walllightmap.png1.2690.592passespasses
Ground_4K.jpg1.0980.761transcodedtranscoded
envs/Garden.jpg4.4836.552refusedrefused, harder

A sweep over the plausible causes found it exactly. With outputColorSpace set to Linear-sRGB instead of sRGB, the harness returns hardwood.jpg at 7.441, max 66, 19.88% of channels over 8 — the published row to three decimals. The earlier oracle wrote linear-light values into an eight-bit framebuffer and differenced those.

The last row is why this matters more than a rounding correction. Six of the seven moved down and one moved up, because an sRGB/linear confusion is not a scale factor: it stretches the shadows and crushes the highlights. Garden is nearly all highlight, so the harness that was too harsh on everything else was too kind to the one texture whose refusal C1 had to argue for. And light_fine_wood.jpg changes verdict: the pixel reason to refuse it has gone, and it stays uncompressed only for the architectural reason C1 recorded separately — texture_cache still cannot hold a CompressedTexture.

What now prevents it is not care. Every run renders the source and differences it against the source's own decoded pixels first. A transparent path returns zero and does: 0.000 across the calibration set, 0.014 worst case across the tree. Under Linear-sRGB output that residual is nowhere near zero, so the run fails before it reports a single codec figure. The check costs one extra frame per texture and would have caught this the first time it ran.

P-3 · The repointer only goes one way med measured

B5 wrote repointJson to move an image reference from a source to its transcode, because a texture that was encoded stayed encoded. A per-asset refusal is a verdict on a measurement, and measurements change — so the first attempt to revert eight textures left eight containers naming files that were no longer there. repoint --check named all eight, which is the safety net working; it is not the same as being able to fix them, and the fix by hand is editing the JSON chunk of eight GLBs.

It now returns an image to its source, moves the texture off KHR_texture_basisu back onto source, and drops the extension from extensionsUsed and extensionsRequired when the last KTX2 leaves a container — a container declaring an extension it does not use is refused outright by strict loaders. The BIN chunk is still copied through byte for byte, so B1's geometry guarantee holds by construction in both directions.

P-4 · Three budgets were lowered on this encode med measured

git log on tools/budget.json shows B5 (e6541a8) lowering three limits in the same commit that transcoded the eighteen:

LimitBefore B5 (17688b3)B5 setNeeded nowRestored to
public-total6,200,0005,870,000~6,122,0006,200,000
public-largest330,000271,000314,335330,000
demo-total13,860,00013,740,000~13,684,00013,860,000

Not one of them goes a byte past where it already was. A ratchet exists to stop a limit drifting up while nobody is looking; it does not exist to make a quality regression permanent by pricing the fix out, and a limit set by a saving that failed the project's own gate is not a limit that was earned. demo-total is restored even though the tree fits under B5's value, because 0.4% of headroom is a tripwire for whichever unrelated commit arrives next — applying the argument to two of the three and not the third would just move the failure somewhere it explains nothing.

P-5 · Eight times wrong, in the direction that does not matter low measured

encode-textures.mjs says a KTX2 “stays compressed in memory at roughly 1 bit per pixel against RGBA8's 32”, while the arithmetic three lines below charges one byte per pixel. The arithmetic is the one that runs, and it is right for ASTC 4x4 and BC7 and twice the true cost of the BC1/ETC2 this catalog actually transcodes to — conservative, which is the correct direction for a budget. The prose is simply wrong, and it is the sentence a reader would quote.

§ 31 · SPRINT

One sprint

Delivered in one pass. There is no second sprint because there is no second question: the deferral RM-005 handed forward was “has anybody looked at these”, and looking is one task.

D1

Measure the eighteen, and keep the instrument

doneP-1P-2P-31 weekno dependencies

Objective. Render every texture the encoder has ever considered against the source it was encoded from, act on whatever fails B4's 3.0 gate under B1's per-asset rule, and leave the measurement in the repository so the next encode cannot skip it.

ACCEPTANCE · OBSERVABILITY · DoD
  • M-20 = 0. No texture ships compressed while measuring past 3.0 RMS, and the claim is a command rather than a spreadsheet
  • M-21 = 0.000. The rendered source matches its own decoded pixels, per texture, or the run reports nothing
  • M-22 = 21 of 21. Every GPU texture the encoder considered — shipped compressed or refused — has a rendered measurement on file
  • No limit moves past a value it has already held, and the commit says which commit each number comes from
  • Rollback. Per texture. Each refusal is one entry in REFUSED, one source file and one repoint
LANDED — D1
  • Nine of eighteen were past the gate, and the sprint's first act was to distrust its own instrument. The new harness was calibrated against C1's published figures before being pointed at anything, it failed, and the failure was worth more than the pass would have been — see P-2. Two programs of texture verdicts were reached through a frame the application never renders.
  • The oracle is a tool now, not a script. npm run oracle, in the shape of the five --check tools already in tools/. It recovers its own sources from the commit that deleted them, which is what makes it usable at all against a tree where the encode already happened — the encoder unlinks the source in the same run that writes the container.
  • Two traps are handled and both were real. TextureLoader hands back flipY = true and KTX2Loader hands back false, and a compressed texture cannot be flipped on upload — so comparing them as loaded differences an image against its own mirror. Both orientations are scored and mirrorTells records how confidently they were separated; it runs 10× to 86× on real content, so the trap would have quadrupled every figure. And the server 404s rather than serving an SPA fallback, which is the trap B4's oracle hit and had to be moved off vite preview for.
  • Eight ship as JPEGs again, one is re-encoded, nine were already fine. B1's per-asset rule, applied for the third time after the model catalog and Garden. cb-archnight-white_baked.png is the good case: quality 192 takes it from 3.392 to 2.728 and from a 187 KB PNG to a 55 KB container, so it is both better looking and smaller than either alternative.
  • The path bug the reverse repointer shipped with was caught by the check that exists for it. The first run wrote textures/textures/oak_wood.jpg — a doubled directory, because the finder returned a path and the caller joined it onto a directory again. repoint --check named all eight containers before anything else ran. A writer can be wrong; that is why the reader is a separate command.
  • Adding a KTX2 without measuring it now fails in four seconds. The render stays behind npm run oracle -- --check because it costs a browser and two minutes — the same reason ledger:check is a command. But the cheap half is a test: is there a measurement for this file, did it pass, and was the render path transparent when it ran. Confirmed by breaking all three.
  • Three budgets went back to values they had already held, and the VRAM ceiling did not move: Runtime assets 5.28 → 5.84 MB against 5.91, Largest single asset 252 → 307 KB against 322, Deployed tree 12.44 → 13.05 MB against 13.22, Texture VRAM 16.15 → 27.38 MB against an unchanged 45.15. The VRAM is the price of the correction and it is paid out of headroom that was already there.
  • 1,271 headless tests in 30 files (6 new) and 62 in the browser, five pipeline --checks green, ten budgets green, lint and typecheck clean, the type ledger at 0 of 0. No public signature, saved design or asset name changed — the eighteen live inside .glb containers and are never named by a document.
  • What this leaves, priced and then closed. Two room textures are now inside the gate rather than one — light_fine_wood.jpg at 2.639 and walllightmap.png at 0.592 — so the cache redesign C1 reverted “for want of a consumer” has two. Both were encoded to measure the prize rather than estimated: 43.7 KB of disk and 0.500 MB of VRAM. An earlier draft of this line said “exactly one consumer, worth about 0.7 MB”; it was wrong on the count and on the number, and the correction is the reason for encoding rather than arithmetic.
  • Against that, the cost of taking it, which C1 never had to price. acquireTexture would need a page-wide KTX2Loader, and formatSupport() returns null wherever the device cannot report its formats — Node and jsdom, which is every headless test that builds a Floor or an Edge. That is a failure mode the module does not have today. And unlike the eighteen, a room texture is named in saved designs: light_fine_wood.jpg is in src/catalog/textures.json, so compressing it is a retirement, and un-retiring one is harder than reverting a model texture. This program has just spent a sprint undoing an over-eager encode; committing a second one to a save-format surface for 43.7 KB would be the same mistake with the same shape.
  • So the answer is 0.500 MB against 17.77 MB of VRAM headroom, and no. Written down with both sides measured so it stops being rediscovered: the blocker is no longer the codec and no longer the absence of a consumer, it is that the consumer is worth 2.8% of headroom already sitting unused. If a room texture is ever added that is large and inside the gate, that number changes and this is the note to re-read.

One week. What is worth carrying out of it is not the nine textures — it is that a measurement nobody can re-run stops being a measurement. The oracle was correct all three times it was written and thrown away all three times, and in the gap the project made two texture decisions it could not check and one of them was wrong. The fix was not more care; it was git add.

PRODUCT ROADMAP · DRAWING Nº RM-007

A planner for anyone's home

Six programmes took a 2014 demo to a tool with gates, budgets and an instrument for everything it ships. None of them asked what a person who wants to design their own home needs from it. This drawing does. It audits what the application can do today, sets that against a Coohom-class planner and the free reference the field already has, and lays out eight programmes, 42 weeks, from a floorplan demo to a floor and house planner anyone can use — 2D and 3D, fully customisable, free without a catch.

Rev B, same day. The audience was fixed as web desktop only. Sprint L1 — the phone and tablet shell, 2.5 weeks — is withdrawn; Q-7 stays on the log, declined by decision rather than deleted; the shell was then measured at 1024×768, 1280×720 and 1366×768 and holds at all three with no overflow. 44.5 → 42 weeks, 26 → 25 sprints, M-31 re-pointed at a laptop viewport.

§ 32 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What it takes to be the planner people reach for

The aim, in the words it was given: a floor planner like Coohom but not that deep — one anyone can use to design their home and view it in 3D, with everything a person may need, no premium tier, no product linkages, absolutely free. Every finding below was produced by reading the tree at 8510642 or by running the application in Chromium and looking at what it drew.

0 of 2
items placed in 3D that appear on the 2D plan. Two were added, the status bar counted two, the plan drew neither — the plan view has no code path for items at all (floorplanner_view.js:588)
5 + 2
wall and floor textures offered, two of them the same image at different scales. No paint colour, no ceiling material, no normal or roughness map anywhere
1
storey. Model owns one Floorplan (model.js:77) and the save format has no word for a level. Stairs are three furniture models
0
ways to get a picture out. No image of the 3D view, no panorama, no PNG, SVG or PDF of the plan. OBJ and glTF export the geometry, which is not what a person shows their family
42 wk
eight programmes at the single-developer cadence RM-001 was planned at. ±40 % at this altitude; each programme is re-estimated in its own drawing before it starts

What is already there is not small, and this roadmap gets all of it for free. A library that draws walls, straight and curved, joins them into rooms with names and areas, slopes them by corner elevation, textures both faces of each wall and every floor, cuts holes for doors and windows, and renders the lot lit, shadowed, tone-mapped and fogged, in orbit, orthographic and first-person — with undo across everything, autosave to IndexedDB with honest recovery, five display units, a traceable backdrop image, OBJ and glTF export, and a catalog of 168 models. Under it, the things a product programme usually has to build first and never gets to: 1,333 headless and 62 browser tests, coverage and size ratchets, an asset pipeline that compresses, measures and refuses, stable identity for walls and rooms across edits, one change event per gesture. RM-001 to RM-006 bought that. What they did not buy is a single feature a homeowner would notice, and that is what the next 42 weeks are for.

“Like Coohom, but not that deep” is a precise brief once Coohom is read literally. Its own floor-planner page names the product: draw or upload a layout, edit walls, rooms, doors and windows, wall thickness, door and window sizing, thousands of furniture models, 2D and 3D, high-resolution renders, 360° panoramas and walkthroughs, templates, a project dashboard, multi-storey with stairs, custom units, export of 2D drawings and renders. Behind that sits a 600,000-model commercial catalog, a cloud render farm, an AI that drafts a plan from a photo, and a login. Not that deep means the first list without the second. Everything in the first list is buildable on what is here, in the browser, against a static host, with no server and no account — and the four things in the second list are the four this roadmap declines by name (§ 36).

The three constraints decide the architecture, and it is the one the project already has. Free, no premium means nothing lives behind a login, so there is no login: designs live in the browser and in files the person owns, and sharing is a file or a URL. No product linkages means the catalog is a data file of CC0 assets with the licence recorded per item, not a feed — which the pipeline already treats it as. Anyone means any desktop browser — the audience is web desktop only, a decision taken with this drawing — offline after first load, no install, and a first hour that needs no manual. Local-first on a static host is what src/app is today; the roadmap keeps it, and it is why the effort is 42 weeks and not a company.

The shape. Five releases, each one a person can use: Plan any home (13 wk) puts furniture, doors and windows on the plan, makes drawing precise, makes openings parametric and gives designs a home; Make it yours (9 wk) is materials, colours and a catalog worth browsing; The whole house (7.5 wk) is levels, stairwells and a roof; Show it (5 wk) is light, photos, panoramas and sharing; Everyone (7.5 wk) is offline, help, languages, keyboard-only editing and a public address. The first sprint is E1 — furniture on the plan: the most visible gap, the best contained, and 2.5 weeks.

Measured on the day

The application was booted in headless Chromium at 1440×900 and 390×844, driven through fifteen states and screenshotted at each. What the pictures showed, beyond the table:

  • Two items placed, none on the plan. A chair and a bed were added from the catalog and selected in 3D, with their dimension labels drawn in the viewport and the status bar reading 2 items. The plan beside them showed an empty room. This is the finding a first-time user makes in their first five minutes.
  • The split view does not re-frame. Zoom-to-fit runs once at mount, at full width; switching to Split leaves the plan half off the left edge and the 3D room cropped. Small, and the kind of thing that reads as broken.Not reproduced, and withdrawn by E1 on 2026-08-18. Measured on both paths a person takes — plan → split and plan → 3D → split — the plan is centred in the pane, off by 8 px and 1 px, clipped in neither: _recentreForResize already handles it. Read off a screenshot taken after a longer sequence, like the cross-view claim two bullets down. Nothing was written for it; a forced zoom-to-fit on every layout change would discard a zoom and pan the user chose.
  • Wall labels read m:5m. The prefix is the midline flag, and nobody outside this repository knows that.
  • Selecting a wall in 3D highlights it on the plan and opens the surface picker — the cross-view selection is already right, and is what E1 builds the other direction on.Wrong, and corrected by RM-008 T-2 on 2026-08-18. A 3D wall click changes 0 of 492,000 plan pixels and a plan wall click changes 0 of 432,000 pixels of the 3D view; the highlight seen here was hover state left over from the previous shot, which clicked the plan. Only the inspector half is true. E1 therefore builds both directions, at 3 weeks rather than 2.5, and programme E is 7.5 weeks rather than 7.
  • The phone viewport is unusable, not merely cramped. The rail, the top bar and a 300 px inspector leave a 40 px plan at 10 % zoom. Declined in rev B: the audience is web desktop only, and the laptop end of that range — 1024×768, 1280×720, 1366×768 — was then measured and holds.
  • The console warns Texture marked for update but no image data found on every frame until the images land. Harmless, and a sign that a needsUpdate is being set on a clone before its source has decoded; worth one look under E1 rather than a finding of its own.

The foundation is the asset — and two of its rules will be felt

The gates, the pipeline and the identity work mean the product programmes below do not start by building scaffolding. Two of the standing rules will bite, and are worth naming before they do. The size budgets are ratchets that may move up with a recorded reason and never down to pass; a catalog that triples and a material library that goes from seven images to ninety will need public-total and demo-total raised, several times, each with the reason in the commit — and they will need a budget that does not exist yet, first-load payload, so that growing the tree never grows what a person downloads before their first wall. The polygon predicates are pinned constants (core/utils.js:44): furniture cannot collide with anything today because pointInPolygon returns false and polygonPolygonIntersect returns false, by a preserved bug the ledger says is left alone on purpose. Collision is a feature people expect from a room planner, and J4 takes it as the deliberate re-baseline the ledger asks for — new predicate, feature flag, characterization tests updated in the same commit — not as a fix.

Q-1 · The plan does not show the furniture high measured

Every planner people compare this to — Coohom, Planner 5D, HomeByMe, Floorplanner, Sweet Home 3D — is used mostly from the top-down view, with the 3D as the check. Here the plan is a wall editor. FloorplannerView2D.draw() walks rooms, walls, corners, the target and the grid; the word item does not occur in src/scripts/floorplanner/. The data is all there: every item knows its footprint (Item.getCorners('x','z')), its rotation and its wall edge, and Model holds the scene and the floorplan side by side. This is a drawing layer and a hit-test, not a model change — which is why it is first and why it is 2.5 weeks and not five.

Q-2 · Doors and windows are furniture high

An in-wall item cuts a hole the size of its bounding box (edge.js:471–482) and that is the whole door model: no sill height as a number, no hinge side, no swing arc on the plan, no frame that follows the wall's thickness. Coohom lists door and window sizing and wall thickness as first-screen features, and Sweet Home 3D computes the wall hole from a parametric opening. F1 replaces the three baked meshes and seven kit pieces as the default with a procedural opening — frame, leaf or sash, glass — that takes width, height, sill, hinge and swing, draws its symbol on the plan, and saves as numbers. The catalog models stay for anyone who prefers them.

Q-3 · One storey high

Model constructs one Floorplan and one Scene (model.js:77–78); every composable, both views and the file assume it. Adding levels touches every layer, which is exactly why it is programme G and not sprint E2: it should land on a single-level editor that is already complete, behind a flag, with a single-level file byte-identical before and after. Stairs (F3) and stairwells and a roof (G2) are what turn floor planner into house planner, and the brief said both.

Q-4 · Seven textures high

The surface picker offers five wall images and two floor images, and Checker and Bricks are the same JPEG. There is no way to paint a wall a colour, which is the first thing most people do; ceilings are one flat tint from the render profile; and every material is a single albedo, so the studio profile's lighting has nothing to catch on. H1 is a material model with albedo, normal and roughness, a colour picker that works on any surface, and a CC0 library of about ninety materials from ambientCG and Poly Haven — each one through the resize, encode and oracle pipeline that already exists, each one inside the 3.0 RMS gate or shipped uncompressed under B1's rule.

Q-7 · No phone, no tablet declined measured

At 390×844 the shell renders the desktop layout smaller: a 52 px rail, a 300 px inspector, and what is left for the plan. The pointer handling underneath is already unified — touch draws walls today — so it would have been a shell problem, not a library one, and rev A priced it at 2.5 weeks as L1. Rev B withdraws it: the audience is web desktop only. The finding stays on the log so it is not rediscovered as a bug, and the desktop end of the range was measured before the sprint was struck — at 1024×768, 1280×720 and 1366×768 the shell holds with no horizontal overflow, the catalog drawer overlays rather than squeezes, and both panes stay usable. The one desktop-width fault seen — the plan not re-framing on a layout change — is already in E1.

Q-11 · Furniture goes through walls med

FloorItem.isValidPosition is documented in the predicate ledger as intentionally inert: pointInPolygon is constant-false, so no item is ever “in a room”, so the early return true always fires and placement is left to the user. Blueprint3d meant that; a person furnishing a bedroom does not. J4 turns collision on as a re-baseline — pointInPolygon2, the sibling that works, is already used for room detection (room.js:277) — with a warning highlight rather than a hard stop, so a rug can still go under a bed.

The rest are smaller in code than in experience, and each is one sprint or less: Q-5 is a metadata pass over a JSON file plus a browsing UI; Q-6 is a second IndexedDB store and a grid of thumbnails; Q-8 and Q-9 are the drawing tools every CAD user assumes and per-wall fields the model already carries; Q-10 is a render-to-texture and a sun vector; Q-12 is controller work on selection; Q-13 is the plan drawn again into an SVG string at scale; Q-14 is four independent, deferrable pieces.

What comes first

E1. It is the finding a new user makes in five minutes, it needs no change to the model or the file, the data it draws already exists on every item, and the cross-view selection it completes is half built. It is also the sprint that teaches the most about the rest of E: once items are on the plan, typed lengths, dimension lines and a PNG of the plan are drawn against a plan that means something. Before E1 there is the drawing for programme E — RM-008 — measured against the tree of the day it starts, in the shape of the six that precede this one.

§ 36 · RISKS & NON-GOALS

What could go wrong, and what this is not

Seven risks, all of them things the six earlier programmes either created on purpose or would recognise; and the list of what the brief's three constraints rule out, so it is not rediscovered one feature request at a time.

RiskWhere it bitesMitigation
The size budgets are ratchets and the asset tree will tripleH1, J2 — every pack and material libraryRaise up with the reason in the commit, as the rule allows; never lower; add first-load (M-30) so the tree can grow while the first download does not; packs lazy by manifest

Non-goals

Named so that they stay named. Accounts and cloud storage — a login is the first thing a free tool grows and the first thing that stops being free. An AI that drafts a plan from a photo — the backdrop tracer is the honest version, and it works today. DWG import — a closed format; DXF may come later as a K-programme item once there is a plan worth importing into. Kitchen and wardrobe configurators — the depth the brief declined. A cloud render farm — H2's Photo is what one browser can do well; a path tracer in the browser is a research sprint, not a promise. Collaboration, comments, multi-user — a server. Product catalogs, prices, links to buy — the brief, in its own words. A 600,000-model library — 500 items a person can find beat 600,000 they cannot, and the pipeline measures every one of the 500.

Forty-two weeks, and the first of them draws the furniture on the plan. What is worth carrying out of this drawing is not the number — it will be corrected by each programme's own sheet — but the shape: local-first, static, CC0, no login is not a constraint the brief imposed on the architecture; it is the architecture the project already has, and the reason a Coohom-class planner without Coohom's company behind it is a plan and not a wish.

PROGRAMME E · DRAWING Nº RM-008

The plan is the product

RM-007 put programme E first because the 2D plan is where a floor plan is made and this one is a wall editor. Measuring it before writing any of it found the reason underneath: the 2D view cannot see the furniture, because a Floorplan has no path to a Scene — and that cross-view selection does not exist in either direction, which RM-007 said was half built. Four sprints, 7.5 weeks, and the first decision is a contract rather than a drawing routine.

§ 37 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring the plan changed about the plan

Seven measurements against the tree at 1d53fc8, five of them run in a real browser against the running library rather than read off the source. Two contradict something this document set already says, and one of those two is RM-007's, written the same day.

0 px
change on the plan when a wall is clicked in 3D, and 0 px change in 3D when a wall is clicked on the plan. Cross-view selection does not exist in either direction — RM-007 said it was already right one way
6 keys
on a Floorplan: runtime, walls, corners, rooms, metaroomsdata, floorTextures. No model, no scene. The 2D view is handed exactly this object, so it cannot reach an item even in principle
0.79 ms
to draw a 36-room, 144-wall plan with 150 item footprints — 4.7 % of a 16.7 ms frame. Furniture on the plan is not a performance question, and measuring it first is how that stops being an assumption
36–69 %
statement coverage across the five files E touches — the least-covered in the library, against floors of 79/68/79/78. Every sprint here must carry its own tests or the ratchet breaks

The finding that shapes the programme. Floorplanner2D is constructed with this.model.floorplan (blueprint.js:234), and a Floorplan holds walls, corners and rooms. Items live on Model.scene, and Scene knows its Model while Floorplan does not — the reference goes one way, deliberately, and it is the same one-way rule that keeps the model layer plain. So “draw the furniture on the plan” is not a drawing task with a lookup in front of it; it is a question about which object is allowed to know about which, and answering it wrongly is how a clean layer boundary is lost for a feature.

The answer this programme takes is a projection, not a reference. Model already owns both halves and already dispatches a typed ChangeSet carrying CHANGE_ITEMS (RM-003 A2). E1 has Model publish a plan projection — a flat array of footprints, each one id, centre, half-extent, rotation, type and label, in centimetres — and has the 2D view subscribe to it. The view draws data it was given; nothing in src/scripts/model gains a back-reference; Floorplanner2D's two-argument constructor keeps working, because the projection arrives by event and not by argument. It is also the shape that makes E1 testable headlessly: a projection can be asserted without a canvas, which the five files this programme touches badly need.

The correction. RM-007 § 33 recorded that selecting a wall in 3D highlights it on the plan, and called the cross-view selection “already right”. It is not: clicking a wall in the 3D pane changes zero pixels of the plan, and clicking one on the plan changes zero pixels of the 3D view. What that screenshot showed was hover state left over from an earlier click on the plan itself — the plan's activeWall is set by its own mousemove and by nothing else. The inspector is the only surface the two views share. E1 therefore builds both directions rather than one, which is why this drawing prices it at 3 weeks where RM-007 priced 2.5, and programme E at 7.5 where RM-007 priced 7.

What is cheap, measured rather than hoped. The plan redraw is 0.112 ms for the default room and 0.593 ms for a 36-room, 144-wall plan — about 3.5 µs a wall. Item footprints cost 0.032 ms for twenty, 0.082 for sixty and 0.197 for a hundred and fifty, so the worst case measured here is 0.79 ms a frame. The 2D path has been coalesced to one draw per animation frame since P6 — nineteen invalidate() call sites against six direct draw() — so E1 hooks invalidate() and inherits that. And the plan's entire output goes through 77 raw canvas calls, 64 of them inside eight primitive and setup methods, with only two outliers (drawCornerAngles, 7; drawOriginCrossHair, 6). That is what makes E4's SVG export one week: implement eight primitives against a second backend, refactor two methods, and every existing drawing routine follows for free.

§ 38 · DECISION LOG

Seven findings, five of them run in a browser

Each row was produced against 1d53fc8. Where the method was a rendered comparison, the two screenshots were differenced pixel by pixel with a tolerance of 6 per channel rather than eyeballed — which is the specific mistake T-2 corrects.

T-5An SVG backend is eight primitives and two outlier methods, not a rewriteclears E477 ctx calls attributed to methodsE4
T-6The save path writes explicit literals, so a field not named in it is silently dropped on round tripmedfloorplan.js:723, readE2 · E3
T-7Only EVENT_ITEM_MOVE_FINISH fires for a moved item; nothing fires during the draglowcontroller.js:451, grepE1

T-1 · The plan cannot see the furniture shapes E1 measured

Constructed in a live page and read rather than inferred from the source: a Floorplan's own properties are runtime, walls, corners, rooms, metaroomsdata and floorTextures. There is no model and no scene. Model has exactly two — floorplan and scene — and Scene carries model, so the reference runs scene → model → floorplan and never back. BlueprintJS hands the 2D view the floorplan alone.

Three ways to close it, and why the third wins. Passing the Model into Floorplanner2D widens a public constructor and points the view at the whole document to read one list. Giving Floorplan a back-reference to Model puts the scene inside the layer whose whole discipline is that it holds plain data with no DOM and no GPU — and every test that builds a bare Floorplan would then be building half a document. The third is a projection: Model computes a footprint list and dispatches it on the ChangeSet it already sends for CHANGE_ITEMS; the view holds the last one it received and draws it. No new coupling, no constructor change, and the drawing code takes plain numbers — which is the only version of this that can be tested without a canvas.

T-2 · Neither view tells the other anything correction measured

RM-007 § 33 said: “Selecting a wall in 3D highlights it on the plan and opens the surface picker — the cross-view selection is already right, and is what E1 builds the other direction on.” The first half is wrong and the conclusion drawn from it is wrong.

ActionOther view, pixels changedInspectorVerdict
Click a wall in the 3D pane0 of 492,000opens “Wall surface”plan unaffected
Click a wall on the plan0 of 432,000opens “Wall”3D unaffected

How the mistake was made, since that is the reusable part. The RM-007 pass drove the application through fifteen states in one session and read the screenshots in order. Shot 13 clicked a wall on the plan; shot 14 clicked a wall in 3D. The plan showed a blue wall in both, and the blue in 14 was read as a response to the 3D click. It was the hover state from 13, still set: Floorplanner2D.activeWall is written by its own mousemove handler and cleared by nothing that a 3D click reaches. A screenshot compared against a memory is not a measurement. Both rows above come from differencing two images captured seconds apart in the same run, with everything else held still.

The consequence for the plan is small and worth stating plainly: E1 builds two directions rather than one, so it is priced at 3 weeks here against RM-007's 2.5, and programme E at 7.5 against 7. RM-007 keeps its figures with a correction note beside them rather than being rewritten.

Adding uncovered code to files already below the project average moves the aggregate down, and branches have 0.77 % of room. This is not an argument for raising the floors — they are ratchets and they move up only when a change earns it. It is the reason every sprint below carries its own test budget explicitly rather than as an afterthought, and the reason the projection in T-1 is worth building for its testability alone.

T-4 · The cost is measured, and it is small clears E1 measured

PlanWallsRoomsms / draw
Default room410.112
Four rooms1640.172

Thirty-six rooms144360.593
Item footprints, drawn as a rotated rect, a facing tick and a label: 20 → 0.032 ms · 60 → 0.082 ms · 150 → 0.197 ms

Sixty draws each, after a warm-up, in headless Chromium at 1200×800. The worst case anyone will hit — a 36-room plan with 150 items — is 0.79 ms, or 4.7 % of a 16.7 ms frame. Every draw is already coalesced to one per animation frame (P6), so this is a per-frame cost and not a per-event one. Measured before the sprint rather than after it, because “furniture on the plan will be too slow” is the kind of objection that is cheap to answer now and expensive to answer once half the sprint is written.

T-5 · The SVG backend is eight methods clears E4 measured

Every mark the plan makes goes through the 2D context, and there are 77 such calls in floorplanner_view.js. Attributing each to its enclosing method: 64 sit inside eight primitive and setup methods — drawLine, drawCurvedLine, drawPolygon, drawPolygonCurved, drawCircle, drawTextLabel, drawBezierObject, drawGrid, plus draw's own clear and transform — and 13 sit in two methods that reach past them: drawCornerAngles (7) and drawOriginCrossHair (6). So E4 is: define the primitive surface as an interface, implement it twice, and refactor exactly two methods onto it. The twelve drawLine callers, eight drawTextLabel callers and five drawCircle callers need no change at all.

T-6 · A field the save path does not name is lost med

Floorplan.saveFloorplan writes an object literal per corner and per wall — {x, y, elevation}, and the wall's own named set. Anything else on the object, and anything a third-party file carried in, is dropped on the next save; DesignDocument.parse does not reject unknown fields, it ignores them. Nothing is broken by this today, and it means E2's per-wall thickness and height and E3's annotations each need an explicit line in the writer as well as the reader. Named here so that “the field is on the model” is never mistaken for “the field is saved” — which is exactly the state per-wall thickness and height are in right now (RM-007 Q-9).

T-7 · Nothing fires while an item is being dragged low

The only movement event for an item is EVENT_ITEM_MOVE_FINISH, dispatched once from Controller.itemMoveFinished when the pointer is released. A footprint on the plan would therefore jump to its new place on mouse-up rather than follow the drag. E1 makes the plan follow live by having the controller mark the projection dirty during a drag — not by adding a per-move event, which would put a dispatch inside a pointermove handler and is the shape RM-002 R-05 spent a sprint removing. The existing event stays the commit point for undo.

§ 39 · SPRINTS

Four sprints, 7.5 weeks

Each carries its own acceptance, its own test budget — because of T-3 — and a rollback that is one revert. E1 is the only one with a new contract in it; E2 to E4 are additions on top of that contract and on top of what the plan already draws.

E1

The plan shows the design

doneT-1T-2T-4T-73 wkno dependencies

Objective. Everything in the design visible on the plan, selectable there, and selection shared with the 3D view in both directions.

  • The plan projection. Model publishes a footprint list — id, centre, half-extent, rotation, item type, label, and the wall edge for a wall-bound item — in centimetres, on the ChangeSet it already dispatches for CHANGE_ITEMS. Nothing in the model layer gains a back-reference (T-1).
  • Footprints drawn. A rotated rectangle with a facing tick and a name, at the plan's own scale; doors and windows drawn as openings in the wall run rather than as boxes on it; on-floor items (rugs) drawn under the rest.
  • Hit-testing and handling. Pick, move and rotate an item on the plan, with the same grid and axis snapping walls already use, and the same undo entry a 3D move produces.
  • Selection in both directions (T-2): a wall, room, corner or item selected in either view is highlighted in the other and shown in the inspector. One selection, two views.
  • Live during a drag (T-7): the controller marks the projection dirty as an item moves, and the plan repaints on the frame it already had scheduled.
  • Two repairs that belong here: re-frame the plan when the layout changes, so switching to Split does not leave it half off-screen; and drop the raw m: / i: / e: prefixes from wall labels, which are the wall-information flags and mean nothing to a reader.
ACCEPTANCE · OBSERVABILITY · DoD
  • M-23 = parity. Items in the scene equals footprints in the projection, for every fixture design, asserted headlessly — and rasterised once in the browser tier beside the existing plan-canvas case
  • M-32 = 0 px drift. Selecting an entity in one view changes the other view's pixels; the two directions asserted by the same pixel-diff method that produced T-2, so the measurement that caught the mistake is the one that guards it
  • Frame budget. A 36-room, 150-item fixture draws in under 2 ms in the browser tier — 2.5× the 0.79 ms measured, so the gate fails on a regression rather than on noise
  • Test budget. The projection is pure data, so it is tested without a canvas; floorplanner_view.js and item.js end the sprint no lower than they start (T-3)
  • Rollback. One revert. No file-format change, no public signature change, no saved design affected
LANDED — E1
  • The projection landed first, alone, before a line of drawing code. That was the commitment and it paid immediately: the contract is pure data, so it is pinned by 24 tests with no canvas, no renderer and no browser, and coverage went up on the commit that introduced the feature — branches 68.77 → 69.31. Model derives the footprints and hands them to the floorplan; nothing gained a back-reference and no constructor changed.
  • T-2 is closed, and measured the way it was found. A wall clicked in the 3D view now changes 5,732 plan pixels where it changed 0; an item clicked on the plan changes 20,224 pixels of the 3D view where it changed 0. Both figures come from differencing two rasters captured seconds apart in one run, which is the method whose absence caused the original mistake. The browser tier asserts the same claim on every build (M-32).
  • Four bugs, three of them older than this sprint, all found by driving the application rather than reading it. Controller.clickDragged guarded a null selection on the line after the call that dereferences it — unreachable until now, because the only way to hold state SELECTED with nothing selected was clearSelection() on teardown. setSelectedObject(null) leaves the state machine in SELECTED, which stops checkWallsAndFloors and makes every wall in the 3D view unclickable; the way out is a new deselect(), because doing it inside setSelectedObject re-enters through onEntry forever — tried, and the suite returned a stack overflow rather than a wrong picture. The pan branch's condition was a list of things that could be grabbed and an item was not on it, so the first drag of a chair panned the plan. And showItemSelected is handed whatever is selected, which useSelection documents may be anything at all.
  • The 3D view renders on demand, which nothing in the plan knew. A position written by a 2D drag sat in the scene graph until something unrelated asked for a frame, so the 3D furniture stayed where it used to be. Main subscribes to EVENT_ITEMS_PROJECTED and asks for one frame; the scene graph is already correct by the time it arrives.
  • Wall labels no longer read m:5m. The prefixes are the wall-information flags, and the m stands for midline. They are empty strings now and still configurable, because an embedder drawing interior and exterior lengths together does need to tell them apart. A characterization test pinned the old default; changing a characterization expectation is normally the wrong move, so the reasoning sits beside the assertion rather than in a commit message.
  • Every file this sprint touched ends higher than it started — the acceptance criterion T-3 asked for. floorplanner.js 63.40 → 68.31, floorplanner_view.js 69.26 → 73.37, model/model.js 78.49 → 82.83, plan_projection.js at 100. Project branches 68.77 → 70.09, statements 80.26 → 80.66. 38 new tests: 28 headless, 10 in the browser tier.
  • One budget went up, deliberately, with the reason in the file. lib-esm-gzip 50,300 → 53,500: the ESM entry grew 3.1 KB gzipped because E1 adds a feature to the library, not to the application. The property that limit guards — three and bezier-js external, an order of magnitude below the ~423 KB a lost externals config produces — is unchanged, and the new ceiling keeps the same ~5 % headroom the limits were set with.
  • What did not land, and why. The re-frame repair: RM-007 recorded that switching to Split leaves the plan half off the left edge, and it does not. Measured on both paths a person takes — plan → split, and plan → 3D → split — the plan is centred in the pane, offset by 8 px and 1 px respectively, clipped in neither. _recentreForResize already handles it. Nothing was written: forcing a zoom-to-fit on every layout change would throw away a zoom and pan the user chose, which is a worse behaviour than the one that was reported and is not happening.
  • 1,385 headless tests and 72 in the browser, lint, typecheck, the type ledger at 0 of 0, three builds, ten budgets and five pipeline checks green. No save-file change, no public signature removed, no saved design affected. Floorplanner2D still takes two arguments.

ACCEPTANCE

LANDED — E2
  • The height half of this sprint does not exist, and finding that out was the sprint's first act. RM-008 priced “per-wall thickness and height in the inspector and in the file”. Thickness is real: HalfEdge sets its offset to half of it, so it moves the faces, the plan and the rooms. Height is not. Measured by building the Edge geometry and reading its bounding box — a wall with height 400 and its corners at 250 drew a mesh 250 tall, and raising the corners to 400 drew one 400 tall while height still said 250. The top comes from the corners' elevations (three/edge.js:461) and nothing else does.
  • So the field is wrong in all three places that read it, whenever a corner has been raised: the wall texture's vertical repeat, the initial vertical placement of a wall item, and HalfEdge.height, which nothing reads at all. Deriving it from the corners fixes all three and stores nothing new — it was written, and it failed the frozen r98 golden for edge.plain, 1.24 against 1.00, because the captured wall had a corner at 310 against a height of 250 and the texture tiled past its top. That makes it a parity change with a fresh capture attached, the same call three/lights.js makes about its own 300 against 250, and three r98 is gone. Reverted and pinned instead. The inspector offers no height field; it says height is set per corner and that two walls meeting at one share it.
  • The file grows for nobody who did not ask. thickness is written only for a wall that was given one — hasOwnThickness is what separates “150 because somebody chose it” from “150 because that was the default”. Every other key in a wall record is unconditional, which is exactly why an additive one cannot be: a thickness on every wall would freeze today's default into every file. M-24 asserts both halves, byte-identical re-save included.
  • Drawing to a number, in three tools. Typed length and bearing while drawing, ending in the same placeDrawTarget() a click ends in rather than a second implementation. Angle snapping at 15°, as its own mode — Shift is taken, it turns on grid snapping, which the README described as axis snapping until this sprint looked — and it wins outright over grid snapping, because the two constrain direction and position and a position rounded after a direction was rounded is at neither. A click-click rectangle tool, four corners and four walls in one batch, that stays selected afterwards.
  • Wall split and join, and alignment guides. A split keeps the original wall's identity, so a bound item or an undo snapshot still names something real, and inherits its surfaces and thickness. A join refuses anything but two straight walls whose corner sits on the line between their far ends — a corner where walls genuinely turn is one somebody drew. Guides line the target up with corners that already exist, within 25 cm, and draw a dashed segment to the corner they found rather than a rule across the canvas: the question is which corner.
  • Four bugs, every one found by driving the pointer rather than calling the method. updateTarget() ran for DRAW and for a MOVE drag and nothing else, so every rectangle was measured from the origin and refused as degenerate — and a test that calls placeRectangleCorner directly passes happily, which is why the suite now drives pointer events. The length field read 0 while the plan drew 1.524 m, because App's pointermove listener is bound before the library exists and therefore runs first, reading the previous event's target; it reads on the next frame now, which is also when the canvas repaints, so the two numbers come from one state. A join removed the wrong corner, because detachWall deletes a corner the moment its last wall leaves. And a fresh click with no move before it used a stale target.
  • Coverage up again: statements 80.66 → 81.16, branches 70.09 → 71.20. 63 new tests, 1,448 total, including the acceptance in all five display units — the field is in the user's unit and the model is always centimetres, and that conversion is where this kind of feature goes wrong. Lint, typecheck, ledger 0 of 0, three builds, ten budgets and 72 browser tests green; no budget moved.

And a design nobody annotated re-saves byte-identical, because dimensions, annotations, north and a room's type are each written only when there is something to write.
  • The per-room ceiling height is not stored, and that is the sprint's finding. E3 was drawn with it as a third persisted field. Building it that way would have repeated exactly the bug E2 measured in Wall.height: a wall's drawn top comes from its two corners' elevations, so a room's ceiling is the elevation of its corners, and a second number stored beside them can disagree with the geometry. Room.ceilingHeight therefore reads the corners and setCeilingHeight writes them, in one batch. Nothing new is persisted — which also means nothing new can be lost, and every file this project has ever written already carries its ceiling heights. The panel states the consequence rather than hiding it: a corner shared with the room next door is one corner, so raising this room's ceiling raises that wall on both sides.
  • The first authored entities in the model, and two things follow from that. Everything else the plan draws is derived from the wall graph — a room is a cycle of corners, a wall label is a distance, a footprint is E1's projection — which is precisely why a plan drawn here could not be read: the drawing stated what the geometry was and never what the person meant. So the ids of a Dimension and a TextAnnotation are persisted, unlike a Room's, because a dimension has no description to be found again by; that is what lets a selection survive an undo, which here is a save and a load. And both collections are omitted from the file entirely when empty, which is the half of M-33 an additive collection usually gets wrong: [] looks harmless and turns every file already on somebody's disk into a different file the first time they open and save it.
  • A dimension that would lie is worse than no dimension. Each end carries an optional corner id and follows that corner when it moves, so a drawing does not quietly go wrong after the first edit. Delete the corner and the dimension falls back to the point it stored — the last place that corner was — rather than vanishing or throwing. The offset line's geometry lives in one exported function that the drawing, the measurement, the label placement and the hit test all call: two copies of that formula is how a dimension ends up clickable somewhere it is not drawn.
  • Two tools, with two different rhythms, and the difference is the point. The dimension tool is click-click and stays armed afterwards, because a plan needs several. The text tool places one and drops back to the pointer, because a label is placed in order to be typed into — and the panel's field takes focus on mount, so the gesture starts on the canvas and finishes in the inspector without a second click. Delete now removes a selected dimension or label as well as a selected item; walls, corners and rooms still need the eraser, deliberately, because deleting a wall silently deletes the rooms it defined and an annotation costs a keystroke to recreate.
  • What is drawn always, and what is drawn only when it is a surprise. The north arrow is on every plan, in screen coordinates fixed to the top right, so panning cannot take it off screen and zooming cannot change its size. A room's ceiling height is drawn only where it is not the document's wall height: a plan carrying the same number a dozen times is noise, and this also means a plan drawn before this sprint looks exactly as it did.
  • Labels give way to each other, which is E1's flagged caption problem answered. E1 shipped one rule — suppress a caption below 34 pixels of on-screen size — and said it does nothing for two items side by side that are both big enough. E3 makes that worse before it makes it better, because a room can now carry four stacked lines and a person can put text anywhere. So text somebody typed, and the measurement on a dimension, are reserved in a pre-pass before anything is drawn; everything derived asks for its box as it draws and does not draw if the box is taken. The pre-pass is the part that matters: reserving in draw order would let “A New Room” beat a label a person typed, because rooms are drawn first, and reordering the drawing to fix that would put the furniture over the walls. Suppression rather than displacement — a label nudged away from the thing it names has lost the one property it cannot lose, and zooming in is the gesture a reader would make anyway.
  • That pass found something that had been wrong since the drawing code was written. A room's name is offset 30 centimetres below its area and both are drawn at a fixed 12 px, so the gap between two lines of type shrank with the zoom: at the default scale 30 cm is about 16 px, which is one line height, and the two labels touched. Invisible for years, because nothing asked — and the moment something did, a room's own name vanished under its own area on every plan. The stack is spaced in pixels now, like every other piece of typography on this canvas.
  • Three bugs found by driving the assembled application rather than the library. E2's four came from driving the library's pointer handlers; these three needed the whole app in a real browser. The label field did not take focus, so typing “Living area” went to the global shortcut map and opened the furniture catalog — the panel mounts during the click that created the label, so a focus() on mount lands and that same mousedown's default action takes it straight back, measured as a focusin followed immediately by a focusout with activeElement settling on <body>. It focuses a frame later, which is after the gesture. Turning north in Settings threw the panel over to the Selection tab, away from the field being typed into, because useSelection rebuilds its {type, object} wrapper on every revision and the panel watched the wrapper rather than the identity. And Delete did nothing for either new kind of selection until it was taught them.
  • Coverage up on all four, and the T-3 files closed out. Statements 81.16 → 82.55, branches 71.20 → 73.19, lines 81.21 → 82.61, functions 78.97 → 80.17. 99 new headless tests and 9 in the browser tier, 1,547 and 81. The two files T-3 named as the least covered in the library finish programme E far above where it found them: floorplanner.js 63.40 → 82.51 and floorplanner_view.js 69.26 → 83.35. model/annotation.js is at 93.25 with every function covered.
  • One characterization test re-pinned, with the reasoning recorded beside it. Two assertions in tests/plan-items-2d.test.js read not.toContain('fillText') — “nothing drew any text at all” as a proxy for “no caption was drawn”. That was true when the only text in the fixture was the caption and is false now that every frame draws a north arrow labelled N. They assert the item's name is or is not among the strings drawn, which is narrower and is what they always meant.
  • Two budgets raised, one of them for a reason worth naming. lib-esm-gzip 53,500 → 59,500, for 5.7 KB gzipped of library feature. demo-total 13,860,000 → 14,140,000, where the tree grew 274 KB for maybe 60 KB of new source — because 6.2 MB of that 14 MB tree is one sourcemap, so that limit tracks source volume rather than shipped weight. The gzipped JS a browser actually downloads moved 353 → 364 KB against a 371 KB ceiling and needed no change at all. Whether a public deploy should carry its sourcemap is a question for whoever sets up the Cloudflare target, and it is recorded rather than answered here.
E4

The plan on paper

doneQ-13T-51 wkafter E3

Objective. A drawing that leaves the application at a stated scale.

  • A backend interface over the eight primitives (T-5), implemented for canvas and for SVG; drawCornerAngles and drawOriginCrossHair refactored onto it.
  • PNG at a chosen resolution, SVG at a chosen scale (1:50, 1:100, custom), print to PDF through the browser, with a scale bar, a title block and the north arrow from E3.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-34 = backend fidelity. The same plan through both backends produces the same geometry — SVG path data compared against the canvas primitives' arguments, not against pixels
  • A wall measured with a ruler on a printed 1:100 sheet is its modelled length, within the printer's own tolerance
LANDED — E4
  • T-5 re-measured, and corrected: eleven primitives, not eight, and 92 raw calls rather than 77. The count that priced this sprint was taken before E1, E2 and E3 each added drawing code, and all three additions are real: E1's door swings and E3's north arrow need an arc, E2's alignment guides need a dash pattern, and E3's dimension labels need rotated text. A fourth is the interesting one and was not foreseeable from a call count — E3's declutter pass has to measure text, and a format with no font metrics cannot. The SVG backend takes a measuring function; the application hands it the live canvas', so a sheet hides exactly the labels the screen hides. The conclusion T-5 drew survives its own correction, which is the useful part: eleven operations and two outlier methods is still a week, and still not a rewrite.
  • The export is not a second renderer. renderTo(backend, project, size) swaps the backend and the projection, calls the same draw() the screen calls, and puts both back in a finally. A sheet walks the same rooms, walls, corners, footprints, dimensions and labels in the same order, so there is nothing to keep in step — and the first time a second renderer fell behind, an exported sheet would quietly stop matching the screen, which is a failure a person only notices after they have printed and handed over the drawing.
  • Both of T-5's outliers turned out to be coupled to canvas state, which is what a second backend cannot honour. drawCornerAngles passed this.context.lineWidth and this.context.strokeStyle back into its own drawLine calls — the state being the parameter. drawOriginCrossHair carried a strokeStyle assignment that fillRect never reads, which is precisely why all four of its rectangles have always been one colour; it is gone rather than translated, and nothing drawn changed.
  • A stated scale is a physical promise, kept in one function. CSS defines an inch as 96 pixels, so a centimetre of paper is 96/2.54 of them and a four-metre wall on a 1:100 sheet is exactly four centimetres — asserted as the arithmetic it rests on, since a ruler cannot be run in CI. A PNG makes no such promise, because an image is pixels and how big one comes out is the printer's business: PNG export therefore offers no ratio at all and says “not to scale”. Both formats carry a scale bar, which is the mark that stays true when somebody photocopies the sheet at 90 % and the printed ratio does not.
  • A sheet carries the document, not the session. The grid, the tracing underlay, the origin marker, the alignment guides and the half-drawn wall under the pointer are all suppressed — and so is every hover and selection colour, through one emphasis predicate that every colour decision on the canvas goes through. A printed drawing cannot arrive with one wall in selection green.
  • Two bugs, both found by running it. The measurer handed to the SVG backend was written as view.backend.measureText(…), and renderTo swaps view.backend for the duration — so once the export was under way that resolved to the SVG backend, which delegates to its measurer, which is that closure. Infinite recursion on the first label. It reads the backend once, before the render. And the north arrow, inset 30 px from the corner because that is right on a screen, landed in the margin of an exported sheet with half of it above the printed border; the inset comes from the sheet now. That one was found by exporting a plan and looking at it.
  • M-34 is met by comparing arguments, not pixels — the only comparison that means anything between a rasteriser and a path writer. A recording backend beside the two real ones asserts that the same plan issues the same primitives, in the same order, with the same arguments, and that every call the canvas backend receives produces exactly one SVG element. 46 new headless tests and 3 in the browser tier, 1,593 and 84; backends.js at 96.02 statements, plan_export.js at 92.07. Two of the four coverage figures moved up and two down by about a tenth, all four well clear of their floors: the dip is useDesignIO's three new functions, which are a blob download, a toBlob and a print iframe.

Seven and a half weeks against RM-007's seven, and the half week is T-2: a claim that a thing was half built, checked, and found to be not built at all. E1 is the only sprint here that decides anything — the projection contract in T-1 is what E2, E3 and E4 all draw on top of, and it is the reason this drawing exists before the code rather than after it.

§ 40 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskWhereMitigation
The projection becomes a second model that drifts from the firstE1Derived on dispatch and never written to; the parity metric M-23 compares it against scene.getItems() on every fixture, so drift is a failing test rather than a wrong picture
Coverage falls through the branch floor, which has 0.77 % of roomall fourT-3 is why each sprint states a test budget; the projection is pure data and testable headlessly; coverage is checked per sprint, not at the end
Selection in both directions turns into two sources of truthE1One selection lives where it already lives, in useSelection; both views render it. Neither view keeps its own idea of what is selected — the plan's activeWall stays what it is today, hover
Live drag repaints put work back inside a pointermove handlerE1The controller marks dirty; the repaint happens on the frame already scheduled by invalidate(). No new event, no dispatch in a move handler (T-7, RM-002 R-05)
Additive fields silently lost on saveE2, E3T-6: every new field gets an explicit line in the writer and a round-trip assertion in the same commit
Two rendering backends divergeE4M-34 compares primitive arguments rather than pixels, so a divergence is caught at the call and not at the eye

What must not change

The one-way arrow: src/app imports src/scripts and nothing goes back, and inside the library the model layer stays plain data with no DOM and no GPU — which is precisely why T-1 is answered with a projection. The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0; E2 and E3 add fields and no reader is required to understand them. Floorplanner2D's constructor keeps its two-argument form; the projection arrives by event. The preserved polygon predicates are untouched here — item hit-testing on the plan is a rectangle test in plan space and needs none of them; collision is J4's re-baseline and stays there. And no metric moves down: the coverage floors, the size budgets and the ten asset budgets are ratchets, and the only number this programme is expected to raise is the count of tests.

First commit of E1 is the projection and its headless test, before a single line of drawing code — because the contract is the part that is expensive to change later, and it is the part that makes the rest of the programme testable at all.

PROGRAMME F · DRAWING Nº RM-009

A door is a number, not a mesh

RM-007 put programme F after E because a plan you can draw and read still cannot say how wide the door is. Measuring the catalog before writing any of it found something sharper than a missing feature: ten of 168 items cut a wall at all, and seven of those ten are unusable — they arrive between 3.0 and 3.9 metres tall and are cut into a wall 2.5 metres high. And an opening larger than its wall does not fail; it makes the wall taller. Three sprints, 6 weeks, and the first decision is a data model rather than a geometry generator.

§ 41 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring the openings changed about the openings

Seven measurements against the tree at ea31d45, four of them run in headless Chromium against the library as the dev server serves it. Two contradict a plan this document set already carries, and one of those two is RM-007's.

10 of 168
catalog items that cut a hole in a wall — every door, window and opening the application has
7 of 10
of those that arrive 303–387 cm tall, measured in a live page, and are cut into a wall 250 cm high
+137 cm
how much taller a 400×250 wall becomes when a 300×387 opening is cut into it. It does not fail; the hole is merged into the outline
0
fields in the save file for a door's width, height, sill, hinge side or swing. There is a mesh URL and three scale factors

The finding that shapes the programme. An opening in this application is a mesh with a scale factor. Edge.createShape (three/edge.js:471) walks the wall's items, takes each one's halfSize, and pushes an axis-aligned rectangle into the wall shape's holes — so the frame and the hole are the same rectangle, and the size of both is whatever mesh the catalog happens to ship, multiplied by whatever scale the file happens to carry. A person who wants a 900 mm door has no way to ask for one, and the file has nowhere to record that they did.

Which is why F1 is a data model first and geometry second. Width, height, sill height, hinge side and swing angle are five numbers. Once they are on the item and in the file, the plan symbol, the wall hole and the 3D frame are all *derived* from the same five — which is the property M-25 asserts and the property the current arrangement cannot have, because a mesh's bounding box is the only thing anything reads. The geometry generator is the easy half and it comes second deliberately: a procedural door drawn from a mesh's dimensions would be the same bug in a new file.

The correction. RM-007 § 35 prices F2 as “half walls via per-wall height”. RM-008 E2 then measured that Wall.height is not the height of a wall — the drawn top comes from the two corners' elevations — and declined to derive it, because doing so fails a frozen r98 golden and three r98 is gone. So F2 cannot be built as RM-007 states it. It is re-drawn below around the corners, which are where a height already lives and already saves, and the parity change stays declined.

What is cheap, and what is not. The generator is cheap: a door leaf, a frame and a pane are boxes, and ShapeGeometry is already in the tree cutting wall outlines. What is not cheap is the item model — Item is 1,100 lines with a size that is read off a loaded mesh, and a parametric item has no mesh to read. That is the seam this programme has to open carefully, and it is why F1 carries three weeks for what looks like a day of geometry.
