U-1 · Ten items cut a wall, and seven of them cannot be used shapes F1 measured

The catalog holds 168 items in eight placement types. Only types 3 (InWallItem) and 7 (InWallFloorItem) reach Edge.createShape's hole loop, and there are eight and two of them. That is the whole door-and-window vocabulary of the application. Each was loaded into a live page against a 400 × 400 cm room whose walls are 250 cm high, and its halfSize read after the loader had finished:

ItemSourceWidthHeightDepthVerdict
Closed Doorlegacy972228a door
Open Doorlegacy972228a door
Windowlegacy12317015a window
Doorway, Doorwayfront, DoorwayopenKenney14630334taller than the wall
Walldoorway, WalldoorwaywideKenney30038727taller than the wall
Wallwindow, WallwindowslideKenney30038727taller than the wall
Centimetres, measured after loading. The wall they are cut into is 250 cm high.

The four Kenney wall pieces measure identically — 300 × 387 × 27 for a doorway, a wide doorway, a window and a sliding window. They are not doors and windows at all: they are wall panels with an opening in them, authored as a full wall segment, and they have been typed as in-wall items. So the application ships one door at one size, one window at one size, and eight things that cannot be used. RM-007 J1 already plans to move “the twelve wall segments” out of furniture; this is the same mistake seen from the other end, and F1 makes it moot for openings by not needing a mesh at all.

U-2 · An oversized opening makes the wall taller high measured

The obvious expectation is that a hole bigger than its shape throws, or produces nothing. It does neither. Edge.createShape builds a Shape from the wall outline and pushes each opening in as a Path in shape.holes; ShapeGeometry then triangulates the contour and its holes together. Run against the exact numbers above:

Wall 400 × 250 with…TrianglesMesh topWhat happened
no opening2250a rectangle
the legacy door, 97 × 2226250cut correctly
a Kenney wall doorway, 300 × 3874387the hole was merged into the outline

The wall grows by 137 cm to swallow the opening. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the plan view is unaffected because it draws the graph rather than the mesh — so this is visible only in 3D, and only as “that wall is the wrong height”. F1 clamps an opening to its wall and says so, which is a two-line guard; the reason it is a finding rather than a bug fix is that it explains why the seven unusable items were never noticed to be unusable.

U-3 · Everything under two units wide is multiplied by 300 med measured

Item.initObject (items/item.js:636) reads, in full:

// An ugly hack to increase the size of gltf models
if(this.halfSize.x < 1.0)
{
    this.resize(this.getHeight()*300, this.getWidth()*300, this.getDepth()*300);
}

Its own comment names it. 142 of the 168 catalog items come from the Kenney kit, authored in a unit system where a chair is under a unit wide, so effectively the whole catalog goes through this branch. Measured live, after the hack:

ItemWHDWhat that is
Stairs547402237a flight 5.5 m wide and 4 m tall
Stairscorner532402428—
Table25298134a table a metre high
Chair legacy467951a chair, and not scaled

A single blanket multiplier cannot be right for a kit whose pieces have different intended sizes, and 300 in particular reads as “three metres per unit” where the kit is authored at roughly one. This is not F's to fix and the drawing says so: per-item real dimensions are RM-007 J1, which already plans them. What F owes is that its own work does not depend on the hack — a parametric door has no mesh, so it does not go near this branch, and F3's stairs replace the four items in the table above rather than scaling them.

U-4 · The file has no door in it shapes F1 measured

Item.getMetaData (items/item.js:1062) writes exactly this per item:

{id, item_name, item_type, format, model_url,
 xpos, ypos, zpos, rotation, scale_x, scale_y, scale_z, fixed, material_colors?}

Three consequences, and each one is a sprint task rather than an observation. Size is a scale factor, so “900 mm wide” is recorded as “0.927 times whatever closed-door28x80_baked.glb happens to be”, and a design opened after that file is re-exported silently changes size. There is no sill: a window's height above the floor is the y of its centre, which is derived from the mesh at placement and never stated. And rotation is a single number — the y angle — so a hinge side and a swing angle have nowhere to live at all, which is why the plan's door symbol has drawn the same arc for every door since RM-008 E1 and said so in its own docblock.

U-5 · Half walls cannot be built the way RM-007 says correction measured

RM-007 § 35 prices F2 as “openings without a mesh, half walls via per-wall height, columns and beams”. RM-008 E2 measured what Wall.height does: a wall with height 400 and its corners at 250 draws a mesh 250 tall, and raising the corners to 400 draws one 400 tall while height still reads 250. The drawn top comes from the corner elevations and from nothing else. E2 wrote the derivation, found it fails the frozen r98 golden for edge.plain, and reverted it — that is a parity change needing a fresh capture, and three r98 is gone.

So a per-wall height field would be a second number that does not reach the geometry, which is precisely the defect E2 declined to entrench. F2 builds half walls on the corners instead: a half wall is a wall whose two corners are at 110 cm, the room inspector already sets a room's corners in one gesture (E3), and the file already carries corner elevations and always has. Nothing is added to the format, the parity change stays declined, and the feature is the same feature.

The cost of that choice is stated rather than hidden: a corner is shared, so lowering one end of a half wall lowers the wall next to it. F2 therefore needs a corner split — give this wall its own corner at the same place — and that is the sprint's real task, not the height field.

U-6 · Nothing here generates geometry from numbers yet low measured

Every mesh in the tree is loaded or extruded from the plan: ShapeGeometry for wall faces and floors, a triangle fan for roof planes, PlaneGeometry for the item size labels, and glTF for everything else. There is no procedural item, so F1 writes the first one and F3 the second, and the two share the seam. That is an argument for building the door generator behind a small, dull interface — numbers in, a BufferGeometry and a material list out — rather than inside Item, so that F3's stairs and any later parametric object are the second caller of something rather than the second copy of it.

U-7 · Wall joins at mixed thickness, and the area a room reports med measured

RM-007 asks F2 for “an audit of wall joins at thickness”, and E2 made mixed thickness reachable. A 400 × 400 room with one wall at 40 cm and the next at 10:

 Interior face runsAt the shared corner
wall A, 40 cm20,20 → 380,20ends at y = 20
wall B, 10 cm395,5 → 395,395starts at y = 5
The room's interior polygon is 20,20 | 395,5 | 395,395 | 5,395 — one point per corner, taken from one wall.

The two interior faces do not meet: the room's floor runs to 395,5, which is 15 cm inside wall A's inner face. On screen that is a notch of floor drawn over a wall. It is invisible today only because nobody has had per-wall thickness for long.

And a second thing fell out of the same measurement. Room.updateArea walks this.corners — the wall centrelines — so the area on the plan and in the inspector is neither the inside nor the outside of the room. A 400 × 400 room at the default 10 cm walls reports 16.00 m² where the floor a person can stand on is 15.21: over by 5.2 %, and by about 19 % at 40 cm walls. Usable floor area is one of the two or three numbers anybody actually wants from a plan. F2 fixes it, and keeps the centreline figure available, because that is what a builder measures.

§ 43 · SPRINTS

Three sprints, six weeks

Effort at the same single-developer cadence as every drawing in this set. RM-007's figures are kept; what changes is what F2 contains, for the reason U-5 gives.

F1

A door is five numbers

doneQ-2U-1U-2U-43 wk

Objective. Width, height, sill, hinge and swing on the item and in the file, with the plan symbol, the wall hole and the 3D frame all derived from them.

  • The data model first, and alone in its own commit. An Opening description — width, height, sill, hinge side, swing angle, style — carried by the item, written explicitly to the file (T-6), absent from every older one, and read back exactly. Nothing is generated until this round-trips.
  • The hole comes from the numbers, not the mesh. Edge.createShape asks the item for its opening rectangle rather than its bounding box, and clamps it to the wall — U-2's silent wall-stretching becomes a clamp and a console note.
  • Then the geometry. A generator behind a dull interface — numbers in, geometry and materials out — producing a frame, a leaf or sash and a pane, in a handful of styles. Deliberately the second commit, not the first: a procedural door sized from a mesh's bounding box would be U-4 again in a new file.
  • The plan symbol follows. The swing arc drawn since E1 becomes this door's swing: hinge side and angle, drawn from the same five numbers, and a sash symbol for a window. E1's own docblock says the arc is a convention until F1; this is where it stops being one.
  • Catalog meshes stay. A parametric door is a new item type, not a replacement, so every existing design opens unchanged and anybody who wants a mesh door keeps one.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-25 = openings are numbers. Every door and window in a fixture round-trips width, height, sill, hinge and swing through the file, and its wall hole matches them to the centimetre
  • M-35 = no opening exceeds its wall. For every fixture and every generated opening, the wall mesh's height equals the corner elevations — the assertion U-2 would have failed
  • A file written before F1 opens with its mesh doors unchanged and re-saves byte-identical
LANDED — F1
  • The description landed first and alone, before a single triangle. That was the sprint's stated first commit and it was worth holding to: U-4 is the finding, and a procedural door sized from a loaded mesh's bounding box would have been the same defect wearing a new file's name. Seven fields — kind, width, height, sill, hinge, swing, style — written explicitly, absent from every older file, read back exactly, and the wall's hole cut from the same numbers rather than from a bounding box.
  • M-35 is met, measured on the geometry Edge actually builds. Every hole is clamped to its wall now. The browser tier places the exact item U-2 was measured with — the Kenney wall doorway, 300 × 387 — into a 400 × 250 wall and asserts the drawn wall is 250 where it was 387. The item is not resized: the clamp is on the hole, not on somebody's furniture.
  • The item's extent is its numbers, not its geometry, and a door is why. A door's leaf is drawn open: a 90 cm door standing 90° open has a bounding box 86 cm deep. A size read off that would cut an 86 cm hole through the wall, hand the plan an 86 cm-deep footprint to draw, and give it an 86 cm-deep target to pick. The leaf sticking out is drawing; the extent is the opening.
  • One bug found by placing a door in a live page. WallItem.boundMove decides an in-wall item's height from its own size — sizeY / 2 + tolerance — which put a 210 cm door's centre at 125 and its bottom 20 cm above the floor. A door hanging in the air, visible only in 3D. The height of an opening is its sill; the sideways clamp is inherited unchanged, so a door still cannot be dragged past the end of its wall.
  • Type 10, and nothing existing moved. Appended rather than filling the gaps at 5 and 6, because an item type number is written into every save file and a number that once meant something else is a trap where a gap is only untidy. The characterization test that pinned “exactly eight types” was re-checked and re-pinned to assert the eight individually plus the addition. Catalog meshes are untouched, and the generated openings live in their own openings.json — catalog.json is the list of model files this build ships, and six suites assert exactly that over it.
  • Coverage up on three of four. Statements 82.44 → 82.59, lines 82.50 → 82.65, functions 80.23 → 80.36, branches 73.23 → 73.21. 39 new headless tests and 4 in the browser tier, 1,632 and 88; items/opening.js at 98.03 statements. Four budgets raised for 2.6 KB gzipped of library code — two of them had been sitting at 0.3 % headroom since E4 and were raised back to the 5 % they were set with, because a limit that fails on the next commit whatever it is trains people to raise it without reading it.
F2

Openings, half walls and the join audit

doneQ-3U-5U-71.5 wk

Objective. A hole with nothing in it, a wall that stops at waist height, and the two things per-wall thickness broke.

  • Openings without a mesh — archway, pass-through, serving hatch — which F1 makes nearly free: they are the same five numbers with no leaf and no pane.
  • Half walls on the corners, not on a height field (U-5). A wall is lowered by lowering its corners, which already save and already draw; the sprint's real work is a corner split, so lowering one wall does not lower its neighbour. RM-007's per-wall height is withdrawn rather than deferred, and E2's declined parity change stays declined.
  • Columns and beams as parametric items, on F1's generator, since they are boxes with numbers and no mesh should be involved.
  • The join audit, with two things to fix (U-7): interior faces that do not meet at a corner where thickness changes, and a room area that is the centreline area and is over by 5.2 % at 10 cm walls and about 19 % at 40. Usable floor area becomes the number on the plan; the centreline figure stays available.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-36 = the room is the floor. A room's reported area equals its interior polygon's area for every fixture, at every wall thickness, and a 400 × 400 room at 10 cm walls reads 15.21 m²
  • Two walls of different thickness meeting at a corner produce interior faces that share a point — asserted on the polygon, not on a picture
  • A half wall lowers its own corners and no others
LANDED — F2
  • M-36 is met: a room's area is its floor. The centreline figure was over by 5.2 % at the default 10 cm walls and by 23.5 % at 40 — a 400 × 400 room reporting 16.00 m² where the floor is 15.21. It is the interior polygon now, and the centreline figure is kept as Room.centrelineArea and shown beneath it, because it is a real number that a builder measures. Eleven characterization tests pinned the old figure; every one was re-checked and re-pointed rather than re-numbered, because those tests are about room detection and the centreline polygon is what answers that question.
  • The join is closed, and only where it was broken. halfAngleVector mitres with the offset of whichever half edge it was called on, so a 40 cm wall's face ended at (380, 20) where the 10 cm wall's began at (395, 5). The correction runs only when the two offsets actually differ; when they are equal the mitre is the one this class always computed, bit for bit, so every existing design and every frozen r98 golden is untouched.
  • Half walls took two failures to get right, and both were measured. RM-007 said per-wall height; E2 had already measured that Wall.height does not set a wall's height. This drawing then said corners, giving a wall its own pair — and that was built and it deletes rooms: two coincident corners break the cycle the room detector walks, and newCorner's merge tolerance meant the split did not survive a save either. Wall.partialHeight caps the drawn top of one wall's faces and touches neither the graph nor the corners nor height, so every room, every neighbour and every golden is unaffected.
  • Openings with nothing in them were already there. F1's description makes an archway the same five numbers with no leaf and no pane, which is what this drawing predicted when it said F2's first bullet would be nearly free.
  • One part was outstanding at the time and is now delivered: columns and beams as parametric items. They needed a new item class, a new type number, catalog rows, an inspector and their own round-trip tests — an F1-sized slice rather than the line RM-007 makes them look like — and shipping a new persisted item type without tests would have been worse than not shipping it. It was recorded here rather than quietly dropped, and cleared after F3 and before programme G started. See the block below.
  • 15 new tests, 1,647 and 88. Branches 73.21 → 73.32; statements, lines and functions flat to within a tenth. No budget moved.
LANDED — COLUMNS AND BEAMS, AFTER F3
  • M-41 = a member is its numbers. Item type 12, and one description for two things: a cross-section of width by depth, a length along the axis, and a soffit — the height of the underside above the floor. The mesh is measured against those four for both kinds across eight sets of numbers. Nothing derivable is stored: the top, the centre and the extent all fall out, and a round column's depth is forced to its width because a circle has one dimension.
  • depth means a different axis for each kind, and that is the right answer rather than a trick. A column's axis is vertical, so its cross-section lies in plan; a beam's is horizontal, so its depth is the vertical dimension. That is exactly what the two words mean on a structural drawing — a beam's depth is its vertical dimension — so one field carries one meaning and lands on the convention for both. The inspector's labels follow the member instead: a column has a height, a beam has a span, and they are the same field.
  • The third caller tested F1's generator seam again, and it held. A rectangular column and a beam are one box each out of items/solid_builder.js. A round column is not, and the 24-sided prism that draws it stays in structure.js with one caller rather than moving to the shared file pre-emptively — the rule that file states is that a piece moves out when a second caller wants it, which is the rule F3 learned by finding box private.
  • The height bug was expected this time, which is the whole point of having found it twice. F1 measured a 210 cm door hanging 20 cm above the floor; F3 measured a railed flight that would have floated 45. FloorItem.resized puts the origin at half the mesh, which stands everything on the floor, and a beam's purpose is not being on the floor. So the elevation is derived in the constructor, in resized() and in placeInRoom(), and the browser tier asserts a beam's soffit rather than trusting that somebody thought of it. A first draft also overrode boundMove; FloorItem does not have one, so that would have been a method nothing ever called.
  • A column is drawn solid and a beam dashed, because a plan is a horizontal section about a metre up: the column passes through it and the beam is above it. Their plan rectangles are otherwise identical, so the dash is the only thing that tells a reader which is which. A round column is drawn round from the same section the mesh is built from, using two of E4's existing primitives — circle to fill, a full-turn arc to stroke — rather than widening one that both backends implement and M-34 enumerates.
  • One bug, found by exporting a sheet and looking at it. A 45 cm round column beside a 40 cm square one came out smaller: the circle's radius came from Dimensioning.cmToPixel, which reads the screen's zoom, while everything around it was drawn through the export projection. renderTo swaps the projection and leaves dimensioning alone, so the column was drawn at its on-screen size on a sheet at 1:100. The radius comes from the projection now, the way drawDoorSwing already took its own, and the regression test halves the scale and asserts the radius doubles.
  • 52 new tests, 1,773 and 100. Coverage up on all four: statements 83.12 → 83.35, branches 73.73 → 74.16, functions 80.82 → 80.98, lines 83.16 → 83.38. No budget moved — but three are thin now (the deployed tree at 0.4 %, the IIFE at 0.7 %, the ESM at 1.5 %) and the next change that trips one should raise it to the ~5 % the limits were set with.
F3

Stairs

doneQ-3U-3U-61.5 wk

Objective. A flight of stairs with a rise, a going and a width, and a footprint on the plan that says which way is up.

  • Straight, L and U flights on F1's generator — the second caller, which is the test of whether that interface was worth having.
  • Rise, going, width, tread count and handrail in the inspector; the going and the rise are what a building code is written in, so they are what the fields say.
  • A plan footprint with the tread lines and an up arrow, drawn through E4's backend so it exports, and a stairwell hint — the rectangle a floor above would need to open — recorded for G2 rather than acted on.
  • The four catalog stair meshes, which measure 5.5 m wide and 4 m tall (U-3), are superseded rather than scaled.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-37 = a flight is its numbers. Tread count × going equals the flight's plan length and tread count × rise equals its height, for every generated flight, to the millimetre
  • A stair round-trips through the file and appears on an exported sheet at the right size
LANDED — F3
  • M-37 is met, and asserted on the geometry rather than on the arithmetic. Tread count × going equals the plan length and tread count × rise equals the height is trivially true of a function that is the multiplication; what is worth asserting is that the mesh anybody would build agrees with it. So every flight is generated and its bounding box read — over the two material groups that are the flight, because a handrail legitimately stands 90 cm above the top nosing — across thirty combinations of shape, tread count, rise, going and rail. To the millimetre, as the metric says.
  • The sprint opened by testing F1's interface, which is what § 44's risk table asked it to do, and the answer is: half right. F1 did draw the boundary in the right place at the call — numbers in, a BufferGeometry and a material list out, nothing about doors leaking through it. What it did not do is share the four pieces underneath: box, appendInto, rotateAboutY and the BufferSink typedef were module-private to opening.js, so the second caller's only options were to copy them or to import from a module named after doors. They moved to items/solid_builder.js unchanged, opening.js became its first caller rather than its second, and F1's 34 tests passed without an edit — which is the test that the move was a move. One function is new rather than moved: a rotation about the horizontal, because a door swings about the vertical and a handrail follows a pitch.
  • The item class needed less than F1's, not more. ParametricOpening had to override objectHalfSize: a door's leaf is drawn standing open, so a 90 cm door's bounding box is 86 cm deep and a size read off it would cut an 86 cm hole through the wall. The drawn thing escapes the described thing. A flight's does not, so the inherited implementation is already right and an override would be a second copy of one number. Making that true cost four lines and 4 cm: a rail the length of the pitch line overhangs its run by half its own section once rotated, and a post centred on the run's foot is half a post outside it — a 400 cm flight measured 404. The plan symbol and the solid occupy one rectangle now, which is the property the four lines buy.
  • Nothing is stored that can be derived, and the stairwell is the one worth naming. The height, the plan length and the landing position all come from the seven saved fields. So does the hint: the floor above sits at the flight's own height, so the opening must cover every tread with less than two metres over it — for the default flight the top twelve treads and not the whole footprint. A stairwell is not the same rectangle as a stair, which is the difference between a hint worth recording and an assumption. Drawn dashed on the plan; nothing in three/ reads it, because there is nothing above the flight to cut (G2).
  • The four catalog stair meshes are superseded rather than scaled (U-3). The browser tier loads one of them and a generated flight into the same page and compares the two, rather than quoting the old measurement — so the assertion stays true whatever the ×300 multiplier does next. Fixing that multiplier is still RM-007 J1's.
  • A bug in E4's own sheet export, found by rendering one and reading it. renderPlanToCanvas painted the paper before calling renderTo, and draw() opens with backend.clear() — so the ground was wiped a moment after being painted and a PNG came out transparent. It survived E4 for two reasons worth recording: the application sets a themed background that draw() paints immediately after the clear, so it only showed for a library embedder who had not styled anything; and the test that counts ink counts it by RGB, under which a transparent pixel reads as ink rather than as a hole. The ground now goes to the backend, which paints it after the clear — rounded up to the bitmap, because a sheet's size is fractional and filling the logical rectangle left exactly one row transparent, measured as 600 pixels on a 600-pixel-wide sheet.
  • 83 new tests, 1,727 and 94. Coverage up on all four: statements 82.58 → 83.12, branches 73.32 → 73.73, functions 80.29 → 80.82, lines 82.63 → 83.16. One budget moved — lib-esm-gzip, 3.9 KB gzipped, with the reason recorded. The three F1 raised did not need to move again, which is what raising them to 5 % headroom rather than to just-enough was for.

Six weeks, unchanged from RM-007, and the shape inside them has moved: F1 is the only sprint here that decides anything. The opening description in U-4 is what F2's archways and F3's stairs both build on, and it is the reason this drawing exists before the code rather than after it — the same argument RM-008 made for E1's projection, and it held.

Delivered, and the sentence above is worth marking against what happened. F1 was the sprint that decided things, three times over: F2's archways cost nothing because the description already covered them, F3's stairs are a second caller of a generator rather than a second generator, and F2's columns and beams are a third that needed no change to it at all. But the boundary F1 drew was only half of one — right at the call and absent underneath it — and that is not something a drawing could have found. It took a second caller, which is exactly what § 44's risk row said and exactly why it named 1.5 weeks as a cheap place to find out. The programme is now complete: F2's outstanding part landed after F3 and before programme G started.

§ 44 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskWhereMitigation
A parametric item and a mesh item become two incompatible kinds of furnitureF1The parametric one is a new item type on the existing Item base, so selection, undo, the plan projection and the file all reach it unchanged. What differs is where its geometry comes from
The generator is written inside Item and F3 copies itF1, F3U-6 is the reason it goes behind an interface in F1 with stairs named as the second caller. If the interface is wrong, F3 is where that is discovered, and 1.5 weeks is a cheap place to discover it
Fixing the room area changes a number every existing design showsF2It does, and that is the point — it is currently wrong by 5.2 % at the default thickness. The centreline figure stays available; the change is recorded as a visible one with the before and after stated, not slipped in
The corner split leaves orphaned cornersF2The same path splitWall already uses (E2), which keeps identity and was built with the join-removal bug that sprint found; the split is asserted on the graph rather than on the drawing
Clamping an opening to its wall silently shrinks somebody's doorF1It is a clamp with a console note and a plan symbol that shows the clamped size, which is strictly better than U-2's silent wall-stretching. M-35 asserts the wall's height instead of the opening's
The ×300 hack is inherited rather than avoidedF1, F3Parametric items have no loaded mesh and do not reach initObject's branch. Fixing it for the catalog stays RM-007 J1's, named here so it is a decision and not an oversight

What must not change

The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0: the opening description is additive and written explicitly, and a file with mesh doors in it opens and re-saves byte-identical. Wall.height stays as it is — pinned by E2 with the measurement beside it — because deriving it is a parity change with a fresh capture attached and three r98 is gone; F2 works on the corners instead. The one-way arrow holds: a generator produces geometry for src/scripts/three and the model layer keeps holding numbers. The preserved polygon predicates are untouched again; collision remains RM-007 J4's re-baseline. And no metric moves down: the coverage floors and the budgets are ratchets, and items/item.js at 63.60 % statements and items/floor_item.js at 36.00 are the two least-covered files this programme touches, which is why each sprint above carries its own test budget rather than an intention.

First commit of F1 is the opening description and its round-trip test, before a single triangle is generated — because U-4 is the finding, and geometry drawn from a mesh's bounding box would be the same defect wearing a new file's name.

PROGRAMME G · DRAWING Nº RM-010

There is no roof, and a level is a number that does not exist

RM-007 calls programme G the widest change in this drawing and puts it last among the structural programmes for that reason. Measuring it first found two things that change its shape. The tree has no roof — it has a two-triangle ceiling plane per room, plus a dead alternative and a comment claiming the live one is commented out. And nothing is drawn at a base elevation: every floor in a loaded design sits at y = 0, so a second storey is not corners with a bigger number, it is every mesh in the scene translated. Against that, two things are cheaper than drawn: a floor opening is one Path, and F3 already computes the rectangle. Three sprints, 6 weeks.

§ 45 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring the levels changed about the levels

Nine measurements against the tree at 6dd9665, six of them run in headless Chromium against the library as the dev server serves it. Two correct a plan this document set already carries, and one of them is this programme's own sprint table.

The programme survives its own measurement, and its first sprint does not. RM-007 prices G1 as “levels in the model with elevation and height”, which reads as a field on the things that already exist. The measurement that argues against it is not an opinion about design: Floorplan has 55 methods and 36 of them read one of its seven collections, so a level field is 36 filters and 36 places to forget one. The measurement that argues for the alternative is that it is already proven — two Models were constructed in one page, loaded with different designs, and stayed independent, which is RM-003 A1's work and is asserted by a suite that already exists.

What is genuinely new is smaller than it looks, and what is genuinely old is worse. The roof is the surprise. The four stair meshes were at least stairs; there is nothing here to supersede, because Floor.buildRoofVaryingHeight() is a ceiling over one room and the file has no notion of a building envelope at all. G2 writes the first roof this application has ever had. Set against that, the stairwell it was drawn to write is nearly free: F3 records the rectangle, ShapeGeometry cuts it, and the measurement below is the eight triangles.

V-1 · There is no roof shapes G2 measured

A four-hundred-centimetre room was loaded into a live page and every mesh in the scene traversed, with its name, its visibility, its triangle count and its bounding box read. Thirty-one meshes, and the two that sit at the top of the walls are these:

MeshBuilt byyExtentTrianglesWhat it is
roofPlanethree/floor.js:178250400 × 4002A triangle fan over the room's corners at their elevations
room.roofPlanemodel/room.js:355250400 × 4002An invisible plane, for picking
Read off a live scene. The room is 400 × 400 with corners at elevation 250.

Both are ceilings over one room, and neither is a roof. Floorplan.roofPlanes() returns one entry for a one-room design, which is the whole of what this application means by the word: a lid on each room, at that room's own corner elevations. There is no envelope over the building, no pitch, no eaves, no overhang, and nothing in the file that could describe one.

Two smaller things came out of the same reading and are worth recording because they will mislead the next person. The call site reads:

this.floorPlane = this.buildFloor();
// roofs look weird, so commented out
this.roofPlane = this.buildRoofVaryingHeight();

The comment is wrong — the line under it runs on every redraw. And buildRoofUniformHeight() sits directly below it, a complete second implementation using ShapeGeometry over the interior corners at the configured wall height, which nothing calls. So the state of the roof in this codebase is: one implementation running while a comment says it is not, and one implementation not running while nothing says so.

What this does to G2. RM-007 prices “a simple roof generator (flat, gable, hip) over the footprint” inside a 2.5-week sprint that also carries stairwells and an exterior view. That price assumed something to build on. There is nothing — but there is also nothing to break, which is the other half of the finding: a roof generator is new geometry from the plan's outline, in the shape F1 and F3 have now written twice, and it does not have to preserve a single existing pixel. The estimate holds; what moves is which part of the sprint is the risk.

V-2 · A floor opening is one Path, and F3 already has the rectangle cheaper measured

A room's floor is one call: new ShapeGeometry(new Shape(interiorCorners)), at model/room.js:367. F3's stairwellHint() was taken from a default straight flight, placed at the centre of a real 600 × 600 room, and pushed into that shape's holes array:

FloorTrianglesOutline
As drawn today2590 × 590 interior polygon
With the stairwell cut8identical
With the hole wound the other way8identical

The hint is {x0: −45, y0: −100, x1: 45, y1: 200} in the flight's own frame — the part of the footprint with less than two metres of headroom under the floor above, which for the default sixteen-tread flight is its top twelve treads. So the two ends of G2's stairwell already exist: the item computes the rectangle and draws it dashed, and the primitive that builds every floor in the application cuts it. What G2 writes is the middle — the rectangle in the room's frame, and which room.

Winding does not matter, which is worth knowing before somebody spends an afternoon on it: three normalises a hole's direction, and the reversed path produced the same eight triangles.

V-3 · U-2 is about ShapeGeometry, not about walls high measured

RM-009 U-2 measured that an opening bigger than its wall is merged into the outline rather than cut out of it, so the wall grows to swallow it. That was recorded as a fact about openings. It is not: it is a fact about the primitive, and the same test run against a floor gives the same answer.

OutlineHoleResulting bounding boxVerdict
400 × 400 floor90 × 190, inside0 .. 400cut
400 × 400 floor600 × 190, straddling−100 .. 500the floor grew 200 cm

So G2 inherits F1's clamp, and inherits it knowingly. A stairwell placed across a wall — which is exactly where a stair against a party wall would put it — would silently enlarge the floor of the room above rather than fail. F1's answer was to clamp the opening to the wall with a note and a plan symbol showing the clamped size; G2's is the same shape, clamped to the room. The value of having measured U-2 is that this one is a known failure with a known remedy rather than a discovery mid-sprint.

V-4 · A level is an offset that does not exist shapes G1 measured

Every flat, room-sized plane in a loaded design was collected with its y coordinate. There are exactly two heights: 0 and 250. The floor is at zero and the ceiling is at the corners' elevation, and there is nothing in between and nothing below.

A corner's elevation is the wall top, not the storey. The file records {x, y, elevation} per corner and nothing else; the floor is drawn at y = 0 with no offset applied. So “levels in the model with elevation and height” cannot be built by giving corners a bigger elevation — that raises the ceiling of the ground floor. A second storey means a base elevation applied to every mesh a level owns: floors, ceilings, wall faces, fillers, and every item's position.

This is the finding that makes G1 three and a half weeks rather than one. The good news is where it lands: Floor, Edge and Item each already build their geometry relative to a plan they are handed, so the offset is a translation applied where the level's contents are added to the scene, not a change to how any of them computes anything.

V-5 · Two models already coexist, and the sprint table says the wrong thing correction measured

A second Model was constructed in a page that already had one and loaded with a different design. The first kept its 400 cm room, the second took a 900 cm one, and the two hold different Floorplan objects. That is RM-003 A1's document ownership work, and it means N floorplans in one page is not a design proposal, it is an existing property with a suite over it (tests/browser/two-designs.test.js).

Against that, the cost of the alternative was counted rather than estimated. Floorplan has 55 methods, and 36 of them read one of its seven collections — walls, corners, rooms, metaroom data, floor textures, dimensions, annotations. A level as a field on those collections means 36 filters, each one a place where forgetting to filter shows up as furniture from the floor below appearing on this one.

ApproachWhat has to changeWhat is already proven
A level is a field (RM-007's wording)36 of 55 Floorplan methods gain a filter; every collection gains a key; every query gains an argumentNothing
A level is a floorplanOne collection on Model, one active index, one base elevation, and a scene that adds N of themTwo independent models in one page, with a browser suite

One thing the second approach does not get for free, and it is worth naming rather than discovering. Configuration is page-wide: the wall height read in the page with two models is one value for both. RM-003 A1 built a per-document runtime for exactly this class of problem, and per-level wall heights are the same problem one layer down. G1 either uses that runtime per level or states that a level's wall height is the document's — and the second is a defensible answer for a first release, provided it is a decision.

V-6 · The file is ready low measured

A design was loaded, exported, re-loaded and re-exported, and the two strings compared: identical. The floorplan record's keys are version, units, corners, walls, rooms, wallTextures, floorTextures, newFloorTextures, carbonSheet. Adding levels beside them is the same additive move E2 made for a wall's thickness, E3 for dimensions and annotations, and F3 for a flight of stairs — and it obeys the same rule those three obey, which is the rule that makes M-26 achievable: write the key only when there is something to write. A single-level design writes no levels and is therefore byte-identical to the file it was before the programme.

V-7 · Undo and autosave snapshot the whole file med measured

useHistory stores the string Model.exportSerialized() produces — the same string the save button writes — and undo is loadSerialized(previous). useAutosave does the same thing to localStorage. Both were built that way deliberately and both are correct; the consequence for this programme is arithmetic. A three-storey house makes every undo snapshot three times the size, and autosave writes three times as much on every debounce.

Recorded rather than solved. It is not G1's job to make history incremental — that is a change to how undo works and it would land on a single-level editor just as well — but a programme that triples the input to both without saying so is a programme that gets blamed for a slow autosave later.

G1 and G3 carry the same obligation below.

V-9 · A room's area would lie again med measured

The 600 × 600 room used for V-2 reports 348,100 cm², which is its interior polygon — the number F2 made the number on the plan, three commits ago, for the reason that the centreline figure was 5.2 % high. Cut the stairwell out of it and the room still reports 348,100, while 27,000 cm² of it is a hole. That is 7.8 % for one flight of stairs, which is the same order as the defect F2 existed to fix.

So the rule F2 wrote applies unchanged: the number on the plan is the floor you can stand on. G2 subtracts its openings from Room.interiorArea(), and the test that pins it is F2's own M-36 with a hole in it.

V-10 · The fixture generator had stopped reproducing its fixtures med measured added on delivery

Found by G3, which is the first sprint since RM-001 to add a fixture and therefore the first to run tools/make-fixtures.mjs. Its module comment states the contract: “corner ids come from Utils.guide(), which is seeded here, so re-running this script reproduces byte-identical files. Regenerate only deliberately; a surprise diff means the model layer changed.” Running it changed all three files.

Not the model layer, and not a surprise once measured: every corner id in all three fixtures shifted by one position — the first id gone, a new one at the end. new Floorplan() draws eight random numbers before a single corner is made, because RM-003 A1 gave every document a DesignRuntime and that runtime an id. Every builder seeded first and constructed second, so the whole sequence moved along by one guide(). The drift has been there for four programmes and nothing caught it, because nothing re-ran the script.

The fix is one line per builder — seed after construction — and the three frozen fixtures come back byte-identical, verified by running the script and getting a clean git diff. The finding is recorded rather than only fixed because the class matters more than the instance: a reproducibility claim that nothing re-runs is not a mechanism, it is a comment, and this project's own rule says prose is not a mechanism. The check is now written down beside the contract it protects.

§ 47 · SPRINTS G1–G3

Six weeks, re-drawn around what a level turned out to be

RM-007 priced this programme at 6 weeks in two sprints. It stays at 6 and becomes three, because the roof and the level are different risks and pricing them together hides both.

G1

Levels

doneQ-3V-4V-53 wk

Objective. A storey is a floorplan with a base elevation, stacked in 3D and switched on the plan, and a single-level file that is byte-identical afterwards.

  • A level is its own Floorplan (V-5), not a field on seven collections. Model gains a level list, an active index and a base elevation per level; every existing call to model.floorplan resolves to the active one, so nothing outside Model changes on day one.
  • The base elevation is applied where a level's contents join the scene (V-4), not inside Floor, Edge or Item — each of those already builds relative to a plan it is handed, and a translation at the join is the change that does not multiply.
  • levels[] in the file, additive and conditional (V-6): written only when there is more than one, so every design anybody has saved re-opens and re-saves unchanged.
  • A level switcher on the plan, with the level below ghosted. E4's renderTo already swaps the backend, the projection and the canvas size; the ghost is that seam plus the floorplan, drawn first at a reduced weight.
  • Per-level wall height is a decision, not an omission (V-5): either the per-document runtime RM-003 A1 built, applied per level, or the document's height for every level, stated.
  • Behind a flag until the fixture suite covers it, and V-7 recorded on the way past: undo and autosave snapshot the whole design, so N levels is N times the payload.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-26 = two levels, one file. A two-storey fixture saves, loads and renders both levels, and every existing single-level fixture is byte-identical on re-save
  • M-38 = a level is where it says it is. Every mesh a level owns — floor, ceiling, wall faces, fillers, items — sits between its base elevation and its base plus its height, measured off the scene, for a three-storey design
  • Nothing outside Model asks which level it is on in order to work: the plan, the 3D view and the file all read the active level through the path they read a floorplan through today
LANDED — G1
  • M-26 is met, on the fixtures rather than on a design written for the purpose. All five .blueprint3d fixtures load, re-save and re-save again byte-identically, and still write only {floorplan, items}. A design with one storey at the default height writes no levels key at all; one that has been named or re-sized writes one, because otherwise renaming the ground floor would be an edit that does not survive a save. And the ground floor's plan is not repeated inside levels[0] — which is not a special case being tolerated but the thing that keeps § 44's promise: a build that has never heard of storeys opens a three-storey house and gets the ground floor, correctly drawn.
  • M-38 is measured off the scene graph, not off the model. Three storeys at 280, 280 and 300 are asserted to have every mesh they own — floor, ceiling, wall faces, fillers, furniture — between their base and their base plus their height. Editing the ground floor's height to 400 moves the two above it and leaves it where it is, because a base is the running sum of the heights below and is never stored.
  • One getter is why nothing else gained a level argument, which is the third acceptance line. model.floorplan resolves to the active storey, so the 2D view, the 3D view, the inspectors, the composables and the file read it unchanged; Main.floorplan does the same one layer up. The two questions those getters cannot answer are asked explicitly instead — scene.allItems() for the whole building (the save file, resolving an id) and scene.getItems() for the storey being edited (the plan, the item count, what a click in 3D can hit) — and each of the twelve call sites was checked against that distinction rather than swept into one of them.
  • The base elevation lands in exactly one place, and V-4 is why that matters. Nothing in this tree was drawn at a base elevation before: every floor sat at y = 0 and a corner's elevation is the wall top. It is applied to a Group per storey inside Scene. Floor, Edge and Item were measured before the sprint to ask a scene for exactly three things — add, remove, needsUpdate — so Scene.levelScene(level) is a three-method façade and not one line of those three files changed.
  • An item asks its own storey for a plan now. placeInRoom, isValidPosition, closestWallEdge and closestCeilingPoint each ask a floorplan a question about this item, and reading model.floorplan would ask it of whichever storey the user happens to be looking at. Six call sites, one Item.floorplan getter, and a fallback to the active plan for an item with no level yet — which is every item mid-construction and every item a test builds by hand, and is the old behaviour exactly.
  • Two bugs found by driving it rather than reading it. A newly created storey's 3D projection was empty: Floorplan3D only subscribes and builds when a change arrives, which was right when there was one of them built before anything loaded and wrong for a view created after its plan already has walls. Measured as three storeys loaded with levels 1 and 2 holding no meshes at all. And the 2D canvas did not follow a level switch — Floorplanner2D holds the Floorplan it was constructed with, in two places — so the switcher moved the model and the 3D view and left the plan drawing the ground floor, which looks exactly like a switch that did nothing.
  • The ghosted storey below arrives as data, not as a reference. A Floorplanner2D is constructed with a Floorplan and nothing else — RM-008 T-1, deliberately — so it structurally cannot reach the level underneath. E1 hit the same wall for furniture and answered it with a projection; this is the same answer. The ghost carries wall centrelines and room outlines and nothing else: no labels, no dimensions, no furniture, because it exists to say where the walls downstairs are. Drawn with the grid rather than with the building, so a sheet of the first floor carries the first floor.
  • The flag gates the affordance, not the feature. With levelsEnabled off, a two-storey file still opens, still stacks, still ghosts and still re-saves correctly; what is withheld is the control that makes a second storey. So turning it on changes no behaviour, which is what makes it a flag rather than a branch, and G3 removes one default.
  • 41 new tests, 1,810 and 105. Coverage flat to within a tenth on all four: statements 83.35 → 83.36, branches 74.16 → 74.13, functions 80.98 → 81.01, lines 83.38 → 83.40. Three budgets raised — the three F2 named as thin, raised to the ~5 % the limits were set with rather than to just-enough, with the reason recorded. The library entries moved 1.4 and 2.3 KB gzipped, the cheapest of the five features this programme set has added, because a level is a floorplan rather than a filter on one.
G2

Stairwells and the first roof

doneV-1V-2V-3V-92 wk

Objective. A hole in the floor where the stairs arrive, and a roof over the building rather than a lid on each room.

  • Floor openings from F3's hint (V-2). The rectangle is already computed and already drawn dashed; G2 converts it to the room's frame and pushes a Path. Two triangles become eight and the outline does not move — measured, not projected.
  • Clamped to the room, the way F1 clamped to the wall (V-3). An opening that straddles a wall makes the floor bigger; it does not fail. Same primitive, same failure, same remedy.
  • The area is the floor you can stand on (V-9): openings come out of Room.interiorArea(), which is F2's rule applied to the thing that now punches holes in it.
  • A roof generator over the building's footprint — flat, gable and hip — on the same numbers-in, geometry-out seam F1 opened and F3 confirmed. There is nothing to supersede (V-1): what exists is a per-room ceiling, and it stays, because a ceiling and a roof are different things.
  • The two stale things in three/floor.js are fixed rather than inherited (V-1): the comment that says the roof is commented out, and buildRoofUniformHeight(), which nothing calls.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-39 = the stairs arrive somewhere. In a two-storey design with a flight on the lower level, the upper floor carries an opening that contains the flight's stairwell rectangle, and the room's stated area is its polygon minus that opening
  • M-40 = a roof covers the building. Every generated roof's plan projection contains the whole exterior footprint, for each of the three types, at every pitch the inspector offers
  • A floor opening never makes a floor larger, at any size or position — the assertion V-3 would have failed
LANDED — G2
  • M-39 is met, and a stairwell is derived rather than drawn. F3 already computes the rectangle — the part of a flight's footprint with less than two metres of headroom under the floor above — so nothing new is persisted. What G2 adds is the frame change: the hint is in the item's own frame and a room is in plan space, so a stairwell under a flight turned thirty degrees is a rectangle turned thirty degrees. The visible floor and the picking plane both come from Room.floorShape(), because a floor you can see through and still click is worse than either.
  • The clamp is the sprint's real content, and V-3 is why. ShapeGeometry does not cut a hole that pokes outside its outline — it merges the hole into the outline, so the floor gets bigger. Every opening is clamped inside its room by bisection on one scale factor, and the containment test is a real one rather than a bounding-box one, because a room can be L-shaped and a rectangle can have all four corners inside such a room while spanning the notch. The third acceptance line — a floor opening never makes a floor larger, at any size or position — is asserted through the primitive that fails it rather than argued about.
  • A test caught a real bug in the new predicate. The first draft tested the centroid of the inner polygon plus “no edge crossings”, which sounds like a proof and is not: a rectangle that encloses the room has its centroid inside the room and no edge crossings at all, because the two boundaries never meet. It was reported as contained and a 1400 cm hole went through into a 400 cm floor. Containment is not symmetric and a centroid cannot tell which way round it is; every vertex is tested now.
  • The predicates are new because the old ones are pinned. core/utils.js' four preserved bugs stay untouched for the seventh programme running — turning them on is RM-007 J4's re-baseline — and model/floor_opening.js carries a fresh, correct pair used by that module and nothing else, which is the rule plan_projection.js already states.
  • The area is the floor you can stand on (V-9), which is F2's own rule applied to the thing that now punches holes in it: a 600 × 600 room loses 27,000 cm² of its 348,100 to one flight's stairwell — 7.8 %, the same order as the 5.2 % F2 existed to fix.
  • M-40 is met by the first roof this application has ever had (V-1). A gable and a hip turned out to be the same solid with one number different: both are the volume between a rectangle at eaves level and a ridge above it, and a hip's ridge is inset from the ends by the hip run while a gable's is not inset at all. Written once with an inset, a gable is the inset-zero case and its two vertical triangular ends fall out rather than being special-cased. Asserted over three kinds × two ridge axes × thirteen pitches; the rise is the half-span times the tangent of the pitch, with nothing stored beside it.
  • The footprint is the plan's bounding rectangle, and that is stated rather than hidden. A gable or a hip over an arbitrary outline is a straight-skeleton problem, which is not two weeks of a sprint that also carries stairwells. roofFootprint() is a separate function for exactly that reason: a later sprint can make it a real outline without touching the three generators.
  • Two bugs found by running it. The first draft wound all four roof slopes backwards, so every slope normal pointed down into the roof; faces are emitted through an outward test against the solid's own centre now, which is exact for a convex body. And Floorplan.update(true) constructs a new Room for every room — identity is derived from its corners, which is finding H-5 — so the openings a room was carrying were on an object that no longer existed, and drawing one wall anywhere on the plan silently filled in every stairwell. Found by placing a flight in a real page and calling update(), which is what a load does.
  • One correction to this sprint's own bullet. It said both stale things in three/floor.js would be cleared. The misleading comment is gone — it claimed the live roof call was commented out while the line below it ran on every redraw — and buildRoofVaryingHeight is renamed buildCeiling, which is what it builds. But buildRoofUniformHeight stays: it carries a frozen r98 golden, three r98 is gone, and deleting it would delete a parity check the project cannot recapture in exchange for removing eleven lines nobody runs. Dead code is untidy; a lost parity check is unrecoverable.
  • 108 new tests, 1,912 and 111. Coverage up on all four: statements 83.36 → 83.42, branches 74.13 → 74.16, functions 81.01 → 81.19, lines 83.40 → 83.44. No budget moved — the three raised for G1 absorbed this sprint, which is exactly what raising them to ~5 % rather than to just-enough was for.
G3

The house, driven

doneV-7V-8V-101 wk

Objective. Take the flag off, on the strength of a suite that drives a three-storey house rather than a unit test that constructs one.

  • A three-storey fixture beside the five that exist, exercised through save, load, undo, autosave, the plan, the 3D view and an exported sheet.
  • The coverage debt this programme lands on (V-8): three/controller.js at 36 % of branches is the file that decides what a click hits, and per-level visibility is a branch in that decision. A sprint with a stated test budget, which is what worked for programme E.
  • An exterior view, which is the one thing in RM-007's G2 that is neither a stairwell nor a roof, and belongs with the walkthrough it resembles.
  • V-7 measured rather than assumed: undo snapshot size and autosave write time at one, two and three storeys, and a decision recorded about whether incremental history becomes its own sprint.
ACCEPTANCE
  • The flag comes off only when the three-storey fixture passes every tier, and coverage on the six files in V-8 has moved up
  • Undo and autosave costs are stated as measurements at one, two and three storeys, not as an expectation
LANDED — G3
  • Both acceptance lines are met, and the flag is off. levelsEnabled defaults to true. It stays in the code rather than being deleted, because it is the line an embedder hosting a single-storey plan turns off and the branch it guards is one v-if — what G3 removes is a default, not a switch.
  • The fixture is the sprint. The other three fixtures are plans; tests/fixtures/three-storey.blueprint3d is a building — three whole Floorplans, a straight flight and a quarter turn, the stairwells those imply in the two upper floors, a column, a beam, a door, a window and a gable roof. Produced by tools/make-fixtures.mjs through the real Model, so it is exactly what the application writes, and driven through save, load, undo, autosave, the plan, an exported sheet and the 3D view.
  • Driving it found four defects, three of them shipped, and none reachable without a building. This is what the sprint was for, so they are listed rather than summarised.
  • 1 — no saved column or beam had ever loaded. Item's constructor calls setScale() whenever a scale is supplied, that calls resized(), and F2's ParametricStructure.resized() reads a description its own constructor has not assigned yet. The catalog path supplies no scale, so placing a column worked and opening one threw. F2 anticipated exactly this window in objectHalfSize() and guarded that one method.
  • 2 — room names on any storey with a stairwell were destroyed on the second load. G2 re-applies floor openings inside Floorplan.update() and put that block above the loop that restores each room's name. setFloorOpenings calls updateArea, updateArea announces an attribute change, and the listener writes the room back into metaroomsdata carrying the name it has at that moment — still “A New Room”. The saved name was overwritten by the default a few statements before it was read: the same read-before-write hazard the comment inside that loop describes, one level up.
  • 3 — the fixture generator had stopped reproducing its own fixtures (V-10), four programmes ago. See the finding; it is recorded rather than only fixed, because the class of failure matters more than the instance.
  • 4 — Controller.deselect() was not idempotent. setSelectedObject(null) switched UNSELECTED → SELECTED on the way in whatever it was handed, so a method named deselect selected — and Main.clearSelection(), which the application calls every time it shows the plan pane, left the machine claiming a selection it did not have. One condition fixes both and makes the recursion that method's own comment warns about impossible by construction. Correction to RM-008 E1, which recorded that this state “stops checkWallsAndFloors and makes every wall in the 3D view unclickable”: measured before changing it, and it does not. mouseUpEvent's SELECTED branch transitions and checks within the same click, so a floor click after clearSelection() still reports the floor. What was wrong was the state, not the click.
  • The exterior view is three things that happen together. Every storey shown, because the outside of a house is not the outside of its ground floor; the roof with them; and the camera framed against Model.buildingBounds() rather than against the plan being edited — the union of the storeys' corners, the eaves at roofBase(), the ridge the pitch implies. The distance comes from the camera's own field of view and aspect, so the box fits a wide viewport and a tall one. Asserted in Chromium by testing all eight corners of the building's box against the camera's frustum, which is what “frames the whole building” actually claims.
  • Per-level visibility was built in G1 and connected in G3, which is what V-8 asked for: Scene.syncLevels has taken an activeOnly option since G1 and nothing passed it, and an untaken branch is an untested one. What it is for is picking — the raycast is offered the active storey's items and the active storey's plan, so with every storey drawn the upper floors are visible and inert. That is a defensible answer and it is the one this build gives; now something says so, in a test that switches storey and watches what the pointer can reach.
  • The plan draws the stairwell it was leaving out. G2 cut the opening from the 3D floor and from the room's stated area and left the 2D plan drawing a solid room, so the two views disagreed about the same building — and the plan is the one that gets printed. Drawn as a void, in the same dashed style drawStair gives the hint on the storey below, because they are the same rectangle seen from either side.
  • V-7 measured, and the decision recorded. A snapshot is 3,137 bytes at one storey, 7,884 at two, 10,331 at three — ×3.29, which is the arithmetic the finding predicted. exportSerialized, the part autosave still does on the main thread, runs in 0.010, 0.020 and 0.024 ms — five readings, stable to the microsecond. Under --coverage the same call reads 0.022 / 0.024 / 0.034, which is the instrumentation and not the code; both are recorded so the difference is not rediscovered. Corrected by H1 to 0.007, 0.019 and 0.024 ms, ×3.3. These were a mean over one timed loop per storey count, which measures the scheduler as well as the work — and the test was flaky at about one run in ten because of it, caught with the one-storey figure at 0.080 ms and therefore above the three-storey one. The minimum over seven repetitions is the fix and is the better statistic: interference only ever adds. The corrected ratio also now matches the byte ratio of ×3.29, which the mean did not. Ten commits held 104,190 bytes, so the 50-entry ceiling is about 505 KiB for this house and about 1.2 MiB with sixty items on it, at the 247 bytes a furniture record costs in legacy-items. Incremental history does not become its own sprint. Half a megabyte of strings and 24 µs a write is not a problem, and the change would land on a single-level editor equally well — the number to watch is the file, not the storey count.
  • All six files V-8 named are up on statements and branches, which was the first acceptance line. three/controller.js 51.65 → 84.43 and 36.14 → 71.42; useAutosave.js 52.94 → 71.56 and 31.25 → 56.25; three/main.js 76.35 → 84.18 and 62.50 → 70.56; useDesignIO.js 48.97 → 50.34 and 30.00 → 34.00; model/model.js 89.45 → 90.87 and 79.41 → 80.98; floorplanner_view.js 85.65 → 85.93 and 71.59 → 71.75.
  • 56 new headless tests and 8 new browser tests, 1,968 and 119. Overall coverage: statements 83.42 → 85.94, branches 74.16 → 76.93, functions 81.19 → 83.32, lines 83.44 → 85.90. No budget moved. The ESM entry is at 0.5 % of headroom, which G2 predicted would be tight; it is within, and it is the first thing the next sprint should look at.

Six weeks, unchanged from RM-007, redistributed: 3 + 2 + 1 rather than 3.5 + 2.5. The week that moved bought a sprint whose whole job is to earn the flag removal, and the reason is V-8 rather than caution — this programme's three heaviest files are the tree's three least-covered, and a level that is switched on before anything drives it is a level that gets found broken by a person rather than by a test.

Programme G is delivered. The week bought what it was bought for: G3 found four defects, three of them shipped in G1 and G2, and every one of them needed a building rather than a plan to reach. three/controller.js went from 36 % of branches to 71 %. The argument generalises past this programme — the fixtures are plans, and the application builds buildings — and it is the reason a sprint whose whole content is driving what already exists earns its place beside sprints that build things.

§ 48 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

What must not change

The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0: levels is additive, written only when there is more than one, and a single-level design re-saves byte-identical — measured, in V-6, before the programme starts. The one-way arrow holds: a level is plain data on Model, and the base elevation is applied where geometry joins the scene rather than inside the model layer. Wall.height stays as it is, pinned by E2 with the measurement beside it, and a level's height is a property of the level and not a second attempt at that field. The per-room ceiling stays: V-1 found it is not a roof, and the answer is that G2 adds a roof rather than that it replaces a ceiling with one. The preserved polygon predicates are untouched for the sixth programme running; collision is still RM-007 J4's re-baseline. And no metric moves down: the coverage floors and the eleven budgets are ratchets, and this programme lands on the three least-covered files in the tree, which is why G3 exists and why it carries a test budget rather than an intention.

PROGRAMME H · DRAWING Nº RM-011

The walls are unlit, and the library does not fit

RM-007 calls programme H “any surface any colour or material, lit like a room, and a picture at the end of it” and prices it at seven weeks. Measuring it first found two things that change its shape. Under the profile this library ships as its default, every wall is unlit — a MeshBasicMaterial, which has no normal map, no roughness and nothing for a light to do — and there is not one PBR map anywhere in the tree. And the material library the programme is priced for does not fit the budgets by two orders of magnitude: today's runtime-asset headroom buys two images, and the programme is written for two hundred and seventy. Three sprints, 7 weeks, and the first task of the first one is a trial rather than a build.

architect3d

§ 49 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring the surfaces changed about the surfaces

Eleven measurements against the tree at 385aa88, five of them run in headless Chromium against the library as the dev server serves it. Two correct metrics this document set already carries, and one of them makes a budget line the wrong instrument for the sprint it would block.

0
PBR maps in the tree. Not one normalMap, roughnessMap, metalnessMap or aoMap across every material in a loaded design
Basic
the material a wall is under the default profile. Unlit — there is no light to tune and no map slot to fill
2
images that fit today's public-total headroom at this tree's own ETC1S mean. The programme is priced for 270
7
textures a three-storey house actually holds on the GPU. The budget that would refuse the library counts all 202 in the tree
9 of 18
furniture textures the oracle refused at the 3.0 RMS gate — four of them wood grain, which is what a material library is made of
388 fps
a furnished design under Studio on the browser tier's software renderer, against M-28's target of 30

The programme survives its own measurement; two of its metrics and one of its budgets do not. RM-007 gap Q-4 reads “seven textures, no colour picker for walls, no ceiling material, no PBR”, and every clause of that is true. What the measurement adds is why the last one is true, and it is not that somebody forgot to set a map. The two render profiles are a deliberate split RM-002 made and this document set has defended twice: classic is what shipped through 1.0.0, down to the constants, and it is the library's default because an embedder who upgrades must get no surprise and because npm run parity renders eleven scenes against frozen r98 goldens through it. Classic's walls are MeshBasicMaterial. A normal map on an unlit material is not a subtle improvement; it is not a thing that exists.

So H1 is a Studio programme, and saying so is the decision. The application already boots Studio (src/app/main.js:38), so a person using architect3d gets physically-based walls today and would get the maps. An embedder using the library gets classic and would get none of it. That is a defensible answer — it is the same answer RM-002 gave — but it has to be an answer rather than a discovery, because the alternative is a parity change against goldens that cannot be recaptured.

The harder finding is arithmetic, and it is the one that moves a sprint. Ninety materials of three maps is 270 images. At the mean size of the ten KTX2 files this tree already ships, that is 9.32 MB against 78,894 bytes of public-total headroom, and 90 MB of computed VRAM at 512 px against a 45.1 MB ceiling with 18.6 MB left in it. Neither of those is a 5 % raise with a recorded reason; the first is 2.6× and the second cannot be raised honestly at all, because texture-vram measures the tree and a library is not a tree. A three-storey house holds seven textures on the GPU and a furnished twenty-item design holds fifteen. The line was right when every image in public/ belonged to a model some design might load. It stops being right the moment there is a catalogue to pick four things out of, and H1 is the sprint that creates one.

§ 50 · DECISION LOG

Eleven findings, five of them run in a browser

A twelfth was added by H1 on delivery, and it corrects part of W-6. W-12 is the encode trial this drawing said had to be task one; it could be run after all, and what it found is the number that sizes the library.

Each row was produced against 385aa88. Where a material is quoted it was read off a loaded scene rather than off the source, and where a frame time is quoted it was rendered by SwiftShader on this machine rather than estimated.

W-1 · The walls are unlit, and that is the default shapes H1 measured

The three-storey house was loaded into a viewer and every mesh in the scene traversed, its material's class and its filled map slots read, once per render profile. The two are not the same scene:

GroupMaterial under classicnMaterial under studion
wall facesMeshBasicMaterial — map, lightMap18MeshStandardMaterial — map, lightMap18
wall facesMeshBasicMaterial — map14MeshStandardMaterial — map14
floorsMeshPhongMaterial — map4MeshStandardMaterial — map4
storey groupsMeshBasicMaterial, no map80MeshStandardMaterial, no map82
Counts are meshes in one loaded three-storey design; the picking planes are the bulk of the last row.

render_profile.js already says this, in a docblock written two programmes ago: “the walls are unlit MeshBasicMaterial and the floors are Phong — decisions from 2014 that no amount of light tuning can make look modern, because unlit geometry has no light to tune.” What is new is the consequence for programme H. Every feature in H1 and H2 is invisible under classic, and classic is the library's default, and it is the default deliberately: it is what the frozen r98 parity grid renders through and what color-pipeline.test.js was written for.

So the decision H1 has to record, rather than discover, is which of three things it means. (a) Materials and light are Studio-only, and the library default does not move — which is what RM-002 chose and what costs nothing. (b) The default moves to Studio — a parity change against goldens captured from a three r98 that no longer exists, so the eleven scenes cannot be recaptured and the grid stops meaning anything. (c) Classic's walls become Standard with the classic constants — which is (b) wearing a hat. (a) is this drawing's recommendation, and the reason to write it down is that a reader six months from now will otherwise read “no PBR” as an oversight.

W-2 · There is not one PBR map in the tree high measured

The same census, asked a narrower question: for every material in the scene, which of map, normalMap, roughnessMap, metalnessMap, aoMap, bumpMap, emissiveMap and lightMap are set. The answer over both profiles is two: map, and lightMap on the eighteen wall faces that carry the hand-painted vignette S8 documented. Zero of every other slot.

That makes Q-4's phrase exact, and smaller than it sounds. MeshStandardMaterial is a PBR material and Studio already uses it; roughness and metalness are already set per surface class, from 0.1 to 0.9. What is missing is not the material model, it is the images — and the images are the part W-4 says does not fit. The code half of H1 is therefore much smaller than the asset half, which is the opposite of how RM-007 priced it.

W-3 · A surface is three fields, and one save key for it is dead cheaper measured

A wall carries frontTexture and backTexture, each {url, stretch, scale}. A room's floor is {url, scale} under its corner-id key. That is the whole description: no colour, no rotation, no offset, no second map. The two dead keys are already documented — wallTextures and floorTextures are written on every save as [] and {} and never read — so a material record is additive beside newFloorTextures, which is the rule E2's thickness, E3's dimensions, F3's stair, G1's levels and G2's roof all already follow.

The colour picker has a precedent in the tree rather than being new: an item's per-slot colours are written as material_colors, painted by Item.setMaterialColor, and offered by ColorField.vue inside ItemInspector.vue. Only slots a person actually picked are written, which is why an untouched item's record is unchanged — the same conditional rule again, and the pattern H1 should copy rather than invent.

How many surfaces there are to pick on, measured rather than guessed: the three-storey house has 32 wall sides, 4 floors and 4 ceilings — 40 pickable surfaces; simple-room has nine. And the catalog they choose from is five wall entries and two floor entries over six distinct images, two of the seven rows being the same file at a different scale.

W-4 · The library does not fit, by two orders of magnitude shapes H1 measured

Headroom in the three budgets H1 would spend, from tools/budget.json against the last build:

Against that, what the programme is priced for. Ninety materials of albedo, normal and roughness is 270 images:

albedo + normal + roughness2709.32 MB18.91 MB90.0 MB
