Disk figures are image count × the measured mean of this tree's own files: 36,182 B for the ten that encoded, 110,732 B for the nine the oracle refused. VRAM is the budget's own formula — compressed texels × 4/3 for mips.

Even at 256 px, ninety materials of three maps put the tree at 49.9 MB against a 45.1 MB ceiling. This is not a budget raise with a recorded reason; it is the wrong shape of number. Two things follow, and they are H1's first two decisions rather than its outcome. The count is set by a trial, not promised in advance — W-6 says the encoder is not even installed, so the honest sequence is B1's: measure, then size the library to what the measurement allows. And texture-vram has to be re-pointed before it can be raised, for the reason W-5 gives.

RM-007 §36 already anticipated the first half of this: “a material library that goes from seven images to ninety will need public-total and demo-total raised, several times … and they will need a budget that does not exist yet, first-load payload, so that growing the tree never grows what a person downloads before their first wall.” That instinct was right and it now has a number — see W-7.

W-5 · The VRAM budget measures the tree, and a library is not a tree correction measured

What a design actually holds on the GPU, read from renderer.info.memory in Chromium after a settled render:

DesignTexturesGeometriesTrianglesDraw calls
three-storey house, unfurnished (studio)71263,532332
legacy-items, 20 pieces of furniture (studio)1526971,270494
The tree holds 202 images weighing 3.06 MB, which the budget costs at 28.7 MB of VRAM.

The line's own note says why it exists and, read today, says why it is about to be wrong: “202 images weigh 5.23 MB on disk and occupy 164 MB of GPU memory once uploaded … That is what a phone runs out of, not the download.” It is a worst case over the whole tree, and that was the right instrument while every image in public/ belonged to a catalog model that some design might load. A material library is different in kind: ninety materials exist so that a person picks four. Costing all ninety as if they were resident over-counts by roughly thirty times, which is exactly the factor between 202 images and the seven a real design holds.

The correction is not to delete the line. It is to make it measure a scene: the furnished fixture loaded in the browser tier and renderer.info.memory.textures read, which is the driver's own count and is already how gpu-memory.test.js works. The tree-level figure stays useful as a download question and that is what public-total already asks. A budget that would refuse a feature for a cost nobody pays is not a ratchet, it is a mistake with a number on it — and the rule this document set follows is that a limit moves up with a recorded reason, never down to pass, which is a rule about limits and not about what they measure.

W-6 · Half this tree's textures were refused, and the failures are wood high measured

tools/encode-textures.mjs carries the ledger RM-006 wrote, and it is a stronger prior than any published compression ratio: of eighteen furniture textures encoded to ETC1S and compared against the source in a rendered frame, nine were past the 3.0 RMS gate. Four of those nine are wood grain — 4.88, 4.88, 4.52 — and one photograph reached 7.00 with a worst pixel 174 of 255. Every encoder setting was swept before any of it was reverted; ETC1S at maximum quality rescued exactly one.

Wood grain is what a material library is mostly made of. Nine of the ninety CC0 materials H1 would ship being oak, walnut, pine, parquet and plank is a conservative guess, and this tree's own measurement says those are the images ETC1S cannot carry. The mean of the ten that encoded is 36,182 B and the mean of the nine that did not is 110,732 B, which is the 3× difference the disk table above prices.

And the same blocker B1 hit is unchanged: ktx, toktx and basisu are all absent from this machine, so nothing in this section could be re-measured against a new image even to check it. This is why H1's first task is the trial and not its conclusion — the same sentence RM-004's method paragraph wrote about B1, still true two years of programmes later, and the reason no number in this drawing is quoted from a codec's documentation.

Corrected by H1, on its first day. The second half of that paragraph is wrong, and it is wrong because the check was wrong: which ktx toktx basisu asks whether the KTX-Software system binaries are installed, and they are not — but RM-004 B5 vendored a WASM encoder two programmes ago and it is a devDependency. ktx2-encoder is in node_modules, npm run encode:textures and npm run oracle both drive it, and H1 ran 48 encodes through it in its first hour. The conclusion the sentence drew still stands — the trial is task one and no number here is quoted from documentation — but it stands for a better reason: the trial could be run, so it was. What it found is below.

W-12 · What the codec does to a material's three maps shapes H1 measured added on delivery

H1's task one, run through tools/material-trial.mjs and recorded in asset-pipeline/material-trial.json: the four material photographs this tree ships, each turned into the three maps a PBR material is, each encoded at three settings, each rendered against its source through the transcode oracle's own harness and differenced in the framebuffer. 48 encodes.

MapHigh-frequency shareBest RMS% of sourceWhat it ships as
albedo0.04142.182 UASTC186 %its source — clears the gate and costs more than it saves
normal, from a JPEG0.12168.827 UASTC—its source — 0 of 4 clear the gate
normal, smoothed0.01951.049 UASTC110 %its source — 3 of 4 clear it, and the container still grows
roughness0.04621.141 UASTC86 %UASTC — the only map worth encoding
ETC1S refused every map at every quality. UASTC transcodes to ASTC 4×4 on this device, which is the good target, so these are not a software rasteriser's numbers.

Two things the trial got wrong before it got them right, and both are recorded in the tool. The first draft encoded a normal map with the options for a photograph — perceptual channel weighting, an sRGB transfer function — and got RMS 35 to 48, which reads as “Basis cannot carry a normal map” and is not a codec finding at all. It is what a perceptual encoder does when asked to preserve a vector field. The second draft derived its normal maps from JPEGs at full strength, which turns that image's own 8×8 ringing into surface detail: the derived map carries three to ten times the high-frequency energy of anything else in the table, and no block codec compresses a 4×4 neighbourhood whose texels all disagree. So the trial now derives the normal map twice and reports both, and the two rows above are the sensitivity made visible rather than a number chosen.

The finding is that the binding constraint is the image, not the codec. Across sixteen inputs the fidelity tracks the high-frequency share and not the format, which is why the same UASTC setting gives 1.049 on one normal map and 12.888 on another. A material library whose normal maps are real bakes can be compressed; one whose normal maps are derived from lossy photographs cannot, and that is a fact about how the library is made.

And here is the number the sprint asked for. Priced from what each map actually ships as, a material is 497,583 bytes with three maps and 103,512 with one. Today's public-total headroom of 78,894 bytes is therefore zero materials — W-4 estimated two images and the per-material figure is harsher still. What the runtime-asset budget would have to become:

LibraryThree mapsAlbedo and roughness only
10 materials10.6 MB6.8 MB
30 materials20.1 MB8.8 MB
90 materials, as RM-007 priced it48.5 MB14.7 MB
public-total is 5.9 MB today. Ninety materials of three maps is an 8.2× raise.
The right-hand column is wrong and H1 measured it wrong on delivery. It is priced at bytesPerMaterialAlbedoOnly — 103,512 bytes, which is one map — under a heading that says two. Thirty materials of albedo and roughness came to 4.50 MB of library and 10.15 MB of public-total, not 8.8, and the raise is 1.80× rather than 1.5×. The left-hand column and the 8.2× verdict are unaffected: they price three maps and that arithmetic was right.

So the library RM-007 named cannot be shipped by a product whose whole premise is a static host and no server, and the trial says which shape can: about thirty materials, albedo and roughness, at 8.8 MB — a 1.5× raise rather than an eight-fold one, with normal maps added later per material as real bakes become available rather than derived. That is H1's recorded answer to “about ninety”, and it is an answer with a measurement under every digit. Every digit except the one that was not measured. 8.8 MB and 1.5× came from the table above, whose right-hand column prices one map under a two-map heading; delivered, it is 10.15 MB and 1.80×. The shape of the answer — thirty rather than ninety, two maps rather than three — is unchanged, and it is the part the 48 encodes actually supported.

W-7 · First load is 407 KB, and the next thing is a 515 KB transcoder med measured

Gzipped at level 9, from the demo build:

What a browser fetches before the first wallRawGzip
index.html1,9511,080
assets/index-*.js1,372,372380,846
assets/index-*.css33,7527,360
asset-manifest.json62,37518,038
first-load payload1,470,450407,324

Then the viewer boots, and its resource timings say it fetches three things weighing 595,263 bytes: basis_transcoder.wasm at 527,333, basis_transcoder.js at 57,529, and rooms/textures/Ground_4K.ktx2 at 10,401. Ninety-eight per cent of what this application downloads after its own code is a transcoder for one ten-kilobyte texture, because the skybox ground is the only KTX2 asset the default scene touches.

That reframes H1's download cost in the useful direction. The transcoder is already paid for, on every boot, for a single image. Shipping the material library as KTX2 does not add it — it is the first thing in this project that makes having it defensible. What H1 must not do is make the first-load figure grow, which is precisely the budget RM-007 asked for and this is its opening measurement: 407,324 bytes gzipped, and a material nobody has picked must not add a byte to it.

Both halves of this were overtaken by H1's delivery. The library ships as JPEG rather than KTX2, because the 515 KB transcoder is paid for by a boot that loads the skybox and would be paid for a second time by a person who picks a material — “already paid for” is true of the boot and not of the picker. And the first-load figure did grow, by 10,724 bytes; what more than paid for it was this line's own first reading, which found 17,065 gzipped bytes of subresource-integrity hashes in the manifest it counts. Moved out of the served file, the payload is 401,316 — 6,008 below the number above, with thirty materials added.

W-8 · The soft shadows are not soft defect measured

three/main.js:301 sets renderer.shadowMap.type = PCFSoftShadowMap. Booting the viewer in Chromium prints “THREE.WebGLShadowMap: PCFSoftShadowMap has been deprecated. Using PCFShadowMap instead”, and reading the property back afterwards gives 1, which is PCFShadowMap, not the 2 that was assigned. The Studio profile's shadowRadius: 2.4 is inert with that filter, so the one number in the profile table that exists to soften a shadow does nothing.

Recorded rather than fixed, because this is a planning pass. It matters to H2 twice over: “softer shadows behind the profile switch” is a defect to repair before it is a feature to add, and any comparison H2 makes between its new lighting and the old will be against a baseline that is not the one the source claims.

Half of this is wrong, and H2's repair measured it. The deprecation and the silent downgrade are exactly as described. shadowRadius is not inert. three rewrote PCF into a five-tap Vogel disk scaled by shadow.radius — which is why the soft variant was deprecated in the first place: the ordinary filter now does what the separate one existed for. Against the profile's own 2.4, radius 1 moves 256 pixels of a 307,200-pixel frame, radius 6 moves 2,394 and radius 12 moves 11,993, monotonically. So this was a defect in what the source says and not in what it does, the repair is a zero-pixel change, and H2's “softer shadows” is a number in a table rather than a feature to build.

W-9 · M-28 cannot fail, so it cannot gate anything correction measured

Twenty frames rendered and timed after five warm ones, at 1024 × 768, composited by SwiftShader on the CPU — which is the browser tier's renderer and therefore the one M-28 names:

DesignProfileFramefpsTrianglesCalls
three-storey, unfurnishedclassic1.07 ms9353,368293
three-storey, unfurnishedstudio1.31 ms7633,532332
legacy-items, furnishedclassic1.65 ms60470,986436
legacy-items, furnishedstudio2.58 ms38871,270494

M-28 as RM-007 wrote it: “the furnished fixture holds 30 fps under Studio on the browser tier's software renderer, or the added effect is off by default.” The furnished fixture holds 388. There is 12.9× of margin, so the metric passes today, passes after any plausible H2, and would go on passing after an implementation that made the view four hundred times slower. A gate with that much slack is not a gate.

H2 re-measured this table with its own method and its own fixture and found the absolute figures are session-relative: the three-storey design comes back at 0.68 ms classic and 1.20 ms studio against the 1.07 and 1.31 here, with identical geometry — 3,368 triangles and 293 calls, 3,532 and 332, to the number. The scene did not change; the run did. The correction below is unaffected and is strengthened by it: a fraction must be taken against a baseline measured in the same session, never against a figure carried over from a document. (Best-of-seven, which G3 settled on after chasing a flake, puts the same two frames at 0.58 and 0.92 ms.)

Corrected rather than dropped, and the correction keeps the number: M-28 becomes relative. Each effect H2 adds states its own cost as a fraction of the frame it was measured in, against the baselines in the table above, and the programme states a total. That is a figure that can move, can be argued about, and can refuse something — which is what a metric is for. The absolute floor stays underneath it as a backstop and will simply never be the binding constraint.

W-10 · North belongs to a plan, and the sun belongs to a building med measured

RM-008 E3 added a north bearing, and it lives on Floorplan — _north, written to the file only when it is not zero, which is the conditional rule. That was exactly right when a design was one plan. Since RM-010 G1 a design is a list of Levels each holding a whole Floorplan, so a three-storey house has three north bearings and nothing stops them disagreeing.

H2's sun needs one. The shape of the answer is the one G1 already used for the roof: a building-wide property on Model, derived-or-owned there rather than added to each plan, with the per-plan value kept as what the 2D sheet draws. Naming it now costs nothing; discovering it while wiring a sun costs a schema decision made in a hurry.

W-11 · No light metadata, no cube camera, and H3's collision is J4's med measured

Three smaller readings, grouped because each is a one-line answer that changes a bullet.

The catalog has five keys. All 168 entries carry exactly format, image, model, name, type — there is no light metadata of any kind, and eight entries are named like lamps. So H2's “light-emitting lamps by catalog metadata” is a sixth key on a file that six suites assert over, which is the same cost F1 paid for keeping openings out of catalog.json and is worth pricing as schema work rather than as lighting work.

The photo capture has a seam and no caller. Main.dataUrl() exists, renders once and returns a PNG data URL; nothing in src/ calls it. Measured on a boot, it produces the canvas at 1024 × 768 at device pixel ratio 1 — 391,170 characters, about 287 KiB. Supersampling it is a render-target change behind a method that already exists. There is no CubeCamera and no equirectangular path anywhere in the tree, so H3's panorama is new construction rather than a setting.

H3 and J4 both claim collision. RM-007 §36 assigns it to J4 explicitly, as the deliberate re-baseline of the two preserved predicates in core/utils.js — “new predicate, feature flag, characterization tests updated in the same commit — not as a fix” — and RM-007's own H3 line also reads “walkthrough with wall collision”. Two programmes owning one feature means it is either done twice or done by neither. This drawing withdraws it from H3: the predicates have been left alone for seven programmes running, and the sprint that turns them on should be the one whose whole subject is that decision.

§ 51 · SPRINTS H1–H3

Seven weeks, re-drawn around what the budgets allow

RM-007 priced this programme at 7 weeks in three sprints and the total does not move. What moves is the order inside H1 — the trial comes first — and what H3 is for, since one of its two bullets belongs to another programme.

H1

A surface is a material

proposedW-1W-4W-5W-6W-73 wk

Objective. Any surface any colour, any material, described by numbers the file keeps — and a library sized by what the encoder actually delivers rather than by a number written before it was run.

  • The trial is task one (W-6). Install the KTX-Software binaries, put a representative material set — wood, tile, plaster, brick, fabric, stone — through resize, encode and oracle, and record the pass rate and the bytes. The library's size is a result of this task, not an input to it. Nine of eighteen refused and four of those wood grain is the prior; if it holds, an albedo-only library is what fits and the normal maps are the thing that gets cut.
  • A material is a description, beside the texture rather than replacing it. {url, stretch, scale} gains a colour, a rotation, an offset and the map set, written only where somebody changed something — the rule E2, E3, F1, F3, G1 and G2 all follow, and the rule that makes an untouched design re-save byte-identical. The precedent for the colour half is in the tree: an item writes material_colors for picked slots only (W-3).
  • A colour picker on every surface, through the field that already exists (ColorField.vue) and the panel that already knows what was clicked (SurfaceInspector.vue). Forty pickable surfaces in the three-storey house; ceilings included, which Q-4 names and nothing offers today.
  • Studio-only, stated (W-1). Maps and colour apply under the profile the application boots; classic keeps the 2014 look, keeps the parity grid meaningful, and gains nothing. Recommendation (a) of the three in W-1, recorded in the code beside the branch that implements it.
  • Two budget lines move and one is re-pointed (W-4, W-5). public-total is raised by the trial's measured bytes with the reason in the commit. texture-vram is re-pointed at a scene before it is touched — the furnished fixture in the browser tier, renderer.info.memory.textures, which is what a GPU is actually asked for. And first-load payload is added as the eleventh budget, opening at the measured 407,324 bytes gzipped (W-7), so that growing the library can never grow what a person downloads before their first wall.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-42 = a surface is its material. Every surface's saved record round-trips byte-identically; a design where nobody touched a material writes no material key at all; and for every combination the picker offers, the mesh's maps, colour and repeat equal the description that produced them
  • M-43 = nothing unpicked is downloaded. The first-load payload does not grow by one byte for a material nobody has chosen, measured as the resource timings of a boot, and the new budget line holds it
  • M-27 stands, extended: every shipped material image passes the 3.0 RMS oracle gate or ships uncompressed, and the count of measured images equals the count of shipped ones
  • The library's size is reported as what the trial allowed, beside the number this drawing could not produce
LANDED — H1, all three slices
  • Task one is done and it corrected this drawing. The encoder was available all along — see the correction under W-6 and the trial in W-12. A material is 497,583 bytes with three maps and 103,512 with one, only the roughness map is worth encoding, and ninety materials of three maps is an 8.2× budget raise. H1 ships about thirty, albedo and roughness.
  • M-42's first two clauses are met. A surface carries a tint, a rotation, an offset and up to two maps beside its image, and a ceiling has a material for the first time. Every key is written only when it differs from its default, decided in one function rather than at three call sites, and all four fixtures re-save byte-identically with no material key anywhere. The third clause — the mesh agreeing with the description — is asserted in Chromium over both profiles.
  • A tint is a multiply, which is what makes clearing one free. White is not a colour, it is the absence of one, so picking it writes nothing and “I cleared it” and “I never touched it” are the same file. It also means the two surfaces that already have a base colour — classic's 0xcccccc floor and the profile's ceiling — keep it.
  • The maps are Studio-only, recorded rather than discovered (W-1). An unlit MeshBasicMaterial has no light for a normal map to bend and no specular term for a roughness map to modulate. Recommendation (a) of the three W-1 set out, asserted in both profiles.
  • Two bugs from driving it. Picking a different image threw the material away, because the first draft of setTexture built a fresh three-key object. And a tinted wall kept a light grey top, because the filler is the top of a wall and was left at the profile's 0xdddddd.
  • One budget raised, and it is the one this drawing said was certain. lib-esm-gzip 73,700 → 78,300 for a measured 74,533 — 1,720 bytes for four of the five clauses in Q-4, the cheapest feature-per-byte of the seven raises in that file. public-total did not move; the library is not in that commit.
  • 42 new tests, 1,986 and 127. Coverage up on all four: statements 85.94 → 86.04, branches 76.93 → 77.01, functions 83.32 → 83.54, lines 85.90 → 86.01.
  • Thirty materials, and the count is a measurement. CC0, from Poly Haven, an albedo and a roughness map each, gated by resize-textures.mjs's own two gates on the way in: worst resample error 0.72 against 2.0 and worst codec error 2.802 against 3.0, over all 60 shipped images. 28.5 MB of 1K sources in, 4.50 MB out. tools/fetch-materials.mjs acquires them; npm run materials:check verifies the committed tree against the report with no network.
  • Two resolutions, because the two maps are not the same kind of image. Measured as the detail a round trip preserves, a roughness map at 256 is more faithful than an albedo at 512 in all six materials sampled, by 1.2 to 7.3 dB. So the smaller map is not the weak link — the albedo already is, at twice the resolution — and it costs a quarter of the pixels: 18,794 bytes against 122,749.
  • JPEG, although this sprint's own trial measured KTX2. UASTC carried a roughness map at 86 % of source and cleared the gate, and it is still not what shipped: a KTX2 drags the 515 KB Basis transcoder with it, which W-7 measured at 98 % of a boot's traffic for one 10 KB texture. Trading 19 KB of map for half a megabyte of decoder is the wrong way round, and M-43 says nothing unpicked is downloaded. The container decision stays per asset, which is B1's rule and C1's.
  • The tiling scale is measured, not invented. Every entry tiles at the material's own published real-world size, so a 1 m brick panel repeats every metre. src/catalog/textures.json carries the demo's 50 and 100 for the same brick image and records no reason for either.
  • texture-vram measures a scene now (W-5). The tree walk put this library at 81.14 MB and would have refused it — for 90 images a scene uploads at most four of. sceneVram() prices the two textures every viewer uploads, the costliest wall and floor material the pickers offer, and the distinct textures of the costliest catalog items up to the item count of the busiest design in the repository: 25,004,576 bytes, every term something a person can actually produce. It is a model, so gpu-memory.test.js holds it to renderer.info.memory on a real scene.
  • Three budgets raised, and the largest overshot this drawing's own estimate. public-total 6,200,000 → 11,180,000 for a measured 10,640,264; demo-total and demo-js-gzip follow it into the deployment. W-12 said 8.8 MB and 1.5×; it is 10.15 MB and 1.80×, because that estimate priced one map under a two-map heading. Corrected in place above rather than replaced.
  • A roughness map belongs to the picture, not to the person. setTexture keeps a tint on purpose — picking a different brick is not a decision to lose the colour you chose — and the map is the opposite, because the bumps in a plaster's map are that plaster's bumps. So every pick writes the slot, to the entry's map or to null.
  • One mislabelling caught before it cost anything. kindOf decided texture by falling through, which was true while every file that reached the bottom was one and stopped being true when a CREDITS.md landed beside the library. Third time this function's kind has been found wrong; first time a test found it rather than a budget.
  • 32 new tests, 2,014 and 131. Coverage up on all four: statements 86.04 → 86.08, branches 77.01 → 77.08, functions 83.54 → 83.61, lines 86.01 → 86.06.
  • M-43 is met in substance and not in letter, and the difference is measured. The eleventh budget line is in: first-load, the document plus the scripts and stylesheets it references plus asset-manifest.json, which useAssets fetches before the viewer can resolve a texture. The library did grow it — 10,724 bytes, 6,554 of catalog and picker in the bundle and 4,170 of manifest entries for ninety new files — so “does not grow by one byte” is not true and is not claimed. The other half of the metric is: a boot's performance.getEntriesByType('resource') contains no material image at all, asserted against the whole catalog rather than a sample.
  • The line found something on the day it was installed, and it paid for the library four times over. 17,065 of the served manifest's 22,208 gzipped bytes were subresource-integrity hashes — 4.1 % of everything a person downloads before their first wall, on every boot, for a feature AssetResolver documents as off by default and which guards nothing whatsoever for a same-origin public/. They are generated into asset-pipeline/asset-integrity.json now, verified there by the same test that always verified them, and never served; npm run manifest -- --integrity writes them into the manifest for the cross-origin deployment that actually wants them. No schema changed — AssetManifest.parse has always read hash defensively — only which builds pay for it.
  • So the first load is 401,316 bytes, which is 6,008 below what W-7 measured before any of this existed. Thirty materials added, and a boot got smaller. That is the whole argument for putting a number on something before arguing about it.
  • H1 is closed. Three slices: the encode trial that sized the library, the material model, and the library with its four budget moves. Gap Q-4 — “seven textures, no colour picker for walls, no ceiling material, no PBR” — is answered in full for the profile the application boots. H2 is next, and W-8 is waiting for it: three/main.js:301 assigns a shadow filter three no longer implements, so “softer shadows” is a repair before it is a feature.
H2

Light that can be seen

proposedW-8W-9W-10W-112.5 wk

Objective. A room lit by a sun that knows what time it is and by lamps that emit, with every effect's cost stated as a fraction of the frame.

  • The shadow filter is repaired first (W-8), because softer shadows cannot be added on top of a setting that is silently ignored. PCFSoftShadowMap is deprecated and downgraded; the profile's shadowRadius is inert with what actually runs. A defect, and the first commit.
  • A sun by time of day and orientation, with one north for the building (W-10). The per-plan bearing E3 added stays as what the 2D sheet draws; the sun reads a building-wide value on Model, which is the shape G1 used for the roof.
  • Lamps that emit, by a sixth catalog key (W-11). Eight of the 168 entries are named like lamps and none of them carries anything a renderer could read. Priced as schema work over a file six suites assert about, not as lighting work.
  • Ambient occlusion behind the profile switch, and Studio-only for the same reason H1 is: there is no aoMap anywhere and an unlit wall has nowhere to put one.
  • A photo capture through the seam that exists. Main.dataUrl() is called by nothing and renders the canvas at its own size — 1024 × 768, 287 KiB, at device pixel ratio 1. Supersampled and saved is a render target behind a method already written.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-28, corrected (W-9): each effect states its cost as a fraction of the frame it was measured in, against this drawing's baselines — 2.58 ms furnished under Studio — and the programme states a total. The 30 fps floor stays underneath as a backstop it will never bind
  • A shadow's penumbra visibly changes with the sun's elevation, asserted on pixels rather than on the setting that was assigned
  • Every light this sprint adds is off, or free, under classic
LANDED — H2, all five bullets
  • The repair is done, and it cost zero pixels. three/main.js names PCFShadowMap, which is what the renderer has been running all along: three deprecated PCFSoftShadowMap and WebGLShadowMap.render assigns the replacement over the top of the value it was given, on the first frame, with a warning. So the property read back as 1 while the source said 2. Naming what runs moves nothing a user sees and nothing a golden capture holds — asserted by asking for the deprecated constant, letting three substitute, and differencing the two frames: 0 of 307,200 pixels.
  • W-8's second sentence is wrong, and this is the correction. It said the profile's shadowRadius: 2.4 is inert with PCFShadowMap, so “the one number in the profile table that exists to soften a shadow does nothing”. It does something. three rewrote PCF into a five-tap Vogel disk scaled by shadow.radius, and that rewrite is precisely why the soft variant was deprecated — the ordinary filter now does what the separate one existed for. Measured against the profile's own 2.4: radius 1 moves 256 pixels, radius 6 moves 2,394, radius 12 moves 11,993, of 307,200. Monotonic, which is what separates “the number reaches the shader” from “the frame is noisy”.
  • So H2's “softer shadows” is not blocked and never was. The knob works; what H1's drawing thought was a missing feature is a number already in the table. That changes what the rest of this sprint has to build, which is the whole reason a repair goes first.
  • One dead property removed beside it. renderer.shadowMapSoft = true — three has had no such property since around r73, and S5 removed its two siblings (shadowDarkness, shadowCameraVisible) while leaving this one. It was an assignment onto a renderer that nothing has ever read.
  • M-28's first entry: the repair costs 0 % of the frame, and it is zero by construction rather than by measurement error — the same filter, the same frame, byte for byte.
  • And a note on how the fractions must be taken. Re-measured with W-9's own method and its own fixture, the three-storey design renders in 0.68 ms under classic and 1.20 ms under studio, against the 1.07 and 1.31 in the table above — with identical geometry, 3,368 triangles and 293 calls, 3,532 and 332. The scene did not change; the session did. So an effect's cost is a fraction of a baseline measured in the same run, never of a number carried over from a document. Best-of-seven puts the same two frames at 0.58 and 0.92 ms, which is G3's finding about interference showing up again.
  • A sun, and it is a description rather than a light. model/sun.js is a latitude, a day and an hour plus the arithmetic that turns them into a bearing and an elevation; Main.syncSun() hands the direction to Lights. Deliberately not an ephemeris — Cooper's declination and an hour angle in local solar time, no equation of time and no longitude, which is the honest model for “does the morning sun reach this room”.
  • Presence is the switch. No enabled field: Model.sun is null by default and the key light then sits exactly where the profile puts it, which is what every design did before H2. "sun": {} is meaningful rather than empty. All four fixtures re-save with no sun key anywhere. The defaults describe themselves — latitude 45, day 81, hour 12 is exactly 45° due south, and the first draft's day 80 landed at 44.60, which is close enough to look right.
  • One north for the building, and no new save key (W-10). Model.north reads the ground floor's and writes every storey, so the three bearings a three-storey house could hold cannot disagree. Derived rather than added; the per-plan value is still what each 2D sheet draws.
  • The acceptance is on pixels. A room with a wall down the middle at 12:00, 9:00 and 7:00: each step away from noon moves more of the frame than the last, monotonically, so a frame that merely flickered would not pass. Under classic the frame is identical with a sun and without one — the third clause, asserted rather than assumed.
  • A sun below the horizon does not move the key underground. Held at the horizon, dimmed to nothing, and the intensity assigned on every pass rather than inside the branch — otherwise taking a night-time sun away would leave the lights off.
  • Lamps that emit, and W-11's count was right. Eight of the 168 rows are lamps and the other 160 keep exactly the five keys they had, asserted row by row. items/lamp.js follows the shape opening, stair and structure set: a row says only what differs, three of the eight say {}, and the record is saved with the item so a design carries its own lamps rather than depending on a catalog that has moved on.
  • Brightness is in lumens, because it means something outside this repository — a 60 W incandescent is about 800, and three's PointLight.power is documented in lumens and divides by 4π itself. The bulb's position is a fraction of the item's height and is never stored: a chandelier lights from near its bottom, a standard lamp from near its top, and both survive a resize.
  • Studio-only and shadowless, and the bulb is not built at all under classic. A point light there would reach the Phong floors and nothing else — a lamp that lights the carpet and not the room. And a shadow-casting point light is a cube of six renders, so four lamps would be twenty-four; lights.js declined the same trade for its fill light.
  • Ambient occlusion is new construction, and it is off. W-2 found no aoMap anywhere, so screen-space is the only occlusion available and Main has never had a post-processing chain. three/post.js is three's GTAOPass behind an EffectComposer. M-28's second entry: +68 % of the frame — 0.22 ms to 0.37 ms on a six-metre room, measured in the same session, the largest single cost in this programme. Under classic it would be wrong as well as expensive: multiplying an unlit MeshBasicMaterial by an occlusion term is a grey stain rather than lighting.
  • The whole frame moves, not only the corners, and that is stated rather than hidden. A composer ends in an OutputPass where renderer.render applies tone mapping itself, and the two are not bit-identical: 781,416 of 786,432 pixels differ by something, mean 4.4/255. The occlusion is the 51,153 past the oracle's visibility threshold of 8. Both are asserted, so a pass that quietly changed the tone response would show as the first number moving.
  • The first-load budget earned its keep on its second sprint. The chain's four modules were static imports — 10.6 KB gzipped on every boot for an effect no default turns on, which is exactly what M-43 forbids. Dynamic now, and the two lines disagreed in the way that proves it: first-load fell while demo-js-gzip rose, because one asks what the bundle weighs and the other what a person waits for.
  • A photograph, through the seam that existed. Main.dataUrl() had no caller and produced 1024 × 768 at ratio 1 (W-11). It supersamples by raising the pixel ratio and leaving the CSS size alone — which is what a device pixel ratio is, so the camera, the picking and the controls stay correct. The restore is in a finally: a toDataURL that throws on a tainted canvas would otherwise leave the viewer rendering at four times its size for the session.
  • H2 is closed, and programme H with it. The repair, a sun, lamps, occlusion and a photograph. Two budgets raised (lib-iife-gzip, demo-js-gzip — an IIFE cannot code-split) and one coverage exemption recorded explicitly, which is what vitest.config.mjs asks for rather than letting a number drift. H3 is next: a 360° panorama, and eye height and a teleport in the walkthrough.
H3

Out of the window

proposedW-111.5 wk

Objective. Stand anywhere in the design and look all the way round, and take that view away as a file.

  • A 360° panorama from any point — a cube camera, an equirectangular projection and a PNG. New construction: there is no CubeCamera in the tree (W-11), which is honest pricing rather than a warning.
  • The walkthrough gets eye height and a teleport click. The first-person rig already carries friction, gravity, a jump and a 160 cm eye height preserved from the fork; what it has no way to do is go somewhere, which is the thing a person walking a plan actually wants.
  • Wall collision is withdrawn from this sprint (W-11). RM-007 assigns it to J4 as the deliberate re-baseline of two preserved predicates, and the same document also put it here. It belongs to the sprint whose subject is that decision, and the week it frees is why this one is still 1.5 rather than 2.
ACCEPTANCE
  • A panorama captured from a point inside a room contains every wall of that room, asserted by sampling the six faces rather than by looking at it
  • The walkthrough is still exactly the fork's physics: friction 10/s, gravity 980/s², walk 3000, jump 350, eye 160 — a teleport moves the walker and changes nothing else
LANDED — H3, both bullets, and programme H closed
  • The projection is pure and the capture is not, and the line between them is the module boundary. core/equirect.js is six faces of bytes in and one 2:1 image out — no three types, no renderer, no canvas — and three/panorama.js is the part that needs a GPU. Same one-way arrow model/sun.js sits behind, and it is what let this sprint be tested exactly rather than by looking at it: coverage went up on all four lines, where H2's GPU-only post.js needed a written exemption.
  • Six cameras of our own, from three's own vectors. CUBE_FACES is copied out of CubeCamera.updateCoordinateSystem(), and each face's right vector is computed as forward × up rather than typed — so the table has six lines of input and no arithmetic to get wrong. A test builds a real CubeCamera, asks three to orient it, and compares all six: a version bump that re-orders or re-orients them fails there rather than producing a panorama that is rotated for no visible reason.
  • three's CubeCamera has a negative field of view, and that is the reason this does not use it. fov = -90, and a negative field of view negates both axes of the projection — measured: a point at NDC (0.2, 0.2) through a +90 camera arrives at (−0.2, −0.2) through a −90 one. That half-turn is how three writes each face in the order a GL cube map stores it. Copying it across would have produced a panorama upside down and back to front.
  • And the deeper reason: a render target gets neither tone mapping nor the output colour space. Read WebGLPrograms.getParameters — toneMapping is forced to NoToneMapping and outputColorSpace to the working space unless currentRenderTarget is null. The studio profile renders through ACESFilmicToneMapping, so a WebGLCubeRenderTarget would hand back six faces that are not what the screen shows, and a panorama that does not match the view it was taken from is a bug that looks like a colour preference. So the six faces are rendered to the canvas, through the same call a frame makes, and gl.readPixels reads them straight back. The alternative was a full-screen pass duplicating three's ACES and sRGB chunks by hand.
  • One limitation, stated rather than hidden: the panorama has no post-processing, so H2's ambient occlusion is absent from it. Not only a shortcut — screen-space occlusion is computed from one frame's depth buffer, so each 90° face would occlude against its own view and the six would not agree along the seams. A panorama with six visible edges is worse than one without the effect.
  • Nearest-neighbour sampling, and the sizing is what makes that enough. A face spans 90° over size pixels and the output spans 360° over width, so at width = 4 × size the two match exactly at the centre of a face — and everywhere else on a face a perspective projection is denser than at its centre, never sparser. 4096 × 2048 from 1024-pixel faces is the default for that reason and not by taste.
  • The acceptance, and it is worded as a method. Four walls of one room, each tinted a colour of its own through H1's surface material; the eye in the middle; each wall then looked for in the direction it is actually in — faceSample says which of the six faces that direction lands on and where, and the pixel there has to be that wall's colour. Four right-angled walls come back on four different faces. A panorama that were upside down, mirrored or a quarter-turn out would pass a blankness test and fails every assertion in that file, because every one of them ties a compass direction to a pixel.
  • A measurement overturned the test rather than the other way round. The first draft read 0, 0, 0 for every wall and the tempting fix was to loosen the threshold. The cause was elsewhere: a classic wall is an unlit MeshBasicMaterial with map set, and a Texture whose image has not arrived samples as zero — three says so on the console and renders it anyway. So the tint was being multiplied by nothing. The suite now polls the face it is about to assert on until the texture has landed, which is a wait for a fact rather than a sleep for a guess.
  • Eye height is a property of the person, not of the building, so it is not in the save file. It lives beside the theme and the workspace layout — in this browser, for this reader, across designs — because two people opening the same plan should walk it at their own eye level, and a file carrying one of their heights would quietly change the other's view. Asserted as a decision: a design re-saves byte-identical after the walker has changed height.
  • A teleport writes a position and the floor under it, and nothing else. Not the velocity — a walker who was moving arrives moving, which is what carries the sense that the room changed rather than the person. Not the orientation. Not _canJump, which the next frame decides from the position just written. Each of those is asserted by measuring the motion after the teleport, not by reading a field back.
  • A second number, so the fork's arithmetic is untouched. The rig clamped to characterHeight outright, which is right for a design with one storey and wrong since RM-010 G1: a walker teleported to the first floor fell straight through it. groundHeight defaults to 0, which makes the fall identical to the fork's, and a click on an upper floor now lands on that floor.
  • The five constants are measured off the motion rather than read back off the object, which is the difference between a characterization test and a restatement. One held key for one step of 0.1 s moves the walker exactly 30 cm, so the acceleration is 3000. Two equal steps in the ratio 1 − k·dt give friction 10/s. A step of 0.5 s from rest falls 245 cm, so gravity is 980. The jump's first step recovers 350. And the eye stands at 160.
  • The aim is the centre of the screen, because a pointer-locked walkthrough has no cursor. The crosshair is where you are looking; looking at the floor and clicking is the gesture every first-person tool already uses. Floors are collected from every storey shown — visibility checked up the whole parent chain, because showStoreys(false) hides a level group and a teleport onto a floor nobody can see is a teleport into the dark.
  • Wall collision stays withdrawn (W-11), with J4, whose subject is the two preserved polygon predicates. Eight programmes now without touching them.
  • One budget raised, and H2 said which one. lib-esm-gzip 78,300 → 83,000. H2's note named this line as thin at 2.0 % and left an instruction — “the sprint that trips it should raise it to ~5 % rather than to just-enough”. It went one sprint later. The entry measured 76,761 → 78,999, and every one of those 2,238 bytes is this sprint's own code: Raycaster and PerspectiveCamera were both already in the bundle, so no three module came with it. first-load took 2.5 KB of the same change and sits at 3.2 % — the next line to watch, and the obvious answer of splitting the capture out is not taken, because package.json publishes exactly two files and a chunk would not be shipped at all.
  • 60 new headless tests and 10 in the browser: 2,126 and 169. H2's own note said 2,067 and 168; both were re-run at that commit in a clean worktree and are 2,066 and 159, so the browser figure was out by more than this whole sprint added. Coverage up on all four lines — statements 86.13 → 86.35, branches 77.28 → 77.32, functions 83.80 → 84.09, lines 86.11 → 86.33 — which is the pure/GPU split paying for itself in the only currency that shows.
  • Programme H is delivered, all three sprints. H1 gave a surface a material and a library to pick from, H2 gave the room a sun, lamps, occlusion and a photograph, and H3 lets you stand anywhere in it and take the whole view away as a file.

Seven weeks, unchanged from RM-007, and unusually the split is unchanged too: 3 + 2.5 + 1.5. What moved is inside the sprints. H1 starts with a trial because the number it was priced against cannot be produced without one, and it spends a third of itself on budgets rather than on features — which looks like overhead until you notice that under today's ceilings this programme ships two images. H2 opens with a repair. H3 gives a bullet back to J4 rather than doing it twice.

§ 52 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskWhereMitigation
The encode trial comes back badly and the library is a fraction of ninetyH1That is the trial working, not failing. The prior is already measured — nine of eighteen refused, four of them wood — and the sprint is written so the count is an output. An albedo-only library of thirty good materials is a better product than ninety that band, and B5 already learned this the expensive way: shipping the source was both smaller and better looking for all eight it tried
texture-vram is re-pointed and something real slips past itH1The tree-level question does not disappear, it moves to public-total, which already asks it and already has a ceiling. What the scene-level line adds is the number a GPU is actually asked for, read from the driver by a suite that exists. Both lines, not one instead of the other

Fixing the shadow filter changes every rendered frameH2It does, under Studio, and that is the point — the profile asks for a soft filter and gets a hard one. Classic is untouched, so the eleven-scene parity grid and color-pipeline.test.js are unaffected. A Studio frame has no frozen golden to break

What must not change

The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0: a material is additive and written only where somebody changed something, so an untouched design re-saves byte-identical — M-26's rule, now on its sixth programme. The classic profile is untouched, in constants and in output: it is what npm run parity renders through and what color-pipeline.test.js was written for, and the r98 goldens behind both cannot be recaptured. The preserved polygon predicates stay pinned for the eighth programme running, which is why H3 gives collision back to J4. The oracle gate does not move: 3.0 RMS is the number B4 chose and RM-006 enforced by reverting eight files, and a material library is the worst possible occasion to discover a reason it should have been 4. And no budget moves down — two move up in H1 with their reasons in the commit, one is re-pointed at what it should have been measuring, and one is added.

PROGRAMME J · DRAWING Nº RM-012

Twenty-two items of headroom, and a collision that is a comment

RM-007 calls programme J “enough furniture to furnish a home, found by room, with the licence on every item; and the handling — select, copy, mirror, align, stack, snap, collide — that makes placing it quick” and prices it at 7.5 weeks. Measuring it first found three things that change its shape. Today's asset headroom buys 21.9 more items at this catalog's own measured mean, and the programme is written for between 232 and 432 more — which is a deliberate decision about how large a static deploy may be, not a 5 % raise with a reason. The catalog index is in the bundle, so J1's metadata on 600 rows costs more gzipped than the whole first-load budget has left, and the sprint order as drawn ships that regression before the sprint that would undo it. And the collision J4 is priced to re-baseline is not gated by the predicates it names: FloorItem.isValidPosition returns true on every path it has, because its only return false sits inside a block comment. Four sprints, 7.5 weeks, and what moves is the order and what J2's number is allowed to be.

§ 53 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring the catalog changed about the catalog

Nine measurements against the tree at 38be485, every one of them run rather than read. Two of them re-price a sprint, one re-orders the programme, and one is good news: the pipeline J2 is costed to build is already installed and already green.

0 of 168
catalog rows carrying a category, a tag, a dimension, a source or a licence. M-29 asks for 100 %
21.9
more items today's public-total headroom buys at this catalog's own measured mean. J2 is written for 232 to 432 more
17,264 B
gzipped growth of the bundled index at 600 metadata-bearing rows, against 13,292 B of first-load headroom
true
what FloorItem.isValidPosition returns on every path. Its only return false is inside a block comment
152 of 168
models already Draco-compressed, and 11 already KTX2. Both encoders run from node_modules
4 loaders
glTF, OBJ, Draco and KTX2, all already constructed by Scene. J3 needs none of them written

The programme survives its own measurement; one of its metrics does not, and its order does not either. RM-007 gap Q-5 is about breadth and Q-11 and Q-12 are about handling, and every clause of all three is true. What the measurement adds is where the cost actually is. It is not in the encoders — npm run encode:check reports 152 encoded, 13 deliberately unencoded and npm run encode:textures:check reports 11 transcoded, all matching the report, both green, both from npm packages rather than from the CLI binaries RM-011 W-6 correctly found absent. It is not in the loaders: model/scene.js constructs GLTFLoader, OBJLoader, DRACOLoader and KTX2Loader at boot, so “GLB, glTF and OBJ from disk” is a storage problem wearing a loader's clothes. The cost is in two places nobody has costed: how big the deploy is allowed to get, and what the index weighs on the way in.

The arithmetic that moves J2. The whole catalog — every model, every thumbnail and every texture a .glb points at, counted once each — is 4,385,565 bytes for 168 items, a mean of 26,105. That mean is not a soft number: 152 of the models are already through Draco and 11 of the textures are already KTX2, so it is the cost of an item after the pipeline, and there is no compression left to find. Against 570,674 bytes of public-total headroom that buys 21.9 items. Reaching 400 needs 6.06 MB more and reaching 600 needs 11.28 MB, which takes the tree from 10.61 MB to 16.7 or 21.9 MB — 1.5× to 2.0× today's limit, and demo-total with it, from 19.21 MB to 25.3 or 30.5 MB. That is not impossible and it is not a 5 % raise. It is a decision about how large a free static deploy may be, and it belongs at the front of J2 rather than in week two of it — which is exactly what RM-011 did to H1's “about ninety materials”, and for the same reason.

The finding that re-orders the programme is smaller and sharper. src/catalog/catalog.json is imported by useCatalog.js, so vite inlines all 168 rows into the application bundle: 3,347 bytes gzipped today, 21 bytes a row. Add J1's five metadata keys to every row — measured on a synthetic augmentation, not guessed — and the same 168 rows become 5,771. At 600 rows they become 20,611, which is 17,264 bytes more than today against 13,292 bytes of first-load headroom. The index alone breaks M-43 before a single model is fetched. J2's own wording already contains the remedy — “packs loaded lazily by manifest” — but as drawn J1 lands the metadata first and J2 splits the file afterwards, so the programme ships the regression and then removes it. The split moves to the front of J1.

And J4 is priced against the wrong risk. RM-007 calls its collision “the deliberate re-baseline of the polygon predicates”, which reads as though the predicates are load-bearing and repairing them is the dangerous part. Run against every caller in src/, they are not. polygonInsidePolygon has no caller anywhere. polygonOutsidePolygon has one and it is commented out. pointInPolygon and polygonPolygonIntersect have one live call each, both inside FloorItem.isValidPosition — whose two live branches both return true, so repairing them changes nothing anyone can see. Room detection uses pointInPolygon2, the sibling nobody refactored, which verifies RM-007's own claim rather than assuming it. The re-baseline is therefore cheap and the collision is expensive, which is the opposite of how the sprint is written.

§ 54 · DECISION LOG

Eight findings, and two of them are good news

Each row was produced against 38be485. Where a byte count is quoted it was gzipped at level 9 by this pass; where a predicate is quoted it was called rather than read; where a pipeline is quoted its own --check was run.

X-1 · Five keys, and none of them describes the thing med measured

Every one of the 168 rows carries exactly name, image, model, type and format. Eight also carry lamp, which RM-011 H2 added and which is the only precedent in the file for a key that says something about what an item is. There is no category, no tag, no real dimension, no source and no licence — M-29 asks for 100 % and the measurement is 0 %, which is worth stating as a number because it makes the metric a target rather than a description.

Two consequences follow from the absence rather than from the plan. A dimension cannot be shown without downloading the model, because an item's size is read off its loaded mesh — so a drawer that wants to say “90 × 60 × 75” beside a thumbnail must either fetch the .glb or be told. And the licence is nowhere in the shipped product, although the assets are CC0 and the obligation is light; RM-007's own objective puts “the licence on every item” in its first line, and there is currently no place to put it.

The eight placement types are in use unevenly: 91 rows are FloorItem, 27 are the bare Item, 18 each are wall and wall-floor items, 8 are in-wall, and three types hold three, two and one row. Two rows are both called Chair. And the twelve wall segments RM-007 wants moved out of furniture are exactly twelve, findable by name and by model path — eight typed as Item and four as in-wall — totalling 63,348 bytes. They are Kenney kit architecture sitting in a furniture list, and moving them is a catalog edit rather than a feature.

X-2 · The headroom buys twenty-two items shapes J2 measured

An item's cost was taken the way check-budget.mjs takes it — the model, the thumbnail, and every distinct image the .glb's own JSON chunk points at — and then summed across the catalog with each file counted once, because a shared texture is one file on a disk. The catalog is 4,385,565 bytes for 168 items, a mean of 26,105. Sharing is almost absent: 147 of the 168 models carry no external image at all, and across the whole catalog exactly two textures are reused, so the deduped mean and the naive one differ by 8 %.

TargetItems to addBytes at the measured meanTree after× today's limit

RM-007's lower figure, 4002326,056,36016.67 MB1.49
RM-007's upper figure, 60043211,277,36021.89 MB1.96

The mean is a floor, not a guess. 152 of the 168 models already declare KHR_draco_mesh_compression and 11 already declare KHR_texture_basisu; 139 are KHR_materials_unlit. This catalog has been through the pipeline twice already, in RM-004 B1 and B5, so 26,105 bytes is what an item costs after compression and a new pack will not come in under it by being encoded harder. The costliest six are 363, 363, 362, 314, 198 and 153 KB; the median is 9,633, so the distribution is a long tail of small Kenney meshes with a handful of textured pieces on the end, and curation has real leverage on the mean even though compression does not.

demo-total moves with it, because the deployed tree contains public/: 19.21 MB today against a 19.99 MB limit, going to 25.26 or 30.48 MB. Neither budget can absorb this and neither should be raised quietly. What J2's first task therefore is: decide the deploy's size, in the open, and let the item count fall out of it — the same substitution RM-011 W-4 made when it withdrew H1's “about ninety materials” as a number and made it the output of a trial.

X-3 · The index ships in the bundle, and the metadata does not fit re-orders J measured

useCatalog.js does import catalog from '../../catalog/catalog.json', so vite inlines the whole file into the application chunk. Compacted the way a bundler emits it, that is 25,218 bytes raw and 3,347 gzipped — 21 bytes a row, which is cheap and has never been worth a thought.

It becomes worth a thought twice over. A synthetic augmentation was built — the same 168 rows with a room, up to three tags, a {w, d, h}, a source, a licence and an author added to each — and gzipped by the same call:

IndexRowsRawGzippedPer row, gzipped
today16825,2183,34719.9
with J1's metadata16850,5195,77134.4
with J1's metadata400120,28313,74034.4
with J1's metadata600180,42520,61134.4

17,264 gzipped bytes of growth against 13,292 of headroom. first-load is M-43, added by RM-011 H1 and already the thinnest line in budget.json at 3.2 %; the index alone at J2's row count exceeds it before one model is fetched, and it does so on a payload every visitor downloads whether or not they ever open the drawer. This is precisely the failure M-43 exists to catch, and it is the second time in two programmes that the line has caught something in a draft — H2's ambient occlusion was the first.

The remedy is in J2's own sentence: “packs loaded lazily by manifest”. What the ordering gets wrong is which sprint does it. As drawn, J1 puts metadata on every bundled row and J2 splits the file afterwards, so the programme ships a first-load regression in week two and removes it in week four. The split comes first: a small index in the bundle carrying only what the drawer needs before a click, and per-pack detail fetched when a pack is opened. Then the metadata can be as generous as it likes, because it is no longer in the payload.

X-4 · The encoders are not missing cheaper measured

RM-004 B1 recorded that no codec had been run, and RM-011 W-6 measured which ktx toktx basisu and found nothing. Both were right and both are still right — ktx, toktx, basisu, draco_encoder, gltfpack and gltf-pipeline are all absent from this machine as command-line tools. It would be easy to carry that forward as “J2 cannot encode”, and it is not true.

Both pipelines are npm packages and both are wired up. tools/encode-assets.mjs runs Draco through @gltf-transform/* and draco3dgltf; tools/encode-textures.mjs runs KTX2 through ktx2-encoder. Run here: “asset encoding is up to date (152 encoded, 13 deliberately unencoded)” and “11 textures transcoded to KTX2, all matching the report”. The GLB census agrees from the other side — 152 containers declare Draco and 11 declare Basis. J2's “through Draco, KTX2, oracle and budget” is therefore a pipeline that exists, is deterministic, has a committed report and has a --check gate, which is a different sprint from the one H1 had to write.

One asymmetry with H1 is worth naming, because it points the other way. H1 refused KTX2 for its material library on the grounds that a .ktx2 drags a 515 KB Basis transcoder into a boot that would not otherwise want one. For furniture that argument does not apply: decoder-total is 838,923 bytes already in the tree, and any design with furniture in it already fetches the Draco decoder. Additional compressed models and textures cost no new machinery at all.

X-5 · The placement check is a constant, and the predicates are not why re-prices J4 measured

The four preserved predicates were called rather than read, and they behave exactly as core/utils.js's ledger says: pointInPolygon false for a point at the centre of a square, polygonPolygonIntersect false for a square against itself, polygonInsidePolygon false, polygonOutsidePolygon true, and pointInPolygon2 correct in both directions. Eight programmes have now left them alone.

What has not been measured before is who calls them, and the answer changes what J4 is:

PredicateReturnsCallers in src/Effect of repairing it
pointInPolygonalways false1 — floor_item.js:64sets a local flag that leads to return true either way
polygonPolygonIntersectalways false1 live, 1 commentedsame expression, same outcome
polygonOutsidePolygonalways true0 live, 1 commentednone — the caller is inside /* */
polygonInsidePolygonalways false0none — nothing calls it
pointInPolygon2correct1 — room.js:554n/a — this is the one room detection uses

FloorItem.isValidPosition returns true on every path it has. It walks the rooms, sets isInARoom, takes an early return true when the flag is false with a comment saying placement is up to the user, and then — past a block-commented item-to-item test — returns true again. The only return false in the function is inside that comment. So the constant is not a consequence of the broken predicates; it would still be a constant if all four were repaired this afternoon.

Two things follow. Item.showError(), the red halo the fork built for a refused placement, has exactly one caller and that caller is unreachable — dead code since the fork, found by asking who calls what rather than by reading a file. And RM-007's framing of J4 inverts the risk: the re-baseline it fears is nearly free, because nothing observable depends on the four constants, while the collision it treats as the payoff has to be written, from a commented sketch, against geometry that has never run. The characterization tests still change in the same commit as the flag — that discipline is not what this finding relaxes; what it relaxes is the estimate of how much behaviour moves when they do.

X-6 · One selection, and three verbs that already have a home med measured

useSelection holds a single selected ref and select(type, object) replaces it; there is no multi-selection anywhere in the application, and eight selection types share that one slot. Multi-select is therefore not a control on top of an existing set — it is the set, and every consumer of selection.value is written against exactly one object or null. That is the largest single piece of J4 and it should be priced as a state change rather than as a gesture.

Three of the seven verbs are cheaper than they look, and the drawing should say so. Elevation is already in the file: an item saves xpos, ypos and zpos, so “elevation for free items” is a control over a field that round-trips today, not a schema addition. Copy and paste has a working relative: useItemActions.duplicateSelected re-adds from getMetaData() at a 30 cm offset, which is the same mechanism a paste needs with a clipboard in front of it. And mirror is representable, because scale_x, scale_y and scale_z are all saved — at the cost the drawing should name rather than discover: a negative scale reverses triangle winding, so a mirrored item needs its material's side handled or it renders inside out.

What has no home at all: group, align, distribute, item-to-item snap, wall snap and stacking. And rotation is stored as a single Y angle in radians, so nothing here can tilt an item — correct for furniture, and worth writing down before somebody designs a mirror about an arbitrary axis for it.

X-7 · J3 needs a store, not a loader cheaper measured

model/scene.js constructs GLTFLoader, OBJLoader, DRACOLoader and KTX2Loader in its constructor, wired to the loading manager RM-003 A1 gave it. So all three formats RM-007 names for J3 — GLB, glTF and OBJ — already have a reader in the bundle, and the sprint writes none of them.

What it does not have is anywhere to put the bytes. An item's model is model_url, a relative URL resolved through AssetResolver; a file picked off a disk has no URL, so J3 needs a store, a scheme for referring to it from a save file, and a rule for what happens when a design is opened where the store is not. The mechanism exists — src/app/persistence/draft_repository.js already speaks IndexedDB for autosave — and the one <input type="file"> in the application is TopBar's design opener, which is the pattern to copy. This overlaps K2's .zip bundle deliberately: a design that carries its own assets is the same problem seen from the export side, and the two should share one answer rather than inventing two.

X-8 · The thumbnails are already uniform, and M-30 has already shipped low measured

Two small readings, grouped because each removes work from the plan rather than adding it.

All 168 thumbnails are exactly 300 × 225. The headers were decoded rather than the filenames trusted; the set is 147 PNG and 21 JPEG, 1,012,146 bytes in total at a mean of 6,025. The drawer renders them two to a row inside a 380 px panel, so they display at roughly 175 px — a shade under 2×, which is right for a high-density display and not waste. RM-007 asks for “thumbnails rendered by a tool rather than collected”, and the reason to do that is now consistency of framing and lighting across a much larger catalog, not consistency of size, which is already there. The mixed formats are worth normalising while a tool is being written.

M-30 was delivered by another programme. It reads “a new first-load limit in budget.json, set at today's payload plus the shell's growth, that no pack may enter”, and that is exactly what RM-011 H1 added as M-43 and what X-3 above has just used to catch a regression before it was written. It is withdrawn here as a duplicate rather than restated, and J2's gate points at M-43.

§ 55 · SPRINTS J1–J4

Seven and a half weeks, re-ordered around what ships in the payload

RM-007 priced this programme at 7.5 weeks in four sprints and the total does not move. What moves is the order inside J1, what J2's item count is allowed to be, and which half of J4 is the expensive one.

J1

An index, and then something to say about each thing in it

proposedX-3X-1X-82 wk

Objective. Know what each item is, where it belongs and who made it — without any of that arriving before somebody asks for it.

  • The index splits first (X-3). A small bundled index carrying only what the drawer shows before a click, and per-pack detail fetched on open. This is J2's “packs loaded lazily by manifest” pulled forward, because doing it afterwards means shipping a first-load regression and then removing it.
  • Then the metadata (X-1): room category, tags, real dimensions, source, licence and author on every row. 0 of 168 carry any of it today, so M-29's baseline is zero and every row is a write.
  • Browse by room, and remember. The drawer already has a search box and a filter by placement type; what it has no notion of is a room. Favourites and recent are session state, beside the eye height H3 added, rather than design state.
  • The twelve wall segments come out of furniture — exactly twelve rows, 63,348 bytes, eight typed Item and four in-wall. A catalog edit, not a feature, and the two rows both named Chair get distinguished while the file is open.
  • A thumbnail tool, for framing and lighting rather than for size: all 168 are already 300 × 225 (X-8). Normalise the 21 JPEGs against the 147 PNGs while it is being written.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-29: category, dimensions, source and licence present on 100 % of rows, checked in the asset-integrity suite, from a measured baseline of 0 %
  • M-44 (new): the bundled index is a budget line of its own, so a row count or a key can never enter the first-load payload unnoticed again
  • The first-load payload does not grow by one byte for metadata nobody has opened a pack to see — M-43, the line X-3 used to find this
LANDING — J1, the index split
  • The split is a generator, so the two files cannot drift from the one they came from. catalog.json is still the only place a row is authored; tools/split-catalog.mjs divides it into catalog-index.json, which vite inlines, and catalog-detail.json, which is a dynamic import. npm run catalog:check regenerates and compares, and a test runs it — the mechanism tsconfig.json's ledger drifted five times for want of.
  • The line was decided by gzipping each candidate key rather than by taste. Added to all 168 rows and measured at level 9: format +40 B (168 identical strings), room +369, tags +116, size +907.Two of those four are wrong, and correcting them is the second slice's own measurement. Priced against the vocabularies that actually shipped — eight rooms, fourteen tags — room costs +131 and tags +178, and the ordering is the other way round. Rooms arrive in runs, twenty-seven consecutive kitchen rows among them, which is the case gzip is best at; a tag list is an array and pays four bytes of brackets and quotes per row before a word is spelled. Both were priced against a vocabulary guessed at, and neither guess survived the data. So the index keeps everything the grid filters on and everything the placement path reads — which keeps addItem synchronous, worth far more than the 40 bytes format costs — and the detail keeps what a person reads about one item. The keys that filter turn out to be the cheap ones because their vocabularies repeat; the expensive ones are exactly those nobody reads until they click.
  • The two budget lines disagreed, which is the evidence the split worked. demo-js-gzip rose 405,606 → 408,761 because the detail chunk is now in the build, and first-load rose 408,108 → 408,473, 365 bytes, because it is a chunk nobody fetches until the drawer opens. One line asks what the bundle weighs and the other what a person waits for; H2's ambient occlusion produced the same pair of readings.
  • M-44 is the twelfth budget line, at 3,580 with 3,408 measured — the index compacted and gzipped, which is what a bundler emits. Set at the usual ~5 % deliberately: a ceiling with J2's whole row growth pre-authorised inside it would notice nothing, and this line exists to make a key crossing back into the payload a decision somebody records.
  • The dimensions are measured, not authored — the one J1 field nobody should type. Each model's bounding box is computed by walking its glTF scene graph and transforming all eight corners of every primitive's own accessor bounds, which survives Draco because the extension replaces the buffer view and leaves the accessor's metadata alone. 168 of 168 measured, including the three plain .gltf files a binary-only reader missed.
  • And the catalog turns out to be authored in two units, with a 28-fold gap between them. The largest extent of the small population is 1.82 and the smallest of the large is 51.42: 141 models in metres, 27 already in centimetres. Both check out against real furniture — at ×100 a basin is 34 cm wide and a stack of books is 15; at ×1 a double bed is 140 × 200 and a door is 97 × 222. This is what Item.initObject has been guessing at since the fork, with if (halfSize.x < 1.0) resize(×300) under a comment calling itself an ugly hack, and RM-009 U-3 measured the 300 wrong and assigned the fix here. At ×300 that stack of books is 45 cm wide.The two populations are real and the gap is real; the factor for the small one is wrong, and the second slice found it. The Kenney kit is not in metres — it is on a 2 m grid, so the factor is ×200, and 141 of 168 rows shipped at half their size. The corroboration above is exactly why it got through: a basin at 34 cm and a stack of books at 15 are both plausible, and so are the same two at 68 and 30. A basin cannot tell the two readings apart. Architecture can — at ×100 the kit's floor tile is a metre square under a 1.29 m ceiling — and six standard heights then agree on ×200 to within 5 %. The fix is not a better threshold: the scale is now declared by the kit in sources.json, which is only possible because the same sprint put source on every row.
  • The band between the two populations is left ambiguous on purpose. A model whose largest extent lands between 2 and 40 units is reported and the run fails rather than being silently assigned a unit. The rule is fitted to this catalog and J2 is going to add packs it was not fitted to.
  • The drawer shows the size, in the unit the person is working in, and shows nothing until the chunk lands — which is the split working rather than a defect. 21 new tests; coverage up or level on all four lines.
LANDING — J1, the metadata itself
  • M-29 met, from a measured baseline of zero. All 168 rows carry a room from a closed list of eight, at least one tag from a closed list of fourteen, a source that resolves, and a measured size. The vocabularies are closed for a reason X-3 priced rather than for tidiness: eight words repeated is what makes the key affordable in the bundled index at all. Seven assertions in the asset-integrity suite hold it there, and split-catalog.mjs refuses to write either generated file for a catalog that fails the same check — a gate on the generator and a gate on the tree, because a generator can be bypassed by editing what it produced.
  • The licence lives once per kit, not once per row, in a new src/catalog/sources.json, and each entry carries the evidence for its own identification rather than an assertion. The blueprint3d demo models: the upstream repository holds exactly 25 model files and all 25 of this catalog's js-glb rows match one by basename. The Kenney kit: its page states 140 files and CC0, and 139 of this catalog's 142 gltf rows draw only from one shared 14-name material palette — excluding the two that share none leaves exactly 140. The duck: the Khronos sample set's own README, which is Sony's 2006 copyright under the SCEA Shared Source License.
  • Two rows ship on a licence nobody could establish, and the test names them. SimpleCabinet.glb and chandelier.gltf fail every check the kit passes — foreign material names, a mesh called Untitled.068, the only PascalCase filename in the directory, the only row in the catalog with no thumbnail of its own. They are recorded as unknown rather than assumed CC0 by resemblance, because not doing that is the entire point of writing provenance down. Whether they ship at all is a decision for J2, which is the sprint about what this deploy may carry.
  • The dimensions this sprint shipped eight days ago were wrong for 141 of 168 rows, and this is the correction. The extent rule read the Kenney kit as metres; the kit is on a 2 m grid. What let it through is instructive: the sanity check was run against a basin and a stack of books, and both are plausible at either reading. Architecture is not. floorFull is exactly 1.000 × 1.000 units and wall is 1.000 × 1.290, so ×100 is a room tile one metre square under a 1.29 m ceiling. Six standard heights then agree to within 5 %: kitchen base unit ×200.0, bar stool ×200.0, door frame ×201.1, round table ×204.5, fridge ×195.7, desk ×195.1.
  • And the cross-check that settles it costs nothing. At ×200 the Kenney door frame is 97.2 cm wide; the blueprint3d door — a different kit, authored in centimetres, measured independently, and named closed-door28x80 after its leaf in inches — is 97.1. Two catalogs drawn by different people in different units agreeing on the width of a door to one millimetre is not something a heuristic produces.
  • So the scale is declared rather than detected — unitScale on the kit, overridable on a row — and that is only possible because the same sprint put source on every row. X-1's provenance is what fixes X-3's measurement; the two halves of J1 turn out to be one thing. Four rows override their kit and each is a model that is not really of it: two Blender exports in centimetres, a cabinet of unknown origin that is on the kit's grid, and the duck, declared at ×10 with the note that a test asset has no real-world size to be authored at. The extent rule survives only as a band — between 5 cm and 6 m or the run fails — which is the check the first slice needed and did not have, because it verified the guess against the thing being guessed at.
  • The building came out of the furniture, as a catalog edit and not a feature. RM-012's twelve segments — eight typed Item, four in-wall — plus the panel, the six openings and the four flights that are the same argument: 23 rows whose room is structure, which is the eighth room and is not a room. And the two rows both called Chair are distinguished, along with two more the count had missed that differed only in the case of one letter — Dining Table and Dining table. All three new names were read off the models' own thumbnail filenames rather than invented.
  • M-44 raised 3,580 → 3,940, measured 3,408 → 3,759, which is the raise the line was set tight in order to force somebody to write. room and tags are in the index because both are read before anybody clicks — one is the filter, the other is what the search box matches besides the name. Everything read about one item went to the detail, so the whole metadata pass cost the payload 544 bytes; first-load ended at 410,277, the other 1,260 being the controls below.
  • The drawer browses by room, and remembers. Eight room chips, plus Starred and Recent, which are a third axis rather than a ninth room — the point of a favourite is not having to remember which room it was filed under. Both are stored where the eye height H3 added is stored: in this browser, for this person, across designs, and never in a design file, because they describe whoever is furnishing rather than the building. Keyed by model URL, which is the one field that is already a row's identity everywhere else — not by name, which this sprint has just spent a commit making unique, and not by index, which moves the moment a row is inserted.
  • The search box matches tags as well as names, so seating finds twenty-five chairs that do not contain the word. Whole-word against the closed list rather than substring, which for this catalog is the difference between four results for bed and eleven.
  • Placement type moved from twelve chips to a <select>, and nothing was removed. It is the filter an embedder reaches for; the eight that answer "what goes in a bedroom" are the ones that deserved the row.
