The three generated sections gained a room too, so somebody browsing for a door finds the parametric ones beside the mesh ones instead of only the three with a model file.
  • axe caught the star. Drawn first as a control inside the tile — which is itself a button — it read fine and violated nested-interactive on all 193 tiles: a button inside a button is one element to a screen reader and the inner one cannot be reached. It is a sibling positioned over the tile now, and the accessibility suite is back to zero violations with the catalog open. Second time the browser tier has caught something the headless one structurally cannot; the first was H1's black walls.
LANDING — J1, the ×300 hack
  • Two guesses were stacked in four lines, and both are gone. Item.initObject read if (halfSize.x < 1.0) resize(×300) under a comment calling itself an ugly hack. Which models needed scaling was decided by one axis of one item — so a wide flat rug authored in centimetres has no axis under 1.0 and a tall thin lamp on the kit grid has two, which means the test answered a question about units by measuring a shape. And how much was 300, which RM-009 U-3 measured wrong and this sprint has now measured properly. At ×300 the Kenney dining chair is 141 cm tall; at the declared ×200 it is 94.
  • The number is declared, and it arrives before the model does. split-catalog.mjs resolves each row's unitScale from the kit it came from and writes it into the bundled index, not the detail — because it is read at the moment an item is placed and addItem is synchronous by construction (X-3). 60 gzipped bytes across all 168 rows, there being three distinct values in it, which is the cheapest key in the file after format.
  • A design somebody already saved does not move. scale_x, scale_y and scale_z are absolute and include this conversion, so a chair placed under the hack is recorded at 300 and stays at 300. Applying the kit factor again on load would multiply an item by 200 every time a file was opened, which is the one way this change could have damaged something a person owns; the constructor records whether the scale came from a document and applyUnitScale returns when it did. Two copies of the same chair in one design, one placed before this and one after, are genuinely different sizes — and both are exactly what their record says. Written up in docs/save-format.md rather than left for somebody to discover.
  • A method lost its cover and got some. Item.resize was only ever exercised because the hack called it, and the inspector's own tests stub it out — so removing the hack would have quietly left the width, height and depth fields untested. Three tests were written for it directly, including the tenth-of-a-centimetre tolerance that stops a field round-tripping 49.99999 from reading as a resize. Coverage up on all four lines: 86.43 / 77.48 / 84.22 / 86.41.
LANDING — J1, the thumbnail tool · sprint complete
  • All 168 thumbnails are rendered from the models the rows actually place. tools/render-thumbnails.mjs drives headless chromium over SwiftShader at 600 × 450 and box-filters down to the same 300 × 225 X-8 measured, one model at a time. Not about size, then: about framing, which is the thing a collected thumbnail cannot be consistent in and a catalog several times larger cannot be kept consistent in by hand. One camera, one margin, one background, for every row.
  • Two numbers inside the render were measured rather than chosen, and they pull against each other. The first draft framed each model by its bounding sphere, which is one line and wastes the frame in exactly the cases a furniture catalog is full of — a sphere round a 200 × 30 × 90 bed takes the half-diagonal for a radius, so the bed is drawn at the size of a cube that would hold it. Fitting the projected box instead took mean frame coverage 15.8 % → 20.9 % and cost 243 KB. Supersampling twice rather than three times gave 179 KB of that back: every extra sample level invents more part-covered edge pixels and each is a colour PNG has not seen before, and at the 150 px a tile is drawn the third sample buys nothing anybody can point at.
  • The honest limit was measured before the tool was written, and it is half of what RM-007 asked for. 139 of the 168 models declare KHR_materials_unlit, so no light reaches them: lighting consistency is not available here and saying otherwise would be a claim the file contradicts. The 29 that are lit get a soft frontal rig; the rest ignore it, which is also what they do in the scene.
  • Every thumbnail is PNG now, and that is not tidiness. 19 were .jpg and 2 were .JPG — the uppercase pair a 404 waiting for a case-sensitive host — and a JPEG cannot carry the alpha the other 147 have. The drawer paints tiles on a surface that changes with the theme, so a baked-in background is a light-theme background sitting in a dark-theme panel.
  • Four budget lines moved and none was raised. public-total 10,609,326 → 10,926,439 and demo-total 19,313,259 → 19,629,535 — +317,967 net, 1,330,113 bytes of renders against 1,012,146 deleted. Headroom on those two falls to 2.3 % and 1.8 %, which is the number J2 needs in front of it: X-2 already says that sprint's first task is the deploy-size decision, and a third of the remaining room is now spent before it starts. Deliberately not raised here — the ceiling is J2's to move with the arithmetic beside it, and moving it now would spend a decision nobody has taken.
  • And catalog-index went down, 3,819 → 3,553. A thumbnail is named after the model it was rendered from, so image and model are nearly the same string on every row and gzip charges almost nothing for the second. The rename paid back 266 bytes — most of what room and tags cost together, recovered by a change made for a different reason entirely. first-load fell with it, 410,394 → 409,933: a boot got smaller in the commit that put a quarter of a megabyte into the tree, which is the split working for the third time this sprint.
  • The report is the gate, because re-rendering is minutes. asset-pipeline/thumbnails.json records every row's bytes, hash, and the coverage and clipped readings that check framing by arithmetic rather than by somebody looking at 168 pictures. None empty, none clipped, mean coverage 20.9 %. And it records what each render replaced: P6's compression report names five of the deleted files as things it produced, so the chain is written down and the older report left true, which is the arrangement B5 already established and this is the third pass to join.
  • And the render caught the catalog lying about two of its own rows. Sectional – Olive renders white, and so does Media Console – Black. Neither is a rendering fault: 4 of the 25 demo models carry no texture and no base colour factor at all — those two, plus Open Door and Wardrobe – White, which are white anyway and so went unnoticed — and an untextured glTF material is three's default white. The collected thumbnails were product photographs of the real furniture, so for eight years they showed an olive sofa and a black console that the files have never contained. A person placing either got a white one and had no way to know why. This is the tool paying for itself on its first run, and the fix is an acquisition question, so it is recorded for J2 rather than taken here.
  • V8 stopped the first draft. It accumulated all 168 buffers and pulled them across in one page.evaluate: 2.43 MB each at the 3× it was then rendering is 408 MB raw and about 544 MB base64'd, and the serialiser threw ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG. One at a time is 1.1 MB a call at today's 2×, and it lets a model be disposed the moment its picture is taken rather than after 167 more.
  • Two browser characterizations were re-stated rather than loosened, both because the ×300 hack was in their numbers. U-3's stair: at the measured ×200 the Kenney flight is 267.9 cm, still too tall to stand under a 250 cm wall and now too short to reach the 280 cm a storey rises — it fits neither end, which is a sharper form of the finding than the hack produced. U-2's opening: the same kit's wall module is 257.9 cm rather than 386.9, so the clamp is still the thing under test and the opening still oversized, by 8 cm rather than by 137. Both docblocks keep the figures as they were measured and record why they moved, which is the rule this document set applies to itself.
  • Sprint J1 is complete. Five bullets in the drawing and a sixth RM-009 U-3 assigned to it, all landed across three commits. 2,186 headless and 169 browser tests; twelve budgets within limits with none raised for the last slice.
J2

How big is this allowed to be

proposedX-2X-41.5 wk

Objective. As much furniture as the deploy can carry, with the size of the deploy decided on purpose.

  • The count is withdrawn as a number. RM-007 says 400–600; today's headroom buys 21.9 more items and reaching those figures is a 1.5× to 2.0× raise of public-total and demo-total (X-2). The first task is the decision about deploy size, taken in the open with the arithmetic beside it; the item count is its output. Same substitution RM-011 made to H1's “about ninety materials”.
  • The pipeline is not built, it is run (X-4). Draco and KTX2 both encode from node_modules, both have committed reports and both have --check gates. And unlike H1, compression costs no new client machinery: the 839 KB of decoders is already in the tree and already fetched by any design with furniture.
  • Curation is the lever, not compression. The median item is 9,633 bytes and the mean is 26,105, so the tail is where the budget goes; a pack is admitted on its measured mean rather than on its name.
  • Packs are fetched, not bundled — the mechanism J1 built, now carrying content.
ACCEPTANCE
  • Every raise of public-total or demo-total states the decision it implements and the item count it buys, in tools/budget.json, before the acquisition runs
  • M-45 (new): every added item's full cost — model, thumbnail and textures, deduped — is recorded, and the catalog's measured mean is reported before and after each pack
  • M-43, unchanged: a pack nobody has opened costs a boot nothing, measured as the resource timings of a boot
LANDING — J2, task one: the deploy's size
  • The decision is taken and it is 1.5× — public-total 11,180,000 → 16,770,000 and demo-total 19,990,000 → 29,985,000, recorded in tools/budget.json before any acquisition runs, which is what this sprint's own gate asks for. The item count is the output rather than the input, the same substitution RM-011 W-4 made to H1's “about ninety materials”.
  • Nothing external binds, and that is the finding. Cloudflare Pages on the free plan allows 20,000 files a site and 25 MiB a file; the deployed tree is 626 files and its largest asset is 307 KB, and at 600 items it would be about 1,490. The build takes 1.44 s against a 20-minute timeout. And a visitor downloads the same 400.3 KB either way, because J1 made a pack a fetch — first-load is unmoved by anything in public/ that nobody opens. The one permanent cost is git, measured at 1.13× the bytes added (H1's material library put 4,504,845 raw bytes into a 5,072,108-byte pack delta), so 53 → 60 MiB at this ceiling. The line that protects a visitor is first-load and it is untouched; this one protects the decision.
  • The ceiling was chosen to make curation compulsory. 5,843,561 bytes of headroom buys 209 items at the measured mean of 27,997 and 521 at the median of 11,218. RM-007 wants 400–600, so 1.5× reaches the top of that range only if packs come in near the median — a heavy pack has to be trimmed or refused. Understated, and corrected by the admission gate that re-ran this arithmetic rather than quoting it: 232 items are needed for the LOWER figure and the headroom buys 206, so neither end of RM-007's range is reachable without curation, not merely the top. That strengthens the case for 1.5× rather than weakening it — a ceiling that reached 400 by standing still would not impose the constraint this one was chosen to impose. Stated as prices: a new item may average 24,863 B to reach 400 and 13,352 B to reach 600, against a catalog that costs 27,997. That is X-2's point turned into a constraint rather than an aspiration: 152 of 168 models are already Draco and 11 already KTX2, so nothing arrives under the mean by being encoded harder. 2.0× would have bought 432 at the mean and noticed nothing, which is the argument against it.
  • M-45 is an instrument, not a line. tools/catalog-cost.mjs records every row's full cost — model, thumbnail and every distinct image the container names — and prints the movement against the previous run: “168 → 216 items, mean 27,997 → 24,110, tree +1,204,880 B”. It exists because the division above is only honest while its divisor is, and the divisor has already moved once with nobody deciding to: X-2 took this arithmetic against 26,105 and J1's rendered thumbnails made it 27,997. A test re-runs the division and fails if a later sprint makes items dear enough that the ceiling stops buying what it was raised to buy.
  • Two costs, because they answer two questions. Within an item a texture used twice is one download; across the catalog a texture used by two rows is one file on a disk. Today they differ by 7.7 % — 147 of the 168 models carry no external image at all and exactly two textures are reused — and only the second belongs in a division against public-total. Worth watching rather than fixing: a pack of variants on one texture set would open that gap wide, and the naive figure would then overstate what admitting it costs.
LANDING — J2, packs are fetched, not bundled
  • No catalog row is in the bundle any more. tools/split-catalog.mjs divides the catalog a second time — J1 split it by tier, this splits both tiers by pack — and writes eight files to public/catalog/. What the application imports is catalog-manifest.json: one line per kit, naming it, its licence, its row count and its two URLs. 575 gzipped bytes for four packs. The rows are fetched the first time somebody opens the drawer, index first and detail after, which is the same staging J1 had between the bundle and a chunk, moved to two fetches.
  • The tier split alone would have run out, and the arithmetic says when. X-3 measured J1's metadata on 600 rows at 17,264 gzipped bytes of growth against 13,292 of first-load headroom, and noted that split by tier the index half is 9,857 — which fits. That is the trap rather than the answer: it fits until the sprint that adds rows, and the sprint that adds rows is this one. The old line grew by ~34 gzipped bytes per row; the manifest grows by ~90 per kit and by nothing at all per item. Acquiring two hundred chairs now moves the payload by one line, which is what turns “packs loaded lazily by manifest” from a promise about future restraint into a property of the arrangement.
  • A pack is a source, because a licence is a property of a kit. The unit somebody admits or refuses, the unit a licence is recorded against and the unit the fetch is grouped by are the same unit — which is J1's provenance work paying for a second thing. Four packs: kenney-furniture-kit 140, blueprint3d 25, unattributed 2, khronos 1. Each carries its own provenance rather than pointing at a shared table, so acquiring one is a file dropped in and a manifest line, not an edit to a file the pack does not own. And it makes J1's recorded finding actionable: the two rows nobody could establish a licence for are now one pack and one manifest line, which is what deciding whether to ship them will amount to.
  • M-43's gate is a measurement now, not a claim. tests/browser/first-load.test.js already asserted that a boot fetches no material; it asserts on the same instrument that a boot fetches none of the four packs, by name and by path, and — the case that stops the other two being a tautology — that the drawer's first open fetches all four. A pack URL that 404s would also never appear in a boot's timings, and nothing but this tells the two apart.
  • One budget line is re-pointed and one is added, and neither is a lowering. catalog-index becomes catalog-bundled, 3,940 → 2,600 with 3,553 → 2,451 measured — the same distinction RM-011 H1 drew when it re-pointed texture-vram: the number under the line is a different number, because the file it named no longer exists. Like for like the catalog in the payload went 5,429 → 2,451 gzipped, the index plus the three generated sections against a manifest plus the same three. The ceiling comes down with it deliberately, since one with the old line's per-row growth pre-authorised inside it would notice nothing. And catalog-packs is the thirteenth line, 9,935 measured against 10,450: J2 moved a cost rather than removing one, and what a person waits for the first time they go looking for a chair was a number nothing here was asking for. 59 gzipped bytes a row across both tiers, so RM-007's 600 rows is about 35 KB of drawer-open — worth a wait, worth knowing about, not worth discovering.
  • first-load fell rather than held. 409,941 → 406,565 gzipped, because the rows left the bundle and only a 575-byte manifest replaced them. Task one's arithmetic said a visitor downloads the same payload whether the ceiling is 1.0× or 1.5×; this says the payload is now independent of the row count as well, which is the stronger claim and the one J2's remaining bullets need. public-total moved the other way by the packs' 74 KB on disk, which is what a ceiling raised for exactly this is for.
  • And the packs resolve like every other asset. They are fetched through AssetResolver, so ?assetBase= moves the catalog to a CDN along with the models it describes. A pack acquired later is a file in that tree, and there was no reason for it to be the one thing pinned to the document's origin.
LANDING — J2, curation is the lever
  • A pack is admitted by a command, not by a judgement. tools/admit-pack.mjs measures a candidate the way catalog-cost.mjs measures the catalog — same filesFor, so a pack's mean and the catalog's mean are the same kind of number — and answers one question: after admitting these N items, would more packs at this price still reach RM-007's 400? Not “is this pack expensive”, which is a question about a pack in isolation and has no answer. A large pack of cheap items passes; a small pack of dear ones fails, because it spends headroom the remaining items need at a price that will not get there.
  • It corrected task one's own sentence on its first run. That landing said 1.5× reaches the top of RM-007's range only with curation. Re-run rather than quoted: 232 items are needed for the bottom of it and the headroom buys 206. Neither end is reachable standing still. The correction is above, in place; what it changes is not the decision but how much of it was load-bearing — and it is the second time in this sprint that re-running an arithmetic instead of citing it moved a number, which is what M-45 was added for.
  • The gate is set at a price a kit in this tree is actually had at. Reachable at what price is the whole question, and today's catalog mean is the wrong benchmark because task one deliberately chose a ceiling it does not reach. So the gate uses the cheapest shipped pack of ten rows or more: the Kenney kit, 12,285 B an item, 140 CC0 rows already through Draco. Proof by existence rather than an estimate — the only kind of evidence about a price that cannot be optimistic. At that price the headroom buys 469, so 400 and 600 are both reachable and npm run admit:check fails the day they stop being.
  • And the first run found where the mean lives. blueprint3d is 25 rows, 14.9 % of the catalog and 55.7 % of its bytes, at a mean of 104,850 against the Kenney kit's 12,285 — eight and a half times. X-2 said the tail is where the budget goes; this says the tail has an address, and it is the 2014 demo's own models rather than anything acquired since. It reframes what curation means here: the cheapest way to buy items is to re-price twenty-five rows that are already shipped, and that is a J2 decision with a name on it rather than a vague aspiration about future packs.
  • Three refusals that are not arithmetic. A row whose licence nobody established — RM-007's constraint is CC0 with the licence recorded per item, and J1 recorded two rows as unknown rather than assuming it by resemblance. An item over catalog-item-largest, because one 3 MB sofa is a cost paid by whoever clicks it and a pack mean cannot absorb it. And a source that resolves to nothing at all.
  • Two notes that are not refusals, because both have a better answer than no. A candidate whose models are not through Draco has not been priced yet — X-2 measured that this catalog's mean is a post-pipeline number, so the answer is npm run encode and measure again. And a candidate whose mean is more than twice its median is carrying a tail, where trimming the worst rows is cheaper than refusing the kit.
LANDING — J2, the material audit
  • J1 found four; asking all 168 found fifty-two. tools/material-audit.mjs reads every catalog model's materials and counts what can produce a colour: 52 of 417 materials render the glTF default white, across 31 rows. J1 looked at the 25 demo models and found 4, which is what looking at a sample gets you. Most of the 52 are correct — a Kenney sink basin whose _defaultMat is white is a white basin — and that is the finding rather than an excuse: a gate that called every colourless material a defect would have buried the two real ones under fifty that were not.
  • So the gate is about a claim, and a claim is something written down. Two rules. A row whose name states a colour that is not white must have a model that can produce one — Media Console – Black rendering white is a defect, Wardrobe – White rendering white is not. And a material whose own name states a colour must produce it, which is evidence inside the file rather than in the drawer. The second rule found a third row nobody was looking at: the chandelier's material is called black metal and renders white.
  • The history turns the fix from an invention into a substitution. These are not models somebody forgot to colour. Their legacy .js ancestors, read at a25c9fd~1, each name a diffuse map — mapDiffuse: cb-moore_baked.png and three like it — and none of those four files exists in any commit of this repository. S3's conversion then correctly produced a material with no texture because there was no texture to point at, and B1's Draco pass dropped the explicit [1,1,1,1] as a default. Both changes innocent, both semantically neutral. The models have named a texture nobody has since 2014, and the product photographs hid it until J1 rendered them.
  • And the colours are sampled from the photographs J1 retired, which are the only surviving record of what each row claimed. Read out of git at 9ea9f57~1, subject region only, studio background rejected: the console is rgb(26, 24, 23) over 16,647 px and the sectional is rgb(94, 89, 72) over 10,171 — R = G > B, which is olive rather than the grey a white render suggested. Converted to linear, because a glTF base colour is linear and writing 26 sRGB raw would give 0.102 rather than 0.0103 — a dark grey instead of a black. Verified by re-rendering: the new thumbnails measure rgb(33, 32, 31) and rgb(96, 91, 75), within three units of the photographs they were sampled from.
  • Not one byte of geometry moved, and the first attempt did move some. Reading each model through gltf-transform's NodeIO and writing it back re-encodes: cb-moore_baked.glb came out 22,064 → 13,032 and closed-door28x80_baked.glb went 15,728 → 28,396. Those are Draco re-encoded at settings that are not the ones RM-004 B1 measured, whose gate was a worst vertex of 0.38 µm against a 5 µm ceiling — and nothing in a colour fix is worth re-opening that. Reverted, and replaced by a container patch that rewrites the JSON chunk and copies the binary chunk verbatim: +28 to +44 bytes a file, and encode:check, oracle:check and the parity render stay true by construction rather than by re-measurement.
  • One characterization test failed, and re-checking it made it stronger. model-conversion.test.js pins that S3 passed each legacy colorDiffuse through untouched, and the repaint broke it for four models. The rule says a failure there is a signal to re-check the change: the legacy value in all four is [1,1,1] and in all four it was a multiplier on a diffuse map, so white was never the intended appearance. The conversion is as faithful as it was; the shipped file is deliberately no longer its output. So the four are pinned from the other side — they must equal the painted table, and their legacy value must have been a white multiplier on a named map — which is one more assertion than the test had, not one fewer.
LANDING — J2, the licence in the product
  • RM-007's first line for this programme, finally done. The objective opens with “enough furniture to furnish a home, found by room, with the licence on every item”, and J1 recorded that the second half had not been: the provenance went into sources.json, and the licence was nowhere in the shipped product. A licence recorded in a repository is one honoured by the repository's authors; the obligation is on the thing people use. It is light — CC0 asks nothing and MIT asks for the notice — which is exactly why it went eight years undone.
  • Per item on the tile, in full in a dialog, and the split is a decision about where the obligation falls. 193 tiles each carrying a licence line would say the same four things fifty times each and make the grid unreadable, so the per-item answer is on the tile's title — “Add Bathtub — Furniture Kit, CC0 1.0 Universal” — and the readable version is a Credits dialog beside the drawer, which is what somebody looking for terms would actually open.
  • Both are right on the first frame, because the manifest is bundled. Name, licence and row count per kit are in the payload J2's split left there, so credits are complete before any pack has been fetched. The author, the licence URL and the caveat come from each pack's detail file and fill in when it lands — the same staging the grid uses, and for the same reason.
  • A row knows its kit because of where it arrived from. The index tier carries no source, and none was added: useCatalog tags each row with the pack whose file it was fetched in. That costs zero bytes and cannot drift — a key saying which kit a row belongs to could disagree with the file it is sitting in, and a fact derived from the fetch cannot.
  • The kit whose licence nobody could establish is shown, not hidden. It is drawn with a warning rather than omitted or quietly called CC0. J1's entire argument for writing provenance down was that assuming a licence by resemblance is the thing to avoid, and a credits screen that showed three kits and dropped the fourth would undo that in the one place a person would look for it.
  • And axe covers the case that was actually risky. The drawer is deliberately not modal — the point of it is that the scene stays visible — and the credits dialog is. A modal opened from inside a non-modal panel's portal is exactly where a focus scope goes wrong, which is why the credits mount as a sibling of the drawer's root rather than inside its content, and why there is now a browser-tier pass with both open.
J3

Bring your own model

deliveredX-71.5 wk

Objective. A file from a disk becomes an item in the design, and stays one when the design is reopened or sent.

  • No loader is written (X-7). Scene already constructs glTF, OBJ, Draco and KTX2 loaders; all three of RM-007's formats already have a reader in the bundle.
  • A store, and a way to name what is in it. model_url is a relative URL and a picked file has none. The store is IndexedDB — persistence/draft_repository.js already speaks it — and the save file needs a reference form plus a defined behaviour when a design is opened where the store is not.
  • Scale and orient on import, because a downloaded model arrives in whatever unit and whatever axis its author used, and the model layer stores centimetres.
  • Shared with K2 on purpose. A design that carries its own assets is this problem seen from the export side; one answer, used twice, rather than a bundle format invented separately.
ACCEPTANCE
  • A design with an imported model round-trips: saved, reopened in the same browser, and the item is there at the same size and orientation
  • The same file opened where the store is empty says so, by name, and loses nothing else in the design
  • The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0 — the reference is an additive key, written only for items that have one
LANDING — J3, the store X-7 said was the whole of it
  • X-7 held, and it is worth saying which half it was right about. Scene constructs four loaders — glTF, OBJ, Draco and KTX2 — and this sprint wrote none. What it did write is everything X-7 said was left over: somewhere to put the bytes, a form for a document to refer to them by, a defined behaviour when a design is opened where they are not, and the scale-and-orient step the brief asked for. The loaders being free is the reason all four fitted in 1.5 weeks, not the reason the sprint was small.
  • The library change is one branch, and its position is the whole of it. addItem asks the byte store before the asset manifest. Without that ordering every deployment of this application would refuse every imported item on the line below — missing() is true for any name a loaded manifest does not declare, an imported model is by definition in nobody's manifest, and every deployment fetches a manifest. It asks after itemLoader, so an embedder's own pipeline keeps the precedence its documentation promises. And it parses rather than fetching: the bytes are handed over, and wrapping them in a blob URL so the network layer can hand them back is a detour with an object lifetime to manage.
  • One key, 74 bytes, and only on items that have one. An item record is 217 bytes without local and 291 with it, so a design of catalog furniture is byte-identical to the file it was before J3 — the seventh additive key to hold that rule. Each of its three fields earns its place: id is what the store is keyed on; up is the one thing the save format cannot already say, because a scale is absolute in scale_x/y/z and a yaw is rotation, and neither can state that a model is lying on its face. And file exists purely to be read out loud: with the store empty, the document is the only thing left that knows the model was ever called grandmother-chair.glb, which is exactly the case the second acceptance clause is about.
  • The axis is applied to the buffer, not to the object. One line shorter the other way and wrong in four places: objectHalfSize, both label planes and every resize handle measure the geometry, and getMetaData writes rotation.y alone — so an object-level tilt would be the wrong size immediately and gone on the next save.
  • Content-addressed, and it buys three things rather than tidiness. The key is the first 64 bits of the file's own SHA-256. The same chair imported twice is one record; a name can never come to mean different bytes; and — the one that matters most — a recipient can check that a bundle's carried file is the file the design named. A bundle repacked with different bytes under the same name is refused by name, the design still opens, and the plan is untouched. There is no fallback digest: a browser with no crypto.subtle is one with no secure context, which is also one where RM-013 K3's worker never registers, and a second id scheme in one store would be worse than a refusal.
  • K2's rule needed no amendment, which is what “one answer used twice” had to mean. design_bundle.js was never told that imports exist: carry what the recipient will not have, decided against their own manifest routes an imported model to carried on its own, because no manifest declares it. What changed is that readBundle hands the carried bytes back instead of only their names, and that openBundle stores them before it loads the design — the same ordering as the branch above, for the same reason: Scene asks the store while it is placing each item, so a bundle that loaded first would report every model it had just brought as missing.
  • 72 of the 215 models in this tree name a file that is not inside them — and one of them, ik_nordli_full.glb, is a .glb, which is the assumption that census broke. Imported from a disk there is no directory for textures/white_wood.ktx2 to be relative to, so such a model loads with its geometry and without its texture. That is the right failure and a silent one, so the import step reads the file's own reference list — images[].uri and buffers[].uri out of the glTF JSON, mtllib out of an OBJ — and says which files will not arrive. The same argument K2 made about a bundle's carried assets: dropping them silently is the one outcome worse than not reading them.
  • Measured with the loader that will load it. The dialog asks which unit the file was authored in by drawing what each answer would make the model, and the bounds behind that come from Scene.measureModel — the same GLTFLoader, with the same Draco and KTX2 attached, that the placement will use. RM-013 K1 is why: a bounds walk written beside three.js rather than through it disagreed with it on 4 of 15 rows. The browser tier holds the two to five decimal places.
  • 202 of 215 models here are Draco-compressed, so “the loaders were already in the bundle” is only true if a compressed import actually decodes — the decoder is 73 kB of WASM fetched at first use. The browser tier imports one and places it.
  • What it cost, measured on fresh builds at both commits rather than subtracted. first-load 421,549 → 427,341 gzipped bytes, +5,792, inside the limit K2 set with 3.3 % of headroom left. And a second cost worth naming because nothing would have reported it: the deploy grew by 113,922 bytes, which takes 15,216 bytes off the catalog's admission headroom — one item at the curated price, 419 to 418. J2's gate is what noticed, and it noticed because admit:check derives the price from the tree rather than from a number somebody wrote down.
  • Three faults in the suite's own IndexedDB fake, found because a model is the first thing this application stores that is not text. It cloned records with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)), which renders an ArrayBuffer as {}; it weighed them the same way, so a 30 MB model counted as two bytes and the quota refusal in a store where quota is actually likely was unreachable; and it did not roll a transaction back on abort, so a refused write left a record whose bytes had never been written and stats() counted a model that was not there. All three are now what a real IndexedDB does. This is the third time in this document set that a fake has been the thing that was wrong.
  • Sprint J3 is closed and programme J is complete. 2,571 headless and 206 browser tests — 104 and 10 of them new — fifteen gates green, fourteen budget lines within limits with none raised, and coverage at 87.28 statements, 87.29 lines, 78.71 branches, 85.63 functions, which moves the lines and statements floors 86 → 87. A third of this sprint is refusal paths and every one of them is reachable from a test only because the fake above was repaired first.
J4

Handling, and the re-baseline that turns out to be the cheap half

proposedX-5X-62.5 wk

Objective. Place a room's worth of furniture quickly — several things at once, aligned, snapped, stacked, and told when they overlap.

  • Multi-select is a state change, not a gesture (X-6). useSelection holds one object and eight selection types share that slot; every consumer reads exactly one or null. This is the largest single piece of the sprint and it goes first, because align, distribute, group and paste all read the set it creates.
  • Three verbs are cheaper than drawn. Elevation is already ypos in the file; paste has a working relative in duplicateSelected; mirror is a negative scale_x — with the winding reversal named up front, since a mirrored mesh renders inside out unless the material's side is handled.
  • Snapping and stacking: item-to-item, item-to-wall, and onto surfaces. New geometry, and the first thing in this programme that needs the predicates to be true.
  • The re-baseline, re-priced (X-5). Repairing the four constants is nearly free: polygonInsidePolygon has no caller, polygonOutsidePolygon's only caller is commented out, and the two live calls sit inside a function that returns true on every path. The expensive half is that there is no collision code — only a sketch inside /* */. It still lands as RM-007 requires: a new predicate behind a flag, the ledger updated and the characterization tests changed in the same commit, not as a fix.
  • And one piece of dead code goes with it. Item.showError() has one caller and that caller is unreachable. Either the halo becomes the collision warning or it is deleted; what it must not stay is unreachable with a comment claiming it fires.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-46 (new): FloorItem.isValidPosition has at least one path that returns false, asserted — the measurement X-5 made, inverted into a gate
  • The four predicates' characterization tests move in the same commit as the flag, and the room-detection tests do not move at all, because room detection uses pointInPolygon2 — verified in X-5, not assumed
  • Collision is a warning and never a refusal: floor_item.js's own comment says placement is up to the user, and eight programmes of saved designs were made under that rule
LANDING — J4, the selection becomes a set
  • The largest single piece, and it went first because everything else reads it. X-6 measured what multi-select costs here: useSelection held one object, select(type, object) replaced it, and eight selection types shared that one slot. So this is not a control layered over an existing set — it is the set, and every consumer of selection.value was written against exactly one object or null.
  • The migration that did not break the world: selection keeps meaning one thing. It is now the primary — the last thing clicked — and still resolves to ?{type, object}, so the inspector, the plan highlight and the item actions read exactly what they read before. selections is the new surface and is the whole ordered set. All 2,235 tests passed on the commit that changed the shape, before one new assertion was written, which is the evidence that the eight consumers did not have to move. An inspector genuinely edits one thing; a verb like align genuinely acts on many; neither has to pretend to be the other.
  • One kind at a time, as a rule rather than an accident. A set holding a wall and a chair has no meaning for any verb that would read it — align what to what? — so a different kind replaces rather than joining. The rule lives in the composable, because a call site that forgot it would build a set no verb could act on and no error anybody would see.
  • The modifier is read from the gesture, not from the event. EVENT_ITEM_SELECTED and EVENT_ITEM_2D_CLICKED carry no modifier and should not: they come from src/scripts, which has no idea there is a set to add to, and threading one through would put application policy inside the library — the direction the one-way arrow forbids. So a capture-phase pointerdown on the window records whether shift or the platform accelerator was held, and the next selection event consumes it. Capture phase because both canvases handle pointer events and one stopPropagation would otherwise turn shift-click silently back into click.
  • Both views draw the whole set; one member is the controller's. The plan gains selectedItemIds beside selectedItemId and draws every member identically — a set where one member looks different is a set a person has to be told the rules of. In 3D, Main.showItemsSelected gives the primary to Controller.setSelectedObject by the path E1 established and tells the rest to setSelected(), which is the bounding helper and the dimension canvases and nothing else — exactly what membership should mean for something nobody is dragging. Controller.selectedObject stays singular deliberately: it is what a drag moves and what clickPressed intersects against, and making it plural is a different sprint.
  • Delete was repaired in the same commit, because a set breaks every verb that predates it. deleteSelected read the primary, so the moment the selection could hold five chairs it would have removed one and left four highlighted. It now removes the set, over a copy of the list — iterating the live one deletes every other chair — and commits once, so undo returns what one gesture took rather than making somebody press it five times.
  • And mod+A selects every item, which is the operation that makes a set worth having on a plan somebody has already furnished. The alternative is shift-clicking twenty chairs.
  • One bug found by handing the library a better stub. Main.showItemSelected guarded on typeof item.setSelected === 'function' — a note already on that line says it was added because an embedder may dispatch a selection with anything it likes — but Controller.setSelectedObject then calls setUnselected() on whatever it is replacing. So an object with one half of the pair passes the guard, becomes the controller's selection, and throws from inside the library on the next click, with nothing on screen connecting the two. The old fakes carried neither method and never reached it; these carry both, which is what exposed the half-check. Guard completed, and found the way the original was: by running it.
LANDING — J4, copy, paste and the duplicate that never worked
  • Duplicate had never once worked, and this is why nobody noticed. RM-012 recorded it while checking X-6's survey: useItemActions read meta.itemType and meta.modelUrl off Item.getMetaData(), which returns item_type and model_url. Both reads were undefined, so Scene.addItem defaulted the type to 1 and asked the loader for undefined. The test passed for two programmes because the fake returned the camelCase shape the caller wished for rather than the shape the real method returns — the second time in this document set a stub has agreed with the code instead of with the data.
  • The repair is not a rename. A rename fixes it until the next caller. metadataFromRecord in model/model.js is now the one translation between the save record and the constructor metadata, and both the design loader and this file are its callers — so there is nothing left to disagree. The four lines it replaces had been inline in the loader since the format existed, which is exactly how the second caller came to write its own wrong version.
  • And the durable half is a test that pins the stub to the real method. Fixing the fake fixes this suite once; asserting its key set against Item.getMetaData on the real prototype is what stops the next stub agreeing with the code instead of the data. It also asserts the negative — that itemType and modelUrl are not among the real keys — which is the fact the old fake obscured.
  • A copy does not inherit an identity, and that is not cosmetic. useSelection resolves a selection by searching the scene for a designId, so two items carrying one would be a single thing to the inspector, to the plan highlight and to delete. metadataFromRecord therefore takes designId from its options rather than from the record: a loader states it, a copy does not, and inheriting it by accident is impossible.
  • Copy and paste are the same machinery, which makes duplicate a shortcut rather than a third implementation. A copy is the set's save records in a module-level ref; a paste re-adds them with a fresh identity. Each successive paste lands one offset further out, so pasting four times gives four visible copies rather than four in one place — and a copy resets that, because it is a new origin. Duplicate deliberately leaves the clipboard alone: somebody who copied a sofa, duplicated a chair and then pasted means the sofa.
  • The clipboard is this application's, not the system's. Putting a design fragment on the OS clipboard is a serialisation format and a security surface, and RM-007 puts sharing in K2 where a .zip bundle and a URL are already the subject. What a person means by copy and paste inside one plan is this. mod+C, mod+V, both over the set.
LANDING — J4, mirror, and the risk that was already handled
  • The named risk does not exist, measured rather than assumed. RM-007 puts mirror among the three cheap verbs “with the winding reversal named up front, since a mirrored mesh renders inside out unless the material's side is handled”. Against the three in this tree it is handled and not by us: WebGLRenderer computes frontFaceCW from object.matrixWorld.determinantAffine() < 0 and flips the face winding for exactly this case. So no material's side is touched — which matters, because 139 of the 168 catalog models are KHR_materials_unlit and forcing DoubleSide on all of them to fix a problem that does not exist would change how every one of them renders. A test asserts the material is left alone, not merely that mirroring works.
  • The real risk was somewhere else, and it is the size. A negative scale is the whole mechanism — scale_x has been in the save format since the format existed, so a mirrored item round-trips with no new field and no version move. But halfSize was computed by multiplying in the scale, so a mirror made it negative, and halfSize is read by getWidth, by both dimension canvases, by the plan's footprint projection and by Edge.createShape, which pushes a rectangle of it into the wall's holes. A mirrored door would have cut a hole of negative width and nothing would have said so. A half size is a magnitude; it is now restated from the geometry with the sign dropped, on both the relative and the absolute path.
  • Mirrored is the sign of the product, not of one axis. Two negated axes are a 180-degree rotation rather than a reflection — which is what the renderer tests, so it is what this reports. And Y is deliberately not offered: mirroring vertically turns a chair upside down, which nobody laying out a room wants and which boundMove would immediately fight over for a wall-bound item. Rotation is the verb for the other orientations.
  • Each item flips about its own centre, and that is the smaller of two verbs. Mirroring a thing is this. Mirroring a layout — reflecting six chairs across the room's axis — needs the set's own geometry, so it belongs with align and distribute rather than here. m and shift+m, over the set, one commit.
LANDING — J4, align, distribute, group, elevation
  • Align works on edges, not centres, and that is the whole difference. Left means every item's left edge on the leftmost left edge. Aligning centres would leave a wide item overhanging its neighbours, which is not what anybody lining furniture up against a wall means. Six edges — left, right, front, back, and the two centre lines — named for the plan rather than for the axis, because +z is not a direction anybody means. Two items is the minimum: aligning one to itself is a no-op that would still cost an undo entry.
  • Distribute evens the gaps, not the centres. Three items where the middle one is much wider: even centres leave it nearly touching one neighbour and marooned from the other. So the two outermost stay put — they are the span being divided — and the rest are laid out with one equal gap each. Three is the minimum, because two already have one gap and it is already even. A negative gap is not refused: items that overlap more than the span allows get overlapped evenly, which is what the arithmetic says and is better than leaving them piled up.
  • Both move through moveToPosition, not by writing coordinates. So a wall-bound item is still bound to its wall afterwards and a floor item keeps whatever elevation it had. Those are decisions WallItem and FloorItem already make, and align has no business re-litigating them.
  • A group is a shared string, not an entity. Nobody selects the group — they click a chair and mean the six around the table — so the only state it needs is a mark saying which items move together. Which makes it additive in the file, free to delete a member of, and impossible to leave dangling, none of which a Group object holding references would be. Selecting one member selects the group by search; shift-clicking one removes that one, because otherwise a person could never take a single chair out of a wider selection.
  • Elevation was cheap in the file and missing from the product. RM-007 called it one of the three cheap verbs because “elevation is already ypos in the file” — and it is, and there has never been a control for it, so a lamp could be put on a table only by dragging and hoping and a bowl could not be put on a shelf at all. It is a field in the inspector now, offered for everything except the four wall-bound types, whose height WallItem.boundMove derives from their own size and would overwrite on the next drag. A field that silently reverts is worse than no field.
  • And it sticks, for a reason already in the code. FloorItem.moveToPosition preserves this.position.y rather than snapping to the floor on every move, so an item lifted here stays lifted while it is dragged around. Clamped at zero: a floor plan has no basement, and furniture under the floor cannot be clicked.
LANDING — J4, snapping and stacking
  • Not to the grid, to what is already there. Configuration.snapToGrid has done the grid since the fork, and a grid is a property of the paper rather than of the furniture. This snaps to a sofa's edge against the bookcase beside it and a rug's centre with a table's — the alignments somebody furnishing a room is trying to hit by eye. Nine pairings per axis per neighbour: each of the moving item's two edges and its centre, against each of the neighbour's. Nearest wins, so it does what you were aiming at rather than what it would rather you had aimed at, and a tie keeps the first candidate so it does not flicker as the pointer jitters.
  • Pure arithmetic over rectangles, in its own module. No scene, no mesh, no renderer — which is the only way “did it snap to the right line” is a question with an exact answer. The tolerance is Configuration.snapTolerance, 25 cm, which has existed since the fork and was read by nothing but the 2D corner snapping: one number for how close counts as meant rather than a second one that disagrees with it.
  • A snap is horizontal and a stack is not, so they are asked separately. Mixed, an item nudged sideways onto a table would suddenly jump up onto it. stackOn is asked only about the vertical, only when half the moving item's footprint is genuinely over another's — a bowl on the corner of a table is on the table, a bowl beside it with a centimetre of overhang is not — and it returns a height rather than applying one.
  • The reach limit is measured, not chosen. Without one, dragging a lamp across a furnished room teleports it to the top of the tallest thing in it; with only “already up there”, dragging a bowl across a table leaves it on the floor, which is the feature not working. So a surface is stackable if its top is at or below 120 cm — and that number is J1's, from the six standard heights it measured while establishing the Kenney kit's unit scale: above the kitchen unit at 90, the bar stool at 87 and the table and desk at 75; below the fridge at 180 and the door frame at 203. A bowl dragged across a counter lands on it; a bowl dragged past a fridge does not. The line is where this catalog's own measurements put it.
  • Off unless the scene asks, and never for a wall-bound item. scene.snapItems is false by default, so no drag changes for an embedder who has not opted in and no parity capture moves; the application turns it on beside the grid snap it already has, because snap is one idea to a person even though the two snap to different things. And WallItem.moveToPosition derives its position along the wall and then calls up to the base class — snapping after that would pull the item off the wall it is bound to, which is a fight between two rules rather than a feature.
LANDING — J4, the re-baseline, and the halo that had never fired · sprint complete
  • An addition, not a repair, which is what RM-007 asked for and what X-5 explained. The rule is “a new predicate, feature flag, characterization tests updated in the same commit — not as a fix”, and the measurement says why that framing is right: polygonInsidePolygon has no caller anywhere, polygonOutsidePolygon's only one is inside a block comment, and the two live calls sit in a function that returns true on every path. Nothing observable depends on any of the four, so repairing them would change behaviour nobody can see while re-opening a suite that has held for nine programmes. All four stay exactly as they are, and their four assertions are unchanged.
  • Utils.polygonsOverlap is new and is written from the separating-axis theorem, not from the broken edge-intersection path — because edge intersection structurally misses the case that matters most for furniture: one item entirely inside another. A rug under a table has no edge crossings at all. SAT catches it, since a contained polygon has no separating axis either. The same test asserts the broken sibling still says no to that case, which is the whole argument for a new predicate in one assertion. Flush is deliberately not overlapping, because flush is exactly what this sprint's snapping produces on purpose.
  • And it makes dead code reachable rather than adding new code beside it. RM-012 recorded Item.showError() as having one caller and that caller unreachable — it sits behind !isValidPosition(vec3), and FloorItem.isValidPosition returns true on every path. The red glow has existed since the fork with a comment claiming it fires. RM-007 offered J4 the choice, “either the halo becomes the collision warning or it is deleted”; nothing had to be written to draw a warning, because a warning was already drawn and nothing could reach it.
  • A warning, never a refusal. It runs after the move rather than instead of it. isValidPosition says in its own comment that placing an item is up to the user, and eight programmes of saved designs were made under that rule — refusing a move now would make some of them unopenable in the sense that matters, in that the furniture in them could no longer be pushed around.
  • Behind Configuration.collisionWarnings, default off, and offered in Settings rather than on the toolbar because it is not a mode somebody switches between while working. It is the first thing in nine programmes to make a correct polygon predicate observable, with the four broken ones untouched, so whether anybody sees that consequence should be something they turned on.
  • Sprint J4 is complete, and so is everything in J2 that does not require acquiring a pack. Ten tasks in nine commits. 2,298 headless and 174 browser tests, thirteen budgets within limits, and all four coverage floors raised for the first time in four programmes: 79 → 86 lines, 79 → 86 statements, 68 → 77 branches, 78 → 84 functions, measured at 86.61 / 86.62 / 77.77 / 84.45 and rounded down as always. What remains in J2 is the acquisition itself and the two rows on an unestablished licence, both of which need a decision rather than a commit.
LANDING — J2 closed: the acquisition · sprint complete
  • 51 admitted from 200, on a rule stated before anything was measured. Kenney's Food Kit, CC0 1.0, downloaded and checksummed. A catalog row is something a person places in a room and expects to stay there — so tableware, cookware, kitchen tools and counter containers, and 149 of the kit's 200 models are food, drinks, packaging or waste and none of them is furniture. That is what curation means with a rule attached rather than a taste: the kit was not trimmed until it fitted a budget, it was trimmed to what a floor planner is for, and the price was checked afterwards.
  • The unit scale was solved and one model was refused by it. Seven objects checked against their real-world sizes; the two most standardised agree to within a centimetre at ×30 — a dinner plate at 26.8 cm against a 26–28 standard, a cooking pot at 24.7 against 24. The other five land short, which is Kenney's stylised proportion rather than a disagreement about the scale. barrel could not be reconciled at 20.4 cm, which is a tub, so it was refused rather than rescaled — J1's method finding its own outlier a second time.
  • The pipeline is run, not built, and it paid for itself. X-4 said both encoders were installed and green; they were, and the acquired pack went through Draco at 12,718 → 3,561 bytes an item deduped, 51 of 51 encoded. The admission gate's own note fired before it ran — “0 of 51 models are not Draco — this price is a pre-pipeline one” — which is the sequence that note exists to produce.
  • And the pack's sharing broke my own gate, so the gate was hardened. The 51 models share one 10,715-byte colour atlas, so the pack's deduped mean is far below its median. Taken as the benchmark price that reading said the headroom buys 1,619 more items, which is a gate incapable of failing. Neither number is wrong and neither alone is the price of a kit: one with an internal atlas costs its deduped mean, one without costs nearer its median. curatedPrice takes the dearer of a pack's two prices, then the cheapest pack — the assumption that does not flatter an acquisition, which is the only kind a ceiling should be divided by.
  • The two rows nobody could license are gone, and that needed a mechanism. A retirement says the old name keeps working and points somewhere new; A5's contract survives it. This is the other thing and it is the first time this project has done it — a name that resolves to nothing because the file is gone on purpose. So WITHDRAWN is a register with a reason per name, and a test refuses an entry whose file is still in the tree, whose row is still in the catalog, or whose reason is short enough to be a label.
  • What it cost, and what the instruments said about it. M-45: “168 → 217 items, mean 27,995 → 24,096, tree +529,092 B” — the 49 net rows cost 10,798 bytes each against a catalog mean of 27,995, which is 39 % of the price the ceiling was raised at. catalog-packs is raised 10,450 → 12,250, the first raise of a line added four commits earlier whose own note said it would happen; and what it buys improved, 59 → 53.8 gzipped bytes a row. first-load did not move. 49 rows entered the catalog and the payload every visitor downloads did not grow by a byte, which is the pack split holding under its first real test.
  • One acquisition put RM-007's lower figure in reach. Before it, 232 were needed and the headroom bought 206 — neither end reachable standing still. After it, 183 needed and 216 affordable: 400 is now reachable without further curation and 600 still is not. No amount of compression could have done that, which is X-2's point demonstrated rather than argued. And the same movement is recorded from the other side: the median rose 11,218 → 14,013, so 600 at the median is now just out of reach — 371 affordable against 383 needed — which is asserted rather than noted, because the first time a ceiling gets harder to reach is the time to notice.
  • Two of my own passes had to be undone. encode --force re-encoded 48 pre-existing models at settings that are not the ones RM-004 B1 measured against a 5 µm gate — reverted, exactly as the same mistake was reverted in the material audit. And it exposed a real gap while doing it: the encoding report merges, so a model deleted from the tree kept its fidelity record forever and encode:check went on reporting a withdrawn file as encoded. Entries for absent models are dropped now.
  • Sprint J2 is closed and programme J is three sprints of four. 2,301 headless and 174 browser tests, thirteen budgets within limits with one raised for its stated reason, and every gate green. J3 — bring your own model — is what remains, and RM-007 places it in Release 5 beside K2, which shares its answer.

Seven and a half weeks, unchanged from RM-007, and the split moves by half a week: 2 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 2.5 against 1.5 + 2 + 1.5 + 2.5. J1 takes the half-week because the index split belongs in front of the metadata rather than behind it, and J2 gives it back because the pipeline it was costed to build is already installed and green. What moved is inside the sprints: J2's headline number becomes an output of a decision, and J4's two halves swap places in the estimate.

What must not change

The save format stays readable by any build that reads 2.0.0: a room category, a licence and an imported-model reference are all additive, written only where they exist, so a design nobody has touched re-saves byte-identical — M-26's rule, now on its seventh programme. The one-way arrow holds: catalog metadata is plain data, and src/scripts must not learn to import the app's index any more than it imports the material catalog today. item_type stays append-only, which is why moving the twelve wall segments is a re-categorisation rather than a renumbering. The preserved polygon predicates are repaired in this programme and nowhere earlier, under a flag, with the ledger and the characterization tests moving in the same commit — X-5 makes that cheaper, not optional. Placement stays permissive: a warning, never a refusal. And no budget moves down — two are expected to move up in J2 with the decision that justifies them recorded beside the number, one is added in J1, and first-load is the one line this programme must not spend, because it is the only one that measures what a person waits for.

PROGRAMME K · DRAWING Nº RM-013

A design with no name, and a picture that costs more than it

RM-007 calls programme K “many designs, starter plans, a link to send — and none of it behind a login, because there is no login” and prices it at 3.5 weeks. Eight measurements against the tree first, and three of them change the shape of K1. A design cannot carry its own name: four unknown top-level keys parse with zero errors, zero warnings and are then dropped by DesignDocument, so a name written into a file reaches the disk and dies on load — silently, which is worse than a rejection. The thumbnail is the expensive half of a project: a 300 px plan is 17,372 bytes as a PNG against a furnished three-bedroom design of 8,518, and WebP is a third of that. And the plan export draws the view's floorplan, not the one it is handed — measured, 15 paths where 30 belong — which has never mattered because the two arguments have always been the same object, and K1 is the first caller for which they would not be. Three sprints, 3.5 weeks, and the total does not move.

§ 57 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What measuring one design at a time changed about many

Eight measurements against the tree at 2879133, every one of them run: two in headless Chromium, four against the library headless, one against the fake IDBFactory the suite already owns, one a grep. Three re-shape K1, one makes K2 cheaper, and two remove work from the plan rather than adding it.

0 errors
a design carrying name, id, createdAt and modifiedAt. All four are then dropped on load
17,372 B
a 300 px plan thumbnail as PNG, against 8,518 B for the furnished design it depicts. WebP is 5,958
15 of 30
paths in a sheet exported from a view that does not hold the floorplan it was passed. Nothing warned
4,050 B
five starter plans gzipped into the bundle — 41 % of what first-load has left
3.00 GiB
quota measured in Chromium, against the one slot the application stores in it
3,086 chars
a 120-item house gzipped into a URL fragment. K2 needs no server and no library

The programme survives its own measurement and one sprint gets cheaper. RM-007 gap Q-6 reads “one design at a time: no library, no thumbnails, no starter plans”, and every clause of it is true. What the measurement adds is which of the three is actually the work. It is not the store — src/app/persistence/draft_repository.js has spoken IndexedDB since RM-003 A5, its interface is already two implementations wide, and Chromium offers this origin 3,221,225,472 bytes against the roughly 14 KB a project costs. It is not the application's document handling either: the single-design assumption lives in five places, one of which is a single line. It is the two things nobody has had to answer yet — what identifies a design, and what a picture of one costs.

The identity finding is the sharp one, because the failure is silent. A saved design's top-level keys are floorplan and items, plus levels, roof and sun where they exist. Adding four more and running the real validator returns ok: true, no errors and no warnings — and DesignDocument's constructor then reads seven fields, none of which is one of the four. So the document format will accept a name, transport a name, and lose it on the way in, with no diagnostic anywhere. That is not a bug to fix in K1: it is the reason a project's identity must live beside the document rather than in it, which is also what keeps M-26's rule intact on its eighth programme — a design nobody has touched re-saves byte-identical.

The thumbnail finding re-prices the sprint's second half. Rendered for real in Chromium rather than reasoned about: the same three-bedroom plan at 300 px is 17,372 bytes as PNG, 11,624 as JPEG and 5,958 as WebP. PNG is the format every other thumbnail in this project uses and it is the wrong one here, for a reason RM-012 already measured from the other side — a supersampled line drawing is mostly part-covered edge pixels, and each is a colour the palette has not seen. The same render also returned a 300 × 333 canvas for an 1180 × 860 landscape plan, because fitProjection is building a sheet: portrait, with a title block and a 56.7 px margin at 19 % of the width. Correct for paper and wrong for a tile. K1 needs a thumbnail mode, not the sheet it already has.

And the store cannot be extended the obvious way. A projects object store inside architect3d requires the database at version 2, and A5 wrote a deliberate refusal for exactly that case. Run in both directions: a build at version 1 against a store at version 2 gets {ok: false, reason: "version"}, read() of null, and stats().kind === "indexeddb-unsupported-version" — autosave off for the session, permanently, by design. A build at version 2 against a store at version 1 upgrades cleanly. So the bump is one-way and it is the draft that pays for it. A second database costs nothing and the two have independent lifetimes anyway, which is what K1 will do.

Eight findings, and two of them remove work

Each row was produced against 2879133. Where a byte count is quoted it was produced by compressing something; where a browser figure is quoted it came out of Chromium; where a refusal is quoted the repository was made to refuse.
