Y-1 · One slot, and a bump nobody can walk back shapes K1 measured

draft_repository.js owns one database, architect3d, at STORE_VERSION = 1, with one object store drafts keyed on id, and it writes exactly one record: DRAFT_ID = 'current'. Its own comment calls that “deliberately not a recent-files list”, and the reasoning is still right — a crash recovery is not a document model. What K1 adds is the document model, and the question is where to put it.

The obvious answer is a second object store in the same database, and object stores are created only inside onupgradeneeded, so that means version 2. A5 wrote a rule for that case and this measurement is that rule being read back:

BuildStoreput()read()stats().kind
version 1at version 2{ok: false, reason: "version"}nullindexeddb-unsupported-version
version 2at version 1onupgradeneeded fires — a clean upgrade, nothing lost

The bump is one-way, and it is the draft that pays. useAutosave treats a version refusal as permanent for the session — “the stored draft was written by a newer version of this app, and has been left alone” — which is correct behaviour and exactly the wrong price to pay for a feature the user has not opened yet. Anybody who tries K1 and goes back to a build without it loses autosave until they clear their storage.

A second database costs nothing. architect3d-projects at version 1 leaves architect3d at version 1, so a rollback is a rollback: the library goes quiet and the draft still works. The two stores also have genuinely independent lifetimes — a draft is one slot that is constantly overwritten and expires after seven days, a project is a named record that expires never — so sharing a version number would have coupled two schemas that have no reason to move together. The interface is already the right shape to copy: kind, a refusal as a result rather than an exception, and a --check-able stats().

Y-2 · The document will take a name and lose it shapes K1 measured

A saved design's top-level keys are floorplan and items. levels, roof and sun join them conditionally, which is M-26's additive rule and the reason a pre-G1 design still re-saves byte-identical. DEFAULT_DESIGN — the one starter plan this application has — is 1,678 bytes raw, 435 gzipped.

The same document with name, id, createdAt and modifiedAt added was put through DesignDocument.parse:

InputokErrorsWarningsFields kept
a design plus four identity keystrue00floorplan, items, levels, roof, sun, version, units

Accepted, then dropped, with nothing said. The validator has no notion of an unknown top-level key — which is the right default for a format that grows additively, and is what let levels, roof and sun each arrive without breaking a reader. But it means the failure mode for identity-in-the-file is not a rejection anybody would notice; it is a name that survives the save, survives the disk, and is gone the moment somebody opens it.

So the decision is made for K1 rather than by it: a project's identity lives beside the document. The record carries the name, the timestamps and the thumbnail; the .blueprint3d string inside it is exactly what exportSerialized produces today, unchanged, and a file exported out of the library is a file any build can open. Teaching the model a name field is a save-format change on the eighth programme in a row that has not needed one, and it would buy nothing the record does not already give.

The visible half of the same finding is smaller and free. Every download this application produces is named by a constant — design.blueprint3d, design.obj, design.gltf, plan-1-{scale}.svg, plan.png, view.png, panorama.png. Seven exports, one name each, no matter what is in them. A project with a name fixes all seven in one place, and it is the cheapest thing in the sprint.

Y-3 · The sheet draws the view's plan, not the one it was handed library bug measured

exportPlanSVG(view, floorplan, options) and renderPlanToCanvas(view, floorplan, canvas, options) each take a view and a floorplan, and reconcile them nowhere. planBounds(floorplan) sizes and scales the sheet; view.renderTo(...) then draws whatever floorplan the view was constructed with. RM-008 E4's note explains why the drawing goes through the view — “the export is not a second implementation of the plan, it is this one pointed somewhere else” — and that reasoning is sound. What was never stated is that the second argument is therefore only a bounds source.

Measured by pairing them wrongly on purpose — a Floorplanner2D bound to a 400 × 300 room, asked to export an 1180 × 860 flat:

View holdsPassedSVG bytesPathsWhat came out
the small roomthe small room3,98615correct
the small roomthe flat3,98815the small room's drawing, at the flat's scale, under the flat's title block
the flatthe flat7,20230correct

Two bytes apart from the correct small sheet and three and a half thousand from the correct large one — a plausible-looking document that is wrong about its own subject, produced with no warning. It has never fired because the only caller is useDesignIO, which reads both out of the same store in the same expression. K1 is the first caller for which they would differ, because a library of thumbnails is by definition a set of designs that are not the one on screen.

Two things follow, and they are separate. The library gets the repair — one argument, or two that are checked — because an API that silently produces a wrong document on a wrong call is worth an hour whoever calls it next. And K1 gets the constraint regardless of the repair: a thumbnail is captured while its design is open, because the alternative is loading a design into a live view to photograph it, which is the whole cost of opening it. Save writes the picture; the grid reads it.

Y-4 · The picture costs more than the design shapes K1 measured

An 1180 × 860 three-bedroom plan rendered through renderPlanToCanvas in Chromium at three widths, and each canvas encoded three ways by the browser itself:

WidthCanvasPNGWebP q85JPEG q82WebP as a data URL
200200 × 26011,6854,4307,4895,931 chars
300300 × 33317,3725,95811,6247,967 chars
480480 × 46422,4336,84216,0339,147 chars

The design it depicts is 8,518 bytes. So at 300 px the PNG is more than twice the document, the WebP is less than three quarters of it, and the format choice is a 3× difference on the larger half of every record the library stores. PNG is what all 168 catalog thumbnails are and it is the wrong answer here — not because PNG is bad at line art, but because this line art is antialiased at tile size, so the sheet is mostly part-covered edge pixels and each one is a colour the palette has not seen. RM-012's thumbnail tool measured the same effect from the other direction when it chose 2× supersampling over 3×.

The other number in that table is the aspect. An 1180 × 860 landscape plan came back as a 300 × 333 portrait canvas, because fitProjection is building a sheet: a page-shaped frame with a title block along the bottom and a chromeInset of 56.7 px, which at 300 px wide is 19 % of the width on each side. Correct for something that gets printed; wrong for a grid, where the tiles must share an aspect and the title block renders as an illegible smudge. K1 therefore wants a thumbnail projection beside the sheet projection — same drawing code, no title block, a fixed aspect and a small margin — rather than a smaller sheet.

Y-5 · Five starter plans, and 41 % of what first-load has left med measured

RM-007 names five: studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom, duplex. Five distinct plans of those shapes were built, closed, updated and serialized through saveFloorplan, each also with fourteen furniture records in the shape savedItems writes:

PlanCornersWallsBareBare, gzFurnishedFurnished, gz
studio762,9316726,490990
one-bedroom1183,9658437,5241,162
two-bedroom1394,4879408,0461,261
three-bedroom14104,9319858,5181,308
duplex13104,8619738,4201,296
all five, one module——23,6773,32144,0204,050

first-load is at 411,551 measured against a 421,400 limit — 9,849 bytes of headroom, still the thinnest line in budget.json at 2.3 %. So the five fit, and that is the honest reading: this is not a wall, it is a 41 % bite out of the last thin margin, taken for content most visitors never open, on a set that is open-ended — the templates are five and the samples are however many get drawn.

It is X-3's argument arriving one programme later, and the answer is the one J1 and J2 already built: a manifest and a fetch. Templates live under public/, the bundle carries their names and nothing else, and M-43's resource assertion is extended to say that a boot fetches no template — the same sentence, about a different directory. That also settles what a “sample design” may weigh: nothing, until somebody clicks it.

Y-6 · Three gigabytes, against one slot cheaper measured

navigator.storage.estimate() in Chromium on a cold profile: quota 3,221,225,472 bytes — 3.00 GiB — usage 0, and indexedDB.databases() empty. Against the 5 MiB Web Storage cap that RM-003 A5 was written to escape, this is the escape working.

At Y-4's WebP thumbnail and Y-5's furnished three-bedroom, a project record is about 14,500 bytes, so the quota holds them on the order of two hundred thousand. Whatever eventually limits this library, it is not the store, and K1 should not pretend otherwise: no pruning policy, no LRU, no size cap, no quota manager. What it owes a person is a count, a delete, and the refusal path A5 already wrote for the day a browser says no anyway — which is a real day, because private browsing and embedded webviews both produce it and the localStorage fallback cannot hold a library at all. That case gets a sentence in the UI, not a mechanism.

Y-7 · A house fits in a link cheaper measured

K2's first clause is “a compressed design in the URL”, and the thing worth knowing before that sprint is whether it needs a backend. The same three-bedroom plan at four furniture counts, compressed and encoded the way a fragment would carry it:

ItemsDesigngzip -9brotli q11base64url of the gzip
04,0368617771,148 chars
147,3851,1671,0111,556 chars
4013,6641,4531,1881,938 chars
12033,0442,3141,6053,086 chars

A design compresses to about 7 % of itself, because it is repetitive JSON with long stable key names and UUID corners. A 120-item house is a 3,086-character link, and CompressionStream('gzip') is in every browser this project targets, so K2 needs no compression library, no shortener and no server. Worth measuring now rather than in five weeks, because a server is the one thing that would have contradicted the programme's own objective — “none of it behind a login, because there is no login”.

Y-8 · Five places assume one design low measured

Grepped rather than guessed. The boot path is App.vue's onMounted calling io.newDesign(), then history.reset(), then offerDraft(); the New action calls io.newDesign() and clearDraft(); useDesignIO.newDesign is one statement, loadSerialized(DEFAULT_DESIGN); and useAutosave holds a module-level repository so that readDraft can run before anything is mounted. That is the whole of it.

Five places, one of them a single line. A project library is not a rewrite of this application's document handling, because there is barely any document handling to rewrite — the same shape X-6 found for selection and X-7 found for imported models, and the third time in one programme's worth of measurement that the expensive-sounding part is the cheap one. What K1 spends its time on is the two things above it: what a project record is, and what its picture costs.

§ 59 · SPRINTS K1–K3

Three and a half weeks, and the total does not move

RM-007 priced this programme at 3.5 weeks in three sprints and none of the three changes length. What changes is what K1 builds first, where it puts it, and one library repair it inherits on the way past.

K1

A design becomes a thing with a name

deliveredY-1Y-2Y-3Y-4Y-51.5 wk

Objective. Many designs, each with a name, a picture and a date — and a shelf of starter plans to begin from, none of which arrives before somebody asks for it.

  • A second database, not a second store (Y-1). architect3d-projects at version 1, so architect3d stays at version 1 and a rollback keeps its draft. Same interface shape as draft_repository: a kind, a refusal that is a result rather than an exception, and a stats() worth asserting on.
  • Identity lives beside the document (Y-2). A record is an id, a name, two timestamps, a thumbnail and the .blueprint3d string exactly as exportSerialized writes it. Nothing is added to the save format, because the format would accept it and lose it.
  • A thumbnail projection beside the sheet projection (Y-4). No title block, one aspect, a small margin, WebP with a PNG fallback for a browser that will not encode it. Captured on save, because Y-3 says a sheet drawn from a view that does not hold the design is a document that lies.
  • And the repair that finding earns (Y-3). exportPlanSVG and renderPlanToCanvas stop accepting a view and a floorplan that disagree. An hour, and it is the last hour anybody spends on it.
  • The library itself: a grid of tiles, open, rename, duplicate, delete, a count and a date. No pruning and no quota manager (Y-6) — but the refusal path is real, because a browser that will not store gets a sentence rather than a broken grid.
  • Templates and samples, fetched (Y-5). Studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom, duplex, on a manifest under public/. The bundle carries their names and nothing else.
  • The name reaches the seven exports (Y-2). design.blueprint3d becomes the project's name, and so do the other six.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-47 (new): a boot fetches no template — asserted in the browser tier off performance.getEntriesByType('resource'), the same sentence M-43 makes about packs, about a different directory
  • M-48 (new): a project round-trips — write, list, open, rename, duplicate, delete — against the real IndexedDB in Chromium and against the fake IDBFactory headless, which is how A5's repository is already tested at both tiers
  • The draft store stays at version 1, asserted: a build that has never heard of projects still reads its draft after the library has been used
  • Every template opens through loadDocument with zero errors and zero warnings, and a design saved out of the library is byte-identical to the same design saved before it — M-26, on its eighth programme
LANDING — K1, the repair Y-3 earned, and three of our own tests it caught
  • The two export functions stop accepting arguments that disagree. exportPlanSVG and renderPlanToCanvas each take a view and a floorplan and reconciled them nowhere; they now agree or throw, and null means the view's own. The finding said this had never fired because the only caller reads both out of one expression — and it was wrong about that in the most useful way, because three tests in this repository were passing on the wrong drawing.
  • plan-levels-2d asked for a sheet of the ground floor while the canvas held the first floor, and asserted the ghost layer was absent from it. It was — from the first floor's drawing, inside the ground floor's frame. The setup now shows the ground floor before exporting one, which is what an application would have to do.
  • three-storey's “each draws its own plan” was not testing that. It switched storeys on the model with useLevels unmounted, so the canvas drew the ground floor three times; the three sheets still differed, because planBounds reads the argument, so new Set(sheets).size === 3 passed on three frames around one drawing. It mounts useLevels now — the wiring the application has — and counts paths as well as comparing strings. Its savePlanSVG case had the same shape.
  • None of the three is a changed expectation. Each setup now does what App.vue does, and every assertion got stronger rather than weaker. This is the case the standing rule is written for, seen from the other side: a characterization failure is a signal to re-check the change, and re-checking it found the tests were the thing that was wrong.
  • A tile is not a small sheet (Y-4). thumbnailProjection takes both dimensions, scales by whichever axis binds and centres the rest, so a long plan and a square one both come back as pictures of the whole building at one aspect. renderPlanThumbnail draws through it at 320 × 240 — the catalog's own 4:3, because a grid that mixes two aspects reads as a mistake — and renderTo gains a chrome flag so the north arrow, 56 px of a 320 px tile, stays off it. That flag is deliberately separate from exporting: a sheet is an export and still wants the arrow, because a plan that does not say which way the building faces is not a drawing.
LANDING — K1, a project is a record, in a database of its own
  • architect3d-projects at version 1, not a second store in architect3d (Y-1). Both halves of the finding are assertions now rather than notes: the databases are named differently and both are at version 1, and a draft written before the library is still readable after it — checked headless against the fake IDBFactory and in Chromium against the real one, where indexedDB.databases() is asked directly.
  • Two object stores in it, because a grid and an open want different bytes. cards carries id, name, dates, thumbnail and size; bodies carries the document. Measured in Chromium: eight 40-item designs list in under a tenth of what they store, and every card still knows how large its own document is without holding it.
  • Identity lives beside the document (Y-2), so the save format gains nothing at all — the first programme in eight for which that is true, and the finding is the reason: the format would have accepted a name silently and dropped it on load.
  • No pruning, no LRU, no cap (Y-6). What is real is refusal: UnavailableProjectRepository is a stated absence rather than a degraded library, because the Web Storage fallback that saves one draft cannot hold many designs and one that silently began losing them would be worse than one that says so.
  • storage.js extracted beside them — the REASON_* vocabulary, byteLength, classify, estimate and promisify — and re-exported from draft_repository, so no caller changed. The vocabulary is shared; the schemas deliberately are not, which is Y-1 as a file layout.
LANDING — K1, the picture is taken while the design is on screen
  • Captured on save, not rendered on demand (Y-3). A picture of a design that is not open means loading it into a view first — the whole cost of opening it, paid once per tile — and before the repair the same call would have drawn whatever plan the view did hold. WebP on Y-4's measurement, 5,958 bytes against 17,372 for the same tile, and toDataURL falls back to PNG by itself where it must.
  • Saving is an act. The draft next door writes every two seconds and on every tab hide; that protects somebody between decisions, and this is the decision. No autosave into the library, no silent overwrite of a project somebody opened to look at.
  • Three behaviours worth naming, each a decision rather than an implementation. A template is adopted rather than becoming the project, so saving creates a record instead of overwriting the studio plan for whoever opens it next. Duplicate does not open the copy, because duplicating from a grid is the first half of trying something and being yanked elsewhere is the wrong second half. And deleting the record you are looking at leaves the design on screen and unkept, because deleting a record should not throw away work.
  • Y-2's cheap half, delivered with it. The seven exports stop being constants: design.blueprint3d, design.obj, design.gltf, plan-1-100.svg, plan.png, view.png and panorama.png all take the project's name, through one documentName ref and a fileNameFor that strips only what a filesystem will not take.
LANDING — K1, five starter plans and two samples, and both corrections they cost
  • Fetched, not bundled (Y-5), and M-47 is the assertion, not the budget. A boot fetches no plan and not even the manifest — the shelf is behind a click, unlike the catalog drawer whose first screen J1 had to keep bundled. The line exists because the plans fit: a build that bundled them and one that fetched them look identical on disk and both stay inside every limit.
  • Built by a tool, not committed as JSON. Each plan is drawn by calling the library's own Floorplan, so what ships is what the model produces, stamped units: cm at whatever version the build declares, and the rooms are whatever closing the partitions actually finds. Rooms are named by asking pointInPolygon2 which one contains a point — the correct sibling, the one room detection itself uses — and the tool refuses to write a plan whose named points miss. Ids are seeded, so --check is a gate rather than a coin toss.
  • The furniture cost two corrections, both found by measuring rather than by reading. A saved ypos is the item's centre, and Item's constructor calls setScale for any document scale, which calls resized(), which for a FloorItem assigns position.y = halfSize.y. So a floor item ends up at half its own height whatever the file says, and the file should say that: writing the midpoint of the box instead put Beddouble at 24.5 where the library settles on 37.5.
  • And half the height has to be measured the way three.js measures it. A union over every POSITION accessor in the file agreed for eleven of fifteen rows and disagreed for four — Beddouble 50.5 against 37.5, Chairdesk 41.76 against 60.76, too big and too small at once, which is the signature of node transforms rather than of arithmetic. modelBounds now walks scenes[].nodes, accumulates each node's TRS or matrix, and transforms all eight corners of every instanced primitive's declared box. All fifteen agree exactly, and the browser tier is what says so.
  • Samples are floor items only, and it is gated. A wall item positions against an Edge, and a document that names one without choosing a wall is asking the library to guess — a sample whose kitchen units drift into a wall is worse advertising than a sample without them.
  • The fourteenth budget line, templates, at 8,774 measured against 9,220. Deliberately tight, because the failure mode it exists to catch is a shelf of seven quietly becoming a shelf of seventy.
LANDING — K1, the library on screen · sprint complete
  • Two shelves, because they are not the same kind of thing. Your designs are records and opening one continues it; starter plans are documents and opening one puts it on screen unsaved. One dialog, because they answer the same question; two tabs, because the answer to “what happens when I click this” differs.
  • Rename and delete happen on the tile. Not window.prompt and not window.confirm — the application sets configSystemUI to false precisely so this stops reaching for those, and a modal on top of a modal to ask “are you sure” is worse than a second click on the thing you are already pointing at.
  • Unsaved comes from the history stack, not from the model's events. useHistory commits one entry per edit and resets after every load, so its depth is the number of edits since the design arrived — and undoing back to the depth a save happened at correctly leaves nothing to save. Listening to the model instead would have marked a furnished project dirty a second after opening it, as its items arrived.
  • The UI suite found two real defects while it was being written. A template ref inside v-for resolves to an array, so field.value.focus() would have thrown on the first rename and the caret would never have landed in the box. And the shelf was chosen only on a false-to-true transition, so a dialog mounted already open showed an empty grid to somebody with nothing kept.
  • What it measures. Coverage 86.72 / 86.69 / 77.50 / 85.06; functions crosses a whole number and is raised 84 → 85, which is what a sprint of new modules does. Branches went the other way, 77.70 → 77.50, and the floor is unmoved and the dip recorded: the new refusal paths need a browser to produce, the fake IDBFactory reaches several of them and not all, and a floor is not a measurement.
K2

A link, and a way to look without touching

deliveredY-71 wk

Objective. Send somebody a design without sending them a file, and let them look at it without being able to break it.

  • The design in the fragment (Y-7). CompressionStream('gzip') and base64url — 3,086 characters for a 120-item house, measured. No server, no shortener, no library.
  • A read-only mode: the viewport and the plan, no tools, no inspector edits, and an offer to copy it into the library rather than a silent switch into editing.
  • A .zip bundle carrying custom assets, which is J3's problem seen from the export side. RM-012 X-7 already recorded that the two share one answer; whichever ships first writes it.
ACCEPTANCE
  • A design round-trips through a fragment and re-serializes byte-identical
  • A link too long for a browser is refused with the size in the message, not truncated Restated on delivery. No browser refused one: Chromium kept a 2,000,000-character fragment whole. The ceiling is this application's judgement about what survives an inbox, so the refusal states the count and the limit rather than blaming the platform.
LANDING — K2, the link, and the state the plan never had
  • deflate-raw, not gzip, and it was measured. Same sample: gzip 1,759 bytes, deflate-raw 1,741. The 18 bytes are gzip's header and its CRC trailer, and neither earns a place in a fragment — base64 decoding, inflating and JSON.parse all fail loudly on a link somebody broke across two lines, so 24 characters for a second opinion is not a trade worth making. Chromium's gzip was also confirmed byte-identical to Node's, which is what lets the two tiers compare figures at all.
  • The fragment, not the query, and that is the privacy. A fragment is never sent to a server, so a shared design is not in the host's access log and not in the referrer of every outbound link. RM-007's objective for this programme is “none of it behind a login, because there is no login”, and putting somebody's floor plan in a log to achieve that would be the wrong kind of serverless.
  • MAX_LINK_CHARS is a policy and says so. history.replaceState was driven at 2,000, 8,000, 32,000, 100,000, 500,000 and 2,000,000 characters in Chromium and every one was kept whole — the browser is not the constraint. 8,000 is where three things line up: every design this build ships fits several times over (largest 2,346, a 400-item house 7,451), it is the request-line limit that tools which rewrite and log links apply even though a fragment never becomes one, and past it a file is the honest answer. The refusal states the number, because “too long” is an unexplained house rule.
  • The plan had no non-editing state at all, which is the finding this sprint could not have been built without. Six modes, and all six mutate — MOVE included, because MOVE is what drags corners, walls, footprints, dimensions and notes. The 3D half has had Controller.enabled since the fork, used by switchFPSMode so a walkthrough cannot shove a sofa; the asymmetry was only that nobody had needed the plan's.
  • And the gate is three guards, not one, because the first version was wrong. mousedown returning early stops everything that grabs, and mousemove pans precisely when nothing is grabbed — so panning and zooming survive by construction rather than by enumeration. But activeCorner and activeWall are set by hover, so a read-only plan still had one under the pointer and the drag branch moved it: a corner moved 182 cm in a plan nobody was allowed to touch, caught on the suite's first run. The comment claiming one guard was the whole gate is corrected in place rather than deleted.
  • Controller.enabled gained a second owner. Read-only and the walkthrough both turn it off, and a single assignment meant the second event won — so leaving a walkthrough inside a shared design handed the pointer back and made the furniture draggable again.
  • Leaving is a copy, never a switch. The fragment is cleared exactly then: while somebody is viewing it stays, so a reload re-opens what they were sent and the link is still there to copy, and the moment they make it theirs it goes — because a URL that would restore the sender's version over their own edits is a trap with a keyboard shortcut. A link also displaces the recovered draft rather than consuming it; two documents competing for one screen is not a choice worth offering.
LANDING — K2, the bundle, and what it turned out to carry
  • A zip written by hand, because the compression was already here. CompressionStream('deflate-raw') emits exactly what a zip entry stores — method 8 is a raw deflate stream — so a library would have been brought in for the container, and the container is two structs and a checksum. Local headers, a central directory, an end record, CRC-32, UTF-8 names flagged, and no timestamps, so two identical bundles are identical bytes. An entry is stored rather than deflated when deflating made it bigger, which is the ordinary case for a Draco model and a PNG and is what stops a bundle exceeding the files inside it.
  • What it carries is the finding, not the format. The asset closure of the largest sample here is 19 items, 20 distinct files, 146,946 bytes — every one already in the app that would open the bundle. So the rule is not “carry the assets”: it is carry what the recipient will not have, decided against their own AssetManifest. Today that set is empty and the manifest says so in three lists — expected, carried, missing — and when J3 lands, an imported model is by definition an asset in nobody else's build and the same rule picks it up unchanged. That is what RM-012 X-7 meant by the two sharing one answer.
  • Reading names what it cannot place. A bundle's design loads; its carried assets are listed rather than loaded, because there is nowhere to put one until J3 builds a store — X-7's own measurement. Dropping them silently is the single outcome worse than not reading them, because a design quietly missing three models looks like a bug in the application rather than a feature that has not shipped.
  • The honest limit, stated rather than discovered. The closure is the URLs the document names, not the images inside a .glb — reading those means fetching and parsing every model to build a bundle. It cannot bite for the imports J3 will produce, because a person picks one file and one file is self-contained.
  • A .zip and a .blueprint3d arrive through the same control, because “open a design” is one intention and making somebody choose the right of two buttons for a distinction the file itself declares is an interface asking them to do the computer's job.
LANDING — K2, the budget, and a number K1 got wrong · sprint complete
  • K1's first-load claim was measured against a stale build. npm run budget does not rebuild, so the figure it reported was the dist from before the sprint. Re-measured on fresh builds at four commits rather than subtracted from each other — which is the rule H3 wrote after doing the same thing to H2's test counts:
CommitWhatfirst-loadΔ
2879133before K1401.9 KiB—
73a4251K1 complete407.5 KiB+5.6
c83c207K2 codec and read-only407.7 KiB+0.2
5b81bd7K2 viewer and share UI410.2 KiB+2.5
—K2 bundle, deferred410.8 KiB+0.6
  • The line caught the right thing on its way past. With the container statically imported the payload went to 412.2 KiB and failed — so design_bundle.js and zip.js went behind a dynamic import() and ship as a 2,065-byte chunk. That is RM-011 H2's move on the ambient-occlusion chain applied to the same kind of thing: machinery nobody touches until they click Export. The link codec is deliberately not deferred — it is small, and a boot carrying a link must decode it before first paint.
  • Two limits raised, deliberately, with the breakdown recorded. first-load 421,400 → 441,700 and demo-js-gzip 423,200 → 439,800, both to the ~5 % every line in that file was set at. The 8.9 KiB is a project library, a starter-plan shelf, a share codec, a share dialog and a viewer — product surface reached from the top bar, deliberately in the payload. What is not in it is content: the starter plans are fetched and M-47 asserts it.
  • One test fixture moved, and it is not a weakened assertion. The admission gate's “small pack of expensive ones” priced its synthetic pack at 130,000, and K1's starter plans grew the tree by 50 kB — enough that 40 × 130,000 crossed the tree ceiling first, which admit() reports instead of the reachability rule because a negative headroom makes that arithmetic meaningless. Correct behaviour, and a fixture that had stopped isolating the rule it names; the price is derived from the tree now.
  • And the ratchet bit, for the second time in the project's history. The codec, the container, the read-only state and two components landed at 84.44 functions and 76.83 branches - under both floors, and under the functions floor K1 had raised one sprint earlier. Neither came down. What the failure pointed at was two components with no test at all, ShareDialog at 21 % and ViewerBanner at 0 %, and a bundle path exercised only in the browser tier where this measurement cannot see it. Twenty-three tests later: 86.89 / 86.88 / 78.12 / 85.18, and branches crosses a whole number and is raised 77 → 78. Worth recording that branches went down before it went up - a sprint of refusal paths adds branches faster than a sprint of tests covers them, and the floor is what makes the second half happen.
  • What it measures. 2,419 headless and 196 browser tests, against 2,361 and 186 at the end of K1. Fourteen budgets within limits, two raised with reasons, and every gate green.
K3

Still there with the network off

delivered1 wk

Objective. The shell boots from cache, assets join the cache as they are used, and the browser is allowed to offer an install.

  • A service worker over the built shell, with the catalog packs and models cached on use rather than precached — public/ is 19.35 MB and precaching it would be a worse first visit in exchange for a better second one.
  • An install prompt, offered rather than nagged.
  • The draft and the library are already offline, which is what makes this a shell problem rather than a data one.
ACCEPTANCE
  • A second load with the network disabled reaches an editable plan
  • A deploy invalidates the cache — asserted, because a stale shell against a new asset tree is the failure mode this feature has
LANDING — K3, offline, and the rule the check disproved
  • Three strategies, because there are three kinds of URL, and the difference between them is not whether to cache but what staleness means. The document is network-first, so a deploy is picked up the moment somebody reloads. Content-addressed assets — index-BUHeTH6a.js — are cache-first and cannot be stale by construction; this is the one place “cache forever” is a fact rather than a hope. Everything else the app serves keeps its name across deploys, so it is stale-while-revalidate: the stored copy is served instantly and a fresh one lands behind it.
  • There is no per-deploy cache wipe, and that is a choice. The obvious design stamps a version at build time and deletes every other cache on activate. It needs a build step, it re-downloads everything after a deploy that changed one file, and it is less correct: it makes staleness a property of the deploy rather than of the resource. CACHE_VERSION exists for the much rarer thing — a change to the rules themselves — and is bumped by hand with a reason, exactly like STORE_VERSION in the persistence layer.
  • Source maps are never cached, and the number is why. They are 7,408,803 bytes across eight files — 36.1 % of the deploy — and the only thing that ever asks for one is a devtools panel somebody opened on purpose. Caching them would roughly triple what an offline copy costs to hold.
  • “Nothing is precached” was written, and the acceptance check disproved it. npm run offline:check failed at the reload with net::ERR_FAILED, for a structural reason rather than an incidental one: a worker does not control the navigation that installed it. The document, the module entry and the stylesheet are all fetched before the worker exists, so a cache holding 2.3 MB of models was unreachable because the three files that name them were missing. install now precaches exactly those, and the note in cache_policy.js says it was found by running the check rather than by thinking about it.
  • What to precache is read out of the document, not from a build manifest. shellAssets parses the module entry and the stylesheets out of index.html — which Vite generates and which is therefore the authority on what the shell is. A manifest would be a second list of the same thing kept in step by hope. The lazily-imported chunks are deliberately absent: GTAOPass and design_bundle are deferred precisely so a boot does not pay for them, and precaching them would undo that on the install instead.
  • A second entry, unhashed, at the deploy root. A worker's URL is both its identity and its scope: hashed, a deploy would register a different worker rather than update the installed one, and a worker under assets/ would control every URL the application does not serve. Built rather than dropped into public/ so it can import the policy the headless suite tests — a copied file would have meant either a second copy of those rules or a hand-rolled inliner, and the first is how two implementations of one decision start.
LANDING — K3, the check that is the sprint · programme K closed
  • Both acceptance clauses are one command. npm run offline:check serves dist-demo/ from a plain Node server with cache-control: no-store on everything — an HTTP cache would make this pass whether or not a worker existed, which is the one thing it must not do — then takes the browser offline rather than stopping the server, which would leave the page a live socket and prove less.
  • It asks questions only a working application can answer. The shell rendered, the plan canvas is there, twelve tools drew, a worker is in control, and the draw tool arms and takes a click. “Reaches an editable plan” is a claim about editing, and the difference between a picture and an application is whether the next click does anything.
  • And it names the gap rather than hiding it. Five files cannot be reached on a first-visit-then-offline run — the four room textures and asset-manifest.json — because they are fetched while the worker is still activating. The application is fully usable without them and the next online visit caches them, but a silent hole is how “works offline” becomes a claim nobody checked.
  • The second clause is asserted in the half that matters. A deploy cannot be simulated by rebuilding mid-run, so the server gets an overlay: different bytes at the same URL is exactly what a deploy does to a browser. Both halves are checked, and the second is the one worth having — that an online reload shows the new build is obvious; that the cached copy was replaced too is what stops a version being picked up online and reverting the next time somebody is offline, which is the failure nothing would ever report.
  • An install offer, once. beforeinstallprompt is kept rather than allowed to fire, because preventing it is what buys the right to ask later and where it fits; the offer goes in the toast stack rather than becoming new chrome, and it is raised once, because a browser that keeps asking is why people learn to dismiss without reading. An update is offered and never applied — the same distinction useAutosave draws about a recovered draft.
  • The icons are rendered, not committed. One SVG — the accent square and lucide's ruler, the two elements the top bar has carried since S7 — through the same headless chromium the thumbnails use. Full bleed for the maskable one, so a platform cropping it to a circle keeps the glyph: 6.9 % of the tile is ink and it sits inside the middle 80 %.
  • One coverage exclusion, and it is checkable. src/app/sw.js is twenty lines of addEventListener; every decision it makes is in src/app/offline/ and is covered by 31 cases over three strategies, five pass-through rules, precaching, the shell fallback and a browser that refuses a cache. Whether the exclusion is honest is a question about how thin that file is, which is why it is that thin.
  • What it measures. 2,467 headless and 196 browser tests. first-load 410.8 → 411.7 KiB for the registration and the two notices, well inside the limit K2 raised. Fifteen gates green, two of them new: icons:check and offline:check.
  • Programme K is delivered, all three sprints. K1 gave a design a name, a picture and somewhere to live; K2 gave it a link and a way to be looked at without being touched; K3 means none of it needs a network. RM-007 asked for “many designs, starter plans, a link to send — and none of it behind a login, because there is no login”, and there is still no login and still no server.

Three and a half weeks, unchanged from RM-007: 1.5 + 1 + 1. Y-3's repair is inside K1's 1.5 rather than beside it, and Y-6 and Y-7 each removed something the sprints would otherwise have had to build — a quota policy and a compression dependency — which is what paid for it.

DELIVERED — K1, five commits
  • 2,361 headless and 186 browser tests, against 2,309 and 174 before the sprint. Fourteen budget lines within limits, one of them new, and first-load did not move — which for a programme about content nobody has asked for yet is the correct outcome rather than a good one. Wrong, and corrected by K2. npm run budget was run without rebuilding, so it measured the dist from before the sprint. Re-measured on a fresh build at 73a4251: 401.9 → 407.5 KiB, so K1 cost 5.6 KiB. What did not move is the templates, which is what M-47 asserts and what Y-5 was about — the library UI is product surface and belongs in the payload. The claim was too broad and the measurement behind it was stale; both are K2's to fix and are fixed there.
  • Every gate green: lint, typecheck, ledger:check, catalog:check, catalog:cost:check, manifest:check, encode:check, thumbnails:check, admit:check, materials:audit:check, oracle:check, templates:check and budget. The type ledger went 137 → 142 files, all checked, still zero errors.
  • The save format gained nothing, which is the first time in eight programmes and is Y-2 rather than restraint: the format would have taken a name silently and lost it. M-26 holds by doing nothing.
  • Five findings became assertions rather than notes. Y-1 is a test that a draft survives the library; Y-3 is a throw and the three tests it caught; Y-4 is the tile's aspect and the arrow it does not draw; Y-5 is M-47, and Y-6 is the absence of a quota manager, stated in code.
§ 60 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskSprintWhat is done about it
The project store is added to architect3d and every rollback loses its draftK1Y-1 measured the refusal in both directions. A separate database at version 1, and an acceptance clause that a build without K1 still reads its draft after the library has been used
A name is put in the save format, and a design opened elsewhere comes back unnamedK1Y-2 measured the drop: ok: true, no warnings, four keys gone. The record carries identity; the document is untouched, which is also M-26
A thumbnail is rendered from whatever view happens to be mounted, and the grid fills with pictures of the wrong planK1Y-3 is the measurement that says this is possible and silent. The capture happens on save, and the two export functions stop accepting arguments that disagree
Thumbnails as PNG, and thirty projects weigh half a megabyteK1Y-4 priced all three formats in Chromium. WebP, with a PNG fallback, and the record's size is part of what stats() reports
Templates go in the bundle because they are small, and first-load loses 41 % of its marginK1M-47 is a resource assertion, not a size limit: a boot that fetches a template fails the suite. The same instrument M-43 has used against packs since RM-011
A browser that refuses IndexedDB shows an empty library and no explanationK1The refusal is a result, not an exception — A5's rule, reused. The localStorage fallback cannot hold a library, and saying so is the correct behaviour rather than a degraded one
A shared link outgrows what a browser will takeK2Y-7's table is the size curve. The refusal states the length; it does not truncate a design into a plausible, broken one
A service worker serves a stale shell against a redeployed asset treeK3Cache invalidation on deploy is an acceptance clause rather than an implementation detail, because it is this feature's whole failure mode

What must not change

The save format stays exactly what it is. This is the first programme in eight that adds no key to it at all, and Y-2 is the reason: the format would have taken one silently and dropped it. A design exported from the library is byte-identical to the same design exported before the library existed, and that is M-26's rule holding by doing nothing rather than by being careful.

The draft keeps working, at version 1, with its seven-day expiry and its one slot. A project library does not replace autosave — a named project is something a person decided to keep, and a draft is what protects them between those decisions. useAutosave's own note has said so since A5 and it is still right.

And first-load does not move. It has been the thinnest line in the budget since RM-011 added it, it has now caught two features before they were written — X-3's metadata and Y-5's templates — and the correct outcome for a programme about content nobody has asked for yet is that the number is the same afterwards. Half wrong, and K2 measured which half. What must not enter the payload is content, and none did: the starter plans are fetched and M-47 asserts it, and the zip container is a 2,065-byte chunk behind a dynamic import because this line caught it. What did enter is product — a library, a shelf, a share dialog, a viewer — for 8.9 KiB across K1 and K2, and the line was raised deliberately with the per-commit breakdown recorded in tools/budget.json. The sentence should have said that content does not move it; a programme that adds features to the shell moves it by definition.

PROGRAMME L · DRAWING Nº RM-014

1,818 words, and the package that speaks English

RM-007 calls programme L “everyone: onboarding, help, other languages, and keyboard-only operation” and prices it at 4 weeks in four sprints, one of which rev B already withdrew. Seven measurements against the tree first, and they move the programme in both directions. The words are countable and they are not the problem: 327 distinct user-facing strings, 1,818 words, 5,466 gzipped bytes a language — against 14,359 of first-load headroom, so a language is fetched rather than bundled, which is the third time this programme set has reached that answer. 54 of those words are the library's, and it is a published package: messages in src/scripts that no dictionary in src/app can reach, which is the finding that takes L3 past a week. And two of L4's three clauses are in different states — reduced motion is already delivered by one media query, and the plan has no keyboard path at all: five pointer listeners, a dblclick, and a keydown that handles Escape and Shift. Three sprints, 3 weeks becomes 3.5, and the reason is one hook in the library. Two sprints, and 2 weeks. L3 is withdrawn on 2026-08-20: the product stays in English, permanently, and a drawing whose headline is a word count now describes a sprint that will not be built. The measurements below stand — they were run, and they are facts about this tree whether or not anything is translated. What is withdrawn is the plan they fed. The half-week Z-2 added goes with it, and the hook it added it for was built, proven and then reverted to the byte; § 63 records what that cost and what it showed.

§ 61 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What counting the words changed about the programme

Seven measurements against the tree at ab7e466, every one of them produced by running something: an extractor over every template and script in src/, four greps whose output is a census rather than a sample, and the budget tool. Two findings make a sprint cheaper, one makes a sprint bigger, and one says a clause is already delivered.

327
distinct user-facing strings — 1,818 words, 5,466 B gzipped as a keyed catalogue
54 of them
are in src/scripts, which is a published package. No dictionary in the application reaches them
14,359 B
what first-load has left. Two bundled languages would take 76 % of it

keydown handlers on either canvas. The one keyboard-operable custom control is the pane splitter
31 tips
AppTip uses across six components, each carrying its own shortcut. The hints L2 is priced for largely exist
