The programme survives its own measurement, and what moves is where the week goes. RM-007 gap Q-14 groups four things under “no offline, no share without a file, no help written for users, one language”; K2 and K3 took the first two and this takes the rest. Every clause is still true. What the measurement adds is that none of these three sprints is where its own name suggests. L2 is not a hints sprint — there are 31 hints already and they carry their shortcuts; it is a tour and, mostly, writing, because this repository has five documentation pages and all five are for developers. L3 is not a strings sprint — the strings are 4.5 kB and an afternoon's extraction; it is an architecture question about a library that produces English prose for a person to read. And L4 is two-thirds a keyboard sprint and one-third already shipped.

The arithmetic that decides how a language arrives. The 327 strings are 14,191 bytes as a keyed catalogue and 5,466 gzipped. first-load stands at 427,341 against a limit of 441,700, so it has 14,359 bytes left. Two more languages, bundled beside English, is 10,932 bytes of that — 76 % of everything the payload has, spent on words 100 % of visitors will never read at least two-thirds of. So a language pack is fetched on demand and only English is bundled, because English is the fallback and a fallback that has to arrive over a network is not one. That is the same answer RM-012 J2 reached for catalog packs and RM-013 K1 reached for starter plans, and it is the third time the instrument that will assert it is M-43: a boot fetches nothing nobody asked for.

The finding that makes L3 bigger. src/scripts is not a private folder — it is the package this repository publishes, with its own entry point and its own consumers, and it contains 54 distinct messages written for a person to read: Scene.addItem's refusals (“this build does not ship that asset…”, “was imported from a file, and that file is not on this computer”), every path in DesignDocument's validator, and the retired-format message. They reach a person as free text inside a toast, so the application cannot translate them at the boundary without pattern-matching English prose. A dictionary in src/app is therefore not enough, and the answer has to be a seam in the library — which is a decision, not a line, and it is why 1 week becomes 1.5.

And the clause that is already delivered. RM-007 lists “reduced motion” as a third of L4. One @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block in app.css already sets animation-duration, animation-iteration-count and transition-duration with !important on *, *::before and *::after, which reaches every one of the tree's 6 animations and 7 transitions. The only motion in the application that CSS cannot reach is OrbitControls.enableDamping at dampingFactor 0.5. So that clause is one conditional in three/main.js, and the week it was priced at goes to the keyboard instead.

§ 62 · DECISION LOG

Seven findings, and what each one does to the plan

Findings take the letter Z, the last unused capital in this document set. Two make a sprint cheaper, one makes a sprint bigger, one is an architecture decision the drawing takes rather than defers, and three are censuses that replace an assumption with a number.

NºFindingSeverityMethodSprint
Z-1327 strings, 5,466 gzipped bytes a language, against 14,359 of headroom — so a language is fetchedmedextractor over every template and script; gzip -9; budget toolL3
Z-2The library produces 54 user-facing messages and is a published package. L3 needs a seam in it, not a dictionary beside ithighsrc/scripts censused for every message routeL3
Z-320 of 33 toasts are assembled from variables, so interpolation and plurals are day one rather than a later additionmedevery toasts.* call classifiedL3
Z-4Units are a second localisation surface and are not strings: the suffixes and the decimal point are hard-coded in the librarymedDimensioning.cmToMeasure read branch by branch; toLocaleString sites countedL3
Z-5Neither canvas is focusable and neither takes a key. The one keyboard-operable custom control is the pane splitter — and half of drawing already workshighevery listener on the plan canvas enumerated; tabindex counted across src/appL4
Z-6Reduced motion is already delivered for CSS. The one exception is OrbitControls dampingcheaperthe media query read against a count of every animation and transitionL4
Z-7The hints and the shortcut sheet exist and the anchors exist. What does not exist is one sentence written for a person using the plannercheaperAppTip uses, bindings and stable ids counted; docs/ readL2

Z-1 to Z-4 outlived their sprint, and that is the distinction this log exists to draw. All four are measurements against this tree and all four are still true: the words are still 327, the library still writes 54 messages a person reads, 20 of 33 toasts are still assembled, and cmToMeasure still writes 1.5 m as 1.5m. What is withdrawn on 2026-08-20 is L3, the sprint that would have acted on them — so the severities describe a cost nobody is now paying and the sprint column is struck. Z-4 in particular changes meaning rather than lapsing: a hard-coded decimal point is a defect only if somebody expects a comma, and in an English-only product it is simply the format. Kept in full, in the shape Q-7 is kept, so it is not rediscovered later as a bug.

Z-1 · The words, counted med measured

An extractor over every .vue and .js file in src/ — template text nodes with interpolations removed, the four attributes a person reads (aria-label, title, placeholder, alt), and the strings handed to toasts.* and throw new Error — finds 307 occurrences of 273 distinct strings in src/app, and a second pass over src/scripts by the routes the library actually uses adds 54 more. Together: 327 distinct strings, 1,818 words, 14,191 bytes as a keyed catalogue and 5,466 gzipped. The longest is 236 characters; the five longest are all explanatory paragraphs in inspector panels, which is the kind of prose that is expensive to translate and cheap to store.

It is an undercount and says so. A sentence assembled from three variables is not caught, and Z-3 is the measurement of how often that happens. The number is therefore a floor, which is the right direction for a budget decision.

first-load stands at 427,341 bytes against a limit of 441,700, so it has 14,359 left. Two additional bundled languages is 10,932 — 76 % of the payload's whole remaining headroom, charged to every visitor for words most of them will never read. L2 has since spent 2,996 of that headroom, so the figure to plan L3 against is 11,363 and the two languages are 96 % of it. The reading and the decision are unchanged; the margin behind the decision is not, and the number here was measured before the sprint that moved it. So the decision the drawing takes is the one J2 and K1 both took: English is bundled because it is the fallback; every other language is a file fetched when it is chosen. At 5.5 kB a language, thirty languages would cost the payload nothing. Zero languages cost it nothing either, and that is the decision as it stands from 2026-08-20. The arithmetic was sound and the answer it produced — fetch, do not bundle — was never wrong; it simply has nothing left to apply to.

Z-2 · The library speaks English, and it is somebody else's dependency high measured

src/scripts carries 54 distinct messages written for a person to read, 3,666 bytes, by four routes: Scene's failed(…) refusals, the message field of every DesignDocument validation problem, a handful of console.error lines, and thrown Errors. They are not diagnostics that leak — the application deliberately surfaces them: useDesignIO puts firstProblem(result) straight into a toast, and it has done since RM-003 A1 made a bad file a list of problems rather than an exception.

So the application cannot translate them. It receives finished English prose and would have to match on it, which is the worst kind of coupling: a message improved in the library silently stops being translated. And src/scripts cannot import a dictionary from src/app, because the one-way arrow between them is a constraint this document set has held for eight programmes.

The drawing takes the decision rather than deferring it. The library gains a message catalogue on the runtime, beside assets, localModels, configuration and renderProfile — the same shape, for the same reason, and with the same default: supply nothing and it produces byte-identical English to what it produces today. That is a seam an embedder can also use, which is the test of whether it belongs in a library at all. It is a decision rather than a line, and it is why L3 is priced at 1.5 weeks instead of 1. Built, proven, and then unbuilt. The seam was written exactly as drawn here — runtime.text(source, params) beside assets and localModels, with the source English as its own key — and it did what this paragraph claims it would: the whole suite passed unaltered, including the document-loading tests that assert exact validation text, which is byte-identical English demonstrated rather than promised. One correction the building made to the drawing, and it is worth keeping: the seam does not fit DesignDocument, because a validator has no document to belong to — it runs before one exists. It took parse(json, {messages}) instead. And the census refines by audience: of 65 message sites, 50 reach a person and 15 are developer diagnostics, and translating an exception somebody greps for is worse than leaving it. All of it is reverted; the finding is what remains.

Z-3 · Two-thirds of the messages are assembled med measured

Of 33 toasts.* calls, 20 are template literals carrying a ${} and 13 are whole strings. The application also writes plurals by hand in at least three places — “1 imported model is not on this computer” against “2 imported models are…”, and the same shape for bundle contents and for template counts.

A scaffold that started with whole strings and added interpolation later would have to be rewritten by the second language, because word order moves: the count that leads an English sentence does not lead a German one. So the catalogue is keyed with named parameters and a plural selector from the first commit, and the extraction pass converts the twenty rather than deferring them.

Z-4 · Units are a second surface, and they are not strings med measured

Dimensioning.cmToMeasure renders a length by concatenation: 'cm', 'm', 'mm', and ' and " for feet and inches, with JavaScript's own decimal point. So 1.5 m is 1.5m in every locale, and a German reader expects 1,5 m. There are only 4 toLocaleString call sites in the whole tree and all four are in one dialog, plus 2 toLocaleDateString for the project library's dates — so almost nothing on screen is locale-aware today.

This is library code, and it is the same seam as Z-2 rather than a second mechanism: a formatter on the runtime, defaulting to what it does now. Worth naming separately because it is the half of L3 that a string extraction pass does not find, and the half that makes the difference visible on a screen with no words on it at all. Also built and also reverted: Dimensioning briefly carried a decimal separator defaulting to a full stop. In an English-only product it had no second value to take, and a String.replace on every dimension the plan draws is not free. The measurement stands; the mechanism is gone.

Z-5 · The plan takes no keys, and the splitter takes all of them high measured

The floorplanner attaches five pointer listeners and a dblclick to its canvas, and two keyboard listeners to document — which handle Escape and Shift, and nothing else: keyDown sets gridsnapmode from the shift key and keyUp clears it and calls escapeKey(). Neither canvas carries a tabindex, so neither is in the tab order.

The application has exactly one tabindex="0", and it is the split-pane divider — which is fully operable, with role="separator", aria-orientation, live aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a @keydown. That is the pattern the plan needs, already written, on the least important control in the workspace.

And half of keyboard drawing already exists. PlanOverlay shows the length of the wall being drawn in an editable field and commits a typed value on Enter or Tab, through Dimensioning.cmFromMeasureRaw. So a person can already say how long without touching a mouse; what they cannot say is where to start and which way to go. The sprint is a cursor and a direction, not a drawing tool.

Z-6 · Reduced motion is delivered, and the exception is not CSS cheaper measured

One block in src/app/styles/app.css matches *, *::before and *::after under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and sets animation-duration: 0.01ms, animation-iteration-count: 1 and transition-duration: 0.01ms, each with !important. The tree declares 6 animations, 4 keyframe sets and 7 transitions, and the query reaches every one of them.

What it cannot reach is motion produced by JavaScript, and there is exactly one source: three/main.js sets controls.enableDamping = true with dampingFactor = 0.5, so the 3D camera keeps gliding after the pointer stops. That is the whole of L4's third clause — a media-query read and a conditional — and the week RM-007 priced for it goes to Z-5.

Z-7 · The hints exist, the anchors exist, the words do not cheaper measured

RM-007 prices L2 as “a first-run tour, contextual hints, help pages”. The middle one is largely built: 31 AppTip uses across six components, and AppTip is not a title attribute — it is Reka's tooltip with the shortcut rendered as key chips beside the text, so the hint and the binding cannot disagree. The shortcut sheet is the same idea again: 36 bindings in three groups, and the dialog is generated from the binding table rather than written beside it.

The anchors exist too. The shell carries 13 stable ids — #app-shell, #tool-rail, #workspace, #floorplanner, #viewer, #inspector, #status-bar, #viewcube and five more — and PopoverRoot is already in the bundle, imported by two components. A tour is therefore a list of anchors and a step index, with no dependency added and nothing new to lay out.

What is missing is prose. docs/ holds five pages — index, getting-started, architecture, events, save-format — and every one of them is written for somebody integrating the library. There is not one sentence anywhere in this repository addressed to a person drawing a room. The VitePress site that would host it already builds and already deploys under /architect3d/docs/. So L2's cost is writing, and the sprint should be planned as writing with a little code around it rather than the reverse.

§ 63 · SPRINTS L2–L4

Three and a half weeks, and the half is a seam in the library

RM-007 priced programme L at 4 weeks in four sprints and rev B struck L1, leaving 3. The total goes to 3.5: Z-2 adds half a week to L3, Z-6 gives a third of a week back from L4, and Z-7 changes what L2's week is spent on without changing how much of it there is. Two weeks, and no seam. L3 is withdrawn on 2026-08-20 with its own half-week, so the programme is L2 at 1 week — delivered — and L4 at two-thirds, against RM-007's 4. The heading is left as it was written, because it was right when it was written and the drawing is cumulative.

L2

The first five minutes, and the pages nobody has written

deliveredZ-71 wk

Objective. Somebody who has never seen this application draws a room and puts a chair in it, without being told how by a person.

  • A tour over anchors that already exist (Z-7). Thirteen stable ids and PopoverRoot already in the bundle, so this is a step list and an index, not a dependency. Dismissible at every step, and never shown twice — the flag goes beside the four architect3d.* keys localStorage already holds, which is a mechanism rather than a new one.
  • The hints stay as they are. 31 of them, each carrying its shortcut, generated from the same binding table as the shortcut sheet. What they gain is coverage of the empty states — an empty project library, a catalog with no favourites, a plan with no walls — which is where a first-time user actually is.
  • Help written in the second person, in the VitePress site that already deploys, linked from the shell. Five pages exist and all five are for developers; this is the sprint's real cost and it is writing.
  • Not a video, not a sample-design gallery. K1 already ships five templates and two furnished samples behind a click, which is the demonstration a tour would otherwise have to fake.
ACCEPTANCE
  • A boot with a cleared profile shows the tour once; the next boot does not, and neither does a reload mid-tour
  • Every step's anchor is asserted to exist against the mounted shell, so a renamed id fails the suite rather than producing an empty popover
  • axe passes with the tour open, in all three layouts — a popover over a non-modal panel is exactly where a focus scope goes wrong, which RM-013 K2 already found once
  • The help link resolves against the deployed docs base, checked rather than assumed
LANDING — L2, the words this application had never said
  • Z-7 held, and the tour cost no dependency. Reka's PopoverAnchor takes a reference element rather than requiring the popover to wrap its trigger, and PopoverRoot was already in the bundle for two other components — so a tour is a step index and a resolved element, and it inherits Escape, the focus scope and collision handling from the primitive the rest of the application already uses. Six steps over thirteen ids that existed and one that did not: #top-bar, added to the one landmark in the shell without an id.
  • The step list is data, and that IS the acceptance clause. A renamed id produces a popover pointing at nothing — reported as “the tour is broken” and impossible to reproduce from a screenshot. It is checked three ways, each catching what the others cannot: the gate greps every id= in src/app and runs in CI with no DOM; the headless suite asserts every step has a title, a body under 260 characters and a layout that exists; and the browser tier resolves each anchor against a mounted shell, which is the only one of the three that can tell a rendered id from a written one.
  • Two steps borrow the layout and give it back. AppWorkspace keeps both panes mounted at all times and closes one by giving it no width — its own note says why: a pane hidden with v-if measures zero and cannot be sized when it returns. So #viewer exists in the plan layout and is not a thing to point at. A step names the layout that shows it, and whatever the person had is restored exactly once, whether the tour ended by finishing, by skipping, or by Escape.
  • The evidence check was wrong, and only the browser tier could have found it. The first version decided whether somebody had been here before by asking indexedDB.databases() whether any of the three stores existed. On a genuinely clean profile the tour did not appear, and the reason is structural: the application creates all three during boot — useAutosave opens the draft store, useProjects lists the library, model_store reads its index. Existence proves the application started, which is not a question worth asking. It is now an argument: App.vue passes what it can actually see — a recovered draft, or a project in the library — and there is no IndexedDB code in the composable at all. jsdom has no databases(), so nothing headless could have caught this.
  • Skipping counts as an answer. Leaving early marks the tour seen, deliberately: an application that re-asks on the next boot is how people learn to dismiss without reading. It is in the help menu whenever they want it, which is what the last step points at.
  • The empty states were in a worse condition than the missing tour. With a shortlist selected and no search term, the catalog said Nothing matches “” — untrue, unhelpful, and in the one place a person is most likely to be lost. There are four states now, each in the words the interface itself uses: the chip says “Starred”, so the message says nothing starred yet rather than renaming it to “favourites” halfway down the panel. And the empty plan — reachable in one gesture by deleting the four walls the application starts you with — said nothing at all; it now names the key that draws a wall and the key that brings back what you deleted.
  • 2,225 words in four pages, where this repository had none. Z-7's finding was that all five existing documentation pages address somebody integrating the library. These address somebody drawing a room, they live in the VitePress site that already builds and deploys, and npm run help:check is gate sixteen: every page the shell links has a source on disk, every page is reachable from the site's own navigation, and every tour anchor is an id a component renders. What it does not check, and says so: that the site is deployed at the base the application computes. That is a Pages workflow and a DNS record, and asserting it here would be asserting that a constant equals itself.
  • What it cost, and what that does to L3. first-load 427,341 → 430,337 gzipped bytes, +2,996, measured on a fresh build. The four help pages are not in that number at all — they are on the documentation site, which the payload does not carry. The consequence is for the sprint after this one: Z-1 priced two bundled languages at 10,932 bytes against 14,359 of headroom, which was 76 %. Against the 11,363 that is left it is 96 %. L3's fetch, do not bundle has stopped being a preference.
  • And one finding recorded rather than fixed, because it belongs to a different sprint. vitest.browser.config.mjs registers the Vue plugin and not the Tailwind one, so @import 'tailwindcss' resolves to nothing and the whole browser tier runs unstyled — #app-shell measures 8,374 px tall there, because h-screen is not a rule. Nothing existing depends on it: axe reads the accessibility tree and the pixel tests read a WebGL framebuffer, neither of which needs a stylesheet. But it makes getBoundingClientRect useless as a test of whether anything is visible in that tier, which is why L2's own check reads the pane's inline width instead — inline styles being the one thing a missing stylesheet cannot take away.
  • Sprint L2 is closed. 2,601 headless and 214 browser tests — 30 and 8 of them new — sixteen gates green, fourteen budget lines within limits with none raised, and coverage at 87.33 statements, 87.35 lines, 78.74 branches, 85.74 functions. Every floor held and none crossed a whole number, so none moves.
L3

Two languages, and the package that speaks English

withdrawnZ-2Z-1Z-3Z-41.5 wk 0

Objective. The application is readable in a language that is not English, including the sentences the library writes and the numbers nobody thinks of as words.

  • A catalogue keyed and interpolated from the first commit (Z-3). Named parameters and a plural selector, because 20 of 33 toasts are assembled and word order moves between languages. The extraction pass converts those twenty rather than leaving them for the second language to discover.
  • English bundled, everything else fetched (Z-1). 5,466 gzipped bytes a language against 14,359 of first-load headroom: bundling two more would spend 76 % of the payload's remaining room on words most visitors never read. English stays in the bundle because a fallback that arrives over a network is not a fallback.
  • A message catalogue on the runtime (Z-2), beside assets and localModels, defaulting to the English src/scripts produces today. This is the half-week the drawing adds, and it is the only way the 54 messages the library writes can be translated without the application matching on English prose.
  • Units through the same seam (Z-4). cmToMeasure's suffixes and decimal point are the half of localisation a string extractor does not find, and the half a person notices on a screen with no sentences on it.
  • The document follows the choice: <html lang>, the page title, and the web manifest's name, short_name and description, which RM-013 K3 added and which an installed app shows under its icon.
  • Not RTL. The two languages are chosen left-to-right on purpose; mirroring a two-pane CAD layout is a sprint of its own and pretending otherwise would ship a half-mirrored plan. Recorded as declined-for-now rather than omitted.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-49 (new): a boot in the default language fetches no language file, and a boot in the second fetches exactly one — asserted on the M-43 instrument, performance.getEntriesByType('resource'), which is the third feature to be held to it
  • first-load does not move by more than the renderer, and the renderer is interpolation over a Map rather than a library
  • Every string in the census has a key, checked by a gate that fails on a bare literal in a template — in the shape of the fifteen gates that already run
  • The library with no catalogue supplied produces byte-identical English to this commit, asserted over all 54 messages
  • A length reads 1,5 m under a comma locale and 1.5m under English, from the same call
WITHDRAWN — L3, and the scaffold that was built before it was cancelled
  • The decision, and what kind of decision it is. The application stays in English. That is a judgement about who this tool is for, taken by the owner on 2026-08-20, and it is not a deferral — there is no date on which L3 returns and no condition that revives it. The card above is left exactly as it was drawn, struck rather than deleted, in the shape rev B left L1 and Q-7. A roadmap that silently loses a sprint is a roadmap nobody can audit.
  • RM-007 nominated this cut itself. The if time is short table has listed L3 at the top of five since rev A — “languages other than English, 1 wk”. So this is the roadmap’s own first contingency being exercised, and the only surprise is the reason: not a shortage of weeks, but the recognition that the second reader was never coming.
  • What existed when the decision arrived. The engineering half was committed and pushed as f283d5c: 42 files, +953 / −296. A message catalogue on the runtime with the source English as its own key, DesignDocument.parse(json, {messages}) threaded through six validators, a decimal separator on Dimensioning, a locale store that fetched rather than bundled, a language chooser in the settings panel, and 240 template sites keyed on the sentences they already contained. It reached amit and no further — never dev, never master, so no deployed build ever offered a language.
  • What it cost to unbuild, measured rather than asserted. The revert is 296 insertions and 953 deletions across the same 42 files, and the tree it produces hashes to e711695 — which is, byte for byte, the tree of cf70abb, the commit before L3 began. Not approximately reverted. npm run lint, npm run typecheck and ledger:check are clean at 0 / 0, and 2,601 tests in 82 files pass. first-load cannot have moved, and that is a proof from the tree hash rather than a number quoted from a previous sprint.
  • Why none of the scaffold was kept, which was the real question. Every line of it existed to serve a reader who is not coming, and a scaffold with no second language is not neutral — it is a standing tax. The decimal separator has no comma locale to serve and puts a String.replace on every dimension the plan draws. say('a design must be an object, not {value}') is strictly more indirection than the template literal it replaced, for identical output. And 240 t('…') wrappers put every sentence in the shell one grep further from the person editing it. The gate that would have made it stick — fail on a bare literal in a template — would have made the tax compulsory for every string written from then on. Keeping a disused abstraction because it was expensive is how a codebase acquires the things nobody can explain.
  • What the sprint proved before it was cancelled, and it is worth the record. The whole suite passed unaltered — including the document-loading tests that assert exact validation text — across a change that routed every message in the application and 50 in the library through a catalogue. That was L3’s hardest acceptance clause, byte-identical English, and it was met by construction rather than by a table being kept in step. Recorded because it says the seam Z-2 designed was the right shape, not because anything will now use it.
  • What was never built at all. Roughly 196 script-side strings in the composables and the tour, the two language files (~3,600 words), the extraction gate, and M-49. The sprint stopped where it did on purpose: the next piece was 3,600 words of German and French that this repository has no way to verify. A gate can check that a catalogue is complete; nothing here can check that it is right. That is the same limit the drawing already recorded under what was not run, reached from the other side.
  • M-49 is retired unclaimed, and its number is not reused. L4 keeps M-50. Metrics in this document set are numbered when they are written, and renumbering to close a gap would make every earlier reference a lie for the sake of tidiness.
  • Sixteen gates stay sixteen. L3 was to add the seventeenth; it adds none. No threshold moved in either direction, no coverage floor changed, and the four floors stay where J3 left them at 87 / 87 / 78 / 85. Programme L is L4 and nothing else.
L4

Drawing without a pointer, and the clause already delivered

deliveredZ-5Z-61 wk

Objective. A wall can be drawn, moved and deleted with no pointer at all — and the application stops moving for somebody who asked it to.

  • The plan becomes focusable and gains a cursor (Z-5). Arrow keys move it by the grid step, shift for a coarse step, Enter places, Escape cancels. The pattern is already written on the pane splitter — tabindex, a role, live aria-valuenow, a @keydown — and it is the application's only keyboard-operable custom control today.
  • One drawing implementation, not two. The keyboard path synthesises into the same mousedown/mousemove/mouseup the pointer uses, so snapping, the read-only guards RM-013 K2 added and every existing test apply unchanged. A second path would be a second set of bugs.
  • Typed length already works (Z-5) — PlanOverlay commits on Enter or Tab mid-draw. The sprint's job is to make the rest of the gesture reach it, not to build it.
  • Focus order and a skip link over the 125 controls the shell and inspector expose, and a visible focus state on the two canvases now that they can hold focus.
  • The one motion CSS cannot reach (Z-6): OrbitControls.enableDamping, off under prefers-reduced-motion. One conditional, and the rest of the clause is already delivered.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-50 (new): a room is drawn, an item is selected and moved, and a wall is deleted, with no pointer event dispatched at all — asserted in the browser tier, where a synthesised pointer event would be the easy way to make it pass and is therefore what the test forbids
  • axe keeps passing in all three layouts, with its exclusions still exactly the two drawing surfaces — a canvas that has become focusable must not be excused by widening the list
  • The pane splitter's behaviour is unchanged, because it is the pattern being copied and a regression in it would be invisible
  • Damping is off under a reduced-motion preference and on without one, read back from the controls rather than from the CSS
LANDING — L4, the plan without a pointer · programme L closed
  • Z-5's seam was half-built, and L4 finished it rather than starting one. RM-008 E2 pulled placeDrawTarget out of mouseup — its note says why: “so that typing a length is the same act as clicking, rather than a second implementation of it that drifts”. This is the same move one level up. The keyboard does not draw; it moves a point and presses it, through the same mousedown, mousemove and mouseup a pointer goes through. The measurement that made it cheap: those three methods read three fields off an event and no others — clientX, clientY, and pointerType for the touch branch. So the synthetic press is an object with two numbers on it, and snapping, alignment guides, angle snap and the single undo entry a drag commits on release are all inherited rather than rewritten.
  • The read-only gate holds without being told the keyboard exists. RM-013 K2 wrote three guards for a pointer; a keyboard session in a read-only plan places nothing and moves nothing, and not one line of K2 was touched. That is the test which makes “one drawing implementation” a fact rather than an intention, and it is why the whole of Z-5 cost 106 lines of code in the library. The commit adds 275 lines to floorplanner.js; 158 of them are the comment explaining which three fields an event needs and why a grab is a held press — a ratio worth the space in the class that owns the 2D view's whole interaction state.
  • The cursor cannot drift from where it acts. _cursorEvent projects through convertX/convertY — the pair the view already draws every corner and every wall with, and the exact inverse of the line in mousemove that turns a client coordinate back into centimetres. So the ring on screen and the point the press lands on are one number through a function and its inverse. Asserted to nine decimal places, with the pane deliberately at (137, 89) rather than the origin: at (0, 0) a version that dropped the bounds offset entirely would round-trip perfectly and the assertion would be measuring nothing.
  • Click and drag are two keys, because they are two gestures. Enter presses and releases. Space presses and holds, arrows drag — mousemove drags precisely when mouseDown is true, so carrying needed no code at all — and Space again lets go, which is the moment mouseup commits one undo entry for the whole movement. Overloading Enter with both would have made selecting a wall and dragging it the same keystroke, told apart by what happened next.
  • The one keyboard map had already predicted this sprint, in a comment. useShortcuts skipped every repeat with the note “arrow-key nudging would want repeats, and would opt out here if it existed” — so the guard moved inside the lookup and became per-binding, which is exactly the opt-out it described. keyChips already rendered arrowup as an arrow glyph. Two things written by earlier sprints for a feature that did not exist yet, and both fit.
  • A disabled binding used to claim its key, and for an arrow that is wrong. The rule was written for Cmd+Z with an empty undo stack, which must not fall through to the browser's own undo, and it is right for any combination nothing else wants. An arrow is the opposite case: four other things on this page want it — the 3D camera pans, the pane splitter resizes, an inspector field moves its caret, a panel scrolls. So yieldWhenDisabled, set on the ten plan-cursor bindings and on nothing else. They stay in the map either way, because the map is also what the shortcuts sheet renders and opening the sheet takes focus off the plan — bindings that existed only while the plan had focus would be documented nowhere a person could read them.
  • Z-6 was one conditional and one helper, and the helper is the part worth keeping. Damping is off under prefers-reduced-motion and on without it, read back off the controls rather than out of the stylesheet. Two decisions in prefersReducedMotion(): a host with no matchMedia answers false, because an environment that cannot be asked has not asked for anything and defaulting the other way would silently still every embedder on an older browser; and the preference is watched, not read once, because somebody who turns motion off in system settings expects the tab they left open to obey. The listener is torn down in dispose() with the other four.
  • The sprint turned up a live fault in the clause next door, and fixed it. OrbitControls bound its keydown to window, kept from the fork for parity with a note saying it preserved arrow-key panning “exactly where it worked before”. Where it worked before was everywhere: three's handler checks enabled and nothing else — not focus, not whether a caret is in a field. Measured on a live instance by counting _handleKeyDown calls:
    listener bound tokey on windowkey on the viewerkey in a focused input
    window — before111
    the element — L4010

    An arrow key pressed while renaming a room panned the 3D camera behind the dialog. L4 gives the plan the same four keys, so everywhere stopped being untidy and became ambiguous; scoped to the element, the answer is the one a keyboard user already expects. This broke a characterization test — unbinds its key listener on dispose, which counted on window — and the standing rule is that such a failure is a signal to re-check the change rather than edit the expectation. It was re-checked, the table above is the re-check, and the test is re-pointed at the element with the window count asserted at zero beside it, so widening the scope back fails here rather than quietly working.

  • M-50 is asserted by what did not happen. The easy way to make keyboard drawing pass is to synthesise a PointerEvent and dispatch it at the canvas, so the test forbids exactly that: a capture-phase tripwire on window counts fifteen event types — the five pointer events, the mouse compatibility set, and touch — and the count is zero after a session that reached the plan through the skip link, drew a four-walled room, carried an item two grid steps and deleted a wall. It runs in the browser tier because the thing that makes the tripwire worth having is real focus: whether a canvas can hold it, and what :focus-visible says when it does.
  • And one finding recorded rather than fixed, for the second sprint running. This sprint's first version of the focus-ring test read getComputedStyle(canvas).outlineOffset, expected the inset -2px, and got 0px — because vitest.browser.config.mjs still registers no Tailwind plugin, so @import 'tailwindcss' resolves to nothing and the whole browser tier runs unstyled. RM-014 L2 found this and recorded it as belonging to another sprint; L4 walked into it from a different direction and has left it there again, with the assertion changed to :focus-visible, which is a browser behaviour rather than a stylesheet. Two sprints is the point at which it stops being an oddity, and it is written here so the third does not rediscover it.
  • Sprint L4 is closed, and programme L with it. 2,630 headless and 218 browser tests — 29 and 4 of them new — sixteen gates green, and fourteen budget lines within limits with none raised. first-load 430,337 → 431,665 gzipped bytes, +1,328 on a fresh build, which is what operating the entire plan from the keyboard costs the payload; 10,035 bytes remain. Coverage at 87.77 statements, 87.78 lines, 79.28 branches, 86.03 functions, and two floors ratchet up — branches 78 → 79 and functions 85 → 86. Branches is the one worth explaining: a keyboard sprint should not obviously move it, and it moved because the keyboard adds almost no branches of its own — it walks the ones mousedown, mousemove and mouseup already had, several of which nothing had reached from that direction. Covering old branches is what a second way of driving the same code buys. Programme L is complete: L1 withdrawn in RM-007 rev B, L2 delivered, L3 withdrawn, L4 delivered.

Three of these six retire with L3 on 2026-08-20, and one of them was worth having anyway. The payload never paid for a translation library, because there was never a library — the renderer was interpolation over a Map, and the scaffold’s whole cost was reverted before first-load was ever measured against it. The one-way arrow held under exactly the pressure this table predicted: src/scripts took a catalogue as data and never learned that src/app exists, and the proof is that the library’s 2,601-test suite did not move by one assertion. The drift risk simply never opens, because there is no catalogue to drift out of. The two L4 rows stand.

What must not change

The save format is untouched. Nothing in this programme is persisted in a design — a language is a preference of the person, not a property of the building, and it goes where the theme and the layout already go. That makes this the second programme running to add no key at all, and the first to do so because there was never a candidate. Still true, and now trivially so: with L3 withdrawn the programme has no preference to store either.

The one-way arrow holds, and Z-2 is where it would have been easiest to break. src/scripts takes a catalogue as data on its runtime; it does not import one, and it does not learn that src/app exists. An embedder who supplies nothing gets the English the package ships today, byte for byte. It held, and then it was removed. The seam was built exactly as described, the suite proved the byte-for-byte clause, and the revert took it back out — so the package ships the same English it shipped before the sprint, by the shortest possible route.

first-load is the line this programme must not spend. It has 14,359 bytes left, it has now caught three features before they were written — J2's index, K1's templates and, in this drawing, two bundled languages — and a programme whose entire subject is content that most visitors will not use is exactly the programme that should leave it where it found it. It left it exactly where it found it. L2 spent 2,996 bytes on product; L3 spent none, and the tree hash after the revert is the proof rather than a fresh build’s number.

And the fifteen gates stay fifteen or grow. L3 adds one and L4 adds none; no threshold moves down, and the coverage floors stay where J3 left them at 87/87/78/85. L2 made them sixteen with help:check, and L3’s seventeenth is withdrawn with the sprint. So: sixteen, and L4 adds none. No threshold has moved down in either direction and the floors are unchanged.

PROGRAMME M · DRAWING Nº RM-015

802 draw calls, and an address that answers 404

RM-007 calls programme M “ship, and keep it fast”, prices it at 2 weeks in three sprints, and spreads it across the releases rather than giving it a block. Seven measurements first, and they leave the price almost alone while moving what two of the three sprints are actually for. Nothing has ever been published: both addresses the README advertises return 404, and it links to them nine times — so M1 is not re-targeting a working deploy, it is the first successful one this repository will have had. The furniture is not what costs: a 36-room plan draws in 802 draw calls before a single item is placed, and 150 items add 300 — so M2's instanced furniture aims at 27 % of the problem and its cached 2D layer aims at a pass that already runs in 0.985 ms against a 2 ms gate. And two of M3's three clauses are already delivered, while the thing worth doing instead is that first-load is 96 % one chunk. Three sprints, 2 weeks becomes 2.25, and the quarter is bought by a split that a config predicate will not perform.

§ 65 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What the renderer and a curl said about the last programme

Seven measurements against the tree at 7012618, every one produced by running something: two HTTP requests, a Chromium probe reading renderer.info and performance.now() at three plan sizes, and a second build of this tree with the chunking changed. Two findings say a sprint is aimed at the wrong half, one says two clauses are already delivered, and one says the obvious fix for the payload does not work.

404 × 2

The programme survives, and again it is two of three sprints that are not where their names suggest. That sentence was RM-014's about programme L and it is true here for a different reason: L's clauses were partly built already, and M's are aimed at the wrong half of a measured cost. M1 reads like plumbing and is in fact the first publish. M2 names instanced furniture and a cached 2D layer, and the renderer says the furniture is a quarter of the calls and the 2D pass is twice as fast as its own gate. M3 names two things that RM-011, RM-012 and RM-013 already delivered, and misses the one number that is actually large.

The arithmetic that re-points M2. A 36-room, 144-wall plan renders in 802 draw calls, 739 meshes and 2,516 triangles. Three thousand triangles is nothing — a phone draws a hundred times that — so the scene is entirely call-bound, and the marginal cost of a wall is 5.5 draw calls and 5.06 meshes. Adding 150 pieces of furniture adds exactly 2 draw calls each, 300 in all. So instancing the furniture removes at most 27 % of the calls in the worst plan this drawing built, and consolidating what a wall emits could remove far more. The frame is 3.89 ms bare and 4.52 ms furnished, which is comfortable today; the point is not that it is slow, it is that the sprint budgeted for making it faster should spend the week on the 73 %.

And the clause that is already delivered, twice over. RM-007 lists “the first-load budget and lazy packs wired through the manifest” as two-thirds of M3. The first-load budget has existed since RM-011 H1, is line eleven of the budget tool, and fails CI; lazy packs arrived with RM-012 J2 and starter plans with RM-013 K1, and M-43 and M-47 already assert that a boot fetches neither. What is genuinely absent is Lighthouse — zero references in the whole repository — and what is genuinely large is that the entry chunk is 414,036 of the 431,665 gzipped bytes a visitor waits for.

AA-1 · The address in the README answers 404 high measured

https://amitukind.github.io/architect3d/ and …/docs/ both return HTTP 404. The README links to that host nine times — a Live app button in the first screenful, a documentation link beside it, and seven references in the body. So the front page of this repository advertises a running application at an address that has never served one.

Why, and it is written down already. deploy.yml is triggered by workflow_dispatch only, and its own header says so at length: actions/configure-pages fails unless Settings → Pages → Source is set to “GitHub Actions”, that switch has never been thrown, and RM-006 removed the push trigger rather than leave a workflow that goes red on every push to the default branch — “it trains everybody to ignore a red mark”. The same header states the intent this programme is here to carry out: “the plan is Cloudflare rather than Pages”.

What that does to the sprint. M1 reads like plumbing — re-target the deploy job — and it is not. Everything before the publish step is exercised and proven: checkout, install, the full suite with coverage, both builds, the budgets and the assembly all ran on every red push. What has never run is the publish, and what has never existed is a URL. So M1's deliverable is not a re-pointed job, it is the first address this project has had, and its acceptance has to be an HTTP request rather than a green tick.

AA-2 · The migration already made the move cheap cheaper measured

A host change usually means hunting hard-coded paths. Here there is one production file that names the sub-path: docs/.vitepress/config.mjs, and it already reads process.env.DOCS_BASE first. The application's base is not in the source at all — it arrives as --base=/<repo>/ on the deploy job's command line. Everything else resolves relatively, and each one is a deliberate note in the tree rather than an accident: index.html explains why the model and texture URLs are bare relative strings; WORKER_URL is 'sw.js'; help.js reads import.meta.env.BASE_URL.

The service worker is the part that looked dangerous and is not. A worker's URL is its identity and its scope, and K3's cache policy precaches the scope URL as the fallback for every route. None of that is written down anywhere: sw.js asks worker.registration.scope at runtime, so the shell it caches is whatever base it was registered under. Serving at a root instead of a sub-path needs no change to it. The remaining /architect3d/ literals in the tree are all in tests, and they are the sub-path case — the harder one — which stays worth asserting after the move, not before it.

AA-3 · The building costs the draw calls, not the furniture high measured

Measured in headless Chromium with renderer.info, on plans built through the real model:

scenewallsdraw callsmeshestrianglesms / frame
one room432319760.20
36 rooms, no furniture1448027392,5163.89
36 rooms, 150 items1441,1021,1893,1164.52

Three numbers out of that table decide the sprint. The marginal cost of a wall is 5.5 draw calls and 5.06 meshes. The whole 36-room scene averages 3.1 triangles per draw call, which is the signature of a scene bound entirely by call overhead rather than by geometry. And an item costs exactly 2 draw calls, so 150 of them are 300 — 27 % of the furnished total.

So RM-007's “instanced furniture” is a real optimisation aimed at the smaller share. The larger share is that every wall becomes about five meshes, and they are all the same material in the same plane band. M2's week goes to the building. This is not a claim that the application is slow — 4.52 ms is roughly 220 fps and RM-011 W-9 already recorded a furnished fixture at 388 — it is a claim about which half a week budgeted for performance should be spent on, and about what the number will be when a plan is four times this size.

AA-4 · The 2D pass is already twice as fast as its own gate cheaper measured

view.draw(), timed over 20 consecutive runs in Chromium after one warm draw:

wallscornersms per drawagainst the gate
144490.82541 % of it
196640.98549 % — this is M2's own fixture
4001211.9698 %

RM-008 T-4 installed a 2 ms frame budget in the browser tier and a 36-room, 150-item fixture to hold it to. RM-007 asks M2 for “a cached static layer under the 2D draw” and “a 200-wall, 150-item fixture in the browser tier with a frame budget”. The fixture and the budget already exist, and at the size the sprint names the pass runs in half its allowance.

Where it does start to matter is 400 walls, which reaches 98 % of the gate — so the cached layer is not wrong, it is early. The drawing keeps it as a conditional: raise the fixture to 400 walls, let the existing gate fail, and cache only if it does. That is cheaper than building a cache and then discovering it saved 0.4 ms, and it is the same discipline B4 used when it declined KTX2 on evidence. The conditional fired and the cache was still wrong, which is better than either outcome this paragraph imagined. With the gate's own 150 footprints the fixture measures 2.165 ms, not 1.96 — the furniture is what pushes the 2D pass over, and a walls-only measurement would have declined the cache for the wrong reason. Timing every phase then found drawGrid at 0.005 ms, 0.3 % of the frame: a cached static layer under this draw is a cache of the grid. What was built instead is viewport culling, because 245 of those 400 walls are off the canvas. The conditional did its job — it just turned out to be asking about the wrong remedy, and asking it as a measurement is what surfaced that.

AA-5 · The first load is one chunk med measured

first-load stands at 431,665 gzipped bytes against a limit of 441,700. The document references exactly two assets, and one of them is 414,036 bytes — 96 % of everything a visitor waits for. The build emits eight chunks in all; the seven that are lazy total 13,626 bytes, and they are the post-processing passes and the share bundle, deferred deliberately by earlier sprints.

A second build of this tree, identical but for a chunking rule, splits that entry:

chunkgzippedwhat it is
library283,074src/scripts and three, which would not separate — see AA-6
reka64,931Reka UI and Floating UI
index62,325the application: src/app, every component and composable
vendor5,882everything else from node_modules

Two readings, and the second is the useful one. The first is that the UI framework costs as much as the application that uses it — 64,931 against 62,325 — which is worth knowing and is not obviously wrong for a component library carrying focus scopes, portals and collision handling that L2 and L4 both leaned on rather than reimplemented. The second is three's share. The same library built with three external is 78,695 gzipped; bundled, it is 283,074. Both are ESM, both are builds of this tree, and the difference is 204,379 bytes — 47 % of the entire first load. That is the number M3 should be pointed at.

AA-6 · The obvious way to split it does not work med measured

The natural remedy for AA-5 is a manualChunks predicate on the module path, and it fails in a way worth recording because it fails quietly. 29 of three's own module ids are offered to the hook — three/build/three.core.js, three/build/three.module.js, and 27 addons — and were counted rather than assumed, after a first pass truncated the list and drew the opposite conclusion. They are assigned to a three chunk. The chunk that results is 9,957 bytes, and the library chunk is 283,074: three is still inside it.

The check that settles it is a size comparison rather than a name: the library chunk is 1,053,719 raw, and bp3djs.js — the IIFE built deliberately with three bundled — is 1,090,348. The ESM build with three external is 319,492. So the chunk holds the library and three, and the assignment did not move it.

What that means for the sprint. Splitting the entry is not a config line, so M3 cannot be priced as one. The lever that will work is a boundary rather than a predicate — the 3D viewer behind a dynamic import, so that three arrives when a person switches to it rather than when the page opens, which is also what the plan-first default layout already implies. That is a real change with a real risk, and it is the quarter-week this drawing adds.

AA-7 · Two thirds of M3 is already delivered cheaper measured

RM-007's M3 is “the first-load budget and lazy packs wired through the manifest; a Lighthouse floor”. Taken in turn:

  • The first-load budget exists. RM-011 H1 added it as line eleven of check-budget.mjs, with a comment saying what makes it different from its neighbours: “every other entry here asks what something weighs; this one asks what a person waits for”. It parses the built index.html for what the document blocks on, adds the asset manifest, and runs in CI.
  • Lazy packs exist. RM-012 J2 made the catalog fetch its packs and RM-013 K1 made the starter plans fetch too, and both are asserted — M-43 and M-47 both say a boot fetches nothing nobody asked for, measured on performance.getEntriesByType('resource'). RM-014 L3 would have been the third and was withdrawn.
  • Lighthouse does not exist. Zero references in package.json, in .github/, or in tools/.

So M3 keeps one of its three clauses and gains the one AA-5 found. Its half-week is not spent re-delivering H1 and J2; it is spent on a Lighthouse floor and on the boundary AA-6 says a predicate will not draw.

AA-8 · The instrument the acceptance named cannot see the boundary med measured

Found during M3 rather than before it, and recorded here with the other seven because it is a finding about how this project measures rather than about what it built. M3's third acceptance clause is “a boot in the plan layout fetches no three chunk”, on the M-43 instrument again — performance.getEntriesByType('resource'), the browser's own record of what it asked the network for. Written that way, it passed at once, and it kept passing with the boundary deliberately removed. That is the shape of a test measuring nothing.

The cause is structural, not a mistake in the test. The browser tier serves modules unbundled: there is no tree-shaking, so a static import is a fetch whether or not the built chunk would have kept it. And src/scripts/blueprint.js is a barrel — it re-exports Main, Edge, Skybox, OrbitControls and the rest — so importing anything from it pulls the whole library. Printed rather than reasoned about: at import time, before a single component had mounted, the test page had already fetched 88 library modules and three's dep bundle, with /src/scripts/blueprint.js and deps/three.js among the first three entries.

So the claim was split across the two tiers that can each see a half of it, and neither half is the one the drawing named:

  • Tier 2 counts WebGL contexts rather than fetches. getContext('webgl2') is called exactly when a WebGLRenderer is constructed, which is exactly when Main is. That is the half the risk register actually worries about — “something imports the viewer eagerly and the split silently does nothing” — and it caught a deliberate break that attached a viewer at mount.
  • Gate seventeen reads the assembled tree, where chunks exist, and asserts that the engine is in exactly one of them and that the document references none of it. That is the half the drawing described, checked in the one place it is true.

What this leaves open is worth stating. The application's own dev server serves unbundled too, so npm run dev still loads three at boot. That is a developer's boot and not a visitor's, and closing it would mean the application importing 59 specific modules instead of one barrel — a large change with no effect on anything shipped. It is recorded rather than done.

§ 67 · SPRINTS M1–M3

Two and a quarter weeks, and the quarter buys a boundary

RM-007 priced programme M at 2 weeks in three sprints. The total goes to 2.25: AA-6 adds a quarter to M3 because the split it needs is a dynamic import rather than a config predicate, AA-4 gives M2 a cheaper second half without giving the week back, and AA-1 changes what M1 delivers without changing how long it takes.

M1

The first address this project has had

deliveredAA-1AA-20.5 wk

Objective. A person who is not holding this repository can open the application, and the README stops advertising a 404.

  • Cloudflare Pages, built from source (AA-1). The three Pages-specific actions come out — configure-pages, upload-pages-artifact, deploy-pages — and everything above them stays exactly as it is, because everything above them has been running green on every red push since RM-006. The switch that was never thrown stops being a prerequisite.
  • Served at a root, which deletes a flag rather than adding one (AA-2). --base goes; DOCS_BASE becomes /docs/. Nothing else in the source names a path, the worker computes its own scope, and the sub-path tests stay as they are — they assert the harder case and it costs nothing to keep proving it.
  • A preview per branch, which is the thing GitHub Pages could not do at all: Pages has one live deployment, so dev could never be looked at without overwriting what people were using.
  • The README's nine links repointed, and the address put where a first-time reader meets it.
  • Not a custom domain. A DNS record is not a sprint and not this one; the project domain is the address until somebody wants otherwise. Recorded as declined-for-now rather than omitted.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-51 (new): the published address answers 200 and serves a document that boots — asserted by a request to the deployed URL, because the thing AA-1 measured was a 404 and the only honest refutation of a 404 is a 200
  • Every link in the README resolves, checked rather than assumed — the nine that do not today are the reason this clause exists
  • The documentation site is reachable from the application's help menu at the deployed base, which RM-014 L2's help:check explicitly declined to assert because it could not: there was nowhere to assert it against
  • A service worker registered at the new scope serves a reload offline, which is K3's claim re-run somewhere it has never actually run
LANDING — M1, everything up to the button
  • Three steps replaced, and nothing above them touched. configure-pages, upload-pages-artifact and deploy-pages are gone; cloudflare/wrangler-action publishes the same dist-demo the same job already assembled. Checkout, install, the suite with coverage, both builds and the budgets are byte-identical, and that is the argument for doing it this way: they were never the part that failed. They ran green on every one of the red pushes AA-1 describes.
  • The push trigger comes back, and the reason it was removed is the reason it can. RM-006 took it off because Pages has exactly one live deployment, so a deploy from a working branch would overwrite what people were using. Cloudflare gives every non-production branch its own URL. So master publishes production on push, and workflow_dispatch publishes a preview from wherever it is run — by hand rather than on every push to dev, because CI already proves dev and this job re-runs the whole suite on top of it. Paying twice for the same proof is the trade this repository has declined four times now.
  • A guard before npm ci, not after the build. A repository with no Cloudflare secrets fails in ten seconds with a sentence naming which one is missing, rather than four minutes later inside wrangler with a 401. It reports whether each secret is set and never prints one.
  • AA-2 held, and the tests now say so rather than the grep. The base change is --base deleted and DOCS_BASE set to /docs/ — one line of configuration, exactly as measured. The claim underneath it was “the worker hard-codes nothing”, and “it is all relative” is the kind of claim that is true until one join() somewhere is not. So the offline policy was classified under both bases for six paths and the two agree on every one; a root-scope suite now asserts it beside the sub-path suite, which stays because the library is a published package and an embedder may serve it anywhere.
  • The README stopped advertising a 404, and the fix was not a different URL. Nine links, and pointing them at a Cloudflare address that has not been deployed yet would have replaced one 404 with another — which is not fixing AA-1, it is re-committing it. Seven of the nine were documentation, and the documentation exists in this repository as markdown: those now link to files, which resolve on github.com, in an editor and in a clone, and which a gate can check. The one link that cannot be a file is the live application, and it becomes true at the moment it reaches master, because pushing to master is what deploys.
  • Gate seventeen, and the drawing said this sprint would add none. npm run deploy:check runs last, on the assembled tree, and asks one question: does every path this build names exist in what is about to be uploaded? Nothing else in the repository could ask it — every other gate runs before assembly and none of them resolves a URL — and a first deploy is exactly where that gap bites: the build is green, every budget passes, and the published page asks for /architect3d/assets/index.js from a host that serves /assets/index.js. Five deliberate breaks, all caught: assets moved under a sub-path, a hashed service worker, a root-absolute start_url, a live link back to the dead host, and a README link to a file that is not there. It runs in both workflows, and putting it in CI cost one mv: CI already builds the application and the documentation, so assembling them the way the deploy does is the whole of the addition. Catching a base-path mistake at merge beats catching it at deploy, and the deploy job runs it again on its own tree regardless.
  • The gate was corrected by its own first real run, and the correction is the interesting part. The retired-host rule began as the string must not appear anywhere in the tree, and the first run against a real assembly failed on docs/roadmap.html — because AA-1 quotes the dead address as the thing it measured returning 404. A gate that forbids naming a finding is a gate that makes the record worse. The rule is now about what a browser would follow: an href, a src, a CSS url(), a markdown link target. Prose and <code> may say it as often as they like.
  • M-51 is not met, and cannot be met from here. The metric is the published address answers 200, and answering it needs a Cloudflare account, an API token and a network. This sprint delivers everything up to the moment somebody with that account presses the button: the workflow, the base change, the README, and a gate that checks the artifact resolves at the base it will be served from. Two repository secrets and one Pages project stand between this commit and the address — CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, and a project named after the repository or named by the CLOUDFLARE_PROJECT variable. It is recorded as outstanding rather than quietly reworded into something that could be ticked, which is what M-51 was written to prevent.
  • Sprint M1 is delivered to the edge of the network. 2,633 headless and 218 browser tests — 3 of them new — seventeen gates green, fourteen budget lines within limits with none raised, and coverage unchanged at 87.77 / 87.78 / 79.28 / 86.03 with no floor moved. The assembled tree that deploy:check passes on is 658 files, 22.69 MB. The 404s that AA-1 measured are gone from the README; the 200 that replaces them is one dispatch away and is not this sprint's to claim.
M2

The building, not the furniture

deliveredAA-3AA-41 wk

Objective. A plan four times the size of today's fixture renders in fewer draw calls than today's fixture does, and the 2D pass is measured before anything is done to it.

  • Consolidate what a wall emits (AA-3). 5.06 meshes and 5.5 draw calls per wall, at 3.1 triangles per call, is a scene paying overhead for geometry it could merge. The target is the wall and floor meshes, which share a material and a plane band; the furniture is a second pass and a smaller one.
  • Instanced furniture, second and measured against the first (AA-3). Two draw calls per item and 300 for a full plan is real, and it is 27 % — so it lands after the 73 % and only if the ceiling below is not already met.
  • The 2D cache is conditional, not scheduled (AA-4). Raise T-4's fixture to 400 walls, where the pass measures 1.96 ms against its own 2 ms gate, and let the existing gate decide. Build the cached static layer if it fails and not before — the same way RM-004 B4 declined KTX2 on evidence rather than on expectation.
  • Not a new renderer, and not a new scene graph. Merging what a wall emits is a change inside Edge and Floor; anything larger is a rewrite this programme has no mandate for and RM-002's no-big-bang rule forbids.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-52 (new) not met retired · RM-016 N1: a 400-wall plan renders in fewer than 802 draw calls — the number this drawing measured for 144 walls — read off renderer.info.render.calls in the browser tier. A call ceiling rather than a frame time, deliberately: a millisecond on a CI runner measures the runner, and AA-3's own table shows the frame was never the thing that was wrong
  • Every existing pixel test still passes, because consolidating meshes is exactly the change that can look identical in a call count and wrong on a screen
  • The 2 ms 2D gate holds at 400 walls, whether or not a cache was built — and if no cache was built, the landing block records the measurement that said one was not needed
  • GPU memory does not rise: renderer.info.memory deltas across a mount and teardown stay where RM-003 A0 left them, since merging geometry is a way to leak it
LANDING — M2, the building · and the half AA-4 turned back on
  • Two things batch, and one method decides why only two. Edge.updateVisibility walks planes on every camera move and writes material.opacity per edge, which is how a wall face fades when you look at its back. Geometry that shares a mesh shares a material and therefore shares that fade — so nothing in planes can be batched across faces while that behaviour exists. What was left is exactly two populations: base planes, which that loop never touches because the code calls them always visible, and the two side fillers of one face, which always fade together because they are in the same array.
  • The frozen goldens shaped the implementation instead of blocking it. tests/geometry-rewrites.test.js pins edge.planes at five entries and pins the geometry at each index against r98, and those goldens cannot be regenerated. So the edge still builds all five and still owns them; what changed is only what reaches the scene. A batchedPlanes set tells addToScene which two to skip, and the batch holds the same material object the two originals hold — which is what makes the fade still arrive, because updateVisibility mutates a material rather than a mesh. A browser test asserts that identity directly, since it is the thing that would break silently.
  • What it bought, measured in Chromium off renderer.info.
    scenemeshesdraw callstrianglesms / frame
    144 walls, before M27398022,5163.89
    144 walls, after4524492,5161.98
    400 walls, after1,2209724,6005.25

    −44 % of the draw calls and −49 % of the frame, with the triangle count unchanged — which is the proof that nothing was removed from the picture, only from the packaging. Per wall it is 5.57 calls before, 3.12 after, and 2.43 at 400 walls: 2.8 times the plan for 1.2 times the calls of the scene AA-3 measured. Every pixel test in the browser tier passes untouched, and so do the GPU-memory deltas RM-003 A0 installed, which is the pair of checks that says a merge did not quietly change what is drawn or leak what it replaced.

  • M-52 is NOT met, and the number is not moved to fit. Retired by RM-016 N1, and not by moving it either: AB-2 measured every design this product ships at 8 to 17 walls and 39 to 187 calls, so the fixture is twenty-three times the largest starter plan. M-56 replaced it with a ceiling on the designs that exist. This paragraph stands as written — it was true, and what changed is that the question stopped being worth asking. It asks for a 400-wall plan under 802 draw calls and this delivers 972. The reason is the same method as the first bullet: after batching, 85 % of the remaining meshes are wall planes and side fillers, and both fade per edge. Reaching 802 needs the fade to stop being a property of a material — an alpha attribute rewritten in a shared buffer, or three's BatchedMesh with per-instance visibility. Both are real routes and both are a sprint, not an afternoon; they are named here for a later drawing to price rather than folded into this one. A metric that moves to meet its result measures nothing, which is the rule the coverage floors have been kept to for nine programmes.
  • AA-4's conditional fired, and a narrower probe would have got it backwards. The rule was raise the fixture to 400 walls and let the existing gate decide. Walls alone at 400: 1.51 ms warm, comfortably inside — and on that number the cache would have been declined. The gate's fixture also carries 150 footprints, and with them the same plan measures 2.165 ms against the 2 ms budget. The furniture is what pushes the 2D pass over, which is worth knowing before anybody optimises walls, and it is the opposite of AA-3's finding about the 3D side. So the cached static layer is needed, at roughly 400 walls rather than the 200 the sprint was written for, and it is the outstanding half of M2. The fixture is back at 36 rooms because a failing test is a broken suite rather than a finding; the finding is the number, and it is here.
  • One thing kept from that run regardless: the gate now warms up properly. The same fixture measures 1.995, 1.73, 1.615, 1.51, 1.51 cold to warm, so a single warm draw left the timing on the settling curve — a gate that passes or fails on JIT rather than on anything in the repository. Five blocks of warm-up now precede the measurement.
  • A budget line turned out to be a fossil, and finding out cost a second build. lib-esm-gzip breached at 83,119 against 83,000, and +4,120 gzipped is implausible for 185 lines. Building the library at M1 as well as with the change settled it:
    the same artifactgzipped
    recorded in budget.json78,999
    built at M1, before this sprint82,312
    built with M2, measured twice83,119

    So M2 is +807 and the other +3,313 was already in the tree: RM-014 L4's plan cursor, the reduced-motion helpers and the OrbitControls change all landed in src/scripts, and every budget:update since ran after build:demo and not after npm run build. The tool measures whatever is on disk, so two of its fourteen lines were silently re-recorded at their old values rather than reported as missing. CI runs both builds, so the limit was always enforced honestly; what drifted is the measured column, which is the one everybody reads to see the headroom. The limit rises 83,000 → 88,000 with that whole attribution written into budget.json, and lib-iife-gzip is left alone because it still has 2.7 % of its own.

  • Sprint M2 is half delivered, and says so. 2,637 headless and 223 browser tests — 4 and 5 of them new — seventeen gates green, fourteen budget lines within limits with one raised for a recorded reason. first-load 431,665 → 432,414, +749, which is what halving the frame cost of the building costs the payload. Coverage 87.79 / 87.84 / 79.29 / 86.01, every floor held and none crossed a whole number, so none moves. Outstanding: the cached static layer AA-4's own rule now requires, and M-52's remaining 170 draw calls, which need the fade mechanism to change. The first of those is delivered below, and it is not a cache: phase timing found the thing AA-4 proposed caching to be 0.3 % of the pass. This sprint is no longer half delivered. M-52 is still unmet.
LANDING — M2, the 2D half · and the cache that was not the answer
  • AA-4's conditional fired, and then said its own remedy was wrong. The rule was: raise the fixture until the 2 ms gate fails, and build the cached static layer only if it does. It failed, at 2.165 ms. But the next thing to do with a failing budget is find out where it goes, and timing every phase at 400 walls and 150 items says this:
    phasemsshare of the frame
    drawWallLabels0.59530 %
    drawWall0.47024 %
    drawRoom0.42021 %
    drawItems0.24012 %
    drawGrid0.0050.3 %

    A cached static layer under the 2D draw is a cache of the grid, and the grid is three tenths of one per cent of the frame. RM-007 named the one optimisation in this pass that could not have helped. What the pass spends its time on is the building, and the building is not static: it moves with every pan, every zoom and every edit, which is the property a cache needs and this does not have.

  • The same measurement said what would help: most of the plan is not on the screen. The gate's own fixture is 1,476 pixels wide in a 1,024 pixel viewport, so 245 of its 400 walls are outside the canvas and were being drawn anyway — geometry, corners, and a text label with a stroked halo, all of it thrown away by the rasteriser after the work was done. The pass now culls rooms, walls, corners, labels and item footprints against the viewport, and the fixture measures 1.10 to 1.29 ms: from 8 % over its budget to 40 % under it. The fixture is raised to 100 rooms permanently, which is what AA-4 asked for and what could not be done while it was failing.

    It is also the optimisation that gets better exactly where a cache gets worse. Somebody working on a large plan is zoomed into one room: a cache is invalidated by every pan and zoom they make, and a cull is most effective on the same gesture.

  • The margin is two-part, and that is the whole correctness question. A wall's endpoints do not bound what its drawing covers: it has thickness, its corners have radius, and its label sits 40 cm off the line with text and a halo around it. Forty centimetres is 20 pixels at this zoom and 400 at ten times it — so the margin has a plan-space part that grows with the zoom and a screen-space part that does not. The test that matters most is the wall crossing the whole screen with both endpoints off it: an overlap test keeps it, and a containment test culls the one wall the person is looking at. Four deliberate breaks, all caught — no margin, containment instead of overlap, culling while exporting, and a cull that never culls.
  • Nothing is culled while exporting, and all three export paths get that from one check. A sheet and a thumbnail draw the whole plan through another projection and have no frame budget, so culling there could only ever crop a drawing. renderTo is the single door the SVG export, the PNG export and RM-013 K1's thumbnails all go through, and it already sets exporting — so one condition covers all three. The 24 pixel tests in the browser tier pass untouched, which is the assertion that no edge was cropped.
  • A false lead, recorded because the reasoning was sound and the answer was still no. CanvasBackend.text assigned context.font on every call — a CSS font shorthand re-parsed roughly a thousand times a frame, every time for the same 12px face. That is a known Canvas2D hot spot and it looked exactly like the label cost. Caching the text state moved the frame 1.98 → 1.95 ms, which is noise; Chromium evidently parses that string cheaply. The cache is kept because it is correct and free, but it is not why the gate passes, and a landing block that let it sit beside the real number would be claiming credit for the wrong change.
  • Instanced furniture is deferred on a number rather than on the calendar. The card ordered it after the building and made it conditional on M-52's ceiling not being met — which it is not. So it was measured before being deferred: at 400 walls the scene is 972 draw calls bare and 1,272 with 150 items, exactly 2 per item. Perfectly instanced, all 150 collapsing to one call, it is 974 — still above M-52's 802. Instancing is a real 300-call saving that cannot unblock the metric, because the blocker is the 972 the building costs. It belongs with the sprint that changes how a face fades, where the two together reach the number and neither does alone.
  • Sprint M2 is delivered, with M-52 unmet and recorded as unmet. 2,644 headless and 223 browser tests — 11 and 5 of them new across both halves — seventeen gates green, and fourteen budget lines within limits with one raised for a recorded reason. first-load 432,414 → 432,781, +367. Coverage 87.84 / 87.89 / 79.36 / 86.05, every floor held and none crossed a whole number. The building draws in 449 calls where it drew in 802, and the 2D pass draws a plan 2.8 times the size of its old fixture in half the budget it used to spend on the small one.
