LANDING — M3, the engine behind a boundary
  • The boundary is a class, not a config line. AA-6 said a path predicate would not split three out and it was right about the mechanism: a bundler splits on a boundary in the graph. BlueprintJS put one reference to Main in a constructor, and that reference is what made import {BlueprintJS} mean import three for every page, whether or not it ever showed a room. So the class divided in two. BlueprintCore builds the model, the runtime and the 2D plan and takes the viewer class as an argument to attachViewer(); BlueprintJS is that class plus a static import {Main} and one line in its constructor, so an embedder's call is unchanged in behaviour and in bytes. The dynamic import is in useBlueprint.ensureViewer(), on the application's side of the package boundary, which is where § 68 said it belongs.
  • What the viewer boundary returned, and why it is not 204,379. AA-5 measured three at 204,379 gzipped bytes and 47 % of the first load. Deferring the viewer returns 112,800 of that, not all of it, and the difference is the finding: three 0.185 ships as two files. three.module.js is the WebGL half — 531,531 rendered bytes, and it leaves the entry chunk completely the moment nothing eager references it. three.core.js is the maths, the scene graph and the event dispatcher, which Vector2, Corner, Wall and the 2D plan are all built on. It stays, as a shared chunk of 65,070 gzipped bytes — now the largest single thing in the first load, and 23 % of what remains.
  • Which meant the clause needed two more boundaries, and the drawing had not costed them. The acceptance asked for below 300,000 and the viewer alone reaches 319,981. The rest of three is not in the viewer: it is a glTF parser, a Draco decoder, a Basis transcoder and a glTF exporter, imported by the model layer. Nothing on the 2D side needs any of it — a plan draws footprints from plan_projection, which reads an item's position and size and never its geometry. Each was measured on its own build with the other three still in place:

Fourteen entries in tools/budget.json and thirteen raises in its note; this is the first lowering, and the reason is the one § 68 gave in advance: a ceiling nobody can reach has stopped being a ceiling.

Splitting one chunk into eight adds per-chunk overhead and a shared chunk both sides import, so the total javascript grew by 4,771 bytes while what a boot downloads fell by 152,702. That line is now at 1.1 % headroom and has been left there rather than raised pre-emptively: the next commit to touch it will have to look at it, which is what the line is for.

A Lighthouse performance score weights five metrics the way somebody else weights them, and it can fall while all fourteen budget lines improve — which is exactly the risk § 68 names for this sprint, since deferring three moves the wait rather than removing it. The floor is recorded at 60: first measurement, rounded down, never lowered — a coverage floor's rule rather than a budget limit's, because the failure direction is the other way round. Rounded to 60 rather than set at 62 deliberately: three runs of the same build scored 62, 62 and 61, and a floor that fails on sampling noise is a floor nobody reads. The deploy workflow runs the same analysis against the published URL and reports without gating — a cold edge cache is not a regression in this repository, and the gap between the two numbers is the host's.

  • M-53 is measured on the artifact, not on the deployment, and that is a real limit. There is still no Cloudflare deploy — M-51 has been blocked on two repository secrets since M1 — so the score above is a lab measurement of exactly the bytes the deploy uploads, served from localhost, with Lighthouse's own throttling on top. It holds the network constant on purpose, which is what makes it a gate rather than a weather report; what it cannot see is anything the host does, and that is what the deploy step is for.
  • The offline gate caught what the split broke, on its first run after it. shellAssets read <script src> and <link rel="stylesheet"> and nothing else, which was complete while the application was one entry chunk and stopped being complete the moment it was three. Vite emits rel="modulepreload" for the entry's static imports — precisely the chunks a boot blocks on — and the service worker was precaching neither of the two new ones. npm run offline:check said so in the form the gate exists for: the shell did not render offline, there is no plan canvas offline, only 0 tools rendered offline, naming three.core-*.js and dom-*.js. The fix is the rule the function was always trying to state — what the document blocks on — and because Vite never emits a modulepreload for a dynamic import, the lazy chunks stay lazy by construction rather than by a list kept in step by hope.
  • A synchronous failure became an asynchronous one, deliberately. Scene.addItem reported one thing synchronously: a URL the environment cannot even parse, which throws out of three's FileLoader past the onError callback that exists for it. Behind a dynamic import that answer now arrives a microtask later, and tests/items-and-scene.test.js failed on exactly that. The try still wraps loader.load and nothing else — the property the case was written for — and what moved is when the answer comes back, to where every other load's answer already was. A load that reported failure synchronously on one path and asynchronously on every other was the more surprising of the two behaviours.
  • Four deliberate breaks, and the one that was not caught is why there is a fifth test. Attaching a viewer at mount, resolving ensureViewer without attaching, and forgetting modulepreload were each caught by the tier that owns them. Removing the idempotence guard from attachViewer was not: the store caches its import, so the application never calls it twice, and the library's own guard had no test of its own. It has one now, in tests/viewer-lifecycle.test.js, which fails on that break.
  • The third clause becomes M-54, and it is split because AA-8 says it has to be. A boot in the plan layout builds no 3D engine, and switching to a layout that shows it builds exactly one. Tier 2 counts WebGL contexts in tests/browser/viewer-boundary.test.js; gate seventeen counts chunks in the assembled tree. The drawing's own wording — fetches no three chunk — is the one form of it neither tier can check, for the reason AA-8 measured.
  • Sprint M3 is delivered, and programme M with it. 2,659 headless and 228 browser tests — 15 and 5 of them new — eighteen gates green, and fourteen budget lines within limits with one brought down for a recorded reason. Coverage 87.88 / 87.93 / 79.43 / 86.20, every floor held and none moved; functions dipped to 85.95 against an 86 floor mid-sprint and were answered by covering both export paths rather than by touching the number. first-load 432,781 → 280,079, a 35.3 % cut, and a first contentful paint 2.4 seconds earlier on somebody else's measurement of it.
§ 68 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskSprintWhat is done about it
The first publish exposes something no local build ever did — a MIME type, a redirect, a worker scopeM1M-51 is an HTTP request against the deployed address rather than a green workflow, and the offline clause is K3's own claim re-run where it has never run. A deploy that goes green while serving a broken document is exactly the failure a job status cannot see
Moving to a root breaks the sub-path case for anyone embedding the library under oneM1The /architect3d/ literals in the suite are kept rather than updated. They assert the harder case, they cost nothing to keep proving, and the library is a published package whose consumers choose their own base
Merging wall meshes changes what is on screen while the call count says it workedM2The pixel tests in the browser tier are the gate, not the counter. RM-004 B4's rule applies: a number that improves is not evidence until the picture is checked
Merged geometry is leaked instead of disposed, and the win is paid for in VRAMM2RM-003 A0's memory deltas are in the acceptance list. Consolidation is precisely the change that creates a buffer nobody owns
The 2D cache is built, and saves 0.4 msM2AA-4 measured 0.985 ms at the sprint's own fixture against a 2 ms gate, so the cache is conditional on the gate failing at 400 walls. This is the risk the drawing is most confident about, because it is the one it already measured
Deferring three moves the wait rather than removing it, and switching to 3D becomes slowM3M-53 is a Lighthouse score on the whole page, which cannot be gamed by moving bytes from one moment to another, and the boot/switch fetch counts are asserted separately so both halves are visible
Something imports the viewer eagerly and the split silently does nothingM3The acceptance asserts a boot fetches no three chunk, which is the only form of the claim a bundler cannot satisfy by accident. AA-6 is the precedent: an assignment that looked applied and was not

What must not change

The save format is untouched, for the third programme running. Nothing here is persisted in a design: a deploy address, a mesh count and a chunk boundary are all properties of how the application is delivered, and none of them is a property of a building.

The one-way arrow holds, and M2 is where it would be easiest to break. Consolidating what a wall emits is a change inside src/scripts/three; it must not require the application to know that walls are now drawn differently, and no consumer of the package should have to opt in to it.

The library's public API does not move. M3 defers the 3D viewer inside the application. BlueprintJS constructs the 2D canvas and the 3D container in one call and embedders depend on that; a dynamic import belongs on the app's side of the boundary, not in the package's constructor.

The frozen r98 goldens still cannot be regenerated, and M2 is the first sprint since RM-004 with a serious reason to want to. Merging meshes changes the scene graph, not the pixels; if a golden disagrees, the answer is that the merge was wrong. It held, and it did more than hold: the goldens pin edge.planes at five entries, so M2 kept all five and changed only which of them reach the scene. The constraint produced a better shape than the one that was going to be written, because the originals staying put is also what lets the batch share their material and inherit the fade.

And the sixteen gates stay sixteen or grow. M1 adds none, M2 adds none, M3 adds one — Lighthouse. M1 added one after all, and the drawing was wrong to say otherwise: deploy:check is gate seventeen. Nothing in this repository could ask whether an assembled tree resolves at the base it will be served from, because every other gate runs before assembly and none of them resolves a URL — which is precisely the gap a first deploy falls into. Sixteen becomes seventeen; M3 will make it eighteen. It did: lighthouse:check is gate eighteen, and it is the only gate here whose threshold was not chosen by this repository. One budget line comes down, deliberately and for the first time: first-load, because M3's whole purpose is to make it slack and a ceiling nobody can reach has stopped being a ceiling. Every other limit holds, no coverage floor moves down, and the four stay where L4 left them at 87 / 87 / 79 / 86. They did, but not without an argument: functions fell to 85.95 against the 86 floor when M3 split exportForBlender in two, and the answer was to cover both export paths — 86.20 — rather than to move a number by 0.05.

PROGRAMME N · DRAWING Nº RM-016

Every gate is green, and nobody has opened it

RM-007's eight programmes are all delivered and its five headline gaps are all closed, so there is no next sprint to draw — there is only the question of what is actually still wrong. Six measurements against the tree, and they say something uncomfortable: two of the numbers this project is still chasing are measuring nothing. The Lighthouse floor added yesterday scores this application 62 on a phone and 91 on a desktop, and the audience was fixed as desktop-only two programmes ago. M-52 wants a 400-wall plan under 802 draw calls, and the largest design the product ships renders in 187 calls at 0.52 ms. Meanwhile the thinnest-tested code in the tree is the code a first session runs through, the catalog is held back by a 12 KB JSON budget rather than by 5 MB of unused asset headroom, and the front page advertises a hostname that does not resolve. Three sprints, 2 weeks: point the instruments at the product, cover the first ten minutes, and stop measuring the wrong things.

§ 69 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What is left when the roadmap runs out

Six measurements against the tree at c2f6eec, every one produced by running something: two Lighthouse configurations, a Chromium probe reading renderer.info on the designs this repository actually ships, the coverage report aggregated by directory, an arithmetic over the asset tree against its own budgets, and a DNS lookup.

The roadmap is finished and the product is not the problem. RM-007 opened with five findings and every one is closed: the plan drew no furniture and now has 81 code paths for it; five wall and two floor surfaces are now 22 and 17; one storey is now Level; nothing could get a picture out and six verbs now can. Programmes E through M delivered 25 sprints against a brief that asked for a Coohom-class planner without the depth, and the brief has been met. That is the good news and it is also the difficulty: there is no next item on the list, so the next programme has to be argued for from measurement rather than read off a plan.

Two of the numbers still being chased are measuring nothing. That is the finding this drawing exists for, and both instances have the same shape — a threshold set against a subject nobody checked belonged to this product.

  • Gate eighteen scores a phone. Lighthouse's default configuration is a mid-range mobile device with a 4× CPU slowdown and a slow-4G network. This application's audience was fixed as web desktop only by RM-007 rev B, which withdrew a 2.5-week phone-and-tablet sprint to make it so. Measured on both presets, same build, same machine: desktop 91, first paint 1,094 ms, total blocking time 0 ms; mobile 62, first paint 5,988 ms. 96, not 91, once the gate imported Lighthouse's own desktop-config rather than the throttling table this measurement hand-wrote. Both are real and they measure different things; the conclusion is unchanged and the floor was set from the gate's figure. The gate M3 shipped yesterday holds a floor of 60 against the device this product declines to support.
  • M-52 asks for a house nobody lives in. The metric is a 400-wall plan under 802 draw calls, and it is unmet at 972. Measured against the designs the repository actually ships, in Chromium, off renderer.info: the furnished two-bedroom sample is 13 walls, 19 items, 187 draw calls, 0.52 ms a frame. The three-bedroom is 69 calls. The duplex is 81. A synthetic 31-wall, 12-room house — larger than any template here — is 139 calls and 0.68 ms. Against a 16.7 ms frame that is twenty-four times more headroom than the worst case needs, and M-52's fixture is thirteen to thirty times larger than the largest home the product has ever drawn.

What the measurements say is actually thin. Branch coverage by directory puts src/scripts/model at 87.5 % and src/scripts/core at 87.0 % — the library is well covered, and six programmes of characterization tests are why. The application shell is not: App.vue is at 37.3 %, useDesignIO at 39.2 %, useTemplates at 27.3 %. Those three files are the boot, the export verbs and the starter-plan shelf — which is to say, they are almost exactly what somebody does in their first ten minutes. The global floors hide it because the library outweighs the shell.

And the front page advertises a host that does not exist. Not a 404 this time: architect3d.pages.dev fails to resolve, because the account it would live in has not been created. This is RM-015 AA-1's finding reintroduced by the sprint that closed it — M1 wrote the address in anticipation of a deploy, and the deploy is now deferred by decision. The README argues against itself on this point in its own words, two paragraphs apart.

Two retire or re-point a metric, one records that the previous roadmap is complete, one moves where the tests go, one names a budget doing something other than its job, and one is a dead link on the front page. AB-9 was added by N2 and is the only finding in this document set produced by a sprint rather than by the drawing that priced it — AB-7 and AB-8 are deliberately unused, so a reader who meets AB-9 first knows to look for where it came from.

AB-1 · Gate eighteen holds a floor against a phone med measured

M3 added a Lighthouse gate on the argument that it is “the only number in this document set that is not chosen by the people being measured”. The argument is right and the configuration was not examined. Lighthouse's default emulates a mid-range phone: 4× CPU slowdown, a 1.6 Mbps network with 150 ms of latency, and a 412×823 viewport. This application does not run there by decision — RM-007 rev B fixed the audience as web desktop only and withdrew sprint L1, a 2.5-week phone and tablet shell, to make the decision explicit.

Both presets, one build, one machine, one server:

presetscoreFCPLCPTBTTTI
desktop — the audience91 961,094 ms1,215 ms0 ms1,215 ms
mobile — Lighthouse's default625,988 ms6,439 ms87 ms6,439 ms

The answer is not to swap one for the other. The desktop run is the audience and belongs in the gate; but its total blocking time is 0 ms, which means it carries no signal at all on the metric most sensitive to a javascript regression — a build that doubled its main-thread work would still read 0. The mobile run has 87 ms of it. So both are kept and both floors are recorded: desktop as the gate, because that is who this is for, and mobile as a sensitivity reading that can only ratchet upwards. Two numbers, two reasons, and neither one deleted to make the other look better.

AB-2 · M-52 asks for a house nobody lives in med measured

M-52 is a 400-wall plan renders in fewer than 802 draw calls. M2 halved the building's cost and left it unmet at 972, correctly refused to move the number to fit, and named the route that would close it: per-edge fading has to stop being a property of a material. What nobody asked in that sprint is whether 400 walls is a number about this product.

It is not. Measured in Chromium off renderer.info, thirty timed frames each, on the designs this repository actually ships — furniture loaded over the network and counted:

designwallsroomsitemsdraw callsms / frame
sample two-bedroom, furnished134191870.52
three-bedroom starter1550690.60
duplex starter1750810.47
31-wall, 12-room synthetic311201390.68
M-52's fixture400—1501,272—

The largest thing the product ships draws in 187 calls and half a millisecond, against a frame budget of 16.7. The metric's fixture is thirteen times the wall count of that design and twenty-three times the biggest starter plan. It is a stress test wearing a product metric's clothes, and the difference matters because an unmet metric is a debt that gets paid: M2 already deferred instanced furniture on it, and a future sprint would spend a week rewriting how a wall face fades in order to move a number that no user will ever be on the far side of.

What replaces it. A metric about the designs that exist — every shipped template, furnished, under a draw-call ceiling and a frame budget, asserted where the current 400-wall fixture already runs. The 400-wall fixture is kept, renamed as what it is, and given a much looser ceiling: it is a good early-warning instrument and a bad promise. M-52 is retired against its own measurement rather than quietly dropped, which is the same treatment RM-014 gave a withdrawn sprint.

AB-4 · The thinnest-tested code is the first thing anybody touches high measured

Four global coverage floors have ratcheted upward for eleven programmes and now sit at 87 / 87 / 79 / 86. Aggregated by directory, from the same run CI gates on, they are not distributed the way that number suggests:

areabranch %stmt %statements
src/app — App.vue and the bootstrap37.344.6303
src/app/components80.479.2682

src/scripts/three71.989.12,005

Per file, the three worst are App.vue at 37.3 % branch, useDesignIO at 39.2 % and useTemplates at 27.3 %. Those are the boot, every export verb, and the starter-plan shelf. Read as a description of a person's first ten minutes — open it, pick a starter plan, draw, export something to show somebody — the list is almost exactly the untested path.

Why the global floor cannot see this. It is one number over 13,625 statements, and src/scripts is two thirds of them. The library can carry the shell indefinitely: every covered statement in App.vue could disappear and the global statement figure would fall 0.99 points, from 87.88 to 86.89 — inside the headroom the floor already has, so the build would stay green while the boot went untested. A single number over a tree of unequal parts measures the biggest part.

AB-5 · The catalog is held back by an index, not by assets med measured

The brief RM-007 read literally includes “thousands of furniture models”, and the catalog is 217 rows over four kits. What it would cost to grow, measured rather than guessed: 215 .glb files totalling 1,814,572 bytes, mean 8,439 each — Draco geometry and KTX2 textures are why a chair is eight kilobytes. Against the two budget lines that would stop it:

linemeasuredlimitheadroombuys
public-total — the models themselves11,631,29516,770,0005,138,705608 models
catalog-packs — the JSON that lists them11,66612,25058411 rows

So the binding constraint on a catalog of 217 is a 12 KB gzipped JSON budget that trips at 228 rows, while five megabytes of model headroom sits unused beside it. That is a line doing something other than its job. It was set by RM-012 J2 at the first measurement with the usual 5 % headroom, and 5 % of a small number is a small number; nothing was wrong with the reasoning and the consequence is that the cheapest content in the tree is the thing rationed hardest.

This finding does not propose thousands of models. Every row costs a licence check, a thumbnail, a material audit and a place in a taxonomy, and RM-012 spent a sprint learning that curation is the lever rather than count. What it proposes is that the number be a decision somebody makes about content, and today it is a decision an index budget is making by accident.

AB-6 · The front page advertises a host that does not exist high measured

RM-015 AA-1 opened with “nothing has ever been published” and counted nine README links to an address returning 404. M1 removed all nine, re-pointed the deploy at Cloudflare Pages, and wrote the new address into the same first screenful — a Live app button, plus a documentation link at /docs. The landing note flagged it at the time: the claim is true from the moment it reaches master.

It has not, and it now will not for a while: the owner has no Cloudflare account and hosting is deferred by decision. Measured: curl against architect3d.pages.dev exits 6 — could not resolve host, with a control request to github.com/amitukind/architect3d returning 200 from the same shell. This is worse than AA-1's 404: a 404 is a server saying no, and this is a name that has never been registered.

Gate seventeen could not have caught it, and the reason is worth keeping. deploy:check forbids links to the retired host and resolves every relative link into the repository. A link to a plausible future host passes both rules, and no rule that runs offline can tell a real hostname from an aspirational one. So the fix is not a cleverer gate — it is the rule the README already states two paragraphs below the offending button: a link into the repository resolves on github.com, in an editor and in a clone, and it cannot be made wrong by a deploy that has not run yet. That rule was kept for the documentation links and broken for the one at the top.

after one tickviewdesign
settledviewdesign

The mode watcher sees a walk-through over the plan layout and moves the layout, which is right. The layout watcher then sees a layout that is not the plan and calls showDesign(), which is right for every mode except the two that asked for the layout themselves. So the first press of the button produces the orbit view, and a second press works — by then the layout is already 3D, so nothing re-enters the watcher.

This is RM-010 G3's bug, and G3's own comment is the diagnosis. That sprint added the guard for the exterior view and wrote beside it: “toggleExterior sets LAYOUT_VIEW and then frames the building; without this the watcher fires in between and showDesign() puts the mode straight back, so the button lit up and nothing moved.” Two modes arrange their own layout and the guard named one of them. The fix names the class instead: a camera mode that carries its own layout is not a mode this watcher may override.

Why nothing caught it for two programmes. There was no test that pressed the button. The camera composable is well covered and its showWalkthrough does exactly what it says; the shell suite checks that layouts show the right panes; neither drives the tool rail and then reads the camera. It is a bug that lives in the space between two files that are each individually tested, which is the argument for a suite organised by intention rather than by module - and is what tests/app-verbs.test.js is.

§ 71 · SPRINTS N1–N3

Two weeks, and the first one deletes a metric

No parent plan to price against — RM-007 is spent, so this is the first programme since RM-003 whose sprints are argued for from measurement alone. Two weeks in three sprints, and the shortest of them is the one that removes work rather than adding it.

N1

Point the instruments at the product

deliveredAB-1AB-20.5 wk

Objective. Every threshold in this repository measures something this product actually is, and the two that do not are corrected against their own measurements rather than quietly dropped.

  • Lighthouse gates the audience, and keeps the harsher lens (AB-1). Desktop becomes the gate at a floor recorded from first measurement rounded down — 91 measured, so 90 — because desktop is who this is for. Mobile stays as a second recorded floor at 60, not because a phone is supported but because its 87 ms of total blocking time is the only signal either run carries on main-thread work; the desktop run reads 0 ms and would read 0 ms after a regression that doubled it. Two floors, both ratchets, both in tools/lighthouse.json, and the reason for each written where it is read.
  • M-52 is retired and replaced with a metric about a real design (AB-2). The new clause is about every template this repository ships, furnished, and the 31-wall synthetic that is larger than all of them — a draw-call ceiling and a frame budget derived from what they measure today with the usual headroom, not from an aspiration. Retired in place, with the numbers that retired it, the way RM-014 recorded a withdrawn sprint: the point is that somebody reading M-52 later finds out why it stopped mattering, not that it disappeared.
  • The 400-wall fixture is kept and renamed. It is a good early-warning instrument — it is where M2's batching was proved and where the 2D culling was measured — and a bad promise. It keeps running with a ceiling loose enough to catch a tenfold regression and no longer tight enough to demand a rewrite of how a wall face fades.
  • Instanced furniture stops being deferred and starts being declined. M2 deferred it on the arithmetic that it cannot unblock M-52; with M-52 retired, the honest status is that a 300-call saving on a scene that costs 187 is not worth the code. Written down with both numbers so it stops being rediscovered.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-55 (new): a Lighthouse desktop performance score with a floor of 90, gating; the mobile score recorded beside it as a second floor that can only rise
  • M-56 (new): every shipped template, furnished, renders inside a draw-call ceiling and a frame budget measured from this drawing's figures — asserted in tier 2, where the 400-wall fixture already runs
  • M-52 is marked retired in the roadmap, beside the measurement that retired it, and no gate references it
  • No threshold moves in the direction that makes a failing build pass. The Lighthouse desktop floor is new and the mobile floor is the existing 60 renamed; the draw-call ceiling replaces a metric rather than relaxing one
LANDING — N1, two floors and a retirement
  • The gate runs both presets, and the desktop number was not the one this drawing predicted. AB-1 measured desktop at 91 with a hand-written throttling table. The gate imports Lighthouse's own desktop-config instead — a preset upstream maintains, so a transcribed copy cannot drift into measuring a machine nobody else calls desktop — and against that config the same build scores 96. Both numbers are real and they are measurements of different things; the drawing's is corrected in place above rather than quietly replaced.
  • Which turned the floor rule into a finding of its own. M3 wrote it as “first measurement, rounded down to the nearest 5”, and that is the rule that was being applied rather than the rule that was needed. It works at 62: the floor lands on 60, two points clear, and three runs of that build measured 62, 62, 61. It fails at 96: the nearest five below is 95, and four runs of this build measured 96, 96, 96, 95 — a floor a green build touches on one run in four is a red mark somebody learns to re-run rather than read. So the margin is stated instead of hoped for: the largest multiple of five leaving at least two points below the measurement. The test that it is a description rather than an invention is that it reproduces the existing mobile floor of 60 exactly.

  • M-56 is a table of what the product ships, and every row of it was measured. Seven designs, in headless Chromium off renderer.info.render, furniture fetched over the network and counted:

    The ceilings are tight, at about 15 % over, because a draw call is a property of the scene graph rather than of the GPU underneath it: a mesh per wall plane instead of a batch fails every row. The item counts are what stop the whole table being vacuous — a model that 404s makes a scene cheaper, so a ceiling on its own would pass harder with the furniture missing. A deliberate break that stopped the loader running failed exactly the two furnished rows and nothing else.

  • The frame budget is 8 ms and is written to be loose. The largest design measures 0.53 ms. Eight is half of a 60 Hz frame, chosen so the assertion says this scene is still cheap and says nothing whatever about which machine ran it — the rule wall-batching.test.js has stated since M2 is that a millisecond on a CI runner measures the runner. A tight timing gate here would be a fifteen-fold safety margin pretending to be a measurement.
  • The 400-wall fixture kept its ceiling, and the drawing was wrong to propose loosening it. N1 was written to relax it to “catch a tenfold regression”. It should not, and the distinction matters: the 1,100 there was never M-52. It is a ratchet on what M2 actually achieved, it passes at 972 with 13 % of margin, and it costs nothing. What demanded a rewrite of how a wall face fades was the metric, not the assertion. Relaxing a working instrument because a neighbouring promise was withdrawn would be the withdrawal spreading further than the evidence for it. So the fixture keeps its number and loses its claim: the file now says it is a stress case, and points at M-56 for the metric about designs that exist.
  • Instanced furniture is declined, and the arithmetic that declines it is not new. M2 deferred it after measuring that a perfectly instanced 150-item scene is 974 draw calls against M-52's 802 — a real 300-call saving that could not unblock the metric. With M-52 retired there is nothing left for it to unblock: the largest furnished design this product ships costs 187 calls, of which the furniture is 38. Declined rather than deferred, with both numbers, so the next sprint to reach for it finds out why in one paragraph.
  • Sprint N1 is delivered. 2,659 headless and 237 browser tests — 9 of them new, all in tier 2, because every claim here is about a real renderer. Eighteen gates, and gate eighteen now holds two floors where it held one. M-52 is marked retired in place beside the measurement that retired it, and no gate references it. No coverage floor moved, no budget limit moved, and the only threshold that moved at all is the Lighthouse floor rule — which moved to make a floor harder to trip by accident, not easier to pass.
N2

The first ten minutes, tested

deliveredAB-4AB-91 wk

Objective. The code a person runs in their first ten minutes is tested as well as the library underneath it, and a per-area floor stops the shell hiding behind the library.

  • The three thinnest files, in the order a person meets them (AB-4). App.vue at 37.3 % branch is the boot, the layout, the shortcut table and the theme; useTemplates at 27.3 % is the starter-plan shelf, which is the second thing anybody clicks; useDesignIO at 39.2 % is every verb that gets something out. Together they hold 171 uncovered branches of the tree's 1,518, in 550 statements.
  • Error paths first, happy paths second. The uncovered branches in those files are overwhelmingly the failure arms — a template that will not parse, a canvas that will not encode, a download the browser refuses, storage that is full. Those are the branches a first user is most likely to be the first person ever to execute, and the ones a demo never reaches.
  • A per-area floor, which is the part that lasts (AB-4). One global number over a tree of unequal parts measures the biggest part: App.vue could fall to zero and the global figure would move under two points. So the coverage gate grows a second form — a floor per directory, set at first measurement and rounded down, exactly as the global four were. The global four stay and stay where they are.
  • Not a rewrite for testability. App.vue is 1,318 lines because it is the composition root, and splitting it to raise a number would be the tail wagging the dog. Every one of these files is already mounted whole in tier 1; what is missing is cases, not seams.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-57 (new): branch coverage per directory, recorded and enforced; no directory below its recorded floor, and the floors set at first measurement rounded down
  • App.vue, useDesignIO and useTemplates each above 60 % branch coverage, from 37.3, 39.2 and 27.3
  • The four global floors rise. Reaching 60 % on the three covers 65 branches, which takes the tree from 79.43 to 80.32 % — enough to move the branch floor from 79 to 80, and the floors are set to the new measurement rounded down rather than to a target
  • Every new case fails when the behaviour it describes is deliberately broken. The failure arms are the point, so a case that passes against a mutant is not a case
LANDING — N2, and the button that needed two presses
  • The sprint found a live bug in a headline feature, and it is finding AB-9. Walk through did not walk you through. From the plan-only layout — which is the layout everybody starts in — the first press left you in the orbit view, and a second press worked. Traced rather than guessed:

Its comment describes the failure in as many words: “without this the watcher fires in between and showDesign() puts the mode straight back, so the button lit up and nothing moved.” The guard was written for one of the two modes that arrange their own layout and the other one was missed, and it went unnoticed for two programmes because nothing had ever pressed the button. That is AB-4's thesis arriving as a defect rather than as a percentage.

  • A second, smaller one in the same shape. Eight verbs in useDesignIO decline with a sentence when the thing they need is absent — “There is no plan view to export” — and two of them, saveDesign and saveMesh, dereferenced the model unconditionally and threw a TypeError instead. Defensive rather than live: the menu lives inside the tree that owns the store. It is fixed because a family of eight where six say a sentence and two throw is a family with a hole in it, and because the case that found it was written to assert the family behaves alike.
  • Where the coverage went, and why the middle column is the interesting one.
    filebranch, beforeafterwhat was missing

    useDesignIO39.2 %70.0 %every way an export can decline

M-47 asserts in tier 2 that a boot fetches no template and that a click fetches the manifest once, and a browser suite drives the shelf against the real files. Both are real tests and neither counts, because tier 2 is excluded from the coverage report — it runs against a server, so what it can exercise is the path where the server answers. What had never run was a 404, a rejected fetch, a JSON body that is not a manifest, or a row missing a field.

  • The verbs are driven the way a person drives them. Nothing in the new App suite reaches into the setup scope to call a function: where a verb has a button it is clicked, and where it has only a key the key is dispatched at window through the real listener — so the binding is under test as well as the handler. The accelerator is taken from IS_APPLE rather than hard-coded, because jsdom reports no platform and a test that assumed Cmd would have passed on a developer's Mac only if the code were wrong.
  • M-57 is a floor per directory, and it is fifteen lines of config rather than a nineteenth gate. Vitest takes glob keys in coverage.thresholds, so the mechanism already existed and what was missing was the numbers. Each is the largest multiple of five strictly below the first measurement — strictly below because two directories measured exactly 75.00 and 90.00, and N1 spent a paragraph four days ago on why a floor a green build sits precisely on is a red mark somebody learns to re-run. Branches only: it is the lowest of the four everywhere, it is the one that separates this line ran from this decision was tested, and four numbers across fifteen directories would be sixty numbers nobody reads.
  • And it stands on its own, which had to be shown rather than argued. Deleting the new App suite fails four checks — three global floors and the directory one — so it proves nothing by itself. With the global floors temporarily relaxed to where a few sprints of growth would leave them, deleting it fails exactly one: src/app/*.{js,vue} at 38.15 % against 60. That is the measurement AB-4 asked for: the global figure could not see the boot going untested, and now something can.
  • The four global floors rise, and by more than the drawing predicted. N2 estimated 65 branches and 79.43 → 80.32 %; the sprint covered 113 and landed at 80.88, because the three suites reached shared code the estimate only counted once — useToasts, useHistory and the plan's annotation paths are exercised by verbs in all three files. Floors go to 89 / 89 / 80 / 87 from 87 / 87 / 79 / 86, each rounded down from the new measurement.
  • Sprint N2 is delivered. 2,706 headless and 237 browser tests — 47 of them new across three suites, two of them files that did not exist. Eighteen gates plus fifteen directory floors; four global floors raised; two defects found and fixed, one of them user-visible in a feature the tool rail advertises. No threshold moved down, no test was weakened to fit, and the one place a test's expectation was corrected — leaving a walk-through returns to design, not to the plan — was corrected because the code was right and the guess was wrong.
N3

What the front page says, and what the budget decides

deliveredAB-6AB-50.5 wk

Objective. Nothing this repository publishes about itself is untrue, and the size of the catalog is a decision somebody makes rather than one a JSON budget makes for them.

  • The README stops advertising an address (AB-6). Done ahead of the sprint, because a dead link on the front page is not sprint work: the Live app button is replaced by the two commands that run it and a note saying plainly that there is no public address yet and why. The address goes back the day the deploy runs, which is what M-51 has always been waiting for.
  • A gate for the class, not the instance. No offline check can tell a real hostname from an aspirational one, so the rule is the one the README already states about its documentation links: an absolute link to this project's own future address is not allowed in the README at all, and deploy:check learns that shape rather than learning one more hostname to forbid.
  • The catalog's ceiling becomes a decision (AB-5). catalog-packs trips at 228 rows against 5.1 MB of unused model headroom. Either the line is raised with an argument about how large a catalog this product wants, or the index gets cheaper — 53 bytes a row is a JSON object with repeated keys, and a columnar or shortened-key form would halve it. The sprint measures both and takes one, and writing down which is the deliverable.
  • Not a catalog expansion. No rows are added here. RM-012 spent a sprint establishing that curation is the lever and that every row costs a licence check, a thumbnail and a material audit; this removes an accidental constraint and leaves the deliberate one alone.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-58 (new): no absolute link in the README to an address this repository cannot prove it serves, enforced by deploy:check as a shape rather than as a list of hostnames
  • The catalog-packs constraint is either raised with a recorded argument or made cheaper with a measured saving, and the choice is written down beside both numbers
  • Every existing budget line holds, and no coverage floor moves down
  • M-51 remains open and remains honestly reported as open. Nothing in this sprint pretends there is a deploy
LANDING — N3, a shape and a wait
  • M-58 forbids a shape, because forbidding a hostname is how this happened twice. Gate seventeen already refused links to the retired host by name, and a link to a plausible future host passed that rule and every other one in the file — which is how M1 closed AA-1 and reopened it in the same commit. No check that runs offline can tell a real hostname from an aspirational one, so the rule stopped trying: what it forbids is a deployment address for this project, matched as a host under a project-hosting suffix or the project's own name as a domain.

    The line it has to draw is where the interest is. github.com/amitukind/architect3d contains the project's name, resolves today, and is the one absolute link a public repository's README certainly should have — source hosting is not a deploy. And the rule is about links rather than mentions, which the retired-host rule had to learn the hard way on its first real run when it failed on this document for quoting the dead address as the thing it had measured.

    When there is an address, the exemption goes in one named constant, deliberately: publishing one should be a commit somebody makes rather than a line that drifts back in.

  • The cheaper-index route was measured and declined, and that is the honest half of AB-5. The sprint was allowed either road. 53 gzipped bytes a row looked exactly like a JSON object paying for its keys 217 times over, and it is not:
    encoding of all four index filesgzippedsaves
    as shipped4,454—
    every key shortened to one letter4,298156
    columnar — keys once, rows as arrays4,40648

    Fourteen thousand characters of key text buy back 156 bytes. Gzip already ate them, which is this file's own warning about headline ratios turned on the person about to act on one. And the index is not even the larger half: 6,886 of the 11,682 is the detail files, which are licence names, author names and source URLs — unique text, and irreducible.

  • So the limit was re-derived from the wait it protects. catalog-packs exists because opening the furniture drawer fetches all four packs; what it should guard is that first open, and what it was guarding was last year's measurement plus 5 %. On the 1.6 Mbps link Lighthouse throttles to - the slowest network anything here is measured on - 50,000 gzipped bytes is 244 ms. That is the new limit, up from 12,250 against a measurement of 11,666.

    It leaves room for roughly 930 rows, and it hands the decision back to whoever curates: past 50,000 the objection stops being the index is too big and becomes the drawer takes a quarter of a second, which is a sentence somebody can argue with. public-total is the binding constraint again at 608 more models, which is the right ordering — the bytes people download should limit the catalog, not the listing of them. No rows were added. RM-012 established that curation is the lever and that every row costs a licence check, a thumbnail and a material audit; this removes an accidental constraint and leaves the deliberate one alone.

  • The front page was fixed before the sprint, and the sprint is what makes it stay fixed. AB-6 was corrected the day it was found — a dead link on a front page is not sprint work — and the counts beside it were stale too: 168 models and 30 materials against a measured 217 and 32. What N3 adds is the gate, in both tiers: deploy:check refuses the shape, and tests/deploy-checks.test.js refuses it line by line where a failure is legible. Putting the button back fails both.
  • Sprint N3 is delivered, and programme N with it. 2,712 headless and 237 browser tests, 6 of them new. Nineteen gates, fifteen directory floors, and fourteen budget lines — one raised here with its argument and its rejected alternative recorded beside it. No coverage floor moved, no other limit moved, and M-51 is still open: there is no hosting account, hosting is deferred by decision, and every claim this repository makes about a deployed product remains a projection. The difference after this sprint is that the README no longer makes one.
§ 72 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskSprintWhat is done about it
Retiring a metric is how a project stops being honest with itself. Gating on desktop hides a regression that only a slow machine would showN1Which is precisely why the mobile floor is kept rather than replaced. The desktop run's total blocking time is 0 ms and carries no signal; the mobile run's 87 ms does. Two floors, and the cheaper one is the sensitive one

What must not change

  • The save format is untouched, for the fourth programme running. Nothing in this drawing is persisted in a design: a Lighthouse preset, a coverage floor, a draw-call ceiling and a catalog index are all properties of how the product is built and measured, and none of them is a property of a building.
  • No floor moves down and no budget limit moves up without an argument. N1 replaces a metric and N2 raises four; the one line this drawing proposes relaxing is catalog-packs, and only with a recorded argument about how large a catalog this product wants — or not at all, if the index turns out to be cheaper to fix than to fund.
  • The library's public API does not move, and this time nothing here would ask it to. Every finding is about the application, the tests or the measurements; src/scripts is not touched by any of the three sprints.
  • The four preserved bugs in core/utils.js stay preserved, the frozen r98 goldens still cannot be regenerated, and the eighteen gates stay eighteen or grow. N1 adds none and re-points one, N2 adds one, N3 adds one: twenty by the end. Nineteen. N2's addition is fifteen per-directory floors inside the coverage gate rather than a gate of its own — vitest takes glob thresholds, so M-57 is config where a new tool was priced.
  • M-51 stays open and stays visible. The one measurement that would matter most — somebody who is not holding this repository opening it — cannot be taken, and no sprint here pretends otherwise. Every claim about the deployed product remains a projection, and the drawing says so in the same words the last one did.
PROGRAMME P · DRAWING Nº RM-017

Three hypotheses, and the one thing they left behind

RM-016 N2 pressed a button nothing had ever pressed and found a live bug in a headline feature within a day, so this drawing set out to find the rest of them. It did not. Every hypothesis the last programme suggested is false, and each one was falsified by a measurement rather than by an argument: all 46 keyboard bindings fire or are correctly gated, exactly one piece of state in src/app is written from more than one file, and the drawing tool does show a live length and angle after all. What is left is smaller and real — that feedback is asserted by nothing and sits under a decade-old comment saying it crashes, and axe has audited 6 screens of about 20. One week, two sprints, and the drawing says plainly why there is no third.

§ 73 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What a search for the next bug actually found

Six measurements against the tree at fad8333, every one produced by running something: a probe that dispatches all 46 bindings at a mounted application and watches which fire, a scan for state written from more than one file, the coverage report read at four specific lines, and a count of what axe has ever been pointed at.

AB-9 looked like the tip of something. The Walk through button did not walk you through from the layout everybody starts in; two watchers fought over the camera mode; the guard that would have prevented it had been written two programmes earlier for the other of the two modes that need it. It was found the same week somebody first wrote a test that presses buttons. The obvious inference is that the untested wiring is full of these, and the obvious inference is wrong.

  • No dead bindings, out of 46. The probe replaces each binding's run with a recorder, synthesises the event a browser would send for its declared combination, and dispatches it at window through the real listener. Twenty-five fire. The other twenty-one do not, and every one of those reports enabled: false — nothing to undo, no plan focus, nothing selected. Not one binding is enabled and silent, and not one fires while disabled.
  • One piece of shared state, out of forty-nine watchers. src/app has 49 watch calls and exactly one cross-object ref written from more than one file: io.documentName, from App.vue, useProjects and useShare. AB-9's cycle was expressed through methods - showDesign() - rather than through assignment, which is both why a scan like this cannot see it and why there is not a second one to see.
  • And the drawing tool does tell you how long the wall is. This was the most promising hypothesis and the most wrong. drawTarget draws a dot and a rubber band and nothing else, and the status bar carries no length — but the caller draws the label: a live measurement and the angle to the nearest wall, with an arc guide, in the units the plan is set to.

What that last one left behind is the sprint. The block runs under this comment, which is the first line of it:

//Enable the below lines for measurement while drawing, still needs work as it is crashing the whole thing

The lines are enabled. Nothing crashes. The comment is a fossil from the 2014 demo that survived S1's port, seven programmes of refactoring and RM-016's own coverage sprint — and it is a comment that tells the next reader the most-used verb's feedback is broken and not to be trusted. Underneath it, the code is executed exactly once across 2,712 headless tests, incidentally, and asserted by nothing at all. So the situation is the reverse of the one this drawing went looking for: the behaviour is right, and everything written about it is wrong.

The other gap is accessibility, and it is a counting error rather than a defect. tests/browser/accessibility.test.js runs axe over the plan layout, split and 3D, all six steps of the first-run tour, the catalog drawer, and the credits modal on top of it. That is six screens. The application has about twenty: fifteen inspector panels, four dialogs, and the drawer. RM-014 L4 made the whole application keyboard-drivable and this gate is what keeps it that way, over a third of it.

And there is no third sprint, which is the point of writing the negatives down. Two of the six findings are measurements that say nothing to do here. One - the size of the catalog, now that RM-016 N3 stopped an index budget deciding it - is a decision for whoever owns the product rather than an engineering task. One is a watch item. A programme padded to two weeks on that evidence would be the first make-work in this document set, and the method that has overturned a sprint plan in nine of the last eleven drawings is the same method that says stop here.

§ 74 · DECISION LOG

Six findings, and three of them are negatives

Findings take AC. Three say a hypothesis is false and cost nothing to act on; two are sprints; one is a decision for the owner.

AC-1 · No dead keyboard bindings nothing to do measured

The hypothesis was reasonable. AB-9 was a verb no test had ever driven; RM-016's own census found that 24 of 38 declared keys had never been pressed by anything, and a binding table is a set of strings matched against what a browser reports — a shape where a typo is silent, a platform difference is silent, and space against a browser's ' ' is the exact mistake RM-014 L4 already made once in a test.

So it was measured rather than assumed. Each of the 46 bindings had its run swapped for a recorder; the event a browser would send for its declared combination was synthesised - including the accelerator from the module's own IS_APPLE, and the browser spellings ' ', Escape, ArrowUp - and dispatched at window, through the real listener, on a mounted application.

Twenty-five fired. Twenty-one did not, and all twenty-one report enabled: false - undo with nothing to undo, the plan cursor with the plan unfocused, mirror and copy and delete with nothing selected. Zero bindings are enabled and silent; zero fire while disabled. The keyboard table is correct, and the reason nothing had tested it is not that it was neglected but that useShortcuts is a small, well-covered function and the table is declarative.

What this costs the plan. A sprint that would have written forty-six end-to-end binding tests. What it is worth keeping is the shape of the check: it is nine lines, it needs a mounted application, and the thing it proves cannot be proved by reading. It is not added as a gate here, because a gate that has never failed and cannot fail without a typo is a gate that only slows a suite down — and the reasoning is written here so the next person who wonders does not have to build the probe again.

AC-2 · One piece of shared state nothing to do measured

AB-9 was two watchers writing one piece of state: the layout watcher set the camera mode, the mode watcher set the layout, and the order decided which won. The obvious question is how many more of those there are.

src/app holds 49 watchers. Every assignment of the form owner.ref.value = was attributed to the file it is in, and exactly one ref is written from more than one: io.documentName, from App.vue, useProjects and useShare — three files agreeing on what the open document is called, which is a design rather than a race.

And the scan cannot see AB-9, which is the honest caveat and the reason this finding is a negative rather than a proof. That cycle was written as camera.showDesign() - a method call on a composable that owns the state - so no assignment appears in App.vue at all. A tool that found AB-9 would have to follow calls into composables and know which of them write. It is buildable and it is not worth building for a codebase with 49 watchers and one shared ref; what is worth having is the note that the discipline is real, so the next person who suspects a state race can start from the two watchers in App.vue rather than from all forty-nine.

AC-3 · The plan does say how long the wall is, and says so under a note saying it crashes med measured

The most promising hypothesis of the six, and the most wrong. drawTarget draws a hover dot and a rubber band and nothing else; the status bar carries rooms, walls, items, area, cursor, zoom, mode and layout, and no length. Read that far, the core verb of a floor planner tells you nothing about the thing you are drawing.

Read the caller and it does. In draw(), under the DRAW branch, is a live label with the distance in the plan's own units, and beside it the angle to the nearest wall with an arc drawn between them. It is good work — it is what the two tools added by this project's own sprints already do, RM-008 E2's rectangle showing width and depth and E3's dimension showing a length — and it is the oldest of the three.

Two things are wrong with it, and neither is the behaviour.

  • The comment above it is a decade-old fossil, and it is the first line a reader meets: “Enable the below lines for measurement while drawing, still needs work as it is crashing the whole thing.” The lines are enabled. Nothing crashes. It came from the 2014 demo, survived S1's port and seven programmes of refactoring, and what it does now is tell the next person that the most-used verb's feedback is broken and not to be trusted. This project has spent eleven drawings on the principle that a comment which misleads is worse than no comment; this is the oldest one in the tree.
  • Nothing asserts it. The block is executed once across 2,712 headless tests - incidentally, by a case about something else - and no test anywhere claims that a person drawing a wall can see how long it is. It is one of the few behaviours in this application that a person would notice within ten seconds of losing, and it is held up by nothing.

AC-4 · axe has seen six screens of about twenty med measured

The accessibility gate runs axe-core over the real application with WCAG 2 A and AA plus the best-practice set, excluding the two drawing surfaces by selector rather than by turning rules off. It is a good gate. It has six cases: the plan layout, split and 3D, every control in the rail and top bar having an accessible name, all six steps of the first-run tour, the catalog drawer, and the credits modal over it.

The application renders about twenty screens. Fifteen inspector panels - corner, wall, room, surface, item, opening, stair, structure, dimension, annotation, carbon sheet, settings, the texture picker and the field components under them - and four dialogs: share, import a model, the shortcuts sheet and the project library. Not one has ever been audited.

Why that matters more here than it usually would. RM-014 L4 made this application keyboard-drivable end to end, including the drawing surface, and its acceptance was that axe runs with exactly two exclusions and that they stay two. The panels are where the form controls are: every label, every field association, every focus order that a person not using a mouse depends on. The gate that protects L4's work covers the shell around them.

AC-5 · The catalog's size is now a decision, and nobody has made it for the owner

Recorded rather than scheduled. RM-016 AB-5 found a 12 KB index budget rationing the catalog at 228 rows while five megabytes of model headroom sat unused, and N3 re-derived the limit from the wait it protects — 50,000 gzipped bytes, 244 ms on the link Lighthouse throttles to, room for about 930 rows. public-total is the binding constraint again, at 608 more models.

So the question the budget was answering by accident is now open and belongs to whoever owns the product: 217 rows today, against a brief that read “thousands of furniture models” literally and then declined the 600,000-model commercial catalog behind it. Every row costs a licence check, a thumbnail, a material audit and a place in a taxonomy, and RM-012 spent a sprint establishing that curation is the lever rather than count. There is no engineering task here until somebody says how many.

AC-6 · The next line anything will trip watch

demo-js-gzip is at 1.1 % headroom, 435,163 against 439,800, and RM-015 M3 left it there deliberately rather than raising it pre-emptively: splitting one chunk into eight cost 4,771 total bytes while taking 152,702 off what a boot downloads, and the note says the next commit to touch it will have to look at it. This is that note, repeated where the next drawing will read it. No action; the line is doing exactly what it was left to do.

§ 75 · SPRINTS P1–P2

One week, and the shortest programme in this document set

Two sprints, because four of the six findings do not need one. RM-016 was two weeks on six findings; this is one week on two, and the difference is not that the search was less thorough — it is that three of the answers came back negative and one belongs to somebody else.

P1

What the plan says while you draw

deliveredAC-30.5 wk

Objective. The live length and angle a person sees while drawing a wall are asserted where they can be seen, and the comment that says they are broken is gone.

  • Assert it in pixels, not in calls (AC-3). The claim is that somebody drawing a wall can read its length, and the tier that can check that is the one with a real canvas: draw halfway, raster the plan, and find the measurement where it should be. A headless assertion that drawTextLabel was called would pass over a label rendered in the background colour, which is the mistake RM-008 T-2 made and RM-004 B4 wrote the rule about.
  • The angle too, because it is the half nobody would notice losing. A length is missed immediately; an angle guide is missed by somebody drawing a room that turns out not to be square. Both come from the same block and both are covered by the same case.
  • Delete the fossil, and replace it with what is true. The comment predates this project. What belongs there is what the block does, why the label sits at the midpoint, and that the angle is measured to the nearest existing wall rather than to the axis - which is the part a reader cannot get from the code in one pass.
  • Not a redesign of the feedback. It is good and it has been good since 2014. This sprint does not move the label, restyle the arc, or add a numeric entry field; it makes the existing behaviour hold still. Anything else is a product decision and there is no finding behind it.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-59 (new): drawing a wall shows its length and the angle to the nearest wall, asserted off the rasterised canvas in tier 2 — ink, not a call count
  • The measurement reads in the plan's own units, so a document in feet says feet: the same case, run twice
  • No comment in src/scripts claims a live code path is disabled. The one this sprint deletes is the only one; a grep for the claim is part of the sprint, not an assumption It was not the only one. The grep found a second in model/corner.js, above a line that runs 205 times a suite — which is the clause working as written rather than a miss.
  • Every existing pixel test passes unchanged. The behaviour is not being changed, so a golden that moves means the sprint broke something
LANDING — P1, and the second fossil the acceptance found
  • There were two, and the drawing said there was one. P1's acceptance did not say delete the comment, it said no comment in src/scripts claims a live code path is disabled — a grep for the claim is part of the sprint, not an assumption. The grep found model/corner.js:

    “The below line is crashing after makign the changes for curved walls / While release v1.0.0 is stable even with this line enabled” — two sentences contradicting each other, above a live call to mergeWithIntersected(). Measured before deleting, the way AC-3 measured the first: that line executes 205 times across the headless suite, it is the path every corner drag takes, and nothing crashes. A third comment beside it survives untouched, because it is true: it explains why move() is called with its recursion guard off, and the code does exactly that.

    Writing an acceptance clause as a check rather than as a task is what found it. The clause could have read “delete the comment in floorplanner_view.js” and would have been satisfied with the second one still there.

  • The first pixel assertion passed with the label deleted, which is the whole lesson of this sprint repeating itself. The case read ink appears at the midpoint of the wall being drawn, and it does — the rubber band runs straight through that box. Deleting the label left it green. Measured, on the fixture:
    box on the pending wallwith the labelwithout
    midpoint, 120×42921407
    a quarter along, same size417405

    So the band is about 410 either way and the label is the other 500. The assertion is comparative now — the midpoint box against a box of the same size a quarter of the way along the same band — which subtracts the band and is the thing one box cannot do. RM-004 B4's rule is a number that improves is not evidence until the picture is checked; this is its converse, and it cost a deliberate break to notice.

  • And the arc needed the backend, because at that radius no box can see it alone. The angle guide is two marks: an arc struck about the corner at roughly 15 pixels, and the degrees printed on the bisector at about 30. The rubber band leaves the same corner through both. Deleting the arc and keeping the label left the corner-region case passing — a second deliberate break, a second assertion that was measuring the wrong thing. What the raster can honestly say is that the corner region responds to the angle, off-axis against on-axis, and that is what it now says; whether the arc in particular is stroked is recorded through backend.arc, with its sweep asserted to be non-zero so a degenerate call cannot pass a bare count.
  • Eight cases, and each of the three marks is held by the instrument that can see it. The label in pixels and in text; the units in text, in both centimetres and feet, with the distance computed from the tool's own plan coordinates rather than from the pixels the test dragged between - a 300-pixel drag is 609.6 cm at the default scale, and getting that wrong was the first version of the case. Nothing before the first corner is placed, and nothing after the tool is put down: without those two, a build that drew the label unconditionally would pass everything else.
  • Sprint P1 is delivered. 2,712 headless and 245 browser tests - 8 new, all in tier 2 because every claim here is about what somebody sees. Nineteen gates, all coverage floors held, every budget line unmoved, and every existing pixel test passes unchanged, which is the clause that matters most: the behaviour was not touched, only what is asserted and what is written about it. Three deliberate breaks, two of which caught an assertion that was measuring the rubber band.
P2

The screens nobody has audited

deliveredAC-40.5 wk

Objective. The gate that protects RM-014 L4's keyboard work covers the screens the form controls are actually on.

  • Fifteen inspector panels and four dialogs (AC-4). axe over each, opened the way a person opens it — select a corner and the corner panel renders, select a wall and the wall panel does. Driven through the application rather than by mounting each component alone, because half of what axe checks is context: a label's association, a heading order, a focus trap, the landmark a control sits inside.
  • Whatever it finds, in the same sprint. The budget is half a week for the audit and the fixes, because an accessibility finding is usually a missing for, an aria-label or a heading level rather than a redesign. If something needs more than that it is recorded as a finding and drawn separately rather than rushed.
  • The two exclusions stay two. L4's acceptance was that axe runs over the whole application with exactly two selector exclusions - the plan canvas and the 3D canvas, both drawing surfaces - and that no rule is turned off to make it pass. A third exclusion is a finding, not a fix.
  • Not a keyboard sprint. L4 delivered keyboard-only drawing and focus order and this does not revisit it. axe is a static audit of rendered markup; what it adds is coverage of the two thirds of the application that audit has never run over.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-60 (new): axe reports no violation on any inspector panel or dialog the application can open, with the same rule set and the same two exclusions the existing six cases use
  • Every panel is reached by opening it, not by mounting it: a case that renders a component in isolation is not a case about the application
  • The count is asserted, not the list. A twenty-first screen added later must fail this rather than be silently unaudited — which is the failure mode the existing six cases have
  • Any violation that cannot be fixed inside the sprint is recorded as a finding with its rule id and its element, and nothing is excluded to make the gate green
LANDING — P2, and three defects the shell was hiding
  • The application has had no level-one heading since S6, with an accessibility gate running over it the whole time. Not one <h1> anywhere: one h2, twelve h3s, three h4s. The six cases that existed scoped to #app-root, and a page-level rule cannot fire on a subtree; the one case that did scope to the document only ever ran with a modal open, where axe evaluates the dialog rather than the page. Two blind spots that happened to cover each other exactly.

    The fix is a visually hidden h1 in the banner, and where it goes was decided by the tool rather than by taste: placed loose in the shell it failed region, because a heading outside every landmark is a heading nothing owns.

  • Which exposed the second defect immediately. With an h1 present, the inspector's h3 panel titles became a jump - heading-order, moderate - and the h4 subheadings under them a second one. The structure was never right; there was simply no h1 for it to be wrong against. Ten panel headings are h2 now and two subheadings h3, which is what they are: the top heading of the <aside> landmark, and the sections under it. Every one is styled by class, so nothing moved on screen.
  • And a third that only the panels could show: the texture swatches said their own name twice. image-redundant-alt, 22 nodes on the wall list and 39 on the floor list. Each swatch is an <img alt="Fine Wood"> inside a button that already carries Fine Wood in text, so a screen reader reads it twice. The image is decorative within a labelled control - the button is the thing being chosen - so the alt is empty now and the span is the name.
  • Five cases were auditing the settings tab and reporting it as five panels. The third assertion this programme to measure the wrong thing, and the worst of the three. <script setup> exposes its refs and functions on setupState and not its imported bindings, so app.SELECTION_CORNER_2D was undefined; selecting a type nothing matches left the inspector on the tab it boots with, and the guard written to catch exactly that - the panel rendered some controls - is satisfied by the settings tab, which is full of them.

    Found by printing the document's headings during the case and seeing one h1 and nothing else. The constants are imported from useSelection.js now, and the guard asserts the selection tab is open and the panel's own h2 is in the DOM. Both surface panels then failed on the swatch alt immediately, which is how it is known the cases had been auditing nothing.

  • The count is read off the tree, not typed here. The first version of that case asserted screens === 19 against constants written a line above it - arithmetic checking itself. It uses import.meta.glob now, so a twenty-first screen fails the suite until somebody either opens it or adds it to NOT_YET with a reason. Verified by copying a dialog into the tree, which failed it.
  • Fourteen screens audited, five recorded as not. ItemInspector, the three parametric panels and CarbonSheetPanel each need something placed in the scene first - a fixture P2 did not price - and they are named in the file rather than left out of the count. Nothing was excluded to make the gate green: the exclusions are still the two drawing surfaces L4 left, and no rule is off.
  • Sprint P2 is delivered, and programme P with it. 2,712 headless and 259 browser tests - 14 new. Nineteen gates, and gate five covers fourteen screens where it covered six. Three accessibility defects found and fixed, all in markup, none of them visible on screen. No coverage floor moved, no budget limit moved, and five deliberate breaks: the h1 removed, a heading demoted, a screen added with nothing opening it, the swatch alt restored, and the arc from P1 - four caught first time and one only after the assertion that missed it was rewritten.
AND NO THIRD SPRINT
  • AC-1 and AC-2 are measurements that say stop. A binding-coverage sprint and a shared-state sprint were both plausible before the probes ran, and both would have been work with nothing behind it. The probes are described in § 74 in enough detail to re-run, which is the deliverable: the next person who suspects the wiring can spend ten minutes rather than a week.
  • AC-5 is not an engineering task. How large the catalog should be is a question for whoever owns the product, and RM-016 N3's whole purpose was to stop a budget answering it by accident. Scheduling a sprint to add rows before that answer exists would be putting the constraint back in a different place.
  • AC-6 is a line doing its job. demo-js-gzip at 1.1 % headroom is where M3 deliberately left it so that the next change would have to look at it. Raising it now, with no change to justify it, is exactly what this file has refused eleven times.
  • M-51 is open and cannot be closed from here. There is no hosting account, hosting is deferred by decision, and the deploy is built, gated and waiting. It is not a sprint until it is a credential.

The alternative was two more weeks of work with nothing behind it, and every drawing in this set that overturned its own plan did so on exactly this evidence

What must not change

  • The save format is untouched, for the fifth programme running. A label on a canvas and an aria-label on a field are properties of how a building is drawn and described, not of the building.
  • The drawing feedback is not redesigned. P1 asserts what is there and rewrites what is written about it. Moving the label, restyling the arc or adding numeric entry are product decisions with no finding behind them, and this drawing has been careful to say when it has no evidence.
  • The two axe exclusions stay two, and no rule is turned off. That was L4's acceptance and it is P2's.
  • No coverage floor moves down, no budget limit moves up. Nineteen gates, fifteen directory floors, fourteen budget lines and two Lighthouse floors, all as RM-016 left them. P1 adds none and P2 adds none: M-59 and M-60 are cases inside gates that already exist, which is where a metric belongs when the gate is already pointed at the right thing.
  • M-51 stays open and stays visible. Every claim this repository makes about a deployed product is still a projection, the README no longer makes one, and the day there is a credential the deploy is a button. Nothing here pretends otherwise, for the sixth drawing in a row.
PROGRAMME Q · DRAWING Nº RM-018

The gate that decides by coin flip

RM-017 closed by saying that the method which has overturned nine of eleven sprint plans was, that time, saying stop. So this drawing began by running the instrument all nine of those overturns were measured against — and npm run test:coverage fails on the committed tree, one run in three. Twenty-one runs at 2909594, seven red, with nothing wrong: 12,136 statements against a floor that needs 12,137, decided by one line in one file that no test file covers on its own. Six runs compared file by file say the other 168 files never move. The gate has been able to report either answer since N2 set a floor to a measurement that was already a whole number — on a branch CI does not run. Two sprints, one week, and the first is half a day of code.
