§ 77 · EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

What running the gate twenty-one times said

Seven measurements against the tree at 2909594, every one produced by running something: the coverage gate twenty-one times, six of those runs compared file by file, the offending statement's own map read out of coverage-final.json, each suspect suite run on its own, a recorder installed on the function that owns the line, nineteen floors' slack computed against their real denominators, and both builds re-made to price the tightest budget line.

The tree is clean and the gate is red. Not intermittently slow, not red on a machine somebody has configured badly — red on the commit this programme starts from, in seven of twenty-one consecutive runs of the exact command CI runs. All 2,712 tests pass every time. What fails is the threshold underneath them:

runs of npm run test:coverage at 2909594statementsof 13,636verdict
14 of 2189.00 %12,137green
7 of 2188.99 %12,136below the 89 floor

One statement is the entire difference, and it is the same statement every time: src/scripts/model/loaders.js line 110, ktx2Loader.workerConfig = support;. Six full runs compared file by file put a number on how isolated that is — 1 of 169 files moves between runs. The suite is otherwise bit-for-bit reproducible, which is what makes this worth a sprint rather than a shrug: there is one nondeterministic line in this repository and it happens to be sitting on a threshold with no room under it.

The floor has no room because the rule that makes these floors safe did nothing, once. Every threshold in vitest.config.mjs is set by rounding the measurement down to a whole number, and the rounding is where the headroom comes from. N2's measurement was 89.00. Rounded down, that is 89. The config records it in those words — “89.07 lines, 89.00 statements” — and a floor of 89 over 13,636 statements needs 12,136.04 of them, so it needs 12,137 and the build has 12,137. Slack: zero. The ratchet did exactly what it always does and, for the first time in eleven programmes, that produced a floor with nothing under it.

It is not the only one. Nineteen floors are enforced here — four global and the fifteen per-directory branch floors N2 added as M-57 — and computing each one's slack against its own denominator rather than its percentage says:

floormeasuredwritteneffectiveslack
global, statements12,137 / 13,6368989.000
src/app/tour/**, branches9 / 108590.000
src/app/offline/**, branches64 / 709090.001
src/scripts/*.js, branches18 / 208585.001
src/app/import/**, branches92 / 999090.912
the other fourteen———5 to 65

A percentage floor on ten branches is not the number it says it is. src/app/tour has ten of them; 85 % of ten is 8.5, and there is no such thing as 8.5 branches, so the floor written as 85 is enforced as 90 and one new uncovered branch in the tour fails the build. The same arithmetic makes src/scripts/*.js a floor of 85 over twenty branches, which is 17, which the build clears by one. None of this is wrong — a floor is meant to be tight — but four of the nineteen are within two units of red and nothing anywhere says so, which is why the first one to actually trip did so unannounced.

And nothing would have said so, because nothing runs it. CI triggers on pushes to dev and master only, deliberately and with the reason written at the top of the workflow — Actions minutes. Tier 0, the pre-commit hook, is npx lint-staged. All eight sprints of programmes M, N and P were built and committed on amit, where the coverage gate runs exactly when somebody types it. That policy is not the bug and this drawing does not propose changing it; it is the reason a coin-flip gate could be introduced by M3, have its floor set flush against it by N2, and survive N3, P1 and P2 without once being the thing that failed.

Underneath the test flake there is a product one, and it is the same defect. The line that comes and goes reads formatSupport(), whose answer is cached forever by the first caller. Before M3 the first caller was always the renderer: Main calls describeFrom(renderer) as it builds one, and Main itself was built inside the BlueprintJS constructor — so it ran before any model could be loaded, every time, by construction. M3 made the viewer lazy, and the order inverted — a session that opens a plan and places an item before ever attaching the 3D view now decides which GPU texture formats exist from probe()'s throwaway 1×1 context, and the real renderer's answer is discarded when it arrives. core/texture_formats.js already says which of the two is preferred, and why: describeFrom is “preferred, because it asks the context the application will actually draw with rather than a second one that might differ if the browser gave it a different adapter.” The comment is still true. The code no longer arrives in the order it describes.

Everything else on the board is green, and that is measured too: lint, typecheck, ledger:check, help:check, manifest:check, templates:check and catalog:check all pass, npm audit reports zero vulnerabilities with and without dev dependencies, and both builds remade from clean put every one of the fourteen budget lines inside its limit. The tightest, demo-js-gzip, holds 4,581 bytes of headroom — 1.04 %, and it has moved 23 bytes in two sprints.

§ 78 · DECISION LOG

Seven findings, and the first one is a red build

Findings take AD. Two are one defect seen from two sides — a test that flakes and a product that decides in the wrong order — and they share a sprint. Two are negatives that cost nothing. One corrects a number RM-017 published.

AD-1 · The gate that eleven programmes have been measured against is a coin flip high measured

This was not the hypothesis. The intention was to open RM-018 the way RM-016 and RM-017 opened — run everything, see what the numbers say — and the first command run said ERROR: Coverage for statements (88.99%) does not meet global threshold (89%) with all 2,712 tests passing. The tree was clean, at 2909594, the commit that closed programme P and was reported green.

It was reported green, and the runs it was reported from were green. That is all a single run can tell anybody: a failure that happens one time in three hides from any one look two times in three. Twenty-one consecutive runs of the same command on the same commit: fourteen at 89.00 %, seven at 88.99 %. Nothing else varies. The denominator is 13,636 in every run; the numerator is 12,137 or 12,136.

What makes 12,136 fail is arithmetic, and it is worth writing out because the number looks like a rounding artefact and is not. A floor of 89 % over 13,636 statements requires 12,136.04 of them. There is no fractional statement, so it requires 12,137 — and a green build has exactly 12,137. The floor is not nearly at the measurement; it is at it, to the last unit.

And that happened by following the rule, not by breaking it. Every floor in this file is the measurement rounded down to a whole number, and the config records what N2 measured: “89.07 lines, 89.00 statements, 80.88 branches, 87.66 functions”. Rounding 89.00 down gives 89. The rounding is where a floor's headroom comes from, and against a measurement that is already whole it produces none. Eleven programmes of ratcheting, and the one time the rule was a no-op is the one time it mattered.

What this costs the plan. Nothing to build; the sprint is small. What it costs is the assumption every previous drawing rested on — that a green coverage run is a fact about the code. For three sprints it has been a fact about the code and the scheduler, and the two were indistinguishable because the failure needed both a floor with no slack and a line that moves.

AD-2 · One line in one file, and no suite owns it med measured

Six full runs were captured and compared file by file. Of 169 files, one moves: src/scripts/model/loaders.js, statements 12/13 or 13/13 and branches 1/2 or 2/2. Everything else — every count, in every file, on all four metrics — is identical run to run. Whatever this is, it is a point defect and not a property of the suite.

Read out of coverage-final.json, the statement is line 110:

var support = formatSupport();
if (support) { ktx2Loader.workerConfig = support; }

— and the branch that moves with it is that same if. So the question is whether anything, anywhere in the run, builds a set of model loaders at a moment when formatSupport() has an answer.

Nothing that can be attributed to a test file does. A recorder was installed on createModelLoaders that writes the value of support and the current test file on every call. Four consecutive full runs produced the same twenty-two calls each time — model-import 11, imported-model 7, share-composable 3, items-and-scene 1 — and every one of the twenty-two reported support false, while the statement was reported covered. Run alone, each of the four reports 12/13, and the two that were run repeatedly — six times and twice — never reported anything else. So the hit that makes the difference belongs to an execution the recorder cannot see.

The likely reading, marked as a reading rather than a measurement: Scene._ensureLoaders() starts import('./loaders.js') and addItem does not await it, so the loaders are constructed whenever that promise settles — which can be after the test that asked for them has finished, in an environment the recorder depends on and no longer has. Two recorders were written; the first swallowed its own failures in a catch and so reported nothing in exactly the runs that were interesting, which is how that reading was arrived at. Confirming it is the sprint's first task and not this drawing's claim. What the drawing does claim is the part that does not depend on the explanation: the line is covered by nothing a test file owns, and the sequence that decides it is a race. This is not a test to fix; it is a sequence to make deterministic, and the reason it is worth doing properly is AD-3.

AD-3 · M3 inverted an order the code still documents med measured

core/texture_formats.js holds one cached record of what this GPU can decode, and it is first-caller-wins by design — “two viewports must not disagree about the device, and a texture already transcoded for one format cannot be re-transcoded because a later renderer reported another.” There are two ways to fill it: describeFrom(renderer), which asks the renderer the application draws with, and probe(), which opens its own 1×1 context and asks that. The preference is stated in describeFrom's own docblock — not required, “but preferred, because it asks the context the application will actually draw with rather than a second one that might differ if the browser gave it a different adapter” — and main.js:552 is the call that was supposed to guarantee it.

Until M3 the preference was guaranteed by construction. Main was built inside the BlueprintJS constructor, so describeFrom ran before the application could load anything. M3 moved the viewer behind attachViewer() and a dynamic import — correctly, and it is the sprint that took first-load from 432,781 to 280,079 bytes — but the ordering guarantee went with it. The application now attaches the viewer on the first camera change or the first document load, and a person who opens a plan and drops a chair into it before ever switching to 3D reaches createModelLoaders first.

What that costs, honestly. Usually nothing: the probe context and the real one are the same GPU and will report the same extension list. The cases where it is not nothing are the cases the comment was written about — a hybrid-graphics machine that hands a second context a different adapter, or a renderer created with attributes the probe does not ask for. It is a small risk, it is unmeasurable from here without those machines, and it is free to remove, which is the argument for doing it: the fix is to decide the format question in one place at one time rather than wherever the race lands. That is the same fix AD-2 needs.

AD-4 · Four floors are within two units, and two of them read stricter than they are written med measured

Once one floor turned out to have zero slack, the obvious question is how many others do. Every one of the nineteen was computed as covered − ceil(floor × total) — the number of units that can be lost before the build goes red — rather than as a difference of percentages, because a difference of percentages hides the denominator and the denominator is the whole story.

src/app/tour/** has ten branches and nine of them covered. Its floor is written 85. Eighty-five per cent of ten is 8.5; the check needs 9. The floor is therefore enforced at 90, and the tour is one uncovered branch from failing a threshold that says 85. src/scripts/*.js is the same shape at twenty branches, and src/app/offline/** and src/app/import/** have one and two units respectively.

None of this is a mistake and none of these floors should move. M-57's per-directory floors were derived correctly — the largest multiple of five strictly below each measurement — and they did what they were built for, which is to stop one number over an unequal tree from measuring only its biggest part. What is missing is that a floor's real distance from red is invisible: the file records percentages, the report prints percentages, and on a ten-branch directory a percentage is a lie of granularity. The fix is to print the slack, not to change a number.

AD-5 · Five screens unaudited, and one of them is misfiled med measured

P2 took gate five from six screens to fourteen and named the five it did not reach: ItemInspector, OpeningInspector, StairInspector, StructureInspector and CarbonSheetPanel, with the reason recorded as “each needs a parametric item or an imported model placed in the scene first.”

That is true of four of them. CarbonSheetPanel is rendered by SettingsPanel.vue under v-if="carbonSheet", and carbonSheet is floorplanner.carbonSheet — the plan's underlay handle, which exists whenever the 2D floorplanner does. It needs no item at all. Whether it is already being audited inside the settings case is a question the sprint answers by looking, not by reasoning: SettingsPanel is in AUDITED, and if the floorplanner is mounted when that case runs then the carbon-sheet controls are in the document axe is analysing and the count is wrong by one in the safe direction.

The other four are genuinely blocked on a fixture, and it is a fixture tier 2 already builds elsewhere: tests/browser/parametric-stairs.test.js and its siblings place items with scene.addItem(...) and wait for them. The work is to lift that into the accessibility suite once and drive four selections through it.

AD-6 · Why nobody saw it nothing to do measured

CI runs on pushes to dev and master, and on nothing else. There is no pull_request trigger. The reason is written at the top of the workflow and it is a good one — Actions minutes are the constrained resource and the file says so in four places. Tier 0, the pre-commit hook, is npx lint-staged: formatting and lint on the staged files, no tests.

So on amit, where every sprint of programmes M, N and P was written, committed and pushed, the coverage gate runs when somebody types it and not otherwise. Five sprints and two whole programmes landed between M3 introducing the moving statement and this drawing running the command twenty-one times, and for the last three of them — since N2 set the floor flush against its own measurement — a run could have come back red. Each of those sprints did run it, and the figures are in this document; each of them happened to get a green.

This is a finding and not a task. Turning CI on for working branches would cost minutes on a repository that has deliberately traded them away, and it would catch this defect one time in three, which is not catching it. The answer is to make the gate deterministic, which is Q1, and then a single run means what it says again. Recorded here so the next person who wonders why a red build sat on a branch for three sprints does not have to work it out.

AD-7 · Everything else, and a number RM-017 published slightly wrong nothing to do measured

Seven check scripts run and green: lint, typecheck, ledger:check, help:check, manifest:check, templates:check, catalog:check. npm audit reports zero vulnerabilities, run twice — once over everything and once with --omit=dev — so RM-006's ratchet holds and the VitePress vite override is still doing its job. Eight dev dependencies are behind — six by a patch, one by a minor and one, TypeScript, by a major; nothing here proposes a bump, and the ledger gate is what would notice if one broke something.

Both builds were remade from clean and the budget re-run, because npm run budget measures files on disk and a stale dist-demo reports a stale number. All fourteen lines pass. demo-js-gzip is the tightest at 435,219 bytes against a 439,800 limit — 4,581 bytes, 1.04 %.

And the browser tier was run three times too, because a claim that one line in this repository is nondeterministic ought to be checked against the half of the suite that has no coverage gate to expose one. 259 of 259 pass on every run, in 488, 463 and 546 seconds. It cannot flake a threshold because it holds none; what it is, at roughly eight minutes, is the long pole — and that is the budget Q2's fixture has to fit inside.

RM-017 recorded that line at 1.1 % and drew a conclusion from it: “AC-6 is a line doing its job.” The conclusion holds and the number was a little stale. Built at 65fa12b the same measurement is 435,196 bytes, so P2 spent 23 bytes — a visually hidden h1, two attribute changes and twelve heading levels. The line is tight, it is not eroding, and 4,581 bytes is still less than one component.

§ 79 · SPRINT PLAN

One week, two sprints, and the first is half a day of code

Q1 is small and it is first because everything else in this document set is measured through it. Q2 finishes what P2 started and priced. Nothing here moves a floor down, nothing raises a budget limit, and nothing changes the CI policy.

Q1

A number that means the same thing twice

proposedAD-1AD-2AD-3AD-40.5 wk

Objective. The coverage gate reports the same four figures for the same commit, every time; the ordering defect underneath it is decided in one place rather than by whichever promise settles first; and every floor's real distance from red is visible in the run that prints it.

  • Confirm where the covering execution comes from, then remove the race (AD-2). The first hour is the one thing this drawing could not finish: a recorder that survives its own test file, so the execution that covers the line is named rather than inferred. Then the fix, which does not depend on the answer. _ensureLoaders() starts a dynamic import and createModelLoaders asks formatSupport() whenever that import settles — which is the race. The read moves to the caller: Scene asks at the point it decides to load something, synchronously, and passes the answer in. That keeps M3's property intact — the probe context is still opened on the first model load and never on a boot — and it makes the line a function of what the caller did rather than of when a microtask ran.
  • Then cover it on purpose, both arms. A test that builds the loaders with a known support record and one that builds them without, so 13/13 is a property of the suite and not of the scheduler. This is the part that must not be done by moving a number: the statement is real code on a real path, and the honest response to a threshold it keeps tripping is to test it.
  • Settle which context answers, in the browser, in both orders (AD-3). Two cases in tier 2: place an item with no viewer attached, and attach the viewer first. Assert which source filled the record in each. If the answers agree on this machine that is worth recording rather than assuming, and it is the measurement that decides the second half — either the stated preference is restored by having attachViewer settle the question before anything can load, or describeFrom's docblock is corrected to say that a probe is now the usual source and why that is acceptable. The drawing does not pick; the measurement does, and whichever way it goes the comment and the code agree at the end of the sprint.
  • Print the slack (AD-4). The workflow's summary step already prints four coverage percentages. It prints each floor's slack in units beside them, for all nineteen, so a floor with nothing under it is visible in the run rather than discoverable by arithmetic. The effective floors go into the vitest.config.mjs comment as well: src/app/tour is written 85 and enforced 90, and the next person to raise it should know that before they do.
  • No floor moves down, and the global statements floor moves up only if the sprint earns it. If covering the line deliberately puts statements above 89 with real slack, the floor is raised with the measurement written down, exactly as eleven programmes have done. If it does not, it stays at 89 and the slack is honest instead of accidental.
  • Not a CI policy change (AD-6). Running the suite on working branches would cost minutes this repository has deliberately traded away, and it would catch this defect one time in three, which is not catching it. The sprint makes one run mean what it says; that is the fix.
  • And not a hunt for other flakes. Six runs compared file by file say there is one. If Q1's own repeat-run check finds a second, it is a finding and it is drawn; it is not scope taken on speculatively.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-61 (new): ten consecutive runs of npm run test:coverage on one commit report identical statements, branches, functions and lines — run, and the ten figures recorded in the landing note rather than asserted from three
  • loaders.js:110 is covered by a named test in both arms, and deleting either arm fails the suite
  • Two tier 2 cases record which source answered the format question, one per order, and describeFrom's docblock at core/texture_formats.js:178 agrees with what the code now does
  • The CI summary prints slack in units for all nineteen floors. A floor with zero slack is legible without doing arithmetic
  • No coverage floor moves down and no budget limit moves. A floor raised is a floor with the measurement beside it
Q2

The four screens that need a chair, and the fifth that does not

proposedAD-50.5 wk

Objective. Gate five covers every screen this application can open, and anything it still cannot open is named with a reason the suite itself checks.

  • One fixture, four selections (AD-5). ItemInspector, OpeningInspector, StairInspector and StructureInspector each need something in the scene, and tier 2 already builds exactly that: parametric-stairs, parametric-openings and lamps all place items through scene.addItem and wait for them. The work is to lift that into the accessibility suite once and drive four selections through it, in the same one-mount shape P2's panel cases use.
  • Check the carbon sheet rather than reasoning about it. CarbonSheetPanel renders inside SettingsPanel on v-if="carbonSheet", which is the plan's own underlay handle and needs no item. Either the settings case is already analysing it — in which case the count was wrong by one and is corrected in place — or one line opens it. Both are half an hour; the point is that the reason in NOT_YET must be true, and today one of its five is not.
  • Whatever it finds, in the same sprint. P2's clause, and P2 is the evidence for it: fifteen panels and four dialogs produced three defects, every one of them a missing attribute or a heading level. Anything larger is a finding with its rule id and its element, drawn rather than rushed.
  • The two exclusions stay two, no rule is turned off, and the count case keeps reading the tree with import.meta.glob rather than being told how many screens there are.
  • Not a keyboard sprint and not a screen-reader sprint. L4 delivered and gated the first; the second needs a person and a screen reader, and this repository cannot run one. That gap is stated, not closed.
ACCEPTANCE
  • M-62 (new): axe reports no violation on any of the nineteen screens the application can open, same rule set and same two exclusions
  • NOT_YET is empty, or every entry left in it fails a check that proves it cannot be opened — a reason in a comment is what this sprint is fixing, not what it produces
  • Every panel is still reached by opening it. A component mounted alone is not a case about the application
  • Each new case fails against a deliberate break, and the break is named in the landing note
AND NO THIRD SPRINT
  • AD-6 is a policy working as designed. The workflow's own comments argue the trade four times over, and nothing measured here overturns the argument. What overturns it would be a second flake, and there is no second flake.
  • AD-7 is a board that is green. Seven checks, zero advisories, fourteen budget lines. The tightest has moved 23 bytes in two sprints, which is a line doing its job for the second drawing running — RM-017 said so at 1.1 %, and at 1.04 % it is still saying it.
  • AC-5 is still not an engineering task. How large the catalog should be is a decision for whoever owns the product, unchanged since RM-017 asked and unchanged by anything here.
  • M-51 is open and cannot be closed from here. Seventh drawing running: no hosting account, hosting deferred by decision, the deploy built and gated and waiting on a credential. Every claim in this document about a deployed product is still a projection.
§ 80 · RISKS & COMPATIBILITY

What could go wrong, and what must not change

RiskSprintWhat is done about it
Moving the formatSupport() read earlier re-opens a probe context on every boot, undoing part of what M3 boughtQ1It moves to the point Scene decides to load a model, not to its constructor. A session that never places anything still never probes, and the acceptance can check it: no WebGL context is created by a boot that loads no model
Ten identical runs is not a proof of determinism, only twenty-one failures' worth of evidence that it was notQ1True, and stated rather than papered over. Ten is what a run of this suite costs times ten; the claim it supports is “the observed flake is gone”, not “nothing can ever flake”. The slack print is the standing instrument, because a floor with room under it survives a flake nobody has found yet
Covering the line raises statements above 89 and the floor is raised, which makes the next sprint's threshold tighter for a reason that was really a bug fixQ1Then it is raised with that written beside it, which is what every other entry in that file does. A floor earned by covering real code is exactly the kind this ratchet is for — and the slack print means the next person can see what they are being held to
The two contexts agree on this machine and the AD-3 question cannot be settled by measurement hereQ1That is the likely outcome and it is still a result: the sprint then corrects describeFrom's docblock to say a probe is the usual source, records that they agreed where it could be checked, and leaves the preference as a documented preference rather than a guarantee nothing enforces. Agreeing on one machine is not a proof, and the comment will say so
Placing four items in one accessibility mount makes tier 2 slower, and it is already the long poleQ2One mount, four placements, four selections, one axe run each — the expensive part is the mount and the model fetches, and P2's panel cases already share one. If the model loads dominate, the four are grouped and the grouping is recorded, which is the same answer P2 gave and did not need
Four new screens produce a list of violations that does not fit in half a weekQ2Then it does not fit, and the list is a finding with rule ids. P2 is the prior: nineteen screens attempted, three defects, all markup. Nothing is excluded to make the gate green — that clause has now survived two sprints and found three real defects because of it
Q1 changes src/scripts, and the library's public API has not moved in four programmesQ1It still does not. createModelLoaders is internal to the model layer and is not exported from blueprint.js; Scene._ensureLoaders is private by name and by ledger. Nothing an embedder can call changes shape

What must not change

  • The save format is untouched, for the fifth programme running. Nothing in this drawing is persisted in a design. A coverage threshold, a probe order and an axe fixture are properties of how the product is built and measured; none of them is a property of a building.
  • No floor moves down. Not this one, not for this reason. A gate that fails a third of the time is the most tempting argument for lowering a number that this document set has ever produced, and it is the wrong one: the line is real code on a real path, the failure is a race, and the answer to both is a test. The rule that has held for eleven programmes holds here, and the sprint that discovered the exception is the worst possible place to make one.
  • M3 is not reverted and nothing is un-deferred. The lazy viewer took first load from 432,781 to 280,079 bytes and it stays. What Q1 restores is an ordering guarantee that came free before and now has to be written down — which is the normal cost of making something lazy, and cheaper than the 152,702 bytes it bought.
  • The library's public API does not move, the four preserved bugs in core/utils.js stay preserved, and the frozen r98 goldens still cannot be regenerated.
  • The nineteen gates stay nineteen or grow. Q1 adds none — the slack print is a line in a summary step, and the coverage gate it reports on has been in the ladder since RM-002 P1 — and Q2 adds none, because gate five is the one it widens. Nineteen at the end, doing more.
  • M-51 stays open and stays visible. There is still no hosting account, hosting is still deferred by decision, and the one measurement that would matter most — somebody who is not holding this repository opening this application — still cannot be taken. Seven drawings have said so in the same words and this one does too.

Method — RM-004. Three measurements against the working tree at 3cf1c24 on branch amit, all of them produced by running something rather than by reading code. The payload — every one of the 370 manifest entries read and gzipped at level 9, and every .glb walked chunk by chunk, splitting the BIN into buffer views an accessor points at, views an image points at, and the remainder, then a census of accessor componentType per attribute semantic and of index width against each primitive's POSITION count. Wall identity — three fixtures loaded, censused, round-tripped through saveFloorplan() and loadFloorplan() and intersected, plus a constructed two-walls-one-pair case run through the same round trip. The type ledger — npx vue-tsc --noEmit --checkJs, bucketed by area, by error code and by file. What was not run: no codec. Draco, meshopt and KTX2 are named throughout and none has been executed against this catalog, which is why M-12 carries no target and why B1's first task is the trial rather than its conclusion. Two repository inaccuracies were found and are recorded in §21 G-3 rather than fixed, since this is a planning pass: tsconfig.json's SFC subtotal disagrees with the tree and with its own itemisation.

Sources — RM-004. KHR_mesh_quantization · KHR_draco_mesh_compression · EXT_meshopt_compression · KHR_texture_basisu · glTF 2.0 — Binary glTF layout · three.js — DRACOLoader · three.js — KTX2Loader · TypeScript — checkJs

Method — RM-005. Five measurements against the working tree at 5bfb795 on branch amit, all produced by running something. The textures — every .png, .jpg and .jpeg under public/ outside the thumbnail directories read for its header dimensions and costed at four bytes per texel with the 4/3 mip factor, then each file attributed to the module that uploads it by grepping the three call sites in three/. The budget hole — an existing 669×1024 .ktx2 copied into public/rooms/textures/, tools/check-budget.mjs run before and after, and the file removed; the line did not move. The type tier — npx vue-tsc --noEmit --checkJs, bucketed by directory, by file, by error code and by receiver type, cross-referenced against grep -rl "@ts-check" src to separate files that are clean from files that are protected. The ledger — the "//" block parsed the way tests/type-coverage.test.js parses it, its rows summed, and git log -S run on the stale row and the heading that contradicts it. The crash — RoofItem.prototype.closestCeilingPoint called against a floorplan stub returning no roof planes, and the TypeError caught and printed. What was not run: no encoder, and no renderer. The 8.75 MB C1 projects is the encoder's 1 bpp model applied to seven files, not an observed GPU figure — the same arithmetic that produced B5's 30.46 → 7.61 MB, whose disk half was measured at 0.459 and whose VRAM half was not. And the C1 spike's question — whether two CompressedTexture clones are one upload or two — is deliberately left open, because reading a signature is what produced the costing this program is correcting. Three repository inaccuracies were found and are recorded in §26 rather than fixed, since this is a planning pass: the Skybox claim in tools/encode-textures.mjs and docs/architecture.md, the KTX2 claim in tools/budget.json, and the stale NOT YET row in tsconfig.json.

Method — RM-005 C2, added on delivery. The type half was measured differently from everything above it, and the difference is the finding. Every count in §26 J-3 was produced by npx vue-tsc --noEmit --checkJs against a tree where three resolved to any — the package ships no .d.ts and @types/three was not installed, which a five-line probe confirms: new Vector3().notAThing type-checked without complaint. So 355 was never a count of the defects in this codebase; it was a count of what a half-blind checker could see. Installing the types took it to 267, resolving the project's own JSDoc names took it back to 300, and the sprint ended at 0. What was not run: nothing was measured about runtime behaviour. Six defects were found by reading the checker's output and two of them — the RoofItem and WallItem crashes — were reproduced by calling the method against a stub, which is the only place in this program a claim about behaviour is backed by an execution rather than by a reading. The other four are argued from the code and pinned by tests written for them.

Sources — RM-005. three.js — CompressedTexture · three.js — Source · KTX 2.0 container specification · TypeScript — checkJs · TypeScript — JSDoc reference

Method — RM-006. One measurement, run twenty-one times, against the working tree at 3d21b81 on branch amit. Every GPU texture the encoder has ever considered — the eleven now shipping as KTX2, the eight refused here, ps_7.jpg and envs/Garden.jpg — was rendered from its authored source and from its transcode through one WebGLRenderer under SwiftShader, same plane, same orthographic camera at 1:1, NearestFilter, no mipmaps, both textures tagged sRGB and the renderer outputting sRGB, and the two frames read back with gl.readPixels and differenced per channel over RGB. Sources for the eighteen were recovered with git log --diff-filter=D and git show against the parent of the commit that deleted each one; provenance was checked by re-encoding one with the shipped settings and comparing SHA-256 against the committed container, which matches byte for byte. The encoder sweep re-encoded each failing texture at qualityLevel 128, 192 and 255 and once as UASTC, and measured all four the same way. What was not run: no on-screen-size sweep. The gate is defined at 1:1 — codecRms in tools/resize-textures.mjs compares the decoded output against the pixels that went into the encoder — and re-measuring at the size furniture happens to be drawn at, in order to let a failure pass, would be moving the threshold rather than meeting it. Three repository inaccuracies were found and, unlike a planning pass, all three were fixed here: the Linear-sRGB frame behind C1's published figures, the one-directional repointer, and the “1 bit per pixel” claim in tools/encode-textures.mjs. The superseded oracle figures are kept in place with a corrected column written beside them rather than overwritten, because what C1 decided and why is still the record.

Sources — RM-006. KHR_texture_basisu · KTX 2.0 container specification · three.js — Color management · three.js — CompressedTexture · WEBGL_compressed_texture_etc

Method — RM-007. Two kinds of measurement against the working tree at 8510642 on branch amit, and one comparison. The code — every file under src/scripts and src/app read for what it does rather than what it says, with the line references in § 33 and § 34 pointing at that tree; the catalog and texture lists counted by script (168 items in eight placement types, 142 of them Kenney, 25 baked, one duck; five wall and two floor textures, two of them one file). The application — booted under Vite in headless Chromium at 1440×900 and 390×844, driven through fifteen states (plan, split, 3D, catalog open, two items added, item selected, walls drawn, wall selected on the plan and in 3D, walkthrough attempted, shortcuts dialog) and screenshotted at each; the “0 of 2” and “40 px strip” figures are read off those pictures, and rev B added 1024×768, 1280×720 and 1366×768 with the split view and the catalog open, reading the plan canvas width and scrollWidth against the viewport (462, 505 and 334 px of plan; no overflow at any). The comparison — Coohom's own floor-planner page and Sweet Home 3D's feature page were read for what a planner is expected to do, and used as a checklist and nothing more; no figure in this drawing comes from either. Effort is at the single-developer cadence RM-001 was planned at, stated at ±40 % because nothing here has been measured against a sprint yet; every programme gets its own drawing before it starts.

Method — RM-008. Seven measurements against the working tree at 1d53fc8 on branch amit, five of them run in headless Chromium against the library as the dev server serves it rather than read off the source. The structure — a Model constructed in the page and its own properties and its floorplan's read back, which is how “a Floorplan has no path to a Scene” became a fact rather than an inference. The two selection directions — the application driven to one click each way, screenshots of the other pane captured immediately before and after, differenced per channel at a tolerance of 6; both returned zero changed pixels, which is what corrects RM-007. The cost — plans of 1, 4, 16 and 36 rooms built through the real Floorplan and drawn 60 times each after a warm-up, and item footprints drawn 60 times at 20, 60 and 150 into a 1200×800 canvas. The coverage — coverage-summary.json from npm run test:coverage, per file. The primitive surface — all 77 this.context.* calls in floorplanner_view.js attributed to their enclosing method by script.
